en: The Compendium of Dhāraṇīs, Scroll One. This scroll contains twenty-nine seals and dhāraṇīs.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master from India, Atikūṭa, during the Great Tang Dynasty.
1. The Chapter on the Śākyabuddhoṣṇīṣa-samādhi-dhāraṇī from the Mahāprabhāva-dhāraṇī-sūtra; Chapter One: The Śākyabuddhoṣṇīṣa-samādhi-dhāraṇī.
Volume One, Part One: Buddha Section. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with five thousand great arhats, headed by Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Nanda, Āniruddha, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Ānanda, Rāhula, and others.

Furthermore, there was an immeasurable assembly of great bodhisattvas, headed by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Gaganagañja Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, and others.
Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable great kings, headed by King Śuddhodana, King Prasenajit, King Bimbisāra, and the Licchavis.
At that time, the six teachers of heterodox paths—namely, first, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa;

second, Maskarī Gośālīputra; third, Sañjayī Vairaṭīputra; fourth, Ajita Keśakambalin; fifth, Kakuda Kātyāyana; and sixth, Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—approached the place where the Buddha was, desiring to engage in debate with the World-Honored One.
At that time, there was a withered tree in that grove named Āmra.
Then, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa asked the World-Honored One:
"Is it not the case, Gautama, that you are not omniscient?"
"If you possess all-knowledge, will this *āmalaka* tree certainly die?
At that time, the Buddha, knowing [the intent], remained silent and did not answer.

Then Pūraṇa Kāśyapa took a white fly-whisk in his hand, sprinkled water upon it, and fanned the withered tree, causing it to grow back again, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all becoming lush and abundant.
At that time, the non-Buddhist ascetic was walking along with the assembly, plucking fruits from the trees with his hands.
There were many ordinary people in the gathering, each of whom felt doubtful in their hearts:
"If an ordinary non-Buddhist ascetic possesses such supernatural wonders, the Buddha must certainly not surpass him."

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of the assembled multitude, immediately entered the *ābhāsvara-samādhi*. From the crown of his head, he emitted immeasurable light that illuminated the trichiliocosm. Then, with his own hand, the Buddha formed the *uṣṇīṣa-mudrā* and recited the *uṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī*. Within that Buddha-light, he manifested immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* *nayuta* Buddhas. Each of these Buddhas moved, stood, sat, and lay in the midst of space, each emitting immeasurable radiance, emitting water and fire from their bodies, and manifesting various kinds of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual feats.
At that time, that tree remained as before, withered and dry.
Pūraṇa immediately fell to the ground, lying there unconscious and in a stupor, while his disciples wept for one another.
At that time, the devas dwelling in the air scattered flowers as an offering and played various kinds of music; the fourfold assembly was also filled with great joy and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, expounded the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dharma for the assembled multitude:
"This extensive dharma is that which has been taught by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; I now likewise extensively teach such a dharma for the sake of all."
"If one wishes to practice, one should install an image of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa within a clean chamber.

As for the method of making the image: it should be seated in the full lotus posture upon a flower made of the seven precious substances; at the base of this flower-seat, two lions are supported, and these two lions sit upon lotus flowers."
As for that Buddha’s right hand, he extends his arm with the palm facing upward upon his right knee, the fingertips hanging down to rest upon the flower.
As for his left hand, he bends his arm with the palm facing upward, held horizontally below the navel.

On each of that Buddha’s two arms were three necklaces made of the seven treasures; around his neck he also wore a necklace of the seven treasures; and upon the crown of his head was a celestial tiara made of the seven treasures.
The body of that Buddha is the color of pure gold and he wears a crimson *kāṣāya*.

To the right of the Buddha is an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—according to one version, it is an image of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara—with his right arm bent upward holding a white fly-whisk, and his left arm extended downward holding a water pitcher.
The mouth of the vase is placed upon a lotus flower; the tip of the flower reaches up to the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head, resting before his forehead.

To the left of the Buddha is an image of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva. His right arm is bent upward toward his shoulder, holding a white fly-whisk (*cāmara*); his left palm holds a vajra, one end of which stands upright from his upper arm and points outward.
The mantra-practitioner stands before the Buddha on the right side, kneeling with one knee bent and holding an incense burner in his hand.
Above the Buddha’s radiance, there appears the form of devas from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven scattering flowers.
"Once this image has been fashioned, one should adorn a maṇḍala in a pure place on well-prepared ground.

Having installed this image within it, the mantra-practitioner should then perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) for the four cardinal directions as well as the zenith and nadir, establish the maṇḍala, and suspend various banners and canopies."

At each of the four corners of that *maṇḍala*, construct a water altar. Upon each altar, place a water jar filled with pure water, and seal the mouth of each jar with cypress leaves, pear branches, and the like. Furthermore, tie various flower garlands and pieces of silk to the cypress leaves and pear branches at the mouths of the jars. In this manner, perform this rite separately on each day for fifteen consecutive days during the waxing moon.
If the petals of the flowers in the water are not beautiful or have withered, he changes them frequently and replaces them with fresh ones.
To the left of the Buddha, he places a clean box containing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which he reads every day.
The person performing the rite shall bathe every day and sit or lie upon clean grass.
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, one shall invite one bhikṣu each day from the first day onward to partake of a meal; there is no limit to the number invited.

On the first day, perform offerings to the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa three times, reciting the mantra one thousand and eight times each time; once this is completed and the deities have been dismissed, recite the Prajñā-pāramitā sin-eliminating mantra repeatedly.

In this manner, he increased his offerings day by day, doubling them each time, until on the fourteenth day he tied sixteen flower garlands, each two feet in length, and placed them before the image of the Buddha.
Furthermore, he arranged eighteen earthenware bowls; ten of these were filled with scented water and eight earthenware bowls were filled with cow’s milk.
He also set out various kinds of food and drink, arranged one hundred butter lamps, and having finished setting out the agarwood and incense burners, he invited the Buddha.
Having established the seat and performed various offerings, one recites the mantra and then dismisses the deity.

On the fifteenth day, at the beginning of the fifth watch of the night, one again performs various offerings as on the fourteenth day; having completed the water-maṇḍala within the ritual arena, one summons Tiśya-rāśi and establishes him there.

Furthermore, set up a brazier and take one hundred and eight pieces of agalloch incense, each piece one foot long, with both ends smeared with *sugandhaka* (styrax) resin. After reciting the mantra seven times over each piece, burn them in the brazier; continue in this manner until all one hundred and eight pieces have been consumed.
At that time, Tiśya came into the place of practice and appeared before the practitioner, saying to him:
"For what purpose do you perform such a rite?"
At that time, having finished making offerings with the various kinds of incense, flowers, and so forth held in his hands, the practitioner should address the Buddha according to his wish:
"I desire such-and-such a dharma."
At that time, the Buddha granted various requests according to the practitioner's wishes and suddenly vanished.
If the Buddha did not appear, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara would manifest his own body; the granting of vows and other such matters were no different from those described above.
If a practitioner cannot see the Buddha or Bodhisattvas with their eyes, they shall hear their voices;
if they do not hear those voices with their ears, they shall obtain various miraculous signs from the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa.
"If a practitioner does not cultivate according to these supreme dharmas, they shall not obtain spiritual efficacy.

1. The Body Seal of Śākyamuni’s Uṣṇīṣa (First) "Interlace the left and right ring fingers; place the two little fingers within the palms. Straighten the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another. Bend the tips of the two index fingers to press against the backs of the proximal joints of the middle fingers. Stand the two thumbs side-by-side and pinch the sides of the middle joints of the middle fingers. Move the index fingers back and forth, and then recite the Heart Mantra of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa."
The mantra says:
"Namaḥ sarvajñāya oṃ. (1) Oṃ. (2)
tathāgatoṣṇīṣa-anavalokiteśvara-mūrti.
Tiśurāṣi (6) huṃ (7) śvabara śvabara (8)
Ḍāka ḍāka 9. Vidhaka vidhaka 10. Dhara dhara 11.
Vidhara vidhara (12) canda canda (13) binda binda (14)
"Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ pāṭ svāhā. (The sixteenth [syllable] is *svā*, with the departing tone;
the following are all the same, and thus no further annotations are provided. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This mantra can dissolve all mantras—whether those of non-Buddhists or those of Maheśvara—and it can also eliminate all evil ghosts and spirits, as well as rescue sentient beings from the five sufferings and eight difficulties."
If a son of good family wholeheartedly receives and maintains this Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-hṛdaya-samādhi-dhāraṇī mantra, he should protect and maintain the purity of the three karmas.
There are two kinds of protection for the purity of the three karmas.
What are the two? First, external protection; second, internal protection. Regarding external protection:

one must not eat the leftovers of my World-Honored One; one must not eat the leftovers of any noble sages; one must not eat the leftovers of any ghosts or spirits; one must not eat the leftovers of teachers, monks, parents, or any common people; nor must one eat the leftovers of kings or government officials. Furthermore, one should not eat from a vessel passed around among a group of people, nor should one eat the food of the *vināyaka* demons—such as food made by wrapping items in flour, deep-frying, boiling, or roasting them until cooked, such as *modaka* cakes (*huānxī tuán*) and the like—all of which must not be eaten.
If one eats this food, one will not achieve accomplishment in the power of samādhi.
One must not go to the birthplaces of any humans or livestock, nor should one eat there;

one must not go to houses where there have been deaths, houses of the ten evil acts, taverns, houses where the five pungent herbs are grown, houses where the dead are buried, houses that sell funeral implements, impure houses, houses of courtesans, or houses where scriptures and images are being made—none of these should be visited, nor should one eat there.

Those who are impure, those who look upon another's wife, those who handle corpses, and those who cut or slice the flesh from the bodies of living beings—persons such as these must not be approached or touched, nor should one associate with them.
This is called the dharma of purity through external protection. Regarding purity through internal protection:

the body must not commit killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct; the mouth must not engage in false speech, harsh words, divisive speech, frivolous chatter, or idle speculation—none of these should be done; and the mind must not give rise to greed, hatred, or delusion, but should instead give rise only to the minds of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity. This is called the Bodhisattva’s purity of the three karmas through the four immeasurable minds.
Only through the purification of the three karmas can one receive and uphold this samādhi-dhāraṇī, the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mantra-seal.

By the power of this samādhi-dhāraṇī, one is able to completely dispel all mantra-practices of celestial Māras and heterodox paths; one can subdue all enemies and adversaries, and all incantations and arts spoken by Maheśvara, the various devas, ghosts, and spirits can be utterly extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One then expounded the Dharma of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Samādhi Maṇḍala:

"Good son! When practicing this dhāraṇī rite, on the first day of the month in the twelfth lunar month, one should thoroughly purify a room. Excavate and remove the poor soil, fill it with good earth, and firmly compact it until it is level."

Before filling [the site], first sweep and sprinkle it until it is pure and clean; burn agalloch incense and recite the mantra seven times. Standing before the purified ground facing east, the Dharma Master says:

"I, [Name], now perform the repentance of the Buddha-ūṣṇīṣa-samādhi-dhāraṇī maṇḍala at this place. May all non-humans, vināyakas, and various spirits within this ground—in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—now depart far away and not remain here."
"If you have a virtuous mind and wish to protect the Buddha-dharma, you may stay here as you please.

Having spoken thus, he first measured out a space four cubits in length and breadth from the previous location. He then erected a bamboo pole at the northeast corner, and erected one pole each at the southeast, southwest, and northwest corners; if bamboo is unavailable, good wood may also be used.

From the northeast corner, measure upward eight *zhǔ* (approx. 2.4 meters) and tie a cord to the pole; do the same for the other three corners. Once the first circuit ending at the northeast corner is completed, proceed to adorn everything starting again from the northeast corner, successively decorating with banners, flowers, bells, ribbons, pendants, mirrors, and precious vases. When the decoration of the single circuit reaching the northeast corner is finished, leave only the western gate open, while the eastern, southern, and northern gates are all closed.

Next, on the upper part of the pavilion, fasten a banner from the northeast corner to the southwest corner; fasten a banner from the top of the eastern gate to the western gate; again, fasten a banner from the southeast corner to the northwest corner; and again, fasten a banner from the top of the southern gate to the northern gate.
Once the upper part has been decorated, fasten the banners and ribbons individually to the four pillars, extending them from the northeast corner to the northwest corner.

Next, take fresh, pure cow dung—the dung of a calf that has not yet eaten grain or beans is considered the best; one must not use raw cow dung directly. Take a new earthenware jar to draw pure water, using no leftover water, and pour it into a clean basin. Mix the dung with the water to remove the dregs, then add powdered sandalwood.

Take a willow branch and hold it with the right hand; with the left hand, hold a vajra and a rosary. Sit facing east, recite the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-hṛdaya mantra while stirring the water with the willow branch, reciting it one hundred and eight times.

Holding the water vessel for recitation, enter the maṇḍala and scoop up some of the fragrant water from the northeast corner. Rub the ground with your right hand, moving in the direction of the sun's rotation; as you rub, the ground shall dry up immediately, causing the water to suddenly cease flowing.

Having finished sweeping the ground within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one should sweep one step’s worth of ground along each of the four sides outside the site as well. At the four corners, plant markers and tie ropes to establish the boundary; this is called the ground for establishing the boundary through the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-samādhi-dhāraṇī*.
As with the first rubbing, the second and third rubbings are performed in the same manner.

For the rubbing ground, one must not use leftover scented water; instead, one should collect fresh, pure cow dung each day and apply it according to the previous procedure. Water produced in this way is called the "Eight Virtues Water" of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-samādhi-dhāraṇī.

"When the ground of the altar has been dried, take five precious vases, each with a capacity of one *sheng*. If precious vases are unavailable, new, clean earthen jars that have never been used may also be employed. At the appropriate time, fill them completely with pure water, place the five grains in each, add scents of seven colors, and further place realgar in each, the size of a jujube fruit."

In each of the five jars, insert willow branches, cypress branches, bamboo branches, and branches of various flowers and fruits; all must be used with their leaves. Tie four feet of colored silk to each branch of fruit and flower, and place these five jars at each of the four corners.
"Place nine lamps within the *dōjō* (sacred precinct) and recite the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-hṛdaya-hṛdaya-mantra* one hundred and eight times.

First, bring these lamps into the *dōjō*: place one lamp beneath the pole in the northeast corner; place one lamp directly at the eastern gate; place one lamp beneath the pillar in the southeast corner; place one lamp at the southern gate; place one lamp beneath the pole in the southwest corner; place one lamp on the southern side of the western gate and one lamp on the northern side of the gate; and place one lamp beneath the pillar in the northwest corner and one lamp at the northern gate."
Following the previous procedure, place one flower vase in the northeast corner, one in the southeast corner, one in the southwest corner, one in the northwest corner, and one in the exact center.

Take storax, camphor, musk, saffron, aloeswood, sandalwood, benzoin, frankincense, and resin; excluding the storax, blend these eight kinds of incense with small portions of the five grains—namely, barley, wheat, mung beans, rice, and sesame—and place them each in a bottle. Then, take various flower cloths and various incense cloths and arrange them within the western gate.
Take white mustard seeds and ten pebbles as large as chicken eggs; sprinkle them with pure water and place them together with the mustard seeds in one spot.
First, burn *agallochum* incense and *olibanum* incense; before burning the incense, recite the Heart-to-Heart Mantra and seal the incense burner with its mudrā.
Having recited the mantra seven times, holding a censer in his hand, he spoke these words:

"I, [Name], make offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions, all Prajñāpāramitās, all Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattvas, all Bodhisattvas, all Vajragarbha Bodhisattvas, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, and all benevolent deities who protect the stūpas and the Dharma. May they bear witness to my, [Name] Bhikṣu’s, merit in performing this Buddhocchuṣma-samādhi-dhāraṇī, so that it may be accomplished according to my wishes; I pray for their protective empowerment."

Having spoken these words, he then reverently invited the image of Śākyamuni Buddha’s uṣṇīṣa and suspended it precisely at the center of the maṇḍala site. He then burned the eight kinds of incense as an offering and prostrated before Śākyamuni Buddha.
He sat down, joined his palms, and remained with his body upright, gazing up at the World-Honored One and praising him in verse:
"Homage to the Buddha’s wisdom and diligence, To the body like Nārāyaṇa’s strength, a lattice of bones;
To the one who practices the six perfections, The Great Compassionate Father who ever acts for the sake of beings."

"Having thus recited these verses of praise three times, prostrating and reverently clasping his feet, one takes various kinds of powdered incense, holds the incense in one's hands, and recites the heart-mantra seven times while scattering it over Śākyamuni Buddha, all the Buddhas of the ten directions, Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattvas, and others, making a universal offering. This is called the offering of the Incense Samādhi Dhāraṇī."

"Furthermore, forming the Flower Mudrā, holding various kinds of flowers, and having recited the mantra seven times according to the previous method for incense, if one then scatters them as an offering as before, this is called the 'Dhāraṇī Samādhi Flower Offering.'"
"Next, holding a vajra in the left hand and a rosary in the right hand, one says:
'I reverently uphold the Prajñāpāramitā Dharma upon my crown; its myriad virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I now receive from all the Buddhas.'"
Having spoken these words, he immediately raised both hands to his head in reverent salutation; this is called the method of "reverent salutation upon the crown.
He then returned the rosary and the vajra to the precious vessel, prostrated before the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, took leave of the Buddha, and departed.

"Furthermore, having bathed by sprinkling oneself with pure fragrant water, one puts on three sets of new, clean garments: one set from dawn until noon, one set from noon until dusk, one set from dusk until midnight, and another set from midnight until dawn; thus changing them in rotation, beginning again once they are finished."
If the three sets [of robes] are unavailable, two sets may also be used.
The upper and lower garments should both be yellow in color; mixed colors are not appropriate.
Having donned the pure robes, one should immediately protect the body with the mantra of the Seal that Shatters Māra.

2. The Mudrā and Dhāraṇī of the Buddha’s Usnīṣa for Breaking the Demonic Boundary and Subjugating [Obstacles], Part Two. "Following the previous body-mudrā, change only this: extend both index fingers and touch their tips together. With both middle fingers, each press against the back of the upper joint of its respective index finger, crossing them so that they support one another. Then, bend both thumbs and tuck them into the palms."
First, having performed the seal of respectful veneration (*namaskāra-mudrā*), recite the mantra with a sincere mind.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ śrīye svāhā. Having recited the mantra of respectful veneration seven times, seal the left and right shoulders, the heart, below the throat, the space between the eyebrows, the hairline, and finally the crown of the head; do this three times.

This mudrā and mantra are commonly used for protecting the body and establishing the boundary (*sīmābandha*). When Śākyamuni Buddha first attained enlightenment while sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he first employed this mudrā and recited the dhāraṇī to protect his body and establish the boundary, thereby subduing all māras and achieving Perfect Enlightenment.

"This dhāraṇī-seal can resolve all kinds of venomous insects, various malevolent spirits, various *piśāca* demons, and various Māras; it completely dispels the incantations of ghosts and gods, and all forms of sorcery, curses, and verbal strife are entirely extinguished so that they can no longer cause harm."

“If a son of good family swiftly attains accomplishment in the meditative concentrations and liberations of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, when performing the practice of contemplation, he should first empower his seat with the mantra twenty-one times, extending it over both body and mind.

Then, ascending the seat, he shall sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), with his clothing and belt all loosely fastened. Sitting upright, he straightens his body so that the joints of his bones support one another; he holds his neck erect and gazes straight ahead, pressing the tongue against the palate. With the right hand pressing down upon the left, he forms the *prajñā-samādhi-dhyāna-mudrā*.
First, one contemplates the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), seeing that form is ultimately empty and lacks any reality;
next, one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), knowing their nature to be empty and ungraspable—this is the samādhi of the extinction of mind.
Contemplating that the nature of form is ungraspable is the samādhi of the extinction of form.
When one realizes this samādhi, great joy arises in the mind; or, upon seeing various objective realms, one must not grasp at them, thereby extinguishing all heavy karmic obstacles.
If one sees others facing obstacles, one should perform the mudrā for them and recite the dhāraṇī; thus, all their karmic obstacles will be immediately eliminated.

Having completed the protection of the body and the binding of the boundary, enter the center of the maṇḍala through the western gate and prostrate while kneeling on the ground. Then, forming the mudrā of the incense burner, recite the mantra seven times. After burning agallochum and frankincense, say aloud:
"I, [Name], respectfully invoke you to perform this rite for the attainment of all wishes."

With the right hand holding a rosary and the left hand grasping a vajra, one seals them upon the precious vessel containing white mustard seeds while reciting the aforementioned Great Heart Mantra one hundred and eight times; then, one returns both the rosary and the vajra to the fragrant precious vessel.
Form the *māra-vidhvamsana-mudrā* and seal white mustard seeds and pebbles, reciting the mantra over each seven times.
Next, form the *uṣṇīṣa-pāśa-mudrā* and seal the white mustard seeds and pebbles, reciting the mantra over each seven times.

Next, perform the Buddha’s Golden Wheel Seal Mantra and the Buddha’s Sword Seal Mantra, each seven times; then, holding a precious vessel of mustard seeds in one's hand, scatter white mustard seeds from the northeast corner within the maṇḍala.

In this manner, having completed one round of scattering in the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, he performs a second and a third scattering in the same way.

Having finished scattering, he immediately exits the *maṇḍala* and, following the previous procedure, scatters white mustard seeds in the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and above and below. Once the scattering is complete, he takes the pebbles from the northeast corner and sweeps them away with all his might.

In this manner, one places a stone in each of the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and above and below; wherever the stones reach constitutes the outer boundary, and wherever the mustard seeds reach constitutes the inner boundary.

Returning to the maṇḍala, perform the Demon-Subduing Seal (māra-bhañjana-mudrā) and seal the ground; recite the mantra seven times, which is called the binding of the boundary of the earth (*bhūmi-sīmābandha*).

At the four corners and the four cardinal directions, rotate the hand-seal in the air while reciting the mantra seven times; this constitutes the binding of the boundary of the eight directions (*aṣṭadik-sīmābandha*).
Holding the mudrā one chi above the crown of the head, recite the mantra seven times; this is called the "Method for the Superior Boundary.
Next, having completed the general binding of the boundary with the mudrā, hold an incense burner and burn various kinds of incense, saying:
"I respectfully invite those who have bound the boundary to each occupy their respective positions, fully endowed with dignified deportment, and abide according to the Dharma."

3. The Seal for Invoking the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa (Buddhoṣṇīṣa-āhvāna-mudrā), Third. Following the previous body-seal, change only this: straighten both index fingers, keeping them four and a half inches apart; place both thumbs upright, eight *fen* away from the middle fingers, and recite the Heart Mantra of the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
Upon reaching the fourth repetition, gradually bend both index fingers into the palms.

When the mantra is completed seven times, perform the seal with the hands reversed, then prostrate in homage (*vandana*). Disperse the fingers inward as the seal for invoking, then form the Flower-Light Seal (*puṣpa-prabhā-mudrā*) while reciting the mantra.

The mantra is: "Oṃ hūṃ kamala svāhā. (Recite this mantra seven times. 4. The Mantra of the Lotus Foot-Pressing Mudrā (*Padmotsaṅga-mudrā*). This fourth [mantra] is also called the Flower-Light Seal (*Puṣpa-prabhā-mudrā*). [Formation]: Interlace the two little fingers by holding them upright against each other. Extend both thumbs upright, while the remaining six fingers are spread apart and held straight up with the finger joints slightly bent, resembling the shape of a blooming flower.
Recite the mantra seven times, then bend both index fingers into the palms and perform a prostration. Disperse the Lotus Seat Mudrā inwardly toward the seat. The mantra is: "Oṃ kamala svāhā.

(Recite the mantra seven times. 5. The Fifth: The Seat Mudrā. If a person were to prostrate before ten trillion buddhas, the merit they would obtain would not equal the merit obtained by a person who recites this dhāraṇī and performs mudrās while prostrating.

At that time, there were further immeasurable great bodhisattvas, those who have attained the fruits of the four paths, pratyekabuddhas, as well as the hosts of devas, all ghosts and spirits, and various seers and non-Buddhists, who all gathered like clouds and each offered divine mantras, saying:
“I have received and upheld all the divine mantras spoken by the Buddhas of the past.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, moved by great compassion, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Out of your great compassion, you wish to proclaim a divine mantra; now is precisely the right time.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara manifested the body of Hayagrīva (translated into Chinese as Mátóu, “Horse-Head”).

When the divine mantra was being recited, the manifested mantra-deity immediately appeared before them, eclipsing all others; the manifested mantra-deities of all the bodhisattvas and celestial deities were made to disappear, just as when a millstone is placed over a well. How marvelous! How rare!”

"What further dharma is there that can extinguish the World-Honored One’s *Tiśya-rāśi*?
At that time, the World-Honored One told Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:

"This mantra is capable of extinguishing the *Ti-zhu-luo-shi* (Ditthirāsi) and other such dharmas; you all should receive and uphold it with a single mind, conceiving a sense of its rarity.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the Seal of the Golden Wheel Dhāraṇī: "The seal is as previously described.

This dhāraṇī is capable of destroying all phenomena; there is nothing superior to it. As for this seal-mantra, if anyone were to place it herein, it was originally not there.

Place both thumbs together, each pressing against the inner side of the lower joint of a ring finger. Raise the seal and place it upon one's own crown. Move the index fingers back and forth; the mantra is the same as the previous Golden Wheel mantra."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

Reciting the mantra once for each seed, he cast them into the fire; when this count reached one thousand and eight repetitions, the rain immediately ceased.
"Facing north with the image and the mantra-practitioner facing south, perform the rite in an open space.
