Place the hand seal before the right shoulder, stand with the left foot raised, face toward the left, assume a look of great wrath, and cry out 'KṢA! in a loud voice."
Again, turning the *vajra* toward the four directions as if to strike, all winds and rains ceased immediately upon the striking.

17. The *Jñānacakra-mudrā-mantra*, the seventeenth; in the Tang language, "Wheel of Wisdom. First, stand the two middle fingers upright with their tips touching. Bend the two ring fingers so that each presses against the back of the middle joint of the middle finger, their tips separated by one inch and two *fen*. With the two index fingers, each press down on the back of the upper joint of the ring finger, their tips separated from the middle fingernails by three *fen*. Bend the two little fingers into the palms. With the two thumbs, each grasp the inner side of the upper joint of the middle finger, joining the wrists.
The dhāraṇī is as follows: "Oṃ jñīta hūṃ phaṭ.

[In the second phrase of this dhāraṇī, the character *jñī* (知) is pronounced with its half-sound. Regarding this seal-dhāraṇī: when preaching the Dharma, first pay homage to all the Triple Gem and request their empowerment. Then, forming the seal with a sincere mind, recite the dhāraṇī one hundred and eight times or one thousand and eight times. Afterward, preach the Dharma; you will immediately attain fearlessness and unhindered eloquence.
If a person engages in debate with an evil mind, the challenger will naturally be defeated and submit.

Furthermore, if one seals the Buddha’s wheel-throne with this mudrā and recites the mantra one hundred and eight times, and then invites the Buddha to be seated upon it, all the demonic armies will submit without exception; this mudrā is employed throughout the great maṇḍala assembly.

18. Jnanottama Mudrā (Jnanottara-sa-mudrā). The eighteenth. [In Chinese: *Zhìdǐng*]. "As before, with this modification: each tip of the two index fingers presses upon the nail of the middle finger, and each fingertip is aligned level with the tip of its respective middle finger."
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
"Oṃ, mama-mama-mama, hūṃ. Those who are able to recite and uphold this seal-dhāraṇī shall attain supreme wisdom, never losing it throughout their successive lives.

19. The Kāriśāṇī Seal-Mantra, the Nineteenth. Translated into Chinese as "Destroying Sin. Following the previous procedure, change only this: place each of the two index fingers on the side of the upper joint of the middle finger; their tips shall be one cun apart, and separated by four fen from the tips of the two thumbs.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:

"Oṃ kareśanija. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family sincerely forms this seal and recites this dhāraṇī, with each single recitation, the offenses of the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, the icchantika state, and all other karmic obstructions throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of koṭis of nayutas of Ganges-sand kalpas will be entirely extinguished.

If one can recite it a thousand or ten thousand times daily for the duration of a single lifetime, it will cause all karmic obstructions from beginningless time to be entirely extinguished for the practitioner.

20. The Seal and Mantra of Aparājita. The twentieth [chapter], the Seal and Mantra of Aparājita; in the Tang language, "The Invincible. Following the previous [instructions], one only changes the position so that the tips of the two index fingers are separated from the tips of the two thumbs by three finger-widths.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:
"Oṃ abara-cchidi hūṃ phaṭ. If any virtuous man or woman can recite and maintain this seal-dhāraṇī, kings, thieves, ghosts, spirits, and all perilous difficulties shall be unable to cause them harm.

"If one wishes to receive and uphold the aforementioned four dharmas, one should construct a water altar in a secluded and quiet place, measuring four cubits in length and breadth and adorned with various ornaments. Within this ritual site (maṇḍala), one should install an image of the Buddha or the Buddha’s relics and offer various kinds of worship. Kneeling on the right knee before the image, one should recite the mantra with a sincere mind, completing one thousand and eight recitations, or ten thousand recitations; doing so daily in this manner until reaching one hundred thousand or even a million recitations, the fulfillment of one's vows will not be in vain."

21. Commentary on the Dharma-Seal Mantra for the Repentance of Śākyamuni Buddha. Second and Twenty-first: "The index fingers, ring fingers, and little fingers of both hands are interlaced with their tips pointing downward. The two middle fingers are held upright with their tips touching. The two thumbs hook together, the right pressing down upon the left, and the tips of the thumbs of both hands rest against the sides of the right index finger."
The mantra is:

“Namaḥ sarvajñāya | Oṃ | Svabhāvikīye | Svāhā. This Dharma-seal mantra can eliminate all karmic obstacles of the three types of action and extinguish all grave offenses, such as the four pārājikas and the five ānantaryas; it completely eradicates them all.

22. The Dhāraṇī of the Sword Mudrā of the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, Number Twenty-Two. "Interlace the eight fingers of both hands within the palms, with the right hand pressing over the left. Straighten and erect the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another, joining the wrists."
The mantra is:
“Oṃ kakkāramana pramadana-tsiya dhoḍaye svāhā. If the bhikṣus form this mudrā and recite the aforementioned great mantra, [the purpose will be accomplished].

If a person suffers from a disease caused by malevolent spirits (*bhūta-graha*), one should strike the head, chest, and back with the seal, and press and rub with the seal according to the location of the ailment.

Furthermore, one should recite mantras over white mustard seeds and strike the patient’s head, face, heart, and chest with them. Then, holding the white mustard seeds in the hand, one should rub them clockwise on the head, heart, chest, shoulders, and back. Throughout the four or five periods of the day and night, one should burn *agaru* (aloe) incense, circumambulate the body clockwise, and fumigate the nostrils. By performing these rites for seven days, the illness will be cured.

"If deities, demons, ghosts, or spirits are difficult to dismiss, construct a four-cubit altar as previously described and follow the prior ritual procedures: offer eight plates of food and sixteen lamps—one at each of the four corners, two at each of the four gates, and one for the Buddha’s seat at the center, with one at each corner. When lighting the lamps, they must all follow the movement of the sun and must not be turned in the reverse direction."
The rites for binding the boundary and the invocation are no different from those previously described. Instruct the patient to bathe and purify themselves, and have them put on clean garments.

Once they are seated to the left of the mantra-master near the western gate of the altar, the mantra-master gives them an incense burner; they shall burn incense, make vows, and prostrate, performing the *sarṣapa* (mustard seed) rite one hundred and eight times as before.

Then take one bowl of vinegar-rice, one bowl of sweet syrup-water, and one bowl of ice water. Taking the bowl of rice, rotate it clockwise three times around the patient’s head, heart, chest, and body; recite the mantra twenty-one times and briefly place the bowl upon the patient’s head. Have another person hold a clean vessel in front of them and pour the rice from the bowl into the vessel; do the same for the other two bowls.

The mantra-practitioner takes the three substances in a pure vessel, stirs them together until they are blended, and having rotated it three times around his head and body, he dispatches someone to quickly pour it out toward the southwest, ensuring that no one looks back.
"Regarding this method for offering food: perform it twice during the first watch and the fifth watch of the night for a period of seven days.

On the fourth day, offer various kinds of food, drink, and fruit. Install a pure jewel fire-pit at the western gate and burn pure wood; with a sincere heart, invoke Śākyamuni Buddha to sit upon a lotus flower within the fire-pit."

One should take curd, butter, honey, food and drink, fruits, sesame seeds, human oil, and so forth, and recite the mantra over each twenty-one times. Taking a small portion of each, one should recite the mantra once and cast it into the fire, continuing until one hundred and eight repetitions are completed.
One should make offerings at the three periods of day and night—dawn, midday, and the early part of the night—and perform the ritual at each time.

The mantra-practitioner takes white mustard seeds and circles them around his own body, reciting the mantra over the white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times; then all ghosts and spirits will depart far away and find no opportunity to cause harm.
"In all cases where one intends to perform a ritual, it is necessary to properly protect oneself through the ritual.
If one does not do so, there is fear that spirits and deities may find an opportunity to cause harm.
Next, perform the ritual of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Rope Seal."

23. The Vajrapāśa Seal Mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, Number Twenty-Three. "Following the previous Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Sword Seal, change only this: bend the upper joints of the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another, causing the finger tips to be level."
If there is a place difficult due to ghosts or spirits, one should form the mudrā and recite the mantra; all evil ghosts and spirits will be completely dispersed and extinguished.
He then spoke the *sūtra-mantra*, which says:
"Oṃ tuluṅ bandha bandha svāhā. If there is a place difficult due to bandits, one should recite the mantra and form the mudrā; the bandits will be unable to approach people.
If a person suffers from "white clouds" (cataracts) in the eyes for many years, they should take *bīḍa* (long pepper), mix it with well-water, and grind the medicine on a stone.

While grinding, they should recite the mantra over the medicine; once the vessel is filled, they should recite the mantra one thousand and eighty times before an image of the Buddha. By applying this to the eyes, the cataract will immediately be cured.

24. The Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Ghost-Binding Seal Mantra. The Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Ghost-Binding Seal Mantra, Number Twenty-four. "Interlace the two little fingers; place the two ring fingers within the palms; straighten and erect the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another; stand the two thumbs side by side and press them against the sides of the middle joints of the middle fingers;
bend the two index fingers to press down upon the nails of the two thumbs; join the wrists together. Then, recite the mantra: ‘Oṃ viśodhe svāhā. “O Bhikṣus!”

Take a peach branch from the east that is free of sores or disease; seal it with the mudrā, recite the mantra twenty-one times, and strike the patient’s body with it—their illness will be cured immediately.

If one suffers from illnesses caused by fox-spirits, mountain demons, ghosts, or the affliction of *ya-gu* (suppressed *gū*), chant the mantra over white mustard seeds twenty-one times and strike the patient’s head, face, chest, and heart with them. Burn *guggulu* incense and circumambulate the body while fumigating the nose and inhaling the smoke; swallow twenty-one puffs of the incense smoke. Then, using peach branches to strike, first strike the inner elbow of the left arm, followed by the right elbow, the waist, and the armpit; the illness will be immediately cured.

Grind realgar and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times to protect the body and establish a boundary. Dot [the powder] on these seven locations: the crown of the head, the hairline, the left armpit, the right armpit, the heart, below the neck, and between the eyebrows. Perform this ritual three times during the day and night. Beneath the patient’s bed, construct a small altar of one cubit using cow-dung mud; sprinkle it cleanly, place a lamp there, and perform the boundary-binding ritual. Keep the lamp lit separately throughout the night, and the illness will be cured.

25. The Mantra of the Eye Seal of Śākyamuni Buddha, Number Twenty-Five. "Interlace the two little fingers and the two ring fingers within the palms. Straighten and erect the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another. Erect the two thumbs side by side. Bend the two index fingers to press down upon the tips of the two thumbs, with their tips touching."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ vīrucciṇi svāhā. By forming the Buddha-eye mudrā and reciting the aforementioned great mantra, one attains purity of body and purity of the faculty of sight.
If one receives and maintains the Buddha-Eye Seal Mantra with utmost sincerity, one will likewise attain the complete purity of the five eyes, and all sentient beings who see them will rejoice.

If a person suffers from eye ailments or has red, painful eyes, they should form the seal and apply it to their eyes, as well as to medicinal herbs while reciting the mantra; when placed within the eyes, the affliction will be cured.
If one seals water with this mantra and sprinkles it upon the eyes as well as the body, one will immediately be cured.

26. The Seal of Śākyamuni Buddha, Number Twenty-Six. This seal has no mantra; it is not given a specific name. Following the previous "Buddha-Eye Seal," one simply changes the two index fingers by bending them to press against the back of the middle finger joints, while the right thumb presses down upon the left thumb.
27. The Seal of Śākyamuni Buddha, the twenty-seventh. It has no separate mantra name. "As before, with this modification: press the left thumb over the right thumb."
28. The Seal of Śākyamuni Buddha. This twenty-eighth seal also has no mantra. "As before, with this modification: simply bend both thumbs and place them within the palms."

"If one can receive and uphold these three seals and can respectfully make offerings to them day by day, all karmic obstructions will be completely extinguished, and all merits will increase with every thought-moment."
29. The Cakra-vartī Seal Mantra (The Second Ninth). Translated into Chinese as “Wheel-Turning. The seal is the same as the Golden Wheel;
the mantra says: “Oṃ viśaye svāhā. Recite this over the Buddha’s seated wheel twenty-one times;
if reciting over a water jar, one hundred and eight times.

30. The Buddha-Cakrā Seal, the Thirtieth Dharma Seal: "Interlock the two ring fingers with both hands; join the two thumbs and index fingers together; keep the two middle fingers straight and parallel; move the index fingers back and forth while reciting the aforementioned *Uṣṇīṣa* mantra."

This seal can subdue all evil Māras and non-Buddhists; it is used during seated meditation and facilitates the attainment of meditative absorption. The above concludes the original text; the following two seals and mantras are to be added after this.

31. The Dharma-Seal Dhāraṇī for Bestowing Fearlessness upon Sentient Beings by the Tathāgata, Number Thirty-One. “With the right hand hanging downward, the thumb presses upon the nail of the ring finger; with the left hand, the index finger presses upon the nail of the middle finger, while the remaining fingers are held straight upward toward the chest.”

The mantra-practitioner assumes a joyful countenance and kneels with the right knee on the ground; the knees are spread apart as before, the body is inclined forward, and the head is turned slightly to the left.
The fearless mantra is:

"Oṃ vāraṇatele raśi puruṣa mantreya svāhā. Regarding the Dharma-mantra of the Single-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa (the thirty-second): Following the bodily mudrā of Cundā, one makes the same modification at the wrists by opening the palms, and uses the two thumbs to press against the middle joints of the two index fingers from the sides.
The mantra is:

*Bhiling* (the first syllable is pronounced long in the Sanskrit original; as this sound does not exist in the Chinese language, it is pronounced as a conjunct). After performing the invocation at the site where the great mandala is to be constructed, one recites this seal-mantra seven times; thereupon, the mandala ritual is perfected.
Each time you call [the name] once, you should recite the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Body Dharani once; they are equal and without distinction.
When you have completed one hundred thousand recitations, there will be a manifestation of light;
at two hundred thousand recitations, you will be able to extensively benefit all sentient beings.
If one recites various mantras while adding this mantra, and completes one hundred thousand recitations, one will immediately possess great efficacy; the following [text] is the original root.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If anyone can receive, uphold, read, and recite the Samādhi-dhāraṇī, they should construct an altar as previously described and continue to recite the mantra—either three hundred thousand times or seven hundred thousand times—while making various kinds of offerings. Within this, various realms will manifest."

At that time, the practitioner should skillfully settle his own mind and not allow himself to become terrified—whether he sees the flame of a lamp reach one *zhang* and five *chi*, or the incense smoke likewise; or whether the banners and streamers of the *maṇḍala* sway of their own accord; or whether the scattered flowers offered remain unfaded for many days; or whether the branches of various fruit trees do not wither for many days;
or whether there are sounds within the room—he must not give rise to alarm or fear; nor should he be alarmed if there is the sound of thunder without clouds, or if rain falls without clouds.

It should be known that all the practitioner’s karmic obstacles will be completely extinguished, and they will attain the power of samādhi-dhāraṇī. Thereafter, one should establish a five-colored mandala altar and perform offerings of lamps, food, incense, flowers, and various other items exactly according to the previous ritual method. Then, whether it be the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, or Devatās who manifest their bodies before the practitioner, one should offer various petitions according to what is seen at that time.

The Ritual of the Eight-Cubit Altar for the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. Regarding the ritual of the eight-cubit altar for the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa: "Prepare the ground as previously described; erect pillars for adornment, and bury the seven treasures, the five grains, and the eight kinds of incense, all as explained before. Next, prepare white powder and mix it with scented water."

Having entered the maṇḍala together with a bhikṣu who understands the ritual method, one should mark a powder dot six finger-widths below the inner corner of the northeast pillar; the same procedure applies to the other three corners.
Having finished marking the four intermediate directions, take a cord forty feet long and as thin as a hairpin shaft, and soak it in a starch solution.

Once soaked, rinse it out and have the person previously instructed in the method of measurement hold one end of the cord. The Master stands at the southern corner mark and presses down; using his left hand to stretch the cord, he stretches it three finger-widths east of the mark and three finger-widths west of the mark. Then, he withdraws the cord and rinses it out in the starch solution.

The person ahead holds the cord, with its end facing west; he should hold one end of the cord in his right hand above his head and rotate it following the direction of the sun, saying to that person: "Press the cord down according to the mark."

The Master also marks a point on the eastern side and presses down; then, using his left hand, he pulls the cord taut. He marks a point three finger-widths south and pulls the cord taut, then marks a point three finger-widths north and pulls the cord taut. Having gathered the cord, he draws it out from within the powder.

Exit through the western gate with the cord; stand facing south at its front end. The master holds the end of the cord and, as before, presses down according to the marked points. Using his left hand to pull the cord taut, he pulls it one span (three finger-widths) to the west of the mark and another span to the east of the mark. Then, retracting the cord, he draws it out from within the powder.

The person holding the cord presses it down on the mark at the northeast corner; the Master, as before, presses it down at the northwest corner. He then stretches the cord across the mark, stretches the cord three finger-widths north of the mark, and stretches the cord three finger-widths south of the mark.
"Having marked three finger-widths from the south and completed one circuit, fashion a bamboo measuring-stick two cubits in length.

Starting from the outer edge of the northeast corner, lay down one bamboo measure toward the west and make a mark; then, lay down another bamboo measure toward the south and make a mark. Taking the bamboo measure, measure westward from that mark and make a mark at the end of the northward bamboo measure; then, measuring southward from that mark, place a mark where the two ends of the bamboo measures meet.
Do the same for the southeast, southwest, and northwest corners, making a powder-mark at each measurement."

From the eastern side, pull out the cord and, following the previous method, mark the points; mark three finger-widths of ground to the east and three finger-widths to the west, marking them according to the previous method;
mark the southern, western, and northern sides in the same manner.

"When the first enclosure is completed, take back the bamboo-measure and, starting from the first edge at the northeast corner, measure toward the west along the corner; mark a point at the end of the measurement. From that point, measure southward, then again from the corner, measure one bamboo-length southward and mark a point at the end of the bamboo. From that point, measure westward until the two ends of the bamboo meet;
mark a point there. The method for measuring the remaining three corners is likewise."

Having measured as instructed below, take a cord from among the powders on the western side and enter through the western gate. Press it down at the northeast corner; the master aligns the cord toward the western end as before, extending it one span toward the west, then another span toward the west, and yet another span toward the west.
Align the cords in the same manner for the southern, western, and northern sides.
Taking the measure from south to north, from west to east, and from north to south, one completes one circuit along the inner edge;

then, returning, one takes up the bamboo-measure. At the outer corner of the northwest, two bamboo-measures equal three finger-widths are marked with one notch as a sign. Taking the bamboo-measure from that corner toward the west, one places a dot below the notch. Measuring one more degree from that dot toward the south, and measuring from the corner toward the south, one places a dot below the notch. Measuring from that dot toward the west, one places a dot where the two notches meet.
The same procedure is followed for the southeast corner, the southwest corner, and the northwest corner, placing dots according to the notches.

"Again, take a cord from the powder on the western side and enter through the western gate. From the mark at the northwest corner, press down on the end of the cord; the master, facing it, presses along the marks to lay out the cord. Three finger-widths east of the mark, lay out one line;
three finger-widths west of the mark, lay out another line. Do the same for the south, west, and north sides."

When the second cord is finished, take two bamboo spans; measure six finger-widths to make one mark. From the inner edge of the northwest corner of the second outer enclosure, measure six finger-widths toward the west and make a dot below the mark. From that dot, measure southward; then, using another bamboo span, measure south from the corner and make a dot below the mark. From that dot, measure westward, making a dot where the two marks meet.
Measure and mark the corners in the east, south, west, and north in the same manner.

"Take a cord from the powder on the western side; then, from the mark at the northwest corner, press down on the end of the cord. The Master presses the layout-cord toward the southern side, marking every three finger-widths with a press.
The same procedure is followed for the southern, western, and northern sides."

Having finished marking the three layers of the entire perimeter with single points, take the cord again and press its end at the northeast corner. The master presses and holds it toward the west, folds the cord in half, and makes a mark at the point where the cord’s end from the northeast corner reaches. From that mark, measure to the center of the southern corner and drop a powder-mark;
measure in the same manner for the southern, western, and northern corners.

"Mark a central lower point. From the eastern center point, measure one *zhù* toward the north and mark a point at the end of the measure. From the central point, measure one *zhù* toward the south and mark a point at the end of the measure. Take a measuring rod of one *zhù* and four fingers, bend its tip inward, and place the mark in the center. From the northern point, make a mark toward the east; from the head of that mark, make a mark toward the north; from the head of that mark, make a mark toward the east; from the southern boundary point, make a mark back toward the east; from the head of that mark, make a mark toward the south; and from the head of that mark, make a mark toward the east."

"Pull out the cord from within the powder; pull the cord from the northern seal-end toward the south, where the master stands at the southern seal-end. Pull the cord taut in one stretch, and once the eastern gate is completed, proceed likewise for the southern, western, and northern gates.

This applies even to the threefold layout with four gates; as for the method of making the gates, follow the threefold pattern, leaving the body of the western gate open while the other three gates are intended to be closed."

"Once the four gates have been completed, take five-colored powders and mix them with hot water scented with eight kinds of incense. Place the powder vessel in the northeast corner of the outer enclosure and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times."

The Master sat upon the path inside the first courtyard and directed the person ahead to sit in the eastern part of the courtyard. Taking two bamboo measuring rods, he measured one chi from the northern edge of the third vertical line toward the south along the second line;
this marks the outer eastern edge. The inner edge is measured in the same manner.

Join two bamboo tips with one length of cord; measure one length of cord northward for three finger-breadths, then again one length of cord northward for three finger-breadths. Continue measuring southward in this manner, dividing the space into seven sections; do the same for the north and south.
To the south of the western gate, it is divided into three sections;
to the north of the gate, it is likewise divided into three sections.
In the east of the second enclosure, it is measured in the same way and laid out into six sections.
The same applies to the north and south, which are divided into six sections.
To the south of the western gate, two sections are demarcated;
likewise to the north of the gate, two sections are demarcated.

From the northeast corner, one forms the *vajrabhūmi-mudrā* using both black and white powders. Starting from the ground at a distance of one cubit toward the north, where the boundary line is marked with white powder, one repeatedly applies the white powder; next, the red line; next, the blue line; next, the yellow line; and finally, the black line. These five-colored lines are applied once around the outer perimeter.
The second and third outer margins are likewise prepared in this manner.
In the center, create a thousand-petaled lotus using five colors.
Regarding the layout of the four corners of the three enclosures, these are the positions for the Vajrabhūmimudrā.

[Vajrabhūmimudrā-dharmavajrabhūmimudrā-dharma] In the second enclosure, at the northern end of the eastern side: first is Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; second, Prajñāpāramitā Bodhisattva; third, Śākyakacakravartin Buddha; fourth, Śākyadharmacakrapravartana Buddha; fifth, Amitābha Buddha; sixth, Śākyamuni Buddha’s Eye. The positions on the eastern side are complete.

Facing south: second, the Bodhisattva Vajramātā Māmaki; third, the Bodhisattva Śaṅkara; fourth, the Bodhisattva Aṅkuśī; fifth, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; sixth, the Bodhisattva Vajracaṇḍālī; seventh, Cittavajrā. The positions facing south are completed.
"On the second and third positions at the southern end of the western face, both depict vajra-tridents;
on the first and second positions to the north of the western gate, these also depict three-pronged vajra-maces."

Facing north with their heads toward the east: second, Avalokiteśvarī-mātṛ; third, Yaśodharā Bodhisattva; fourth, Avalokiteśvara-bhaginī; fifth, Avalokiteśvara-rāja; sixth, Ekādaśamukha-avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; seventh, Vighuṣṭa-avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

"On the western end of the northern side: second, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva with the Amoghapāśa; third, Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. On the northern end of the outer enclosure on the eastern side:

second, Dhṛtarāṣṭra Devaputra; third, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva; fourth, Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva; fifth, the parasol of Śākyamuni Buddha; sixth, the sword of Śākyamuni Buddha; seventh, the spear of Śākyamuni Buddha; eighth, Śakra Devendra."
Facing south: second, Akinijidvana; third, Virūḍhaka of the south; fourth, Vajrapaṭala; fifth, Vajra-śakti; sixth, Agnimukha-vajra; seventh, Vajrakumāra; eighth, Vajraputra.
To the south of the western gate, the second, third, and fourth [positions] each have one spear and a double-pronged fork;
to the north of the gate, the first and second have one fork and one spear, while the third has a *vīrabhadra*.

Facing north, at the western end: second, the Heart Avalokiteśvara Tārā; third, the Avalokiteśvara Ekajaṭī; fourth, the Citta-anuvartinī Avalokiteśvarī; fifth, the Trident; sixth, Vaiśravaṇa of the North; seventh and eighth, the Single-pronged Spear and the Single-pointed Arrow.

"Place Tiśyaraśmi at the center, and Śākyamuni as the presiding master of the maṇḍala. Light one hundred lamps, and prepare food and drink according to the positions, including various incenses and flowers, various foods and drinks, various bowls of fragrant water, and sixteen water jars; for each of these, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times."
From the northeast corner, descend the lamps, descend the food, and descend the vases; place the vases at the four corners, the four gates, and the center.

Perform the ritual of offering exactly as before: do not sleep for two nights—the seventh and eighth days—and do not sleep for three nights—the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days. Do not eat on the eighth, thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month—except for permitted medicinal foods, such as ghee, milk, and parched grain flour.

Every month on the fifteenth day, at the beginning of the fifth watch, take water from sixteen jars and proceed to the western gate. Seal the jars with the Vajra-mudrā and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, prostrate and make this vow:

"I, disciple [Name], now petition the Buddha for the water of merit from the Samādhi-dhāraṇī to consecrate my body and mind, so that my three karmas may be purified and my practices and vows fully realized."

Then, taking a water jar filled with scented water mixed with cow dung, he ascends the ritual altar, removes his garments, and stands facing due east. Holding the water jar above his head, he pours the water over himself while reciting:
"May all Buddhas of the ten directions bestow upon me, [Name], all the practices and vows of the Bodhisattvas."

"First, one should perform the consecration of body and mind with the *diśūra* (water) from the central vessel; then, taking the other jars in succession, one pours them out until they are exhausted. Having put on the robes and entered the maṇḍala, one performs the ritual practices. When the practitioner attains the fulfillment of their vows and various signs appear, these must not be told to even a single person. Furthermore, the performance of the ritual practices must also not be told to even a single person."

"Furthermore, if one wishes to cause all rākṣasas to rejoice in the Dharma, one should cook a milk porridge of non-glutinous rice; at the western gate of the maṇḍala, one should first recite the mantra over the milk porridge one hundred and eighty times."
From the southern side of the door, take firewood from the *śrīvṛkṣa* tree and kindle it upon the brazier. Invite Śākyamuni Buddha to sit upon a lotus seat within the brazier.
Take a small amount of milk porridge and, reciting the mantra once, cast it into the fire; continue in this manner until one hundred and eight repetitions are complete.

Performing the ritual at dawn, at noon, and in the evening for a full seven days, all the rākṣasas will respectfully invite and welcome [the practitioner], making various offerings and giving rise to great joy.

Furthermore, recite the Dharma-mantra over one hundred and eighty times over storax and benzoin incense. At the western gate, invite Śākyamuni Buddha to sit upon a lotus seat within the precious fire-pit; then, taking the aforementioned storax and benzoin incense, recite the mantra once for each portion and cast it into the fire as an offering.

One may perform this rite during the six periods of day and night, or even five periods; by reciting it one hundred and eight times for each distinct period, all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and others will experience great joy.

The Seven-Day Ritual Procedure: "Furthermore, there is another method: recite the mantra over frankincense one hundred and eighty times, following the ritual procedure as before. At five sessions during the day and night—four sessions being acceptable—one completes the seven days; thereafter, all Brahmā kings and Maheśvaras will give rise to great joy."

"Furthermore, there is another method: recite the mantra over agallochum incense one hundred and eighty times during four periods of the day and night—three periods will also suffice—and for a full seven days; then all the various spirit-kings, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the various ghost-kings, and others will give rise to great joy."

"Furthermore, there is another method: recite the mantra over white resin incense one hundred and eighty times. Having performed the ritual as prescribed for seven full days, all ghosts will give rise to great joy."

"Furthermore, there is another method: recite the mantra over white mustard seeds and salt one hundred and eighty times, rub them upon one's own body and mind, and with each recitation, cast one seed into the fire. Following the aforementioned ritual for a full seven days, all calamitous illnesses, all calamitous obstacles, all legal disputes, and all matters of verbal contention shall be entirely extinguished."

"Furthermore, according to another method: first, recite the mantra over white mustard seeds one hundred and eighty times. Then, taking a small amount, recite the mantra once for each seed and cast it into the fire. Following this procedure as before for seven full days, all officials and all *makhali* beings will be greatly delighted."

"Furthermore, there is another method: recite the mantra over sesame seeds and *śāli* rice flowers one hundred and eight times. Invite Śākyamuni Buddha to sit upon a lotus seat within the fire; take a small portion [of the offerings], recite the mantra once and cast it into the fire each time, until the offering is completed for one hundred and eight times."

Having completed seven days according to the preceding ritual procedures, one’s mental and physical strength will be fully restored, and all bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and celestial benevolent deities will constantly follow and protect them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those who have not yet entered the great maṇḍala of Samantabhadra may not speak this samādhi-dhāraṇī-mantra-seal; they may not hear it, nor may they see the Dharma."
If one were to preach it, they would fall into hell;
those who listen to the Dharma would receive the retribution of folly;
and those who rashly perceive the Dharma would be rebuked by ghosts and spirits.

Although one has personally entered the samādhi maṇḍala, if one does not guard the Dharma with a focused mind and carelessly performs mudrās and mantra rites in exposed places, one will provide an opportunity for malevolent ghosts and spirits to exploit;
however, if one can receive and uphold them with utmost sincerity and firm resolve, all the devas will follow and protect one’s person.
This dharani method is like the sun shining upon frost, or like fire consuming all things.
Just as Mount Sumeru is supreme among all mountains,
so too is this sutra supreme among all sutras.
Among all waters, the great ocean is supreme;
this sutra is likewise the most excellent among all sutras.
Among all stars, the moon deity is the most distinguished.
This sutra is likewise so; it is the most excellent among all sutras.
Just as among all holy beings the Buddhas are foremost, this sutra is likewise the foremost among all sutras.

At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others, as well as the various spirits and ghosts, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated and practiced accordingly.
The *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-dharmas* are concluded. From here below, the *dharmas* of all Buddhas are clarified.
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha: Collection of Dhāraṇīs*, Volume One.
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha: Collection of Dhāraṇīs*, Volume Two. The *Buddha Section*, Part Two.
The Method for Painting the Images of All Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas, translated by the Tripitaka Master Ajita from India during the Great Tang Dynasty.

The images of all Buddha-uṣṇīṣas have bodies that are entirely yellow in color and emit red light. From the center of this light, five blue flames of varying lengths extend outward. They wear a single-layered red skirt that covers their calves and shins, and they don yellow monastic robes with blue linings that hang down to their knees as they sit upon flowers made of a hundred jewels.

Upon that lotus is placed a single square precious side-tablet; on each side of this tablet are two bare feet, shaped like those of one squatting in prostration upon the ground, situated atop the lotus, with a blue ground spread above them.
On the blue ground, on both sides, are established red jewel terraces, adorned with variegated ribbons, flower garlands, and precious brocades, their decorations interspersed in intricate patterns.
Upon each terrace sits a lion, positioned at both flanks, supporting the Buddha’s seat with its head bearing a precious flower.
"The image’s right hand has the index finger and thumb joined to form a hollow; the other three fingers are spread and held upright, with the palm facing forward.

The left hand’s index finger rests against the side of the right thumb’s hollow, with the thumb positioned as if nearly touching it, giving the appearance that they are joined; the middle and ring fingers are bent within the palm, and the little finger is also held upright against the right palm."

The back of the image rests against a precious, embroidered pillow; on each side of the image stands a bodhisattva, their entire bodies golden-yellow in color, wearing crowns and necklaces that emit a blue light.
The attendants, bodhisattvas, and their vajra-attendants on both sides of the image all share the same blue hue in their radiance.
On the left side, the attendant bodhisattva has his right arm bent, holding a white whisk, while his left arm extends downward, slightly curved above the thigh, holding a lotus flower.
She wrapped a blue flower-patterned cloth around her waist and hips, fastened it with a jeweled sash, and wore a skirt of morning-mist silk, draped over her left hip with a light gauze shawl.

Furthermore, she wears a single robe of vermilion-colored chrysanthemum-patterned brocade, with the hem tucked over her right hip and hanging down toward the outside, standing upon a purple lotus flower.

To her right, the attendant Bodhisattva bends his left arm, holding a rosicle of twenty-one beads with his palm extended forward; his right arm is extended upward, resting against his thigh as he brandishes a fly-whisk.
Her two hips are draped with blue floral garments, her waist is bound with jeweled cords, and she wears a skirt of morning clouds (*chāoxiá*) covered by a light gauze shawl.
Beneath her left hip, a strip of green floral fabric extends horizontally across to her right hip and hangs down, as she stands facing outward upon a purple-white lotus flower.

Above each of those two attendant bodhisattvas were śrāvaka deities, their bodies entirely white, wearing yellow robes draped over their shoulders and true crimson skirts; they each stood upon five-colored clouds, scattering various flowers as an offering.

Furthermore, behind each of the two rows of attendant bodhisattvas, there were four bodhisattvas, majestic from top to bottom, sitting upright with bodies composed, assisting the Buddha’s supernatural powers to guide and receive sentient beings.

On the upper part of its left side, there are two bodhisattvas sitting side by side. The front bodhisattva is light yellow in complexion throughout; he wears a flower crown on his head, his neck is adorned with jeweled necklaces, and his ears lack earrings. He has a circular halo of red light and turns his face toward the back, appearing as if he were conversing with the bodhisattva behind him.
He wears a plain white shawl draped over his right shoulder and twisted back around; it hangs down from his left elbow.
His left arm is bent with the hand resting upon his left knee, while his right hand is raised upward, its fingers supporting the wrist of his left arm.
She wears a skirt of morning clouds, sits with her left knee raised upon a white lotus flower.

Behind her is a bodhisattva whose entire body is yellow; he wears a floral garland on his head, has a green halo, and a crimson robe draped over his shoulders. With palms joined in reverence, he wears a skirt of morning clouds and sits cross-legged upon a blue lotus flower.

"Next, below that, paint another bodhisattva, his entire body yellow in color; he has a floral wreath upon his head and green earrings in his ears, and his circular halo is red in color without shoulder straps."
The right arm is bent over the right thigh; the index finger and thumb are joined together, while the remaining three fingers are extended upward and away from the body.

The left arm is bent, resting upon the left thigh and knee; the hand holds a lotus flower, the stem of which reaches across the space between the armpit and the elbow, with the head of the flower facing upward, level with the neck and shoulder.
She wears a skirt of morning clouds and sits with legs crossed upon a pale purple lotus.

Next is another Bodhisattva, whose entire body is yellow; her breasts are large, she lacks a floral crown on her head, and her ears have white rings. Her halo is blue and she has no shoulder-strap ornaments; she is depicted in profile.
Bend the right arm; join the thumb and index finger of the right hand and rest them against the chest, while the remaining three fingers are extended upward and spread apart.
Extend the left arm downward, with the palm resting between the thigh and the knee.
Wearing a skirt of morning clouds, she kneels with both knees upon a red lotus flower.
Above her right side, two bodhisattvas sit side by side; the front bodhisattva is entirely colored light yellow, his face turned back as if conversing with the bodhisattva behind him.
He wears a jeweled crown upon his head, yet has no earrings or rings; his halo is crimson in color, and he likewise lacks a shoulder-cloth.
His left arm is bent, with the elbow resting upon his left knee and thigh; the palm is turned downward, and all five fingers hang straight down.

Place the right forearm upon the left wrist; join the tips of the index and thumb fingers as if pinching together, bend the middle finger, slightly curve the ring finger, and extend the little finger upward.
Wearing a skirt of morning clouds, he sits with legs crossed upon a red lotus flower.
Next, there is a Bodhisattva whose entire body is yellow; his head is adorned with a floral crown, his ears lack earrings, his halo is green, and he uses a crimson shawl to drape over his shoulders.
The right arm is bent, with the hand holding a lotus leaf; within the leaf, five-colored lotus flowers are placed one by one in separate positions.
The left arm is bent over the crossed legs, and in the palm of the hand is made a blue flower, shaped like the form of one who is scattering flowers before an image in worship.
Wearing a skirt of morning clouds, he sits with legs crossed upon a white lotus flower.
Next, a bodhisattva whose entire body is yellow, with a jeweled crown on his head, golden earrings in his ears, and a red circular halo.
Upon his left shoulder he wears a flower garland that hangs down across his right arm and reaches as far as his waist.
His left arm is bent, resting upon his left thigh, with the palm facing his body and holding a white lotus flower that reaches level with his forehead.
The face of this Bodhisattva is shaped like a flower viewed from below.
His right arm is bent, with the hand resting against the side of his right calf, the palm facing outward.
He wears a skirt of morning clouds and sits in the *paryaṅka* posture upon a pale purple lotus flower.
"Next, the Bodhisattva below has a body that is entirely yellow; his head is adorned with a floral wreath, his halo is blue, he wears golden earrings, and his breasts are large and prominent."
The left arm is bent upward with the elbow resting on the left knee, the hand holding a scripture case.
The right arm is bent and rests upon the right knee; the ring finger is bent while the remaining four fingers are spread apart like the palm of a lion.
Wearing a skirt of morning clouds, they sit with legs crossed upon red lotuses.
"The various bodhisattvas mentioned above all wear jeweled bracelets upon their wrists; these are all the retinues of the Buddhas."
Behind the image, two trees are depicted; upon these trees are painted *luheitu jiabosibei* flowers—translated into Chinese as *lingxiao* flowers—which are interspersed among the leaves.
Above the light of the image, another row of jeweled side-panels is fashioned, forming a double-layered structure.

Above these jeweled panels, a separate partition is made, within which three śarīra stupas are depicted; they are constructed of brick, adorned with white jewels, and are five-storied pagodas. Within both the stupas and the gates of the pagodas, the forms of transformation Buddhas are fashioned.

1. The *Sarvabuddha-uṣṇīṣa-mudrā-mantra*. First mantra: *Sarvabuddha-uṣṇīṣa-mudrā*, translated into Chinese as "The Uṣṇīṣa of All Buddhas. First, turn both hands palms upward. Hook the two ring fingers back and bend them into the palms. Each bend the two little fingers and the two middle fingers into the palms. Extend the two index fingers straight, with their tips about one inch apart. Open the two thumbs and move them back and forth.
The mantra is:

“Namaḥ sarvadharmatebhyaḥ (1) arhadvibhyaḥ (2) samyaksambuddhebhyaḥ (3) tadyathā (4) śodhani śodhani (5) sarvadharmaviśodhani sarvapāpaviśodhani (6) śodhe viśodhe (7) sarvadharmaviśodhe (8) svāhā (9). On the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, bathe with fragrant water and construct a water mandala; burn incense and offer various foods and drinks. This extinguishes all sins, eliminates evil poisons and sorcery, and also cures all diseases.
"Recite this mantra over all medicinal herbs; by reciting it seven times before consuming them, abdominal pain will cease immediately upon ingestion, and malignant poisons will be eliminated.

**2. The Heart-Seal Mantra of Śākyamuni Buddha.** *Second: Hold the two thumbs, middle fingers, and little fingers upright with their tips touching one another. Interlace the two index fingers inwardly, pressing the right over the left; do the same for the ring fingers. Extend the wrists four inches apart. This seal is identical to the Heart Seal of Avalokiteśvara and also identical to the Wheel Seal of Vajrānala.*
The mantra is:

“Oṃ sarvasiddhike viśuddharoṇi svāhā. If a mantra-master wishes to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, desires to avoid all obstacles and difficulties, to eliminate all diseases caused by spirits, and to cure all illnesses and pains, they should perform this rite.

If it is known that there is a disease caused by a ghost, construct a water altar four cubits in size; place a brazier at its center and burn cypress branches while reciting the mantra repeatedly, and the patient will immediately recover.
If it does not improve within one day, perform this daily until the seventh day, and it will then be cured.

3. Furthermore, the Buddha’s Heart-Seal Mantra (Buddha-hṛdaya-mudrā-mantra), Part Three: "Form the seal by making a fist with the right hand, grasping the thumb with the last four fingers; the left hand is not used."
The mantra is:
“Tadyathā: amṛte aśvapatige mamara mamara śambara upaśama dundubhi dundumule sāha. If one recites this mantra while traveling on a long journey, one will never grow weary.

If, while traveling on a road, one loses the way due to the wind and cannot discern east from west; or if a ghost comes and leads one astray regarding the path; or if there is a person or horse that dies—then at that very spot, one should erect a stone pillar. Having inscribed this mantra upon the stone pillar, one should recite it one hundred and eight times. If there is no stone pillar, one should instead erect a banner-pole, and likewise inscribe this mantra upon the banner-pole.

If one recites this one hundred and eight times, all evil spirits and ghosts, having heard this mantra, shall never again dwell there; their movements will be free from obstacles and hindrances for twenty years or less.

For children who are ill, one should prepare a consecrated cord (*mantra-sūtra*) using thread of five colors and tie fifty-four knots upon it. Having ground ox-gall (*go-rocanā*) into ink, one should transcribe this mantra onto a piece of silk and place it within the consecrated cord. By tying this around the child’s neck, they will immediately recover.

4. Furthermore, the Buddha’s Heart-Seal Mantra (Buddha-hṛdaya-mudrā-mantra), the fourth: "With the right hand, press the thumb upon the nail of the little finger; extend and separate the remaining three fingers. With the left hand, cross it behind the waist. This may be employed while either standing or sitting as one pleases."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ (1) tisa ta-na (2) kāla-kāra (3) māra-māra (4) sāra-sāra (5) pūra-pūra (6) cchinda-cchinda (7) binda-binda (8) hūṃ phaṭ (9) svāhā (10). If cattle, horses, or other such livestock should suffer from a feverish illness, one should take the hair of a cow, horse, camel, donkey, mule, or similar animal and mix it together with cow’s milk. Beginning at sunset, one should perform a water mandala night after night. Placing a brazier at the center of the mandala, the mantra-reciter faces north and takes a small portion of the hair from the milk.
Having taken it, he should think in his heart: “May the Buddhas of the ten directions save all sentient beings from suffering.”

Having recited this mantra once, one should immediately cast it into the fire. In this manner, performing the rite one hundred and eight times throughout a single night, and continuing daily for seven full days, all sick animals within the kingdom will be cured.

5. Furthermore, the Buddha’s Mind Seal (Buddha-cittamudrā), the fifth: “Bend the right thumb toward the palm; extend the remaining four fingers upward and erect. The mantra is the same as that of the second Mind Seal above.”

"If the King falls ill, he should observe a fast for seven days and construct a water altar four cubits in size. He should place incense, flowers, food, and a hundred kinds of offerings upon the altar, and further install a brazier at the center of that altar."

The mantra-practitioner shall bathe daily with fragrant water, don fresh and clean garments, enter the ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*), and invoke the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others. He shall take one hundred and eight segments of a Bodhi tree—if such a tree is unavailable, a grain tree may also be used—each segment being one chi in length. Taking one segment, he shall smear it at both ends with cow’s milk; as for the method of smearing, he first applies it to the tip and subsequently to the base.

The mantra-practitioner faces north and recites this mantra until the end of the *dumule* section. He then pronounces the name of the king and the phrase "the illness is cured. After finishing with the oral utterance of *svāhā*, he burns [the wood] in the fire—regarding the method of burning: the tip of the wood points forward, and the base of the wood points toward himself. In this manner, he completes one hundred and eight pieces in a single night, continuing for up to seven days; the king’s illness will then be immediately cured.
"If the mantra-practitioner falls ill, by performing the fire-oblation of sesame seeds one hundred and eight times according to the previous method, they will immediately recover.

If a person is about to travel far away, by performing the fire-oblation of powdered *śiṃśapā* wood daily according to the previous method for seven days, once this rite is completed, the traveler will have no fear regarding any obstacles or difficulties."
If one travels on a journey, seven persons or fewer may travel together.
One who practices this rite need not fear any thieves, ghosts, or calamities. If a person suffers from a headache, follow the previous method:

the mantra-reciter takes fragrant flowers and recites the mantra seven times, then gives them to the patient to smell. After they have finished smelling, recite the mantra twenty-one times, burning [the incense] once for each recitation. At the end of the word "Svāhā," state the patient's name; thus the illness will be cured.
If the illness does not subside, it will do so by the seventh day, as it progresses day by day.

6. The Mantra of the Heart-Seal of All Buddhas, Part Six: "Interlace the last four fingers within the palms, pressing the right over the left. Align both thumbs in front and hold them upright. Bring the two wrists together and move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:

“Namaḥ sarvabuddhānāṃ viheṭhanāya | Sara sara | Sura sura | Pura pura | Sarvāpāritāparāye | Svāhā. If a person suffers from a feverish wind-disorder (*vāta-roga*), one should prepare a consecrated cord according to the aforementioned method, reciting the mantra once for each knot, making twenty-one knots. Tying this around the patient’s neck and striking the patient’s head with white mustard seeds, the illness will be cured immediately.
If it is not cured, one should recite the mantra for three days; by striking [the patient] with white mustard seeds, it will then be cured.

If the illness does not subside, take cooked non-glutinous rice and recite the mantra twenty-one times; for each repetition, burn one portion while reciting the mantra, prefixing it with "Svāhā" and the name of the patient. The patient will then be cured.

"If a person suffers from eye disease, they should likewise follow the previous method for seven days: take one hundred and eight grains of añjana (translated in Chinese as *yín kuàng shí*, or silver ore stone), recite the mantra over each one once, and cast them into a fire. After burning them one hundred and eight times, the eyes will be cured."

"Furthermore, there is another method: recite the mantra over all food, fruits, medicines, and so forth, seven times each, and then consume them; thus one shall be free from all illness. Furthermore, there is another method:

if one recites all various mantras while forming this mudrā, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and worthy sages will be simultaneously delighted, and all transgressions committed within the body—namely the four pārājika offenses, the five heinous crimes, the consumption of alcohol, meat, and the five pungent vegetables, as well as the sin of sexual misconduct—shall all be extinguished."

"If there is an enemy, one should fashion an image of them out of clay, making it large or small as desired. Taking *khadira* wood (translated into Chinese as *zǐqiāngmù*, or purple acacia) for a staff, one should strike this person with it. Having struck them, one should immediately burn this staff while constantly reciting the mantra and calling the person's name. By casting white mustard seeds into the fire one hundred and eight times, the evil person will depart far away; this is also effective for curing illnesses."

7. Furthermore, the Heart-Seal Mantra of All Buddhas, the seventh, also known as the Great Heart-Seal Mantra: "Cover both hands, crossing the index and middle fingers back-to-back within the palms. Extend the two thumbs straight toward the body with their tips touching each other. Point the two ring fingers forward with their tips touching each other. Extend the two little fingers so that they do not touch the ring fingers."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ susarvasiddhike apratihate tṛṣṭu svāhā. If a mantra-practitioner, a king, or a minister wishes to be free from physical illness and pain, they should follow the aforementioned ritual procedure, burning all types of incense one hundred and eight times while reciting the mantra; then they will be cured.

"If a person wishes to obtain wealth and property, they should likewise sit facing east according to the previous method, recite the mantra over white mustard seeds, and burn them one by one for one hundred and eight times; that which is sought shall then be attained."

"If you wish to engage in debate with another, burn green achyranthes (chángpú) every day for seven days; recite the mantra once for each burning, and after one hundred and eight repetitions, you will surely prevail over them."

"If a person is bitten by a venomous snake, one should recite a mantra over a branch of a pomegranate tree one hundred and eight times; by rubbing the branch against the lower part of the body and doing this every day, the snake venom will be cured."

"If one wishes to cause others to love and cherish them, one should burn white mustard seeds, reciting the mantra once for each seed burned, for one hundred and eight times; by doing so for seven days, one will attain their wish."

"If a person afflicted by a spirit-disease is unable to speak, take white mustard seeds and recite the mantra over them twenty-one times, then strike the patient with them; in this way, within seven days, they will be able to speak."

8. The Mind-Seal of All Buddhas (Sarvabuddha-hṛdaya-mudrā). The eighth mantra is the same as the second Buddha-heart mantra mentioned previously. According to the previous [instructions], simply change it so that the two little fingers press down upon the two ring fingers, holding them together.
If one recites this mantra every day, others will feel joy and treat one with reverence and respect.

If one wishes to go before a king (*rāja*) or a great minister (*mahāmātya*), first perform the rite of self-protection in a private room; then, at the gate of the king’s palace or the gate of the minister’s residence, recite the mantra over one’s own palms seven times and rub one’s face twenty-one times. Upon entering, the king or the minister will see one and immediately feel joy.

"If there are human or demonic illnesses that are extremely difficult to cure, one should also follow the previous method: take a woolen cord and tie it around all four legs of the bed. Burn white mustard seeds, reciting the mantra once for each burning, for one hundred and eight times. The illness will then be cured; if not cured within three days, it will certainly be cured within seven days."

"Performing the rites day by day for seven days according to the mental dharmas of all Buddhas as previously described, the person who performs this rite must always maintain compassion for all sentient beings, down to the smallest ants; they must not kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, or speak falsehoods, but should instead cultivate the ten wholesome actions and sever the ten unwholesome karmas."
When performing the ritual, one must not eat for the first day among the seven days; thereafter, one may eat for the remaining six days.

Regarding the statement that "each rite is as previously described," this means that for all of them, one should construct a water mandala and perform various offerings, ensuring that the rites are accessible both above and below, according to this method.
"When performing the rite, one must with a profound mind give rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta and feel impartial compassion for all sentient beings.
One who gives rise to such a mind will obtain the desired efficacy;
if one does not do so, one shall not obtain it."

9. The Mudrā and Mantra of the Eye of All Buddhas (Sarvabuddhanetrīmudrāmantra), the Ninth; also known as the Buddha-Mother Mudrā. Join the two ring fingers and the two little fingers straight upward with their tips touching. Extend the two middle fingers straight upward, slightly curved, with their tips touching one another. Place the two thumbs side-by-side, extended and slightly curved, and press the sides of the two index fingers against the backs of the two thumbs so that their tips touch.
The mantra is: "Oṃ śikhāsamaye svāhā.

If a person suffers from eye ailments, one should take *pippalī* (long pepper), pound it into a powder, and mix it with honey. Using an iron tip as large as the head of a chopstick, one applies the medicine to the eyes. Furthermore, one seals the medicine in the eyes with this mudrā and mantra; the affliction will be cured immediately.

10. The Dhāraṇī of the Seal of the White Tuft between the Buddha’s Brows The tenth [chapter] is the Dhāraṇī of the Seal of the White Tuft between the Buddha’s Brows: "Interlace the two little fingers behind within the palms; extend the two middle fingers with their tips touching one another; extend both thumbs side by side; bend the lower joint of the left index finger flatly to press against the tip of the left thumb; curve the right index finger open so that it remains about one inch away from the back of the right middle finger."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ, uṣṇīṣe, nir-male, alu-kite, uṣṇīṣe, svāhā. This is the Great Mind, and it is also called the Great Mantra.
Furthermore, the mantra is recited as:
"Oṃ vāṇi svāhā. This is a minor mantra, also known as the heart-mantra.

"If there is anyone who can daily make offerings, perform mudrās, and recite mantras, at the time of their death, the light between their eyebrows will be like the radiance from the ūrṇā-kośa of Amitābha Buddha."

11. The Buddha-tooth Seal Mantra. Regarding the Buddha-tooth Seal Mantra, eleventh: "It is performed according to the previous Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Sword Seal, with the sole modification that the right middle finger is bent into the palm, while the left middle finger is slightly curved and held upright."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ śatror-vimardaniye svāhā. Construct a water mandala four cubits in size—though one of two or three cubits may also be used for this purpose—and place white mustard seeds, the seven precious gems, and all other requisite items within the mandala.

Next, fashion a mantra-cord; recite the mantra once for each knot until thirty-seven knots are formed. Tie it around the patient’s neck—or it may also be tied on the arm—and the illness will be immediately cured.
Furthermore, by sealing water with this mudrā and drinking it, toothache is eliminated. 12.

Furthermore, the mantra of the Universal Buddha-Eye Mudrā (Sarvabuddhanetra-mudrā-mantra), the twelfth: The Śākyanetra-mudrā is the same as follows: "Interlace the two little fingers behind [the palms] within the hollows of the hands; bend and erect the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another; place the two thumbs side-by-side and erect them straight; bend the lower joints of the two index fingers flatly to press against the tops of the two thumbs, causing their tips to touch; and bring the two wrists together."
The mantra says:
"Oṃ śikhāsamaye svāhā. If one performs this rite and makes offerings daily, one will behold the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
after the end of this life, in every place of rebirth, one shall always obtain the divine eye.

13. The Buddha-vajra Seal and Mantra for Stopping All Venomous Insects, Number Thirteen. "Interlace the two little fingers within the palms; likewise interlace the two ring fingers. Extend the tips of the fingers from the 'tiger mouth' (the hollow between the thumb and forefinger). Hold the two middle fingers upright with their tips touching. Stand the two thumbs upright. Slightly bend the tips of the index fingers so that their middle joints meet at a distance of about one *fen*."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ, jvala jvala, budhavajra, apratihata, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This Dharma-seal mantra can stop all bites from venomous insects and also cure various diseases.

When performing the rite, construct a small altar, burn incense, scatter flowers, and offer food and drink as an offering. By forming this seal and reciting this mantra upon the body of the patient, their illness will be immediately cured; furthermore, one should seal the patient’s person and establish a boundary for protection.
"If a person has various malignant sores or suffers from seasonal epidemics, by sealing them with this seal, those sores and fevers will all be cured without exception."
If one seals a patient, for illnesses above the navel, one should apply seals to all locations according to where the ailment resides;
however, for illnesses below the navel, one must not apply seals, but it is permissible to strike them with a willow staff.

14. Furthermore, the Buddha-Vajra Seal Mantra. Regarding the Fourteenth, the Buddha-Vajra Seal Mantra: "Perform it according to the previous Tejorāśi seal, with the sole modification that the two index fingers are extended and their tips are slightly bent."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ kuruṇiṇa huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Construct a small water mandala and make offerings of various incenses, flowers, food, and drink; burn agallochum and frankincense, but do not use any other incense.
First, polish the blade with dry ashes seven times, without using water.

Then, construct a water altar four cubits in length and breadth. A boy aged eight, twelve, or fifteen years old shall bathe in fragrant water, don new and clean garments, and sit on the eastern side of the altar facing west.

The mantra-practitioner holds the blade across his eyebrows and sits on the western side of the altar facing east; he recites the mantra repeatedly until the desired ritual effect appears upon the blade, which the practitioner does not see, but only the child sees.

15. Furthermore, the Vajra Seal Mantra of All Buddhas, the Fifteenth: "Place the left thumb upon the nail of the little finger. Pass the right thumb through the hollow between the fingers. Grasp the left thumb and little finger with the remaining four fingers. The tip of the right thumb should point upward; the left index, middle, and ring fingers should be held straight and extended. This is the seal of Buddha Amitābha (Vairocana). To form the seal of Buddha Śākyamuni, simply change it so that the right index, middle, and ring fingers are spread and grasped over the back of the right palm, along with the tip of the thumb."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vajra-jihve svāhā. To cure all illnesses caused by ghosts, if one recites this mantra three times on the fifth day of the waxing moon, one will immediately attain the eradication of transgressions.
One may recite the mantra twenty-one times, one hundred and eight times, or one thousand and eight times as desired; by doing so, all obstacles and afflictions can be entirely eliminated.

16. The Mantra of the Staff Seal of All Buddhas, Chapter Sixteen. "Interlace the three fingers behind in the palm; join the two thumbs upright, leaving them slightly separated from the index fingers. The tips of the two index fingers should touch one another, and they should be bent down to press against the tips of the thumbs, with their heads slightly not touching the thumbs."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ, māre māre, māriṇi, dhara dhara, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. By striking all demonic illnesses with this seal, those illnesses will be immediately cured; the efficacy of its application is proven.

17. The Mantra of the Seal of All Buddhas’ Sword-Piercing of All Ghosts, Number Seventeen. "Interlace the two little fingers behind within the palms; extend the two middle fingers straight upward with their tips touching; and bend the right thumb into the palm."
Next, press the left thumb over the right thumb, concealing the tips.
Next, press the right index finger over the left thumb, concealing its tip.
Next, press the left index finger over the right index finger, likewise concealing the tip, and join the wrists.
The mantra says:

“Oṃ kakkāramalaṇa pramadanañcaye dhoḍaye svāhā. If one wishes to practice seated meditation, one should bind the boundary three times, turning the mudrā clockwise, and recite the mantra seven times; this also cures all diseases caused by ghosts and spirits.

18. The Mudrā and Dhāraṇī of the Buddha-śikhara of King Viśuddha (The Eighteenth). Also known as the Akṣobhya-Buddha-śikhara-mudrā: "Interlace the three fingers [ring, middle, and little fingers] behind within the palms; bend the two index fingers so that their tips touch one another; place both thumbs side by side in front, slightly away from the index fingers so that they do not touch, and move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is as follows:

“Namo sarvatathāgatebhyo bhūṣaṇarājāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | Tadyathā | bhūṣaṇe bhūṣaṇe | sarvabodhiprati-bhūṣaṇe | bhūṣite bhūṣite | sarvadharmaprati-bhūṣite | Svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there is anyone who, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, bathes with scented water, burns incense as an offering, and recites this mantra with a sincere heart, they shall extinguish immeasurable sins.
If there is anyone who can recite this daily, no evil spirits or ghosts will dare to approach them, and it shall also cure all diseases.

When treating a disease, first empower white mustard seeds with this mantra seven times; by scattering them in the four directions, a boundary (sīmābandha) is established. Once the boundary is established, the treatment of the disease will be effective.

If a woman experiences difficult labor and the child cannot be delivered, seal a vessel of sesame oil with this mudrā and recite the mantra twenty-one times. Then, rub the oil on her navel while reciting the mantra, and the child will be born immediately.

On the thirteenth day of the waxing moon, bathe with fragrant water, burn incense as an offering, and recite mantras to extinguish transgressions; one will then be able to bind ghosts, wicked people, and thieves.

19. The Mudrā and Dhāraṇī of the Padmaprabha Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, the Nineteenth. "The mudrā is the same as the preceding Golden Wheel Mudrā, with the sole difference that the two thumbs move back and forth."

The mantra is: "Oṃ padmāvalokite 'bharaṇe huṃ. (20) The Seal and Mantra of Vimalaprabhāsa Buddha, the twentieth; translated into Chinese as Wuyoudefo (Buddha of Sorrowless Virtue). "Following the seal of the Moon Deity, one makes this modification: place the two index fingers at the middle joints of the middle fingers, with the tips of the fingers pointing slightly inward, while the thumbs move back and forth."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ śurudharāgate ja vasekara prabhā hūṃ hūṃ bhagavan svāhā. (21) This is the *Ratnaśikhin-buddha-mudrā-mantra*, the twenty-first; in the language of Tang it is called "Candana-deva Buddha. Following the *Hayagrīva* hand-seal, the only modification is to bend the two thumbs and insert them into the palms, with the two middle fingers bent down to press upon the thumbs, while the index fingers move back and forth.

The mantra is: "Oṃ, vilokini, sarasara, ciri cire, sulu sulu, alokini, vilokini, apavāsaya, svāhā. 22. The Seal-Mantra of Vipaśyin Buddha, Number Twenty-Two. Form the seal as follows: Join the wrists of both hands. Slightly curve the index fingers and ring fingers of both hands, interlacing them to the tips of the nails. Extend the two little fingers straight upward with their tips touching. Extend the two thumbs side-by-side with their tips touching. Extend the two middle fingers straight upward, and move the two thumbs back and forth.

The mantra is: "Oṃ (1) dhara dhara (2) sāgaradhvaja (3) kūṭāgāra (4) kṣata kṣata (5) matha matha (6) abhiṣe abhiṣe (7) svāhā (8). 23. The Seal-Mantra of Indradhvaja Buddha. (Indradhvaja Buddha is translated into Chinese as Xiāngdé [相德] Buddha. This is the twenty-third. "Following the Vajrarāja-mudrā, one only changes it by bending the two index fingers so that each presses down upon the tip of the thumb; the index fingers then move back and forth."
The mantra says:

“Namo jñānajñāna-aye (1) oṃ (2) śvāra-paśu-si (3) śvāra-śvāra (4) matha-matha (5) bandha-bandha (6) abhiṣe abhiṣe (7) hūṃ phaṭ svāhā (8–9). 24. The Mantra of the Seal of the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa of the Northern Lakṣmī-Vyuha (The Second Fourteen). “Form the seal by pressing the tip of the left little finger with the thumb; pass the right thumb from below upward through the hollow of the palm; grasp the left thumb and little finger with the remaining four fingers; let the tip of the right thumb protrude from between the thumb and forefinger; extend the left index, middle, and ring fingers straight upward and apart; and move the left forefinger back and forth.”
The mantra is:
"Oṃ vajrāṅkī svāhā. If a person performs this rite daily, they will be able to extinguish the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and other such transgressions.

25. The Seal-Dhāraṇī of the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Buddha, Number Twenty-Five: "Place the eight fingers from the index fingers of both hands interlaced within the palms, with the right hand pressing down upon the left. Keeping the two wrists approximately five inches apart, move the two thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ hulu hulu candali mārīci svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there are persons with many karmic obstacles and hindrances, or women suffering from the perils of difficult childbirth, those who wish to turn misfortune into fortune, or those afflicted by diseases caused by spirits that are difficult to cure—one should fashion a consecrated cord from five-colored threads and bind it around the patient’s neck, hands, feet, waist, abdomen, and so forth. Furthermore, one should instruct them to have an image of the Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru made, transcribe one scroll of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*, and create a banner forty-nine feet long composed of the five colors.

Furthermore, he taught that forty-nine lamps should be lit, arranged in seven tiers in the shape of a chariot wheel, and placed before the image. He further instructed that forty-nine living beings should be released;

thereafter, one should prepare a five-colored mantra-cord (*mantra-sūtra*). Regarding the method for making the mantra-cord: once the thread has been obtained but not yet twisted, one should burn named incense and make a vow. Then, after reciting the mantra forty-nine times and fumigating it with the incense smoke, one twists the thread to form the cord, ensuring that the sound of the mantra does not cease.

Having twisted it into a cord, support it with the mudrā and further recite the mantra over the cord forty-nine times; thereafter, tie forty-nine knots, reciting the mantra once for each knot, ceasing when the count is complete.
One should tie this cord around that person’s body and recite the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* forty-nine times; all their karmic obstacles and hindrances will be liberated.

At the time of childbirth, there will be no suffering whatsoever, and delivery will be easy. The child born will have a handsome and upright appearance, be intelligent and wise, enjoy a long life, avoid untimely calamities, and always abide in peace and security.
Diseases caused by ghosts and spirits will be immediately eradicated.
The Great Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha is as follows:
*Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo Kambile.* (1) Homage to the Triple Gem.
(2) Homage to Kambila.
