" Svāhā. For the twenty-first seal, use the previous seal.

"This Dharma-seal mantra was spoken by the Buddha while he was at Vaiśālī beneath the Music Tree, together with thirty-six thousand people, as well as the twelve divine kings along with their retinues, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others, and great divine kings. Having taught this Dharma within such a great assembly, all who heard it were filled with joy; this is therefore called the 'Mantra for Binding Vows.'"

If there are those who receive and uphold [this], they will be able to uproot all grave sins of past births and deaths within their bodies; they shall no longer undergo the three miserable realms, escape the nine untimely deaths, and transcend all sufferings. They will find peace and happiness wherever they go throughout the worlds of the ten directions, moving with sovereign ease and without obstruction; such is the natural law.

"If good sons or good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite this divine mantra diligently bathe with fragrant water day and night, wear fresh and clean garments, observe all the prohibitive precepts, and having completed one hundred thousand recitations according to the Dharma, they shall prepare the ground according to the Dharma in a pure location."

The method for preparing the site is as described for other altars: dig a circular area several *zhang* in diameter, fill it again with pure earth to make it level, and it is best if the foundation rises above the surrounding ground.
Having finished leveling the ground, he moistened it with pure cow dung mixed with sandalwood water, rubbing it with his palms while turning in accordance with the movement of the sun.

Once the ground had been rubbed smooth, he arranged a thousand lamps upon it. Above the site of practice (maṇḍala) and in its four directions, he adorned the area with various miscellaneous jewels, suspended silk streamers, banners, and canopies, and interlaced them with jeweled nets.

"On its surface, one should distribute five-colored powders all around to construct seven layers of courtyards, each with four gates; the configuration of these seven layers of courtyards is like that of the earth, water, millstone, and wind wheels."

Each courtyard contains numerous partitions, and within each partitioned passage there is the appearance of jeweled staircases and paved floors; in the center of each floor is the appearance of a jeweled lotus-wheel throne. This is what is called the Adornment of the Lower Direction.
At each end of every partitioned aisle, lamps were placed; at every successive interval, lamps were set separately until the total reached one thousand.
Having completed the arrangement of the lamps, various precious vases, jeweled trees, incense, flowers, and other such items were installed.

Having completed the arrangement, place a small bed upon the central seat and cover it with clean materials such as brocade and embroidery. Install an image of the Medicine Buddha (*Bhaiṣajyaguru*) and, using the previously mentioned mudrā, invite him to serve as the presiding master. Perform the boundary-binding and expulsion rites according to the *Samaya* method, as in the ritual for Vajra-Caṇḍālī. Thereafter, settle the mind and offer various incenses, scatter various flowers, and present various foods, drinks, flowers, and fruits; furthermore, burn ghee, honey, sesame seeds, and human [flesh] as offerings.

"If for one day and night, three days, seven days, or seven times seven days, one recites the mantra a full hundred thousand million times, day and night combined, whatever one seeks shall be granted according to one's heart, and immeasurable fruits shall be obtained—except in cases of lack of sincere devotion."
The Dharma should be practiced in this manner; the benefits thereof are inexhaustible, and its remaining functions are fully described as stated in the Sūtra. 26.

The Continuation of the Empowerment of the Mudrā and Mantra (Continuation of the Empowerment of the Mudrā and Mantra, Chapter Twenty-Six): "Bend both thumbs into the palms and press against the nails of the two ring fingers. The middle joints of the two ring fingers face one another, while the tips of the two little fingers touch each other. The two middle fingers are held straight upright with their tips touching. The two index fingers are bent, each pressing against the upper joint of the back of the middle finger."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ, *bhusuṇḍarā*, *somayaṃ*, svāhā. If one wishes to restore the efficacy, every morning at dawn, one should form the mudrā over a water jar, recite the mantra twenty-one times, and pour it over one's own head; thus, it will return to its former state.
**The Preface to the Exposition of the Mahā-cintya-brahma-paripṛcchā Sūtra on Amitābha Buddha, Part One** Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Potalaka—this being the island in the ocean—together with a great assembly of one thousand five hundred Arhats.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with five thousand others, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, surrounded them from before and behind as they approached the place where the Buddha was.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet. Having paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, he circumambulated the Buddha three times and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as all sentient beings, practice wholesome dharmas, they shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha and behold that Buddha.
"How is this attained?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:

"If those of the fourfold assembly wish to be born in that land, they should receive and uphold the seal of Amitābha Buddha, as well as his dhāraṇī and the ritual for constructing the altar; only by making offerings and prostrating shall they attain rebirth in that Buddha-land."
“If the fourfold assembly scatters various flowers upon Amitābha Buddha while making vows and reciting mantras, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit.
What are these ten?
First, one generates a wholesome mind oneself;
second, one causes others to generate a wholesome mind;
third, all the devas rejoice.
Fourth, one’s own body will be upright and handsome, with all six sense faculties complete and free from impairment;
fifth, one’s place of birth and death will be transformed into a precious land;
sixth, in life after life, one will be born in a central land and a noble lineage, encountering the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, and never being born in a borderland or a lowly lineage.
Seventh, he shall become a wheel-turning monarch, ruling over the four continents;
eighth, in birth after birth throughout all lifetimes, he shall always obtain a male body;
ninth, he shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, whereupon he will sit cross-legged upon a flower made of the seven treasures and attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Tenth, having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they sit upon a lion throne made of the seven precious gems and emit a great radiance, equal to that of Amitābha Buddha and no different from him.
These are called the ten kinds of merit from scattering flowers.

"If the fourfold assembly were to take the seven treasures filling the entirety of the world and offer them as alms to all the Buddhas of the ten directions, it would not equal the merit of one who, with a sincere heart, offers a single coin, a single flower, or a single incense stick to Amitābha Buddha."
If one performs these meritorious deeds, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and others will be filled with joy, and at death, one shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
"If a person lights lamps as an offering and is reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, they will immediately obtain the divine eye and see all the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
If a person offers incense as an act of worship and is reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, they will immediately obtain a fragrant body from which clouds of fragrance constantly emanate.
If a person prostrates themselves on the ground in reverent worship of Amitābha Buddha, they will be reborn in that land."

If a person who recollects that Buddha makes various offerings such as incense, flowers, clothing, food, and water mandalas, they will obtain incense, flowers, clothing, and food upon being reborn in that land.

If a person does not make offerings of incense, flowers, clothing, food, and so forth, although they may be reborn in that Pure Land, they will not obtain the rewards of various offerings such as incense, flowers, clothing, and food.

If a Wheel-Turning King were to practice the giving of the seven treasures throughout the four continents for a hundred thousand years, offering them to the Buddhas of the ten directions, it would not equal a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā sitting in meditation for even the duration of a finger-snap, contemplating the merits of Amitābha Buddha with a mind of equanimity and compassion for all sentient beings.

"If any good man or good woman recites and maintains the Amitābha Buddha-dhāraṇī, performs the mudrās and so forth, and makes daily offerings, they shall immediately eliminate the grave sins of the five heinous acts, the four pārājika offenses, and the heavy karmic burdens of births and deaths as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

If you wish to attain the verification of *śamatha*, to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, to obtain a male body that is upright and intelligent, to sit upon the seven treasures, to achieve supernormal powers such as the divine eye and divine ear, and to receive celestial garments no different from those of the Buddha, you should fashion an image of Amitābha Buddha.

Regarding the method for creating the image: first, prepare an altar on the ground using fragrant clay. Summon one, two, or three highly skilled painters and have them bathe daily. Grant these painters the Eight Precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa). The mantra-reciter must also bathe daily, perform mudrās to protect his own body, and likewise perform mudrās to protect the bodies of the painters. Both the mantra-reciter and the painters must not violate the precepts or break their fasts; they must abstain from the five pungent roots, alcohol, and meat.
At the center of the altar, hang a canopy; at the four sides, place offerings of food, drink, fruits, and various musical instruments to make offerings to Amitābha Buddha.
The painter shall wear pure white garments and use various pigments mixed with the juices of incense such as *guggulu* and *agaru*, but must not use animal glue.

"The mantra-practitioner sits outside the altar facing west, while the painter faces east. Before the mantra-practitioner, a censer is placed, wherein various incenses are burned and flowers are scattered; at night, lamps are lit."
The mantra practitioner forms the mudrā of the body of Amitābha Buddha and recites the dhāraṇī mantra, saying:
"Namo āryāya amitābhāya. (1) (2)
Tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya.
Tadyathā: oṃ amṛte hana hana.
Sarvabodhanī kudāha kudāha (10) sarvabodhanī (11)
"Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ (12) svāhā (13). Next, regarding the method for the painting master to depict the Buddha image:

place Amitābha Buddha in the center, seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). His hands form the Dharma-teaching mudrā (*dharmacakra-mudrā*) of Amitābha: the tips of the left thumb and ring finger are pressed together; the tip of the right thumb and ring finger presses down upon the tips of the left thumb and ring finger; and the index, middle, and little fingers of both hands are extended upward.
"To the right of the Buddha, an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with eleven faces was made; to the left, an image of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta was made.
Above the Buddha, a jeweled palace was constructed, all fashioned from the seven precious gems."
Your Highness has constructed a canopy of the seven treasures, entirely composed of the seven treasures and necklaces of jewels.

Upon that jeweled palace, three great jewel-kings are depicted; from each jewel issues light of five colors, and within that light, jeweled palaces and towers are manifested. Inside these jeweled palaces, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are fashioned.
"Amitābha Buddha sits upon a high throne made of the seven treasures; upon that high throne are fashioned seven lotus flowers of solid substance, and Amitābha Buddha sits atop those flowers."

"At the four corners of its inner courtyard stand four trees made of the seven precious substances; at the four sides of the Buddha’s inner courtyard are four palaces made of the seven precious substances. Upon each of these precious palaces are the seven treasures, and from each treasure issues five-colored light. Within each ray of light is a palace made of the seven precious substances, and within each of those palaces reside Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."

"Outside that Buddha’s enclosure, there are four palaces made of the seven treasures; upon each of these palaces are the seven treasures, and from each treasure issues light of five colors. Upon each ray of light is a palace of the seven treasures, and within each of these palaces dwell Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
"To the left and right of Amitābha Buddha stand two Bodhisattvas, each playing music.
Beneath that Buddha is the Water of Ambrosia, from which emerge immeasurable jewel-lotuses; upon each lotus there is a Bodhisattva, and to the left and right there are five hundred flowering trees."
"The form of that Buddha is golden in color, and his monastic robe is crimson.
The halo surrounding that Buddha is composed of five colors, and from the crown of his head, he emits light of five colors."
Those bodhisattvas are yellowish-white in color, and upon their bodies they wear five-colored celestial robes.

To the left of that Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta sits in the full lotus posture; his left hand is placed palm-downward upon his left thigh, while his right arm is bent with the elbow resting on his right thigh. His arm is extended upward, with the thumb pressing against the nail of the ring finger, while the index, middle, and little fingers are held upright and separated, the side of the palm facing forward.

"To the right of that Buddha, paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with eleven faces, seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). His left arm is bent toward his shoulder, the palm turned downward against his back, holding a lotus flower. His right arm is bent at the elbow, resting upon his right thigh, holding a white fly-whisk (*cāmara*), the tail of which extends toward the right."
"On all four sides of that water are immeasurable jewel trees made of the seven treasures, and its banks are likewise formed of the seven treasures.
Above those Buddhas, the various devas scatter flowers."

"Once this image has been fashioned, install it within the Buddha hall. Form the mudrā of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), and using four stakes made of khadira wood—each eight finger-widths long and each consecrated one hundred and eight times with mantras—drive them into the four corners."
Once these stakes have been firmly set, do not remove them again; as it is with one stake, so it is with the remaining three.

Furthermore, take white mustard seeds and pierce holes in the four directions and the center, each about one span deep, and bury them within the holes. For all of this, recite the Great Heart Mantra of the Army-Conquering One (*Cundī*) over the white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times. As in the previous ritual for the wood, the Great Heart Mantra is as follows:

"Recite: *Oṃ vilu vilu tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bandha bandha hana hana amṛte huṃ phaṭ*. After reciting this mantra one hundred and eight times and having finished burying the mustard seeds, then install an image of Amitābha Buddha. Invite four monks to partake of a vegetarian feast—more than four is also permitted without limit—and make offerings every day while reciting the Great Body Mantra (*Mahākāya-dhāraṇī*)."
The mantra says:
"Namaḥ hradantātrāya nama āryāya."

Gamiṇi gagaṇe kṛti-kare sarvaspokasaṃskāre. (12–14)

*Svāhā* (the "sa" pronounced with a departing tone; fifteen syllables). 1. The Body Seal of Amitābha Buddha. First: Place the two little fingers of both hands back-to-back upon the backs of the ring fingers. The tips of the two ring fingers touch one another. The two middle fingers are held straight upright, separated by about one *cun*. The two thumbs are held side-by-side upright. Bend the two index fingers to press down upon the tips of the two thumbs, their tips touching. Move the index fingers back and forth.

2. The Great Heart Seal of Amitābha Buddha. Second: Following the previous body seal, change only by bending the two thumbs and inserting them into the palms, with the two index fingers pressing down upon the nails of the two thumbs. The mantra is the same as the previous one used.

“Construct a water altar measuring four cubits. Place eight butter lamps and five platters of cakes and fruits; set a brazier at the center. The mantra-reciter shall face east, take cow’s milk and honey mixed together, and further take one hundred and eight pieces of *pīlu* wood (herein called the *gǔshù*, or grain-tree), each one foot long. Anoint both ends of each piece with butter and honey; after reciting the mantra once, cast one piece into the fire. In this manner, burn them until the full count of one hundred and eight is reached, reciting the mantra repeatedly throughout.”
If one performs this rite, one will immediately attain *śamatha* and extinguish the sins of the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
On the fifteenth day of every month, bathe and recite the mantra; by performing the rite as previously described, one will be reborn at will in the Land of Amitābha Buddha.

3. The Seal for Amitābha’s Protection of the Body and Boundary-Delimitation (Amitābha-huśen-jiexie-yin), Third. "Following the initial body-seal, change only the two middle fingers so that they touch the palms. Once the protection of the body and the delimitation of the boundary have been performed, one may then sit in meditation."

4. The Seated Meditation Mudrā of Amitābha, Number Four. "Join the palms. Extend the middle fingers and ring fingers of both hands straight upward, ensuring that their joints touch one another. Tuck each little finger against the back of its respective ring finger, with the tip resting upon the upper joint. Place both thumbs side by side, extending them straight upward. Bend the middle joints of the two index fingers so that their tips press down upon the tips of the thumbs. This is used for curing illnesses."

If one has an illness, construct a water mandala four cubits in size. First, perform the body mudrā and invoke the mantras of the images of Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The master sits and recites the mantra over cow’s milk one hundred and eight times, burning it in the fire. This is performed for seven days; every day it is done in this manner. One begins this rite at sunset and ceases at the first watch of the night; one resumes at the third watch of the night and ceases at dawn. Practice in this way for seven days, and the illness will be cured.

5. The Seal for the Extinction of Sins of Amitābha Buddha, Number Five. Join the wrists. Straighten the middle and ring fingers of both hands, ensuring that their joints align perfectly. Extend the two little fingers straight upward. Open the two index fingers and place them upon the backs of the middle fingers without touching them; the tips should be slightly curved. Align the two thumbs vertically, pressing their tips against the second joints of the middle fingers.

When the practitioner sits in meditation, they perform this mudrā and recite the boundary-binding mantra (*sīmābandha-mantra*), consecrating white mustard seeds, water, and fire, and placing them within the room.
When wishing to bind the boundary, one first scatters the consecrated water from the northeast corner, circling clockwise until returning to the northeast corner to rest;
next, one performs the same with the white mustard seeds as before.
Afterwards, holding fire in his hand, he circumambulated it as before. Having thus completed the boundary-binding three times, he immediately sat in meditation.

According to the methods of dhyāna-concentration, he observed and contemplated the defilements of various karmic offenses. Within that state of concentration, a sense of shame and remorse arose in his heart; he performed the seal of repentance to atone for the transgressions committed from beginningless time until the present life. Thereafter, he recited the mantra over all medicinal herbs twenty-one times; upon taking them, [the illness] was immediately cured, and all sins were extinguished. He studied True Suchness as consciousness and practiced the contemplation of the wisdom of non-arising, using these as an aid to the mantra while concurrently cultivating the path of dedication toward Bodhi.

6. The Heart-Seal of Amitābha Buddha, Number Six. "Place the three fingers from the middle finger downward of the right hand together and bend them into the palm of the left hand to grasp the thumb of the left hand. Then, press the right thumb upon the tips of the three fingers of the right hand. Straighten and spread apart the two index fingers."

Construct a mandala four cubits in size, using five colors. In the center of the mandala, place a flower seat for Amitābha Buddha; in the east, place a flower seat for Mañjuśrī, who is also named Mañjuśrī.

7. The Mañjuśrī Seal Mantra, Seventh. "Following the Vajrarāja Seal, one makes this modification: each of the two index fingers grasps the back of the upper joint of the middle finger, while the index fingers move back and forth."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ vākītanama svāhā. To the north, place the eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara upon a flower seat.
8. The Seal and Mantra of Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara, Part Eight: "The seal is the same as that of Prajñāpāramitā; the thumbs move back and forth."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ āruṇi oṃ tejoloke āḥ vijaye sarvasattvānāṃ parimocana karaya svāhā. To the south, place the flower seat of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

9. The Seal and Mantra of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Number Nine. "Interlock the right ring finger with the left ring finger. Insert the back of the left middle finger between the tips of the right index and middle fingers. The right ring finger emerges from the space between the right middle and ring fingers and enters the space between the left index and middle fingers. Hook the tips of both index fingers over the tips of the two ring fingers. Bend the two middle fingers downward to press upon the backs of the two thumbs, with their tips pointing inward. First, bend the left little finger over the back of the right ring finger; then, grasp the back of the left little finger with the right little finger. Move the thumbs back and forth."

The mantra is: "Oṃ lūcīra-mati-te ā vaṃ bha-gavate jñāna-cintā-piṇḍa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Furthermore, the Seal of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Number Ten. It is modeled after the Seal of the Buddha Amitābha’s Uṣṇīṣa below, with the sole modification that the two index fingers each grasp the tips of the middle fingers; the index fingers are slightly bent. Next, place the two thumbs side by side, covering the middle joints of the right middle fingers, and move the thumbs back and forth.

11. Another Seal of Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Eleventh. It is modeled upon the body-seal of Amitābha Buddha; the only difference is that the two middle fingers are held upright and touching each other. Next, the two index fingers are bent behind the middle fingers with their tips touching. Then, the two thumbs are placed side by side, their tips bent inward toward the edge of the second joints of the middle fingers, moving back and forth.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vajravajri ghuṭa ghuti pata pata hana hana dhaha dhaha paṭa paṭa huṃ phaṭ svāhā. One who bathes on the fifteenth day of every month and performs this rite shall immediately attain the stage of *avaivartika*.

"One should construct a water altar of four cubits using five colors. There should be five water jars—one at each of the four corners and one in the center—with a piece of raw silk, one to two feet long, tied around the neck of each jar. One should offer ten plates of food and drink, sixteen lamps, and burn aloeswood incense as an offering."
"The method for constructing the altar is the same as that for other altars. A group of four monks shall form a fellowship to perform the practice;

no more than this number may be included. All four shall wear saffron-colored *kaṣāyas*. If they are *bhadantas*, they shall wear white robes before entering to perform the ritual; furthermore, they must not wear various other colors."
One must not wear the *kāṣāya* robe while using the toilet. One may eat only non-glutinous rice, milk porridge, and fruits, but must not eat vegetables.

One should perform ritual offerings three times each day. Beginning on the eighth day of the twelfth month and continuing until the fifteenth day, once the ritual offerings are completed, one shall take water from the central jar and pour it over the crown of the head of the person receiving the dharma-transmission.
Having donned clean robes, lead [the practitioner] into the *maṇḍala* to perform offerings; when the rites are completed, conclude them and disperse from the *maṇḍala*.
"If one performs this rite, it will be like sunlight shining upon snow, whereby all transgressions are extinguished, and after the end of life, one will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha."
If a woman performs this rite, after the end of her life she will be transformed into a man and be reborn in that land.

This is the Heart-Seal Dharma; the Upālidhaya Dharma—here translated as the "Dharma of the Small Mind"—is the dharma-gate through which Amitābha Buddha attained enlightenment. One who practices it shall realize entry into the stage of non-retrogression.
"Regarding the scattering of leftover food as an offering, those who receive the Dharma should not eat it. 12.

The Crown Seal of Amitābha Buddha, Number Twelve. Following the Buddha’s Sword Seal, change only by interlacing the two middle fingers and extending their middle joints straight; this is the Crown Seal."

When using this to treat illness, construct a water mandala two cubits in size, place an image of Amitābha Buddha within it, and set up a brazier to burn agarwood, sandalwood, and frankincense mixed together.
The patient sits facing west with palms joined.
The mantra-reciter sits facing east and, circling incense around the patient's head, casts the mantra into the fire.
Thus, perform this one hundred and eight times, three times each day; if the patient recollects the Buddha with a sincere mind, the illness will be immediately cured.
This is the *uṣṇīṣa* dharma of Amitābha Buddha.

13. The Mudrā of Amitābha Buddha’s Wheel. Regarding the thirteenth mudrā of Amitābha Buddha: "With both hands, each thumb presses against the tip of the ring finger; the right hand rests upon the left, held at the heart."
If one wishes to preach the Dharma or engage in doctrinal debate, by performing this rite daily, all will rejoice, and upon death, one shall be reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha.

If one seeks wealth, food, drink, or other such things, construct a water mandala four cubits in size and place an image of Amitābha Buddha at its center. Arrange five plates of food—one at the center of the mandala and one in each of the four directions. The mantra-practitioner should face east and perform this rite three times a day for five days. The practitioner’s clothing must be entirely yellow and no other color is permitted; thus, whatever is sought shall be fulfilled as desired.

"Furthermore, if a person has a feverish illness, one should recite the mantra twenty-one times over a five-colored thread, tie twenty-one knots, and fasten it around the patient's neck. While the patient recites the name of Amitābha Buddha, the mantra-master holds an incense burner in hand and makes offerings and praises to the Buddhas of the ten directions; the illness will then be cured immediately."

"If one wishes to cause the eight classes of spirits, devas, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajras to rejoice, one should construct a water mandala four cubits in size. The mantra-practitioner must maintain ritual purity; men and women must not touch one another. At the center of the mandala, place an image of Amitābha Buddha facing west. Set out eight plates of food and twenty-eight lamps. Place a single water jar in the center. Before the Buddha, set up a brazier and cast *sumana* flowers into the fire once for each recitation of the mantra, repeating this one hundred and eight times. If one performs this rite with a mind of impartial compassion for the sake of all sentient beings, divine efficacy will be attained and all will be filled with joy."

"If one daily performs various offerings to Amitābha Buddha, recites the mantra one hundred thousand times, and practices the mudrā rites, one shall immediately attain the extinction of sins and, at the end of life, be reborn in that land."

Furthermore, if one wishes to be born in that land, one should also mold one hundred thousand clay images of Amitābha Buddha to extinguish transgressions; upon death, one will be reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha.
"When making offerings day after day, one should use a rosary made of gold—if that is unavailable, use silver;
if silver is unavailable, use red copper;
if red copper is unavailable, use crystal—consisting of one hundred and eight beads—or, if those are unavailable, fifty-four."
Regarding the "further none" [beads], there are forty-two;

regarding the "further none," there are twenty-one—when counting these beads while reciting the mantra, one takes the beads to represent the ten *pāramitās*, and taking the mindfulness of the Buddha and the recitation of the mantra as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When making offerings to Amitābha Buddha, one should use the aforementioned materials and the like to fashion the beads; no other materials are permitted.
If one uses various other miscellaneous substances, none of them will produce any efficacious results.
Among these, the most excellent are rosaries made of crystal for those who recite mantras; all their transgressions will be extinguished.
Just as the beads are transparent and radiant, so too shall one's own body become.
This crystal bead is universally applicable for the rites of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, Devas, and others. **14.

The Dharma Seal for Healing Illness According to Amitābha Buddha** First, turn the left hand upward with the four fingers bent; then cover the left hand with the right hand, likewise bending the four fingers of the right hand. Hook the two hands together firmly so that the knuckles of both fists rest against the palms, and extend both thumbs straight upward.

This is the Single Dharma Seal that subdues all malevolent spirits and ghosts; if there is anyone who is ill, one should apply this seal, and their illness will be immediately cured. All such seals are accompanied by the recitation of the heart-mantra.
The Buddha Spoke on the Chapter of the Ritual for Making Rosaries. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and all sons and daughters of good family:

"You should resolve to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*, mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha, and the recitation and upholding of my secret dharma-treasury of the Samādhi Dhāraṇī and Divine Seal Mantras. Those who wish to achieve success in rebirth in that land and to collectively protect and mindfully sustain all sentient beings, and who further desire to practice asceticism, should wholeheartedly receive and uphold [this teaching], making offerings daily, with single-minded devotion, and not allowing the mind to wander toward other objects."

Those who practice by reciting sutras, mindfulness of the Buddha, or holding mantras must each hold a rosary in their hand. This is according to the instructions for the Samādhi of Amitābha Buddha, and furthermore, as prescribed in all such dhāraṇīs and the teachings of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and Devas; the number [of beads] must fully possess the required characteristics.
As for their characteristics, there are four kinds. What are the four?
First, gold; second, silver; third, red copper; and fourth, crystal.
The number of beads shall be one hundred and eight; however, fifty-four, forty-two, or twenty-one may also be used appropriately.

If practitioners use such precious objects as rosaries to perform finger-counting, recite mantras, recite sutras, or practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they shall attain the fulfillment of the merits of the ten *pāramitās* and realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in their present bodies.
Among these four kinds, crystal is the foremost.

This crystal possesses incomparable radiance, is pure and free from blemish, and its wondrous color is vast and expansive; because it has attained the vow for the Bodhi of a Buddha, it penetrates that land with perfect clarity, appearing exactly like the characteristic of a jewel.
For this reason, it is called "supreme.

By holding its beads and counting them, one can eliminate the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, all karmic obstructions, and all retributive obstructions of the practitioner who recites the mantra; no evil karma can defile them, for they are illuminated by the light of the bead and do not undergo the characteristics of form.
"If a person constantly practices the recollection of the Buddha, they should use *kataka* seeds as their rosary;
if one wishes to recite mantras for the purpose of upholding them, they should use the four types of precious gems mentioned before as their rosary;
if one performs the ritual methods of a Bodhisattva mantra, they should use *bodhi* seeds as their rosary, or if these are unavailable, they may use lotus seeds in their stead."
If one performs the activities of the Vajra Fire-Head, one should use beads of the color of flesh as a rosary.
These types of rosaries all accord with the characteristics of the Dharma; therefore, by means of this method, I shall protect and mindfully sustain those in the world who uphold the Dharma.

When all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, vajrapāṇis, devas, and others in this assembly heard the Buddha’s teaching on the method of the rosary, they were all filled with joy and simultaneously exclaimed, "Excellent!"
The Buddha said:

"If a person wishes to fashion a rosary according to the characteristics of the Dharma, they should first summon a bead-maker; do not bargain over the price, but ensure that the work is exquisite and fine.

All such precious materials must never have been used before; each and every one must be transparent inside and out, free from cracks or defects, perfectly round, pure, and bright, with the size being as one desires."

First, have the bead-maker receive the Eightfold Precepts, bathe with fragrant water, and don new, clean robes; then provide him with protection for his person. Adorn a ritual site, hanging up various banners and flowers, and prepare a small altar with scented mud. Daily, offer incense and flowers as worship, and also set out one or two trays of cakes and fruit as offerings. Furthermore, separately light seven lamps each night, and fashion the beads into one hundred and eight.

Once the beads have been fashioned, one further makes a single golden bead to serve as the mother-bead, and additionally fashions ten separate silver beads to serve as the marker-beads. This is called the complete and perfect fulfillment of the formal characteristics of the Triple Gem; it enables the practitioner, when counting these beads, to constantly receive the empowerment and protective mindfulness of the Triple Gem—namely, the Buddha-gem, the Dharma-gem, and the Sangha-gem.
Based on these proofs, why worry that one will not be reborn in the Western Pure Land?

"Once this bead has been fashioned, sprinkle it within this altar with various kinds of scented water; furthermore, place seven trays of food and light twenty-one lamps. Invite the Buddhas, Prajñāpāramitā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and all the devas, and offer worship with reverent petitions. Because of the majestic spiritual power of the Triple Gem, all such diverse ritual acts will possess efficacy. Thereafter, carry it with you and keep it ready for use; then all evils will not defile you, and all ghosts and spirits will collectively revere and fear you."
Therefore, the power of merit is fully accomplished and fulfilled; this is called the secret efficacy of the rosary.
Within the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of the Amitābha Buddha-dhāraṇī seal-mantra, this essential core has been briefly extracted, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
"The above concludes the Dharma of Amitābha Buddha; if one practices according to this teaching, the merit shall be infinite."

The Great Cakra-Vajra Dhāraṇī. The Great Cakra-Vajra Dhāraṇī: "Namaḥ samantabhadraye te | Tathāgatāya | Oṃ vīra vīra mahācakravartine | Sata sata | Sara sara | Tara tara | Vidamane | Samparśane | Tarame ti | Siddhāgari-tre | Svāhā. Regarding the pronunciation of the *zhù* (inserted) syllables, one should read them according to the rules for the *zhù* sounds.
"Where a double-consonant cluster is marked with a note, the upper character must be pronounced as a half-syllable and read in conjunction with the sound of the lower character.

Where a half-syllable is marked, it must be pronounced as a fragmentary sound. "If one recites this dhāraṇī twenty-one times, one shall immediately enter all maṇḍalas—herein referred to as *tán* (altars)—and whatever one undertakes shall be accomplished."

When reciting mantras, there are various methods of mudrās, such as the body-seal (*kāyamudrā*) and others; if one performs hand-mudrās and recites the various mantra rites, it is easy to achieve efficacious results.
However, those who have not yet entered the consecration mandala (*abhiṣekamaṇḍala*) must not arbitrarily perform any hand-mudrās.
"If a person recites this dhāraṇī, they are as if having entered the maṇḍala.
To perform mudrās and ritual applications [without this] is to fail in the practice and constitutes stealing the Dharma.

The Chapter on the Dharma Characteristics of the Efficacy of the Vajra, spoken by the Buddha. (In the language of Tang: *Jingangchu*). At that time, the Buddha was at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, preaching in a great assembly the secret treasury of all dhāraṇīs.
Then the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

"World-Honored One, Tathāgata, now that you have preached this subtle, wondrous, and precious Dharma in this assembly, our hearts are filled with great joy; we have attained what we have never experienced before.
All these devas of the desire realm, Māra Pāpīyān, as well as the ghosts and spirits, are without exception struck with awe and trembling."

We reflect that the minds and intentions of the various māras are truly difficult to fathom; whether they deceive or rebel, if we do not take precautions in advance, we fear they will treat our various Buddha-dharmas with contempt.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to bring forth an inconceivable and unfathomable Dharma; by this, I shall be able to protect and uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, subdue all Māras, and prevent them and their like from causing violent chaos throughout the worlds.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Then, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha suddenly caused a three-pronged *vajra* to emerge from the crown of his head, its color like the radiance of gold.
At the moment of his emergence, the great trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the spirits and ghosts seated there all collapsed at once.
The Buddha said:
"Spirits and ghosts!..."

"Do not be afraid. Because I, Vajragarbha, possess such sovereign supernatural powers and great majesty, I have manifested these unfathomable signs; by this, I shall assist and protect my True Dharma."

I now grant my approval and further entrust these seven grains of the true *śarīra* relics of past Buddhas to you, Bodhisattva, so that they may be concealed within it. This shall serve as a token of faith for the recognition of its characteristics and for its protection, guarding against the arrogance of various non-Buddhists, those of the desire realm, and the celestial Māras. For this reason, you are named Mahāvajra; thus, you shall always be able to attend at my side with majesty and repel all demonic activities.

Since there is benefit therein, I further wish that those who uphold my Dharma, as well as those who uphold the dhāraṇī methods of Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and devas, shall all fully possess the characteristics of the Dharma and remain constantly prepared.
The great assembly seated before him all exclaimed, "Excellent!

Regarding the *vajra* and the ritual for merit: "If a person wishes to fashion a *vajra*, they should first take materials of five colors, such as gold, none of which have previously been used to make vessels."
What are the five colors?
First, gold; second, silver; third, red copper; fourth, high-carbon steel (vimala-iron); and fifth, tin.
These are combined and fashioned into the form of a *vajra*.
If these five kinds are unavailable, one may also use the heartwood of the *pīlu* (thunder-fruit) tree.
Furthermore, before fashioning the *vajra*, one must first pre-consecrate objects such as gold or copper by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ mahākāra nāthakubhara svāhā. When the recitation of the mantra is finished, one should act at the time when the moon is about to be eclipsed. First, on the fourteenth day—if such an auspicious day as this cannot be obtained, one should take the thirteenth day of the eighth month, which is likewise an auspicious day—on that morning, one should send the artisan in advance to observe the fast and precepts (upavāsa), bathe with fragrant water, and put on new, clean clothes; the same applies to the one who wishes to invite him to serve as the Vajradhara master.

Once both have been thoroughly cleansed, they are prepared in advance by being repaired and groomed; they are then established in a pure location to perform the ritual for protecting the body and binding the boundary (*rakṣā-sīmābandha*).

On the morning of the fifteenth day, the artisan is again sent to bathe them with fragrant water and dress them in new, clean garments, after which the rituals for protecting the artisan and protecting oneself are performed.

Within the site of practice (maṇḍala), construct a water altar and invite the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā, the great Bodhisattvas, the Vajras, the devas, and others; furthermore, invite one, two, or seven grains of śarīra and place them within that altar.
On the eastern side of the altar, one should fashion a smelting furnace with cow dung mud; next, summon the Fire Deity (Agni) and command him to guard the furnace.
The artisan faces west, while the mantra-reciter himself stands on the western side of the altar, facing directly east, spreading grass as a seat and sitting in the half-lotus posture (hukuei).

Place seven plates of food and drink within the mandala, and set one additional plate of food beside the incense burner. Perform the ritual of protection as usual, and then invite the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā, the various great bodhisattvas, the Vajras, and the devas.

Furthermore, one should offer various kinds of incense, flowers, and ritual seals to the Triple Gem three or seven times; thereafter, one may proceed with the casting, ensuring it is completed in a single pour without allowing for any flaws or defects.
If it is complete from top to bottom, straight, upright, and level, without any deficiency or flaw, this is called the "One Jewel," which is the most preeminent.
If it cannot be cast successfully on the first attempt, then even if one were to recast it later, it would ultimately be useless.

Such a person is likewise unfit to practice my secret treasury of Dharma-gates; even if they should force its application, they will constantly encounter demonic obstacles, achieve nothing, and instead bring calamity upon themselves.

"This vajra should weigh eight *liang*, be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length—measured by the transverse fingers—and have three prongs at both ends; there is also a five-pronged version. This five-pronged one is called the 'Great Vajra' and must be used for lifelong observance by those who maintain the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
If one lacks moral discipline, one must not hold or use the five-pronged version, as it will harm the body."

"These *vajras* must all be made circular at the waist, resembling the shape of a betel nut, with a hollow in the middle large enough to hold about one handful. They must be carved and engraved with all one's strength, seeking only perfection and avoiding anything coarse or crude; once finished and polished, they are to be adorned with pure gold."

At the very center of the waist, a square opening is to be made for the insertion of the śarīra; the ritual application, its form, and the underlying conditions are identical to those of the current model. The practitioner should provide instructions to ensure it is well-crafted, making it with diligent care so that it is prepared without negligence.
"When fashioning the pestle, the chanting of mantras must not cease and the incense smoke must not be interrupted.
As for the artisan's fee, one may demand whatever amount one wishes and need not pay it back; furthermore, the work must be completely finished on that very day."
Upon the completion of the *vajra*, the artisan reports to the mantra-practitioner, saying:
"The mallet is finished.
The practitioner then takes a censer and a casket made of the seven precious gems in his hands, circumambulates the ritual site to the right, and offers this praise:
"The Dharma-treasures of the Buddhas of the ten directions have been accomplished.

With these words, he went forth to welcome the ritual mace with Brahma-sounds; arriving at the side of the incense burner, he scattered various fragrant flowers, performed rites of praise, and reverently entreated it with earnest devotion.
The artisan knelt down and, with both hands, placed [the object] into the seven-jeweled casket held in the practitioner's hand.
Having done so, the artisan prostrated in thanks and said:
"In many respects it was not according to the Dharma; its polishing and adornment were all unsatisfactory. I offer this with joy, wishing that all my transgressions may be extinguished."
The mantra-master replied:
"It is extraordinary and most exquisite; its form is dignified and in accordance with the Dharma, its marks are fully complete, and it is supreme and peerless.

I am truly filled with shame and remorse. I pray that you may eliminate the karmic obstacles of the three actions of this artisan from past lives, so that in birth after birth he may encounter the Buddha and participate in the assemblies of the Dharma."
Having spoken thus, the artisan again prostrated and made vows, saying: “... [and so forth] ... burning incense and joining his palms, he requested the relics.

The mantra-master then rose, circumambulated the altar three times, returned to his original seat, and stood to one side. He then addressed all the Buddhas of the ten directions, Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattvas, the Vajras, the Devas, and others, saying: “... [and so forth].”

Again perform rites of offering with incense and flowers, weeping and shedding tears like rain; take a pinch of camphor and place it within the cavity at the waist of the Vajra, and after that, having taken the śarīra and placed it within the cavity at the waist of the Vajra, once more perform rites of offering with incense and flowers.
Having completed the offerings, he again raised the vajra, circumambulated the maṇḍala clockwise, and went to where the artisan was; kneeling on the ground, he received it and gave it to the artisan.
The artisan, with a sincere mind, treasured it, burned incense, made offerings, and prostrated; he then held the vajra with both hands and closed its opening until it was perfectly secure.
When the task of nailing it shut is completed, [the relic] is returned and offered with both hands to the mantra-master.

The mantra-master prostrates, receives it, and rises; the artisan then performs three more prostrations, takes up the reliquary casket, and makes vows from both heart and mouth, saying: "... and so forth.

The practitioner, holding the precious reliquary containing the śarīra in his hands, circumambulates the maṇḍala three times to the right; having performed the circumambulation, he returns to his original position, completes further offerings with various incenses, flowers, and the performance of mudrās, and then dismisses the artisan.

"Subsequently, he again took the precious reliquary containing the śarīra back to the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa). He personally observed the signs until nightfall, when he lit twenty-one lamps within the altar, arranging them as he pleased, and offered cakes, fruits, and various kinds of incense and flowers as offerings."
When the ritual is completed, the mantra-master sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) on the western side of the mandala.
Holding a vajra in his right hand and counting the beads with his left, he must recite the mantra with all his might and single-minded devotion until three types of radiant signs appear.
What are the three signs?
First, the vajra naturally becomes warm; second, smoke issues forth; third, it emits great radiance.

If the sign of heat appears, the practitioner who wields the vajra will naturally cause all yakṣas, rākṣasas, and human beings to become of one mind in their respectful devotion toward him as if he were a Buddha.
If the sign of smoke appears, the practitioner who wields the vajra will naturally find that wherever he goes there is no obstacle whatsoever, nor shall he suffer from illness.

If the sign of emitting light appears, he will obtain the spontaneous protection of all mantra-deities; the practitioner will be constantly revered by all devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, ghosts, spirits, humans, and non-humans, and among all classes of sentient beings, from the Buddhas downward, he shall be ranked as peerless in six respects.
"However, all those who are able to recite these mantras shall achieve the most supreme and efficacious results, due to the majestic spiritual power of the Vajra-bāzra mace."

"Later, if you wish to employ the vajra, hold the mallet according to the ritual rules. Before using it, recite the Great Heart Mantra of Cundī seven times. Then, using this mallet according to the method for protecting the body, subsequently perform the great boundary-binding rite (mahā-sīmābandha)."
At all times, one must make it a constant rule to protect purity with diligent care; only then will the ritual acts performed for the sake of the Dharma be efficacious.
When treating illness using the *vajra*, one must not exceed the proper limits and must maintain purity at all times.
If used according to the Dharma, the mantra-practitioner’s person will always remain well and secure.
The explanation of the functional efficacy of the *vajra* dharmas is hereby concluded.

*The Mahācitta Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. This *Mahācitta Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* has thirteen seals and nine mantras.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, surrounded before and behind by twelve hundred and fifty arhats, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya great bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others, both human and non-human.
At that time, Brahmā and the great assembly addressed one another, saying:
"We now wish to hear of the merits of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Then the entire assembly was filled with great joy and praised the Brahmā King, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the Brahma King rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now wish with a sincere heart to hear of the inconceivable merit of the *prajñāpāramitā*. I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain to me the inconceivable merit of the mantra-seal (*dhāraṇīmudrā*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Brahma King:
"I have briefly explained the dhāraṇīs and mudrās among the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas; listen attentively, listen attentively! I shall now explain their merits for you."
Just as Mount Sumeru is the king among all mountains, so too is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) the sovereign among all forms of śamatha.
Just as the king of mountains, Sumeru, cannot be shaken by the fierce winds from the four directions; [so too is the perfection of wisdom unshakable].
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise; if one relies upon the Prajñāpāramitā, one will attain firm abiding in śamatha, such that the devas, Māras, and others cannot cause one to waver.
Just as the great ocean is able to contain all streams, so too is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); it likewise is able to contain all Buddha-dharmas.

If one practices according to this teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, one immediately attains the knowledge of abiding in one's abode, whereby one knows that in the past, "I" was born in this place from that place due to those actions.

If one practices according to this teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, one shall immediately eliminate the sins of the three poisons; in every place of rebirth, one shall not hear evil teachings; one shall obtain a body as upright and beautiful as gold, wearing a celestial crown upon the head; one shall be free from avarice and be born among the Kṣatriyas or Brāhmaṇas; all the great assemblies in every gathering shall follow and attend one; one shall not be born in the three miserable realms or within the hells; one shall be reborn at will in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions; in one’s present life, one shall immediately attain the four fearlessnesses and excel above all others in every assembly.
If one can perform this rite daily, in this very life one will realize that all dharmas are without obstruction and attain *śamatha*.
"If a person wishes to attain *śamatha*, they should practice according to the method of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, making offerings daily and performing mudrās while practicing seated meditation."

If one sits in a śmaśāna or among burial mounds beside a corpse, and practices the contemplation of impurity, the contemplation of arising and ceasing, up to the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, and the contemplation of the skillful means of the elements, one will immediately attain śamatha.
If one practices *śamatha* for three years, the light of the formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*) will enter the body, and one will immediately know all matters within the three realms (*tridhātu*).

During these three years, one should eat on one day and abstain from food on the next. On days when one does not eat, one may take medicinal herbs; if one does not take medicinal herbs, it is best to practice the cultivation of vital energy (*vāyu*). If one maintains this alternate-day fasting for the full three years, one will attain *śamatha*.

If one performs this rite daily, burning *sugandhaka* incense and reciting the mantra until it reaches one hundred thousand repetitions, one will attain the *śamatha* of the Great Cloud, the *śamatha* of Compassion, the *śamatha* of the Great Thunderous Sound, the *śamatha* of Lightning Radiance, and the *śamatha* of Blazing Fire.
If one performs various offerings such as mudrās and dhāraṇīs every day, transgressions will be extinguished and one will attain śamatha;
if sentient beings with heavy karmic offenses do not perform various offerings such as mudrās and dhāraṇīs every day, their transgressions will not be extinguished and they will not attain śamatha.
Therefore, I now set forth this expedient means, desiring that all may joyfully hear it so that their vows may be fulfilled.

Regarding the ritual for painting an image of the Great Prajñāpāramitā: "To paint an image of the Bodhisattva of the Great Prajñā, one should select the fifteenth day of the eighth month. Use two or three pieces of fine, high-quality silk as desired; the height and width must be proportionate."

Having completed the water mandala within the vihāra, one recites the Great Prajñāpāramitā mantra over it. Once the silk has been consecrated one hundred and eight times, invite a painter of the finest skill and have him receive the eight precepts. He shall then go once to the toilet and bathe once, put on fresh, clean garments, and be granted a protection-seal.
In the pigments, use a mixture of *kunkuma* (frankincense) and the resin of *guggulu* (bdellium), but do not use glue.

On the altar, scatter flowers of various colors at the three periods of each day, burn aloeswood incense, and recite mantras to make offerings to the Bodhisattva. At night, separately light seven lamps; only then may you paint the Bodhisattva.

As for the body of that bodhisattva, excluding the celestial crown, his height is one cubit—one cubit being equal to one *vitasti* (span) of the Buddha. His entire body is white in color, and he has three eyes on his face; his appearance resembles that of a celestial maiden (*devī*), and his features are as upright and beautiful as those of a bodhisattva. Seated cross-legged upon a lion throne, he wears a celestial crown from which emanates a light like that of a winnowing basket; in his ears he wears earrings of genuine jewels, and around his neck he wears a necklace of the seven precious gems, while his two arms are bent.

The left arm is bent at the elbow and rests against the chest; the left hand is turned upward with the five fingers extended, and within the palm is depicted a casket of the seven precious gems, containing the twelve divisions of the scriptures—namely, the Prajñāpāramitā-piṭaka.
The right hand hangs down over the right knee with the five fingers extended; this is the Bodhisattva’s gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*).

On the Bodhisattva’s body he wears fine gauze and silk brocades, embroidered with a *kacchāhika* (a loincloth). Below the waist he wears a skirt of morning-glory cloth (*prabhāta-śāṭī*), upon which is painted a yellow floral undergarment. Celestial garments (*divyavastra*) are draped over his two arms, crossing at the armpits and emerging at both ends, both directed upward and slightly curved as if in the motion of fluttering. On both wrists, he wears rings and bracelets.

"On the right side of the Bodhisattva is seated the Brahmā-deva King; his entire body is white in color, he wears jeweled earrings, and around his neck he wears a necklace of seven precious gems, standing upon a woolen rug."
His right arm is bent over his shoulder, holding a white fly-whisk;
his left arm is extended, holding a water pitcher.
From the waist down, he wears a skirt of *chaoxia* silk, with his garments adorned with fine gauze, brocade, and embroidery.

The body of that Brahmā deity is draped in a purple kāṣāya, wears a flower crown upon his head, and emits a light like that of a winnowing basket; his hands, feet, and wrists are all adorned with jeweled bracelets.
To the left of the Bodhisattva is seated Śakra-devendra, his entire body white in color, wearing jeweled earrings and a necklace of seven precious gems around his neck, standing upon a woolen rug.
The right arm is bent upward toward the shoulder, holding a white whisk (*śveta-vālavyajana*).

The left arm is also bent, with the elbow pointing to the left; the palm faces the abdomen and is turned upward, firmly grasping a *vajra* in its center. The head of the *vajra* points outward, and it is encircled by flames.

The image of Śakra wears a skirt of *chaoxia* silk from the waist down; his garments are adorned with fine gauze, brocade, and embroidery, draped with celestial robes (*devavastra*). He wears a flower crown upon his head, which emits a radiance like that of a winnowing basket, and his wrists and ankles are all encircled by jeweled bracelets.
"On both sides above the Bodhisattva’s radiance, paint one Srotāpanna deity on each, scattering various flowers and bearing necklaces as offerings.

Beneath the seat of the image, paint incense burners and implements for worship; on the left and right sides of these offering implements, paint eight images of Śrīdevīs (Eight King Spirits) arranged accordingly."

The colors of these spirit-kings were blue, yellow, red, and white, each being a single color; their faces bore expressions of fierce wrath. Each spirit-king wore fine armor of gold and silver in five colors and stood with majestic dignity upon stones of five colors, each grasping a weapon.

"Next, below on the right side, paint an image of a mantra-reciter (dhāraṇī-vidyādhara) sitting in the *hu-kuei* (half-kneeling) posture, holding an incense burner with both hands in offering; his face is turned upward as if gazing up at the venerable countenance of the Bodhisattva."

"Once the image has been painted, one should establish a *bodhimaṇḍa*, hanging silken banners and canopies, and adorning it with various ornaments such as jewel bells and pendants. Having smeared the ground with fragrant mud, one should construct a water altar four cubits in length and breadth, and invite the Bodhisattva to be enshrined upon the altar."

The image faces west while the mantra-practitioner faces east; every day, having bathed in fragrant water to become pure and donned fresh, clean robes, he enters the maṇḍala, performs the rites of self-protection and boundary-binding, recites the mantras, and makes various offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.

One may recite the mantra up to one hundred thousand times, performing separate repentances from time to time to extinguish all past karmic obstacles of the body; thereafter, when performing the ritual applications while reciting the mantra, various efficacious results will be attained.
The method for painting the image is concluded; next, the methods for mudrās are explained. 1.

The Prajñā-kāya Mudrā (First) Join the two forearms together with the palms facing outward. Then, bend the tips of the index, middle, and ring fingers of both hands so that they touch one another. The two little fingers and the two thumbs should each be held straight and extended upward, spread apart.
2. Prajñā-āgama-mudrā. Second: Following the previous body-mudrā, change only this: bring the two thumbs slightly closer together and bend them evenly downward; this is the Bodhisattva-āgama-mudrā.

3. The Seal for Sending the Bodhisattva Away (Bodhisattva-gamana-mudrā), Third. "If one wishes to send the Bodhisattva away, follow the seal previously described; however, change the two thumbs that were formerly bent so that they are slightly spread apart until they reach their maximum extent. This is the seal for sending the Bodhisattva away."
4. The Heart-Seal of Prajñā, Fourth: "As before, simply change it so that the right thumb presses against the index finger; this is the Heart-Seal of Prajñā."
5. The Great Heart Seal of Prajñā, Fifth: "In accordance with the previous [instructions], simply change it so that the left thumb is bent downward; this is the Great Heart Seal of Prajñā."

6. The Prajñā-Head Mudrā (Sixth) "According to the previous [instructions], simply change [the position] by holding the two thumbs upright side-by-side, separated from the index fingers by a distance of about one finger-width; this is the Prajñā-Head Mudrā."

7. The Mudrā for Binding Māra through Prajñā. Seventh: "In accordance with the previous [instructions], simply change the method so that both thumbs each grasp the index fingers; this is the mudrā for binding Māra."
If used for self-protection, no demons or malevolent spirits shall be able to disturb or harass one.

These seven seals are not to be released before a Bodhisattva; after reciting the subsequent Great Heart Mantra, they remove the evil obstructions of the three karmas within the human body and are also employed for the purpose of meditative concentration.

8. The Seal of Subduing Māra through Prajñā, Number Eight: "Sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). First, extend the five fingers of the right hand upward upon the right knee; then, extend the five fingers of the left hand upward as well, placing the side of the little finger horizontally below the navel. This is called the Seal of Subduing Māra."

9. The Ninth Seal of Prajñā-Śamatha First, extend the five fingers of the left hand below the navel. Then, form a fist with the four fingers of the right hand and place it palm-upward within the left palm. With the two thumbs held upright and joined at their tips—these two seals constitute the Seal of Prajñā-Śamatha; they are employed when entering Śamatha to subdue Māra.

10. The Seal of the Prajñā-Śamatha Four Dhyānas, Number Ten. "First, turn the right hand upward and extend the five fingers over the right knee. Then, erect the four fingers of the left hand and bend the thumb into the palm. Next, bend the elbow and straighten the arm, joining the palms behind the back. Within this palm lies the treasury of the Prajñā of all Buddha-dharmas; this is the seal of the Prajñā-Śamatha Four Dhyānas."

11. The Seal of the Prajñā Repentance (Prajñā-paścattāpa-mudrā), Number Eleven: "First, extend the four fingers of the right hand and turn the palm forward; bend the thumb so that it rests within the palm. Then, with the thumb of the left hand, hook it with the right thumb, and further interlace the four fingers of the left hand over the back of the right palm. This is the seal of repentance."

"If there are practitioners who daily perform this seal-method and recite the mantra, they will be able to eliminate all four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes; sins as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will all be extinguished, they will be reborn at will in the pure lands of the ten directions, and draw near to Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

12. The Seal and Mantra of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Prajñā (Prajñā-akṣaya-garbha-mudrā-mantra). The twelfth [chapter], also known as the Eye of Prajñā, the Heart of the Vajra-prajñā, and the Root of Prajñā. [Method: With both thumbs, pinch the tips of the two little fingers. Bend the two little fingers flatly; the lower and middle joints of the two hands should be pressed back-to-back. The two middle fingers and the two ring fingers should each be pressed back-to-back, held straight up, and the two index fingers bent so that their tips touch at the middle joints with their backs joined, aligned with the two little fingers. Form the hands like a scripture treasury placed upon a high seat, and hold them against the heart.
When reciting the mantra, one should focus the mind with single-minded concentration, visualizing that all the *piṭakas* emerge from the seal and enter entirely into the heart.
The *Prajñā-akṣaya-garbha-dhāraṇī-mantra* is as follows: *Namo bhagavate prajñāpāramitāye | Oṃ liri kiṭi citi śrī śūradhā viśaye svāhā.* The Buddha said:
"This dhāraṇī-mudrā has four names:
first, it is named the Inexhaustible Treasury of Prajñā; second, it is named the Eye of Prajñā; third, it is named the Root of Prajñā; and fourth, it is named the Heart of Vajra-prajñā."

This dhāraṇī-seal possesses great merit; if one can receive and maintain it according to the Dharma with a sincere mind and recite it even once, it gives rise to eighteen thousand sūtra-piṭakas. Furthermore, from each of those individual sūtra-piṭakas, twenty-five thousand sūtras are produced; from each of those individual sūtras, one million sūtra-piṭakas are produced; and from each of those individual sūtras, immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, billions, nayutas, and asaṃkhyeyas of sūtra-piṭakas are produced. In this manner, they continue to be produced in succession until immeasurable and inexhaustible sūtra-piṭakas arise, such that the titles, phrases, names, and meanings of the resulting scriptures are each distinct and never redundant.
In this way, it gives rise to the inexhaustible in every thought-moment; therefore, it is called the "Dhāraṇī-Seal of the Inexhaustible Treasury.

This dhāraṇī-seal is the ancestral source of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and the mother of all Prajñāpāramitās. It is constantly worshipped, revered, and praised by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future.

If good sons or good daughters, with a sincere mind, copy, read, recite, and practice according to the teaching, all their heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges-sand kalpas will be completely extinguished without remainder in a mere instant.

If I were to dwell for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas praising all the merits of this dhāraṇī-mudrā, I would still not reach the end; how much less could any other person praise it exhaustively?
"If one wishes to practice the Prajñāpāramitā, one should observe the one-meal fast and precepts, bathe with fragrant water, put on new and clean garments, and enter the place of practice."
One must first recite this dhāraṇī and form this mudrā one million times; thereafter, when practicing other Prajñāpāramitā methods, they will certainly achieve accomplishment.
Therefore, it is called the root of Prajñā.
This dhāraṇī-seal can fully illuminate all dharmas of the Prajñāpāramitā; thus, it is named the Eye of Prajñāpāramitā.

This dhāraṇī-seal can completely destroy all obstacles and can sustain all the merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; thus, it is named the Vajra-Prajñā-Hṛdaya. (Translated by the Dharma Master Raśmiśrī.)

13. The Seal of the Prajñā Messenger (Prajñādūta-mudrā), Number Thirteen. First, employ the Prajñā protection for the body; next, employ the Kuntali method for protection. "First, turn both hands palms upward. Then, hook the two ring fingers together. Bend the two middle fingers and the two little fingers toward the palms respectively. Extend the two index fingers upright so that their tips touch one another. Also, extend the two thumbs upright and attach them to the sides of the index fingers, pressing against the middle joints of the index fingers. By moving the two thumbs back and forth, one treats all illnesses."

“Svāhā! Fifteen. The Buddha said:

If there are men or women who can recite and uphold this mantra, and desire to seek wisdom or seek the eradication of grave offenses, they shall immediately attain wisdom and their grave offenses shall be instantly extinguished.
The Buddha’s words are sincere and free from falsehood. At dawn, cleanse the mouth with *yācī* twigs;

having rinsed the mouth thoroughly, before an image of the Buddha, with reverent single-mindedness, join the palms and fix the mind upon it. Burn various famous incenses, scatter all manner of exquisite flowers, and with a sincere heart, prostrate, kneel on the ground, and recite this mantra twenty-one times. Furthermore, until the time for the midday meal, do not engage in miscellaneous conversation with others. Then, go to a secluded and quiet place, where in a single day you shall be able to recite five hundred verses of scripture.
In this way, after one, two, or three seven-day periods, there will be no lack of efficacy, except in cases where one lacks a sincere heart.
If one wishes to read and recite any of the sūtras, one must first recite this dhāraṇī; one will then immediately attain the power of mindfulness and non-forgetfulness.
For the seal, use the seal of the four dhyānas of śamatha.
