If one recites this one hundred thousand times up to one million times, there will be no lack of efficacy, except in cases where the mind is not sincere.
18. The *Prajñā-śravaṇa-dhāraṇī* (The Dhāraṇī for Hearing and Retaining the Perfection of Wisdom) The mantra says:
*Namo bhagavate prajñāpāramitāyai | tadyathā | śrīye śrīye śrīye śrīye-si svāhā.* 19. The *Prajñā-laghu-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī* (The Minor Heart Dhāraṇī of the Perfection of Wisdom) The mantra says:

“*Tadyathā | Śrīye | Śrīye | Śrī śṭhā svāhā* ||” If a mantra-practitioner wishes to cure a disease, having first performed the self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*), he should construct a water-maṇḍala four cubits in size beside the patient. Once it is fully adorned, having arranged various incenses and flowers, lit forty-nine lamps, and set out various foods and drinks, he should hold an incense burner in his hand, burn incense, and circumambulate to the right. Having completed the offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and spirits of the ten directions, he places the incense burner at the center of the maṇḍala. Sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) on a clean and pure spot, facing directly east—or facing north is also permissible.

Next, having offered burnt offerings of ghee, honey, sesame seeds, rice grains, flowers, and incense, one should next form the Prajñā-body mudrā and recite the aforementioned Great Mantra twenty-one times while contemplating emptiness in the mind—meaning that all phenomena are without marks—and then shoot the breath from one’s mouth at the patient’s body; after seven or twenty-one such applications, the illness will be cured.
If this rite does not effect a cure after being performed once, perform it three times daily and it will surely be cured.

Regarding the food, drink, cakes, and fruits used for the altar, these must be replaced with fresh ones every day; the remnants of these offerings must not be consumed by either the incantation master or the patient, for if they are eaten, the power of the incantation will prove ineffective.
"If one performs this rite, all rākṣasas and various spirits will rejoice and release the patient, who will then recover.
One should give the remaining food to the poor as the foremost act; thus, no spirits whatsoever shall find an opportunity to cause harm."
The practitioner of mantra-dhāraṇī should be fond of memorization and free from forgetfulness.

Regarding the *prajñā* altar ritual: the altar is four cubits in length and breadth, constructed with five colors. Starting from the interior, the colors are applied in sequence—white, yellow, blue, red, and black. This is the standard procedure for all altar rituals.
In the center of the altar, place a flower seat for Śākyamuni Buddha, with an image installed upon it.
To the east of that seat, further place a flower seat, upon which install the personification of the Prajñāpāramitā, holding a scripture in her left hand.
On the northern side of the altar, place another flower seat; upon this seat, place the Great Brahmā Deva, holding a *kundikā* (in the Tang language, a "hú píng" or water jar) in his left hand.
On the southern side, place a flower seat; upon this seat, place Śakra Devendra, holding a *vajra* in his right hand.

In the center, place one incense burner and water jar; at each of the four corners, place one incense burner and water jar. Within each of these five jars, fill them with pure water, the five grains, and the seven treasures, and seal their openings with cypress leaves and pear branches. Bind each of them securely with three feet of raw silk.
There were twelve plates of various fruits and excellent fruits, and sixteen lamps.

The mantra-master should sit at the western gate, facing directly east. To the southeast of the mantra-master, one should place a brazier. In front of the mantra-master, one should arrange three or five plates of various incenses, flowers, ghee, honey, sesame seeds, rice grains, and other offerings such as food and drink, intended for burning as an offering.

Once all the various arrangements have been completed, invite [the deities] in sequence; for each one, perform their respective root mudrā and recite their mantra, and for each one, perform the flower mudrā to welcome them.

When they are all seated in order, perform the great boundary-binding (*mahā-sīmābandha*). Then, in sequence, offer the *kaṇika* and distribute money according to one’s means, performing acts of charity as desired. Once this is finished, next perform the ritual service with incense and flowers as offerings; then burn substances such as ghee, honey, and sesame seeds as offerings. Finally, the Vidyādhara master, holding a rosary in hand, shall recite the Great Heart Mantra one thousand and eight times.

When the recitation is finished, take the water jar from the northeast corner and place it before the image of Prajñāpāramitā. Kneel on your right knee and press your right hand upon the water jar. Having completed one hundred and eight recitations of the Great Heart Mantra, prepare a water altar outside the western side of the mandala, measuring two cubits in length and breadth.

In the center of the maṇḍala, construct a lotus seat. Having completed the offering of scattered flowers, take the water flask and lead the person receiving the dharma outside the maṇḍala. Arriving at the edge of the central lotus seat on the western altar, have them stand facing east, holding the water flask.

Then, have the person receiving the dharma sit upon the lotus seat facing east and make this vow, saying aloud: "I universally pray that all sentient beings may all resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta. Because I now desire to seek śamatha and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I perform this rite for the sake of all sentient beings so that they may leave birth and death behind. May all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and devas bear witness to this."
Having made such a vow, he further required those receiving the Dharma to take this solemn oath:
"I vow that after I have accomplished this Dharma, I shall never teach it to those who slander the True Dharma, those who have severed their roots of goodness, or various evil persons."
"If the teacher [does not act thus], all practices and studies will fail to be accomplished.
If one commits such a transgression, one will swiftly incur a great sin.

Having made this vow, the Vidyādhara master shall place the Prajñā-body-mudrā upon the head of the person receiving the empowerment, placing a flower within the mudrā. Once he has finished pouring water from the ritual jar over their head, he shall again form the body-mudrā to grant them protection. Then, having had them put on new, clean garments, he leads them into the maṇḍala; once the prostrations are completed, they sit in their respective order.

The Vidyādhara sits facing east beside the homa fire-pit. He kindles firewood of grain-bearing trees within the pit and performs the mudrās one by one in sequence. Having invited [the deity] to sit within the pit and completed the offerings of incense, food, drink, ghee, honey, and other substances, he escorts [the deity] back to its original place.
In this manner, continuing until all the devas and others have been addressed, he says aloud:
"I am ashamed that my offerings were not excellent and that I have erred in the ritual procedures.

Having apologized for his transgressions, he takes some ash from the incense burner with his fingers as the Master of Mantras and applies it to protect the body at seven locations: the nape of the neck, the two shoulders, the heart, the throat, the space between the eyebrows, and the hairline. Once the protection of the body is complete, he takes leave of the Buddha, unlocks the enclosure, and after performing the dismissal rites, he immediately sweeps away the altar site with pure water.
"One who performs this rite shall have all karmic obstructions completely extinguished.
As for the residual food from the *maṇḍala*, neither the Vidyādhara master nor those who have received the dharma are permitted to eat it."
If one consumes [the offerings], both the Vidyādhara master and the recipient of the Dharma will lose their accomplishments.

As for the money offered to the *liṅga*, it shall be used for the Buddha; the money for Prajñāpāramitā, for copying scriptures; the money for the Bodhisattvas, for the Bodhisattvas; and the money for the Vajras and the devas, for the Vajra and deva shrines.
Regarding the water jar, it is best for the Vidyādhara to use silk cloth or not at all.
When practicing seated meditation, if one presses the ground with the hand and recites the aforementioned Great Mantra twenty-one times, śamatha will be swiftly attained.
If one performs this rite, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will be delighted.

If one constructs this maṇḍala, it must be done on the fifteenth day of the eighth month. One should recite the Prajñā mantra in a pure location and establish a boundary for that site using the Muñjakeśinī mantra. All bones, hair, shards, stones, and the like must be excavated until they are completely removed, to a depth of either four fingers, one span, or one cubit.

Once all the inferior materials have been exhausted, fill the area with excellent, pure earth, compacting it firmly to make it level. Bury within it the seven treasures and the seeds of the five grains at a depth of one span (vitasti), placing them at the center.
"When you wish to install the jewel, first seal it with the Root Seal of Prajñā, and only then bury it.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was in the great assembly preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā* and explaining these methods for the benefits of mantra-dharmas, he was able to cause all humans and non-humans who heard this dhāraṇī to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi, dedicate themselves toward the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, and surely attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, always dwelling in joy.
At that time, there were sixteen great yakṣa generals within the assembly, whose names were as follows:

The Great Yakṣa General Dharitīraṣṭha, the Great Yakṣa General Kambhīru, the Great Yakṣa General Vajru, the Great Yakṣa General Kambhīru, the Great Yakṣa General Mithūru, the Great Yakṣa General Kaṅkubhi, the Great Yakṣa General Aniru, the Great Yakṣa General Saniru, the Great Yakṣa General Indaru, the Great Yakṣa General Pāyiru, the Great Yakṣa General Maviru, the Great Yakṣa General Kāviru, the Great Yakṣa General Cintiru, the Great Yakṣa General Vaṭaturu, the Great Yakṣa General Vikāru, and the Great Yakṣa General Kubheru—these sixteen great yakṣa generals, each leading seven thousand retinues, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Now, all the devas and humans within this assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, have extinguished all their sins, shall not fall into the three miserable realms, and have planted the seeds of Buddhahood;

we yakṣa generals are likewise, for having received the Buddha’s grace, we take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and shall constantly follow and protect the community of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.

If kings, ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and all sentient beings receive and uphold this Dharma—whether reading it, reciting it, hearing it, contemplating it, or furthermore, practicing mindfulness of the Buddha or sitting in meditation—we, the sixteen yakṣa generals and our retinues, shall follow wherever they go and provide them with protection.

Whether in kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, or in secluded forests and such places as these, if there are those who recollect the name of this Prajñāpāramitā, we and our retinues shall all provide protection for them.
If there should be anyone who encounters any kind of adversity while upholding this Prajñāpāramitā, we, together with our retinues, shall collectively protect them.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who wishes to achieve the accomplishment of the Prajñāpāramitā, we, together with our retinues, shall fulfill their aspirations.
At that time, the Buddha praised the yakṣa generals, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You and your retinues are able to provide protection wherever the Prajñāpāramitā resides, and you have explained the methods of practice for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages."
At that time, the yakṣa kings and others said:

"Whether it be a king, or a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, if they can with deep resolve believe in and understand the sovereign power and the accomplishment of the dhāraṇī of the merits of our Prajñāpāramitā, we must also have our sixteen retinues come to assist in their protection."

If you are able to rely upon this Dharma of mine, perform the protective binding as previously described, extensively establish a site of practice (*maṇḍala*) according to the ritual methods for the altar, and seek all manner of benefits—then the state’s prosperity shall be prolonged, the people shall be peaceful and happy, the four quarters shall be free from trouble, calamities and misfortunes shall not invade, you shall preserve your integrity and diligence, and there shall be no afflictions or sufferings.

"One should invite seven, or even fourteen or twenty-one, pure Vidyādharas—regardless of whether they are monastics or laypeople, as their essential nature is the same—who are of noble virtue and whose conduct is fully matured. They must strictly maintain the observance of the precepts. In a separate location, one should establish a kitchen and provide food and provisions for these masters."

One may select any superior location—whether it be within a spacious hall of a monastery, a courtyard, near a stupa or temple housing relics, a beautiful garden, or a sacred site on a famous mountain—and there establish a place of practice (maṇḍala).
Regarding the ritual for the mandala site: one should excavate and remove all impure substances and level the ground with pure soil.
Once it has been leveled and made even as previously described, one should further smear the ground with a paste of fragrant water mixed with pure cow dung.
"Construct three tiers of courtyards using five-colored powders; each of the three tiers shall have four gates opened.
Within the third tier, construct a circular moon-disk, and place an image of the Bodhisattva Prajñāpāramitā at its center, facing west toward the gate."
To the right of the image, place Śakra; to the left, place Brahmā. On the eastern side, place the messengers; on the western side, place the Vidyādharas.
Outside the first tier, arrange four images of the Four Great Kings on each of the four sides—four on each side, totaling sixteen Great Kings.
If one wishes to paint [the mandala], it is also permissible to paint within the first enclosure.

As for the Vidyādhara master, he enters the third enclosure and stands directly before the image of Prajñāpāramitā; first, he invites the Bodhisattva Prajñāpāramitā, next he invites Brahmā and the others, and then he summons and installs the sixteen Śivas of the four directions, along with their messengers and attendants.

"When one is about to recite, one should first place the hand inside the bowl of scented water and then bring it toward the mouth; doing this three times, the rite will be accomplished.

"If there are those who wish to enter the mountains to practice seated meditation, and should there be evil insects, lions, tigers, wolves, or malevolent demons and spirits that come to harass them, they should recite this mantra one hundred and eight times; then they will have nothing to fear, and all obstacles and difficulties will naturally vanish."
"If there are those who slander the Dharma or commit the five heinous crimes, such evil persons cannot be accepted for repentance; do not teach this teaching to such people.
However, if one can recite this mantra with a sincere heart, they will be able to extinguish the sins of the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and so forth."
“If one were to explain this Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā in full, there would be immeasurable maṇḍalas, mudrās, and dhāraṇī-dharmas; now, I shall briefly explain this Dharma.”
It is like a *maṇi* jewel: if there is one who possesses the unsurpassed bodhicitta and can behold this Dharma, they shall attain the fruit of enlightenment.

If a person wishes to make daily offerings to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and others of the ten directions, whether in their own quarters or within a Buddha hall, they must perform the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) at every place of offering. Using four stakes made of *khadira* wood (translated as purple ginger wood), each eight finger-widths long, empower each stake one hundred and eight times and drive them into the four corners. Once a stake has been driven in, it must never be pulled out again;
once one stake is thus established, the remaining three are treated in the same manner.

In the center of the mandala and at each of the four directions, one should dig holes into the ground, each one cubit deep. Within these holes, one should bury white mustard seeds, having empowered them one hundred and eight times with the Great Heart Mantra of Cundī.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ (1) hulu hulu (2) tiṣṭha tiṣṭha (3) bandha bandha (4) hana hana (5) amṛte (6) hūṃ (7) phaṭ (8). If a person bathes daily with fragrant water and enters the maṇḍala, they should perform the *rakṣā-mudrā* (protection seal) and the following seals, which are auxiliary seals; therefore, the sequence and number of heads are recorded separately below.

The Dharani-Seal Mantra of Amṛtakuṇḍalī for Expelling Vināyakas. Regarding the Dharani-Seal Mantra of Amṛtakuṇḍalī for Expelling Vināyakas: "Bend the right thumb across into the palm; grasp that thumb with the left middle and ring fingers. Then, extend and bend the index and little fingers outward so that the tip of the index finger reaches the side of the middle joint of the middle finger, and the tip of the little finger reaches the side of the middle joint of the ring finger. Immediately extend the arm and rotate it to the right, reciting the mantra seven times."

When performing the rite correctly, press the tip of the thumb against the upper joint of the little finger with the left hand, place it at the side of the waist, and extend the three fingers straight forward with their tips pointing ahead.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ hūṃ hana dhuna māthaya vidambha svāhā uccāṭaya huṃ phaṭ phaṭ. This mudrā and this vidyā-mantra can completely expel all yakṣas and vināyakas; all evils shall scatter and flee, all undertakings will be accomplished, and there will be no fear whatsoever.

The Dharani and Mudra for Binding the Earth Boundary: First, place the right middle finger between the left index and middle fingers with the tips pointing outward from the backs of those fingers. Next, do the same with the left ring finger between the left little fingers. Turn the left middle finger inward, and place the right index and middle fingers together with their tips pointing inward. Then, place the left ring finger between the right little fingers in the same manner. Join the tips of both little fingers and index fingers; join the two thumbs as well, with their tips pointing downward.
When performing the rite, join the tips of the thumbs and place them on the ground, while the elbows support the two upper arms.
The mantra is: "Oṃ kili kili vajra-puṭe pante pante hūṃ haḥ. Recite this mantra seven times and press the seal against the ground; all evil spirits and the like will immediately flee and disperse.

The Dharma Seal and Mantra for Binding the Boundaries of the Four Directions: "Following the previous earth-seal, change only this: extend the two thumbs apart by two inches, with the tips of the fingers pointing toward the body; hold the fingers upright and straight, and rotate them to the right."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ sarasara vajraparākāra hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra seven times and, with this mudrā, direct it toward the four quarters, turning clockwise with the sun; all yakṣas, vināyakas, and the like will immediately flee and disperse.

The Mantra and Dharma-Seal for Binding the Realm of Space. This mantra and dharma-seal for binding the realm of space is also called the "Upper Direction Boundary. Following the previous earth-seal, change only this: place both thumbs against the sides of the index fingers. Then, with this seal, move it above the head, rotating it three times to the right.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ viṣṇupatara kṣa vajra bhañjara huṃ phaṭ. By raising this mudrā above one’s head, circling it three times to the right, and reciting the mantra seven times, all yakṣas, māras, and other spirits who fly through the heavens and the void shall be completely dispersed and driven away.

Each should recite the mantra for sealing seven times and provide twenty-one kinds of offerings to perform a Dharma assembly of the Prajñāpāramitā; according to one's capacity and means, these should be as refined and exquisite as possible.
What are the twenty-one kinds?

First, one should adorn the *bodhimaṇḍa* and install the honored image; furthermore, using various perfumes—namely, camphor, clove, saffron, and aloeswood—one bathes the image with fragrant water and returns it to its original place.
Second, one should construct a water-maṇḍala before the image.
Third, using camphor, aloeswood, and other supreme, exquisite incenses to anoint the body of the image;
fourth, adorning the Buddha’s body with various exquisite flower garlands and necklaces upon the left and right shoulders;
fifth, suspending a celestial crown upon the head.
Sixth, adorning the Buddha’s body with precious bracelets and necklaces;
seventh, precious canopies;
eighth, burning various kinds of incense.
Ninth, hang banners of variegated colors;
tenth, hang parasols;
eleventh, light lamps.
12. Food and drink of a hundred flavors, as well as excellent sweet fruits;
13. Suspended small bells and pendants;
14. Suspended musical instruments.
Fifteenth, various multicolored flowers;
sixteenth, jeweled fans;
seventeenth, diverse garments;
18. Precious mirrors;
19. Precious vases; 20. Pearl nets;
Twenty-one: The White Whisk.

By making offerings with such supreme and wondrous implements as these with a sincere heart, one can cause the various sins of the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes committed since beginningless time by kings and all sentient beings to be extinguished, and furthermore, cause all present aspirations to be fulfilled according to their wishes.
If one cannot provide all twenty-one kinds, five kinds will suffice. What are these five?
First, scented water; second, various flowers; third, incense for burning; fourth, food and drink; and fifth, lamps.
Possessing these five qualities and giving rise to great compassion and pity for all sentient beings, one shall likewise achieve success in making offerings to the Buddhas.
Next, perform the Vajra mudrā to empower all the previously prepared incense, flowers, precious objects, and other offerings;
if a vajra is available, do not use the hand mudrā, but directly use the vajra itself to perform the empowerment.

For *vajra*, one uses the hand-seal (*mudrā*): with the left hand, form the general seal by pressing the thumb against the tip of the little finger, while the remaining three fingers are held straight up and extended.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ amṛte huṃ phaṭ. One should recite this *Cundā* minor-heart mantra seven times to adorn the ritual site (*maṇḍala*). Having arranged various incenses, flowers, lamps, and food offerings in rows, one should next burn incense.
If one wishes to invite the Buddha, one should perform the Buddha-mudrā to invite him;
next, to invite Prajñāpāramitā, one should perform the Prajñā-mudrā;
next, to invite Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one should perform the Avalokiteśvara-mudrā.

Next, invite Vajrapāṇi and the various devas in the same manner; form the appropriate mudrās for each according to their class to invite them, inviting them one by one, and perform the flower-seat mudrā while reciting the mantra for seating.

The mantra is: "Oṃ hūṃ kāmala svāhā. Recite this seven times; after each recitation, invite [the deities] and seat them upon their thrones. Next, perform the Great Boundary-Sealing Mudrā (Mahā-sīmā-bandhana-mudrā) by circling it three times to the right. First, extend both hands palms upward. Then, interlace the two little fingers and the two ring fingers, pressing the right over the left and hooking them back into the palms. Next, extend the two middle fingers with their tips touching one another. Then, place the two index fingers so that they each press against the upper joint of the middle fingers from behind. Finally, bend the two thumbs individually and place them upon the middle joints of the middle fingers, ensuring they do not touch one another.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ śaṅkare mahāsamaye vaṭa vaṭa svāhā. One should recite this seven times. Next, burn incense again; perform the incense-burner mudrā to seal both the incense and the burner, then hold the incense burner and kneel on the right knee before the maṇḍala to make offerings to all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, all Vajras, all devas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and so forth, even extending to the ten directions in the same manner.
Having completed the offerings, set down the incense burner before the altar and prostrate with a sincere heart; if you have incense, flowers, food, drink, and so forth, offer them as such.
If you lack incense, flowers, food, drink, and so forth, perform the seal of universal offering (*sarvapūjāmudrā*) and make offerings while reciting the mantra.
"Next, perform the Seal of Universal Offering (Samantabhadra-pūjā-mudrā).
Join the two hands in *añjali* with a slight space between the palms so that they do not touch.
The mantra is as follows:"

"Oṃ sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite supratihite gagana-gambhīra-samantata svāhā. Recite this seven times, then make offerings of various incenses and flowers, and each performing their respective mudrās, return to their original positions.

Next, having completed the cycle of musical offerings and praises, one should form the Prajñā mudrā and perform repentance for karmic obstacles. Reciting the Great Heart Mantra, one should seal the heart center while verbally confessing the transgressions of the three karmas committed; thus one should constantly maintain these seven factors.
Just as a great fire burning dry grass is completely extinguished when aided by a fierce wind,
so too are the stains of sin eliminated through diligent recitation of the vidyā-mantra.
Furthermore, just as frost, snow, and the darkness of a room are dispelled by fire and the sun,
so too does the recitation of mantras and diligent application of effort extinguish the darkness of ignorance, like the blazing sun. Moreover,

by reciting the Prajñā-mantra and performing homa with substances such as ghee and honey to make offerings to the worthy and holy ones, one eradicates the heavy sins of beginningless birth and death and swiftly attains the realization of unsurpassed Bodhi.
"That vidyādhara should fully and firmly uphold seven dharmas.
What are the seven?
First, the upholding of ethical discipline;..."
Second, patience;
third, refraining from verbal transgressions;
fourth, generating resolute faith in the Buddha-dharma.
Fifth, to resolve upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta;
sixth, to constantly recite mantras and dhāraṇīs while maintaining a sense of shame and remorse within the mind;
seventh, to remain free from physical or mental weariness throughout the four modes of deportment.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch, endowed with the seven treasures, succeeds to the rightful throne and rules over the four quarters of the world;
so too it is with the mantra-practitioner: by possessing the aforementioned seven dharmas, they swiftly attain realization and achieve all their intended purposes according to their application.
“Sit upright and do not move; prostrate repeatedly and praise all Buddhas, saying:

‘May I, in every birth, avoid the eight difficulties; may I always be born with a male body; may I honor the Triple Gem; may my faculties be complete; and may I swiftly attain mastery in all arts and crafts, endowed with the six supernormal powers.’”

If there are those who come to beg, whether it be their head, eyes, marrow, or brain; their kingdom, city, wife, or children; or their elephants, horses, and the seven treasures—he shall give all these to them, according to whatever they desire.

With a mind free from attachment to all desires and endowed with intelligence and wisdom, may all sentient beings who see or hear me resolve to attain Bodhicitta; in every place of birth, may they encounter virtuous friends whom they revere and honor, listen to the True Dharma, and practice according to its teachings.

Adorned with the bodhicitta, their body and mind remain pure throughout the four modes of conduct; they attain the knowledge of past lives and achieve unimpeded mastery. Feeling profound dread toward all evil karmic offenses, they cultivate the ten pāramitās of bodhi and attain great sovereignty.
One shall not receive a female body nor that of a slave; nor shall one be dull-witted, nor dwell in a border region, nor give rise to false views, nor be born into the family of a caṇḍāla.

May I always encounter the Buddhas who appear in the world; may I practice the six perfections and dedicate the merit toward Bodhi. May I provide all wealth and treasures to those in need according to their desires; rather than remaining in poverty and low station while practicing various wholesome dharmas, I would never abide in wealth and nobility while committing evil deeds.

His life shall not be cut short; he will be born into a family of right faith, with a complete circle of kinsmen. He will provide filial support to his teachers and elders, possess keen faculties and wisdom, and have unimpeded eloquence. He will attain right faith in the Buddha and maintain compassionate thoughts for all sentient beings.
May I be endowed with five qualities in every place where I am born. What are these five?
First, merit; second, wisdom; third, the ten powers; fourth, diligence; and fifth, the arousal of the bodhicitta.

"Just as the Buddha has realized the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñā-jñāna*) and the thirty-two marks, I too shall attain them; I shall be born at will in the pure lands of the ten directions and constantly behold all Buddhas.
May it be so for all sentient beings as well, so that all sentient beings may cultivate a wholesome mindfulness of the Buddha."
Having made this vow, one should hold the bead and recite the vidyā. As for the method of holding the beads:

stay at a distance of about four or five chi from the place where the Buddha and Bodhisattvas are enshrined; kneel with the body drawn back and remain motionless. Do not look toward the east or west, do not bring the breath near the mouth, and do not release the "grain-wind" (exhalation) toward the place where the Buddha and Bodhisattvas are enshrined. Sit upright with the body straight, and with single-minded devotion, recollect the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and Devas, no different from entering into śamatha.
"Next, form the mudrā for counting the beads (*mālā-mudrā*).

With the left hand, press the thumb against the top of the ring finger so that it enters the hole through which the beads pass. Then, extend the middle and little fingers straight. Cover the side of the upper joint of the middle finger with the index finger. With the right hand, use the thumb and ring finger to grasp the beads while reciting the mantra; the remaining fingers are held the same as the left."
"If one obtains these ten auspicious signs while thus counting the beads, one should know that efficacy has been attained.
What are the ten?
First, light radiates from the image;..."
Second, although the wind did not blow, the banners within the site of enlightenment moved and fluttered of their own accord;
third, although clouds did not cover the sky, there was the sound of thunder;
fourth, the flames of the lamps within the site of enlightenment reached three or four feet in height.
Fifth, incense smoke emerged spontaneously from within the incense burner even though no one was burning incense;
sixth, various sounds of music were heard in the air;

seventh, the four quarters became peaceful and free of trouble, their blessings and lifespans increased, they were free from all diseases, and lions, tigers, wolves, and various venomous insects could not cause them harm.
Eighth, the mind is free from attachment to the objects of the five desires;
ninth, various demons, ghosts, and spirits cannot cause disturbance, and the illnesses of oneself and others are cured as soon as treated;
tenth, one beholds Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and so forth.

If, within a dream, one sees Buddhas or Bodhisattvas; or ascends a high mountain, or climbs a tall tree, or boards a boat to cross to the other shore; or rides an elephant or horse; or sees one's preceptors, parents, or spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)—if at such times the practitioner and the donor see such signs as these in a dream, they should know that their transgressions have been extinguished. These are all auspicious and numinous omens, indicating that the Vidyārājas are providing protection.
"At this time, while the practitioner is performing the rite correctly, the hairs on their body will all stand on end; they should then know that a sign of efficacy has been attained.

Every morning upon rising, having washed their hands and face, they should chew a willow branch and rinse their mouth thoroughly. Then, entering the Buddha hall, they should perform the rites of offering. Until mealtime arrives, they should dismiss all [deities]. Three times each day, as before, they should manipulate the prayer beads and recite the vidyā one hundred and eight times or one thousand and eight times."

According to one’s capacity, place a homa furnace before the entrance of the maṇḍala. The vidyādhara master sits facing east with his back to the west; on his left, he places scented water and various flowers, and on his right, he places sesame seeds, ghee, honey, śāli rice blossoms, and so forth. Whatever offering materials are available for burning at the site of the altar should all be placed on the right side. Thereafter, having invited the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and others, he forms the flower-seat mudrā and, as required by the ritual, burns offerings within the furnace.
Having made the offerings, he returns to his original seat and says:
"I am ashamed that there are no incense, flowers, food, or drink here.
Only then does he dismiss [the deity].

"Constantly burn incense within the chamber and daily recite the Akṣobhya-buddha-dhāraṇī, the Amitāyus-buddha-dhāraṇī, and others, to eliminate all karmic obstructions such as the five heinous crimes and the four grave offenses within one's body."
"If one wishes to be born in the land of the Buddha Amitāyus, one should daily perform this offering and recite the dharani according to the ritual method.
By constantly performing this rite, all undertakings will be accomplished, and after death, one will be reborn in the land of the Buddha Amitāyus."
If one makes offerings day after day, the merit is so vast that it cannot be fully described.

The merit of recollecting the Buddha is beyond comparison; the power and nature of the merit from reciting mantras is like the light of the sun and moon, whereas the merit of recollecting the Buddha is like the light of a lamp at night—the two cannot be compared.
If one daily makes offerings and recites mantras while simultaneously practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, the merit thereof will be as high as Mount Sumeru and as deep as the great ocean;
if one mindfully recollects the Buddha alone without reciting mantras, the merit will be as small as Mount Gandhamādana and as trivial as Lake Anavatapta, such that they cannot be compared.
If one makes offerings to the Buddhas every day and recites the vidyā to extinguish transgressions, the destruction of those sins is just like fire consuming grass and wood.

If one can perform offerings, mindfulness of the Buddha, and recitation of the vidyā three times each day, this cannot be compared to merely mindful recollection in the air; it is beyond verbal expression, and its merit and benefits are inconceivable.
One should know that the praise for the accomplishment of the merits of Prajñā cannot be exhausted.
*The Compendium of Dhāraṇīs*, Scroll Three;
*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Compendium of Dhāraṇīs*, Scroll Four; Upper Volume of Avalokiteśvara.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Ajita from India during the Great Tang Dynasty:

The Sutra of the Divine Incantation of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara. Commentary on the Sutra of the Divine Incantation of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara: This is the intention of the person [who compiled it]; this is the original text of the sutra. In this fascicle, there are fifty-two seals in total;
fifty are primary, and two seals are secondary (guest). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of immeasurable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, who surrounded him before and behind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, accompanied by countless sages and deities who uphold dhāraṇīs, came to where the Buddha was, surrounded by them before and behind.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves on the ground with their five limbs to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet. Having paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, they circumambulated the Buddha three times and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I possess a heart-mantra named "Eleven Faces," which includes immeasurable great dhāraṇīs, various seal-methods (mudrās), and immeasurable maṇḍalas.

I shall now proclaim it for the sake of all sentient beings: to cause all sentient beings to recollect wholesome dharmas; to cause all sentient beings to be free from sorrow and affliction; to eliminate the illnesses of all sentient beings; to completely extinguish all obstacles, difficulties, calamities, portents, and evil dreams; to eliminate all untimely deaths and diseases; to soften and harmonize all those with evil minds; and to ensure that no obstacles or difficulties arise from demons, ghosts, or deities.
"Bhagavān!

I have never seen anyone—whether among devas, Māras, Śakras, śramaṇas, or brahmins—who is able to receive and uphold such a Dharma as this, whether by reading it, reciting it, copying it for circulation, or using this Dharma to protect their body; or by sealing water with this seal and bathing their body after consecrating it with mantras; or whether entering into battle or being struck by poison.
For one who upholds this Dharma, no calamities whatsoever can take effect, except for those karmic retributions from past lives that cannot be eliminated."
Such a Dharma as this is what all Buddhas keep in mind.
This dhāraṇī method of mine has been prophesied by all Buddhas.
"World-Honored One!..."

I recall that beyond kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha named Śatapatranetra-mūrdhanirāvaraṇaguṇaprabhāsarāja Tathāgata. At that time, I was among the great mantra-holding ṛṣis and served as their king; it was at the place of that Buddha that I first obtained this dharma.
When this Dharma is attained, all Buddhas of the ten directions appear before one’s eyes.
Having seen the Buddhas appear, one suddenly attains a wisdom never before possessed.
One should know that this Dharma possesses such supernatural power and is also able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
Therefore, you should know this:

if there are good men or good women who can diligently recite this [sūtra] day and night without forgetting it, maintaining this Dharma at all times without turning to other objects; and who, having bathed their bodies at dawn and donned fresh, clean garments, receive and uphold this Dharma, perform mudrās to protect themselves, prepare a ritual altar with pure clay—shaping it as they wish, whether square or round, wide or narrow, large or small—and having completed the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), invite Avalokiteśvara to sit upon the altar, burning incense, scattering flowers, making various offerings, prostrating, and reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
One who upholds this mantra shall immediately obtain ten kinds of retributive fruits in this very life.
What are these ten?
First, the body is always free from illness.
Second, they are constantly remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions;
third, all their wealth, clothing, food, and drink are spontaneously sufficient, never lacking anything;
fourth, they are able to defeat enemies and adversaries.
Fifth, they can cause all sentient beings to give rise to a heart of loving-kindness;
sixth, no poisons from sorcery or any febrile diseases can inflict harm upon them;
seventh, no blades or staves can cause them injury.
Eighth, they cannot be swept away or drowned by any water-related calamities;
ninth, they cannot be burned by any fire-related calamities;
tenth, they shall not undergo any untimely death.
These are called the ten.
Furthermore, one obtains four kinds of karmic retribution.
What are these four?
First, one shall not be harmed by any birds or beasts;
second, one shall never fall into the hells;
third, at the time of death, one shall behold all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
"Fourth, after the end of my life, I shall be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life.
'World-Honored One!

I recall that more than incalculable *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas ago, even beyond immeasurable *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas, there was a Buddha named Mandāravagandha Tathāgata. At that time, I was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) under that Buddha, and from him I again obtained this Dharma.'"
Having attained this Dharma, one transcends the limits of birth and death throughout the kalpas of the four directions.
When this Dharma is taught, one attains the Dharma-gate of the treasury of wisdom of all Buddhas’ great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity.

By the power of this Dharma gate, one is able to rescue all sentient beings from the various sufferings of all prisons, confinements, fetters, shackles, and stocks, as well as the perils of execution, water, fire, and so forth; I shall constantly protect them, causing them to attain liberation.

By the power of this Dharma-seal dhāraṇī, all yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others shall cause these yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others to give rise to wholesome minds and become fully endowed with merit, immediately resolving to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"This Dharma of mine possesses such power.

Even if there were someone who has committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, should they be able to uphold this Dharma and recite this dhāraṇī even once, all their fundamental resentments and heavy transgressions will be entirely extinguished."
If those who recite this mantra possess such merit, how much more so for those who, in accordance with the teachings, are able to perform the mudrā rituals and maintain the recitation of the mantra?
One should know that such persons have previously heard this Dharma from tens of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, and now hear it once again.
How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, never forgetting it day or night?
If such a person has any wish in their heart, I shall fulfill that vow.

Furthermore, if there is anyone who, on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the month, bathes their body with fragrant water, puts on new and clean clothes, and after using the toilet once, bathes once more—ensuring these clean clothes do not come into contact with a screen or partition.
When practicing this rite, one should abstain from food for the entire day and perform the seal (*mudrā*) to protect the body.
Having completed the ritual for binding the boundary (*sīmābandha*), one should recite the *dhāraṇī* until dawn.

Within the maṇḍala, one should place an image of Avalokiteśvara, perform the seal for inviting Avalokiteśvara, and recite the mantra while hanging various multicolored banners and canopies and making offerings of incense and flowers.
When first entering the *maṇḍala*, one must with utmost reverence and sincerity invite the Buddhas of the ten directions, earnestly repent, and praise the Triple Gem.

Having performed three prostrations, one should spread a single sitting mat before the image, kneel on the right knee in a respectful manner, and with a sincere mind make vows. Forming the *mālā-mudrā* and holding the beads, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times—reciting one hundred and eight times is also acceptable and faultless.
Next, holding the incense burner and burning incense, he said:
"In this place there are no various offerings nor food and drink of superior flavor; I apologize for this with a sense of shame.
"World-Honored One! [he continued.]

Because of the power of these Dharma seals and mantras, and because my name is so noble and difficult to hear, if there were one person who recited the names of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, and another who for a brief moment recited my name, the merit of those two persons would be exactly equal and no different.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters diligently invoke my name day and night, they shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika). In their present bodies, they shall be freed from all suffering and affliction, all obstacles and difficulties, and all fears; furthermore, the transgressions of the three poisons shall all be healed and eliminated. How much more so for those who rely upon this teaching and practice according to the Dharma?”
"You should know that such a person will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as if it were held within the palm of their hand.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!

You are indeed able to give rise to the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion toward all sentient beings, and thus desire to reveal and teach these dharma-gates such as the Great Divine Mantra and Seal."
"Noble son!

By the power of the skillful means of this Dharma, you are able to rescue and liberate all sentient beings from all their sicknesses, sufferings, obstacles, difficulties, fears, and the evils of body, speech, and mind; furthermore, you shall establish all sentient beings in the resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, free from doubt."
"Good son!
I also rejoice in these dharma-gates such as the dhāraṇī-seals; I likewise authorize you to receive these methods of divine mantras, seals, and so forth."
“Good son! You should now speak of it.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, I shall explain in sequence the ritual procedures and the efficacy of the seal-dhāraṇī maṇḍala.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
