*Pra-ma-sūta-sattva (22) mahā-kāruṇika (23) svāhā (24)* When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara spoke this dhāraṇī,
the assembly of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, vajradharas, devas, and others praised him with loud voices, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is the root dhāraṇī; if one recites it, one shall obtain the meritorious benefits as described above.
Having finished explaining the root dhāraṇī, next I shall explain the ritual for the seven-day altar offering.

"If there be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or sons of good family who recite this secret treasury of the Dharma, which provides the essential instructions for achieving great efficacy; and if kings should develop a resolute mind to repent of their manifold sins and desire to see and hear the Great Dharma-assembly at the Universal Great Maṇḍala site—first seek out a pure, spacious, and vast courtyard, a magnificent mansion, or a fine temple or Buddha hall—even an open space will suffice."

Once the location has been determined, on the first day of the waxing moon at the hour of dawn, the ācārya and his disciples shall bathe their bodies with fragrant water and carry various incense and flowers to that site.
The Ācārya, holding a vajra in his hand, questioned the disciples in succession, saying:
"Do you all resolutely wish to study the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, without giving rise to doubt?"
The assembly replied, "We wish to study the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas; we are resolute and sincere in our faith, and shall harbor no doubts.
Thus it was asked three times and answered three times in succession.

When the response has been thus completed, the *ācārya* next consecrates the hand-seal (*mudrā*), the incense burner, the water, and so forth with mantras. Holding the incense burner in his hands and kneeling on his right knee, he makes this announcement to all Buddhas, Prajñāpāramitā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and all the spirits of the karmic paths:

"This ground is now my ground. I now wish to establish for seven days and seven nights a great Dharma-assembly of the Universal Great Maṇḍala. I shall make offerings to all the World-Honored Buddhas of the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm, as well as to Prajñāpāramitā, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Vajras, devas, and others. Leading my retinue, I shall definitively realize the inconceivable Dharma-gates of the secret Dharma-treasury and thereby attain all forms of realization."

I wish to perform the rite for protecting the body and establishing the boundary; therefore, all *vināyakas*, evil spirits, ghosts, and the like who destroy the True Dharma—whether they be in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below within this courtyard—must all depart to a distance of seven *li* outside my established boundary.
However, those benevolent spirits and ghosts who protect the True Dharma and bring benefit to my Buddha-dharma may remain as they please.
Having spoken these words, he next established the boundary (*sīmābandha*) according to the ritual of Khandali.

Once the boundary was established, he immediately ordered that all impure soil, bones, hair, charcoal, husks, shards, rubble, and other such things within an area of ten cubits be excavated and removed.
If it is excellent ground, dig one span deep;
if middling, one cubit;
if inferior ground, two cubits.
If it is on a lower level ground, dig three cubits deep.
Once all impure substances have been removed, fill it with excellent, pure earth and pack it firmly to make it level; the foundation should be made as high as possible.
On the second and third days, plaster the ground with mud.

"On the fourth day, having finished smearing the ground with fragrant cow-dung mud, one should next take a cord and measure eight cubits around each of the four sides, marking a dot at each corner; then, using another cord, one should pull diagonally from the northeast corner to the southwest corner and from the southeast corner to the northwest corner."

At the lower point of the cord-cross, one should dig the earth to a depth of about one span and bury therein the five treasures along with the five grains. As for the five treasures: first, gold; second, silver; third, pearl; fourth, coral; fifth, amber. As for the five grains:

first, barley; second, wheat; third, rice; fourth, small beans; fifth, sesame. Wrap these treasures and grains together in a single piece of silk, tie the silk with thread of five colors, and bury it.

One end of each of these five-colored threads emerges from the ground to a length of about five finger-widths; these precious objects must never be allowed to emerge. Next, perform the great boundary-binding (*mahā-sīmābandha*). As for the method of this boundary-binding:

holding a *vajra* (in Chinese, *jin'gangchu*, or "diamond scepter"), circumambulate the outside of the altar three times while running swiftly. Perform various *mudrās* for the boundary-binding of the *vināyakas*, sealing the four directions and the zenith beneath the ground. Recite the mantras and form the seals, and perform the rites of invocation, expulsion, and boundary-binding as previously explained, following the sequential procedures of the *Cundī*.
"The ritual procedure for establishing the boundary on the fifth day is the same as on the fourth day, with the addition of smearing the ground with cow dung.
Regarding the method for smearing the ground: rub it with the right hand in a clockwise direction; do not rub it counter-clockwise."
The remaining matters are the same as on the fourth day.

"Next, on the sixth day, the ācārya bathes and first enters the maṇḍala; then two other disciples who are wise and intelligent also bathe themselves clean, put on new, pure garments, and enter the maṇḍala following him."

Once the lime has been mixed with fragrant water on the altar, dip a fine cord into the lime solution; have a disciple hold the end of the cord and press it down at the northeastern corner of the altar, precisely at the point where the first mark was made.

Next, the Ācārya presses one end of the cord against the southeast corner of the maṇḍala, precisely at the point where he first made a mark; he pulls it taut toward the ground and has a disciple grasp the center of the cord and press it down onto the floor.
Next, the disciple at the northeast corner rises and sits facing the southwest corner, performing as before;
next, the ācārya at the southeast corner rises and sits facing the northwest corner, performing as before;
next, the disciple at the southwest corner rises and sits facing the northeast corner, following the same procedure.
Next, at the initial layout site, measure one cubit inward from the outer edge and encircle it again according to the previous method.

Then, take an eight-cubit cord, bend it in the middle, and place a mark on one side of the altar. Further, bend the cord by two cubits and measure from the center mark on that side of the altar, making two more marks to the left and right.

"Next, at one side of the gate wall, leave a space of five finger-widths from the cord marking the altar; next, further bend the gate wall toward the left and right by five finger-widths; next, make the two sides of the gate, left and right, five finger-widths wide."
Next, draw straight lines along the outer edge of the gates; if one side is thus, the other three sides should be understood accordingly.

Next, construct the middle enclosure: the outer cord is four cubits [in length], and between the inner cord of the outer enclosure and the outer cord of the middle enclosure, leave a path one cubit wide.

The walls on the four sides of the courtyard gate and those facing left and right are each three finger-widths thick; the method for joining the cords along the outer edge of the gate is also as described previously.
Within that middle enclosure, at a distance of one cubit from the outer cord, further mark a lime cord.
At the exact center of that altar, construct a courtyard measuring two cubits; do not make a door.
"Next, the Ācārya shall use five-colored thread, reciting the mantra once for each knot, making fifty-five knots using the Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara mantra.
The mantra is:

'Oṃ āmlīdudhi vavava hūṃ phaṭ. Next, wrap the five precious gems together with the five grains in pieces of silk, tie them with the five-colored thread, and fasten them to the consecrated cord; wrap them one by one according to the number of persons."

"Next, erect a single pole at each of the four corners of the mandala; take two bamboo poles from the western gate and bind them with ropes to the poles at the four corners, and suspend multicolored banners upon those ropes."
Atop the altar, banners are fastened to the four cardinal directions—east, west, south, and north—and the intermediate points, interlacing to form a magnificent adornment.
On the southern side of the western gate of the outer enclosure of the altar, two feet away from the altar, a fire pit is to be dug, measuring two feet in length, width, and depth.
Within that furnace, leave a mound of earth; upon this mound, fashion a lotus seat out of plain scented clay.

On the following day, at the time of sunset, the ācārya shall instruct all the disciples to complete their ritual bathing, after which the ācārya will perform the great boundary-binding (*mahā-sīmābandha*).

"On the following day at the appointed hour, one should invoke all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajras. Place an image of the Buddha at the center of the maṇḍala, with Avalokiteśvara in the north and Vajrapāṇi in the south. One should then make offerings to them with various incenses and flowers, five types of food and drink on platters, and sixteen oil lamps."
"Next, outside the western gate, spread out new and clean mats.

Then the Ācārya calls the disciples and has them form the protection-of-the-body mudrā (*kāyarakṣā-mudrā*). Reciting the mantra seven times for each one, he places the seal upon each disciple’s crown, both shoulders, heart, throat, space between the eyebrows, hairline, and the nape of the neck."
Having completed the protection of the body, have the disciples take their seats upon the mats, facing east.

Next, take incense, flowers, and white mustard seeds; the ācārya shall hold the white mustard seeds and recite the mantra over them seven times each, then strike the heads of the disciples three times in succession.
When the striking is finished, further grant them protection by consecrating them with the seal and mantra of Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara.
Next, the ācārya kneels on his right knee and asks the eldest disciple, saying:
"Do you now wish to learn this dharma?"
The disciple replied,
"I wish to obtain it.
In this manner, he questioned each of the disciples in succession, following the same ritual procedure as before.
Next, the ācārya holds fragrant water in his hands and sprinkles it upon the head of each disciple one by one.
He then places his right hand upon the chest of each disciple one by one and recites the Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara mantra for them.
Next, take the mantra-cords and bind them individually to the arms of the disciples—the left for men and the right for women.
Then, apply the fragrant sap of the *śāla* tree to the bodies of the disciples in succession, circling three times clockwise.
Having finished sprinkling the scented water, next perform the circling of the flaming torch, also according to the previous method.
Next, give a willow branch to each, eight finger-widths in length.
Having finished bestowing the flowers, have the disciples sit in a row facing east and instruct them to cast the flowers forward.
Next, chew a willow branch, casting it as before.
If the flower-end points toward the body, it is auspicious;
if it points away from the east, know that demonic obstacles are emerging.
If the tips point toward the south or north, both are inauspicious.
If the part of the willow branch that was chewed faces the practitioner's body, it is auspicious;
if it points away from the practitioner toward the east, one should know that demonic obstacles are arising.
The remainder is as in the Flower Dharma ritual.
Next, provide water for washing the hands; each person takes *vajra*-water in their hand and respectfully thanks [the deities] before drinking it.
Next, the *ācārya* enters the maṇḍala and makes this announcement to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and others:

"I have questioned my disciples in succession and completed testing them through the sequence of ritual procedures; now these disciples wish to enter the maṇḍala to make offerings to the assembly of noble ones."
Having been thus addressed, the disciples were led inside; after performing a brief offering, they were dismissed and sent outside.
The Ācārya said to the disciples:
"Each of you lie down and sleep. If you have any dreams, report them to me individually tomorrow morning."
When the disciples had all lain down to sleep and departed, the Ācārya next entered the maṇḍala and addressed the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and others, saying:

"The disciples wish to enter the maṇḍala again tomorrow to perform extensive offerings. I pray that the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, Devas, and others will ascend into the air; as we wish to offer worship tomorrow, please attend in person at that time to receive these offerings. This was said three times.
Thereafter, dismiss the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and various devas within the maṇḍala.

Next, the Ācārya proceeds to the northern side of the maṇḍala and sits facing south. He sets up a fire pit and recites the Hayagrīva mantra over white mustard seeds; for every single recitation, he burns one seed, repeating this one hundred and eight times. At that time, all the disciples shall immediately attain the extinction of their transgressions.
"Next, the ācārya, together with two disciples, shall, during one night, arrange the maṇḍala within the enclosure using five-colored powders.
As for the method of arrangement: first, starting from the inner court, one uses white; next, yellow, blue, and red; and finally, black."
At dawn on the following day, rise and establish the outer enclosure; construct it by circling clockwise from the northeast corner, using five-colored materials according to the previous method.
In the center of the altar, install the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara as the presiding deity, with a wheel-shaped emblem placed upon a lotus throne.
"Next, in the center of the eastern side of the inner court, install Amitābha Buddha; to the Buddha’s right, install Śākyamuni Buddha, and to his left, install Prajñāpāramitā.
In the center of the northern side, install Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva; to his right, install Avalokiteśvarī, and to his left, install Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara.
In the center of the southern side, install Vajrarāja; to his right, install Vajrī, and to his left, install Vajramuṣṭi."
On the south side of the western courtyard gate, place Tiṣya; on the north side, place Virūḍhaka.

Next, proceed along the eastern side of the outer courtyard: starting from the northern end, first place Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, then Maitreya Bodhisattva, then Candanaśrī Buddha, then Akṣobhya Buddha, then Lakṣaṇaśrī Buddha, then Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, then the Moon Deity, and finally Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva.

"On the northern side of the outer courtyard, starting from the eastern end, first install Mahāsthāmaprāpta (translated into Chinese as Dàbái Guānshìyīn); next, Mahāśrīye; next, the随心 (Sui-xin) Avalokiteśvara; next, Ekajaṭīkara; next, Amoghapāśa (translated into Chinese as Bùkōng Juésuǒ); next, Padmakuṭi; and next, Vimalamati."

"Proceeding south from this courtyard, starting from the eastern end, first install the Fire-Head Vajra; next, Nīlabhadravajra (translated into Chinese as *Qīngjīngāng*, Blue Vajra); next, Mūrdhaṭaka (the name of a Vajra-child); next, Subhasiccharakara; next, Subhūti (also a Vajra-child); next, Aṅkuśi; and finally, Vajrasaṃkara."
Proceeding westward from the outer enclosure, first install Mārīcī at the southern end; next, install the Sun Deity (Sūrya); next, install the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa. Next, install the gate;
on the northern wall of the gate, install the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa; next, install the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī); next, install all the Nāga Kings.
"At each of the four corners of the outer enclosure, place two crossed *vajras* in the shape of a cross.
Furthermore, at each of the four corners of the middle enclosure, as before, place two *vajras*, also arranged in a crossed formation like a cross."
"Next, the Ācārya shall stand at the western gate and observe the affairs within the maṇḍala—what is well-proportioned?
What is not well-proportioned?
What is complete in its circumference?"
"Why is it not complete?"—investigate this thoroughly;
furthermore, dispatch former disciples to remain within the altar to provide protection.

Next, the *ācārya* shall bathe in fragrant water, don fresh and clean garments, wrap his head with crimson silk (it is also permissible for the color to be red), and further encircle his head with yellow silk, tying it at the forehead.
"Next, bind the mantra-cord upon your own left hand, precisely at the wrist joint.
Next, perform the body-protection mudrā to seal yourself, employing the horse-headed body-protection mudrā and mantra for all."
"Next, holding the *vajra*, perform the body-seal of Amṛtakuṇḍalin and circumambulate three times to the right along the outer edge of the maṇḍala.
Next, perform the earth-boundary consecration (*bhūmibandha*) for the four directions and the zenith in succession, while reciting the Hayagrīva mantra."

"Next, take thirteen water jars; fill each with about one *sheng* of pure water. Within them, place a small amount of the five grains, along with a little *nāgakesara*, saffron, and *pomegranate yellow*. Having wrapped these together with the aforementioned five precious gems, place them inside the jars."
The openings of the jars are plugged with willow and cypress branches and leaves, as well as bamboo stalks, which are propped upright and each bound with white silk to prevent them from scattering.

Next, one recites the mantra over the water jars one hundred and eight times, using the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara mantra to consecrate the jars; having thus completed the one hundred and eight recitations, they are brought inside. First, one jar is placed at each of the four corners and the center of the inner court. Then, one jar is placed at each of the four corners and the four gates of the outer court.
"Next, take two silver platters; place fragrant water in one platter and flowers in the other.
Then, take the flowers from within that [second] platter and place them into the single platter of fragrant water, allowing them to soak completely."

Next, take a small portion of those flowers and place them in the palm of your hand; then, forming the body-seal (*kāyamudrā*), first invite the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara at the center of the maṇḍala.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times, form the sitting-seal (*āsana-mudrā*).
Having also recited the *āsana-mantra* seven times, one then releases the flowers and casts them into their respective positions;

once they have been fully installed, next invite [the deities] to proceed eastward in the middle enclosure, each according to the previous procedure. Next invite them to proceed northward, next southward, next westward; having completed these, next invite them to proceed eastward in the outer enclosure, next northward, next southward, and next westward. Thus the general invitation is complete.
"Next, perform the Great Boundary-Sealing Mudrā. Then, take scented water and scatter it before all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and others within the maṇḍala. Next, scatter various flowers."

"Next, place one incense burner at the center of the maṇḍala, and one incense burner at each of the four directions and eight gates. Once all have been burned, the ācārya takes an incense burner, burns various types of incense, and circumambulates the perimeter of the maṇḍala once, keeping it to his right."
After completing the circumambulation, place the incense burner beside the water jar in the west.

Next, take one end of the five-colored thread from atop the water jar at the western gate; wind it clockwise around the bamboo pole on the outer edge of the altar, returning to the western gate to complete one circuit and tie it fast.
"Next, arrange the food and drink: place four dishes of food and drink before Avalokiteśvara at the center of the altar, and place one dish before each of the other bodhisattvas."
"Next, place four lamps at the center, and place one lamp on each side of the seated figures.
Next, offer gold, silver, silk, money, and other such items to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, offering whatever you have."

Next, the ācārya takes the former disciple, who holds incense, flowers, and water, as well as about three or four *sheng* of boiled five-grain rice; once the ācārya has finished offering food and drink to the spirits and deities of the ten directions within the residence, [the ritual continues].
"Next, the ācārya washes his hands and rinses his mouth, enters the maṇḍala, performs three prostrations, and withdraws.

Next, one senior disciple takes a flower and folds it, while another disciple holds a censer and white mustard seeds, following behind the ācārya. One by one, they call the new disciples to come forward and stand outside the northwest corner of the maṇḍala."

"Next, the Ācārya first takes white mustard seeds and recites the Hayagrīva mantra over them seven times; he then strikes the disciple’s head three times and subsequently seals the disciple with the protection mudrā."
"Next, take scented water and give it to him for washing his hands; perform the Avalokiteśvara Samaya-mudrā for the disciple, place a flower within the mudrā, and do not allow it to be discarded."

"Next, wrap the eyes of the disciple with silk; the ācārya then makes a vow with his mind and mouth, dedicating everything toward all sentient beings with a mind of universal, great compassion and equanimity."

"Next, the ācārya leads the disciple into the western gate of the maṇḍala; the ācārya stands on the southern side and the disciple stands on the northern side, while the ācārya recites the Samaya-mantra of Avalokiteśvara."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ bamu-bāyā svāhā. Having recited it seven times, instruct the disciple, saying:
"Scatter flowers before [the image]. Once you have finished scattering them, observe carefully upon which seat the flowers fall."
Having known this, he said:
"The flowers you have scattered have landed upon such-and-such a Buddha and such-and-such a Bodhisattva; remember this well and do not forget it.
As for the other disciples, they were treated according to the aforementioned method.

If, after three rounds of scattering [the flowers], none of them adhere [to the candidate's head], do not untie the silk cloth; instead, expel them at once. Such a person of great transgression is unfit to enter the maṇḍala; instruct them to repent of their manifold sins with a sincere heart.

"After all the people have finished, he again requested the Buddha to admit them; only then were they ushered in. As before, flowers were scattered—those upon which the flowers adhered were granted silk scarves;
those to whom the flowers did not adhere were expelled at once and forbidden from entering ever again."
The ritual procedures for the remaining disciples were as before, and each was completed in turn.
"Next, the disciples shall sit in a row outside the western gate, facing directly east."
Place high-quality charcoal in the fire pit; outside the western gate, upon the consecration mandala, place a single bed, leave a plate of food, and set out four lamps as an offering.

Next, he dispatched two disciples, each holding a parasol—one purple and the other crimson—the crimson parasol covering the disciples and the purple parasol covering the ācārya, as they led the disciples forward one by one in succession.

The ācārya, holding the water flask, goes out to the consecration altar, circumambulates it three times to the right, causes [the disciple] to ascend the platform, and the ācārya also ascends the platform himself.
Standing beside his disciple, he asked,
"Upon which Buddhas' or Bodhisattvas' seats did you previously scatter those flowers?
The disciple replied:
"Recite 'I take refuge in such-and-such Buddha,' and so forth.

Then the ācārya, according to the disciple's response, instructs them to form the mudrā; he seals their crown with it, places a flower within the mudrā, and causes them to recollect with a single-minded heart.
According to the respective principal Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, the Ācārya shall recite the mantras of those Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others.

Having conferred the empowerment, he instructs them to scatter flowers, release the mudrās, put on their robes, enter the maṇḍala to pay homage to the Buddhas, and sit according to their original positions.
The ritual procedures for the remaining disciples are as before.

Once the general consecration is complete, the Ācārya next sits near the fire-pit at the western gate, facing directly east. With body upright and mind focused, he first summons the Fire God (Agni) to sit within the fire-pit; he then offers ghee, honey, and sesame seeds into the fire seven times each while reciting the mantra.
Next, the *Ācārya-hṛdaya-likhita* states:
"The Fire God shall first emerge from outside the hearth and sit near its edge.
Next, invoke Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara to sit upon the lotus throne within the hearth."

"Next, the Ācārya takes the vajra and calls each disciple to him one by one in order. He instructs them to maintain right mindfulness, to kneel with their right knees on the ground and join their palms. He seals the center of their palms with the vajra-mudrā, then gives them sesame seeds, ghee, honey, and so forth, reciting the mantra twenty-one times and commanding them to cast these into the fire. Once this is finished, he tells them to return to their original seats."
The ritual procedures for the remaining disciples are as before.

Next, having returned the Horse-Headed Avalokiteśvara from the midst of the fire to his original position, one then invites the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara from the center of the altar to sit upon the lotus seat within the fire-pit. Having burned sesame seeds and other offerings while reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, one dispatches him back to his original position.

"Next, invite each individual Buddha, then each individual Bodhisattva, and then each Vajra-being and the various devas and so forth. The ritual procedure is as before: for each, burn sesame seeds, ghee, honey, and other substances, reciting the mantra twenty-one times. Once this is completed for each in succession, bid them return to their respective seats."
"Next, for the sake of the Son of Heaven of this land, burn sesame seeds and other offerings, reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times until it is completed.
Next, for the sake of all teachers, monks, parents, and spiritual friends throughout successive kalpas, burn and recite the mantra for each individually, following the same ritual as before."
Next, for all sentient beings of the six realms, burn [the incense] according to the same method as before, reciting the mantra twenty-one times.
Next, for the owner of the residence, likewise burn [the incense] according to the same method as before, reciting the mantra twenty-one times.
Next, the ācārya shall recite the mantra over himself twenty-one times.
From the celestial son above down to the ācārya, all together employ the eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara mantra.

Next, the ācārya takes the incense burner and burns incense; he circumambulates the exterior of the maṇḍala once to the right. Having arrived before the western gate, he prostrates and offers this apology:
"The various offerings of incense, flowers, food, and drink were all performed improperly; I am deeply ashamed."

Thereafter, one dispatches each [deity] from the center of the maṇḍala one by one; for each, one performs their respective original mudrā for dispatching. There is no difference in the mudrās or mantras used when summoning them for dispatching.

"Next, collect the money, wealth, and precious objects offered to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others. If these are items belonging to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they should be used to fashion images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
if they are items belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā, they should be used to transcribe various sutras."
If the acharya wishes to compose sutras of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas himself, he should personally collect materials for the construction of images and the copying of scriptures;
if he does not do so, he shall entrust these matters to the Three Heads of the Community.
Regarding the offering of gold, vajras, celestial objects, and the like: it is permissible for the ācārya to use them himself, or he may not use the foremost [item].

As for the food and drink within the maṇḍala, neither the ācārya nor his disciples shall consume them—if they do eat them, they will not obtain divine efficacy. It is permissible, however, to give them to slaves, other people, or even to animals; it is also permissible for monks who have not entered the maṇḍala to consume them.
Next, the ācārya holds a torch in his hand and shows it to the disciples, saying:
"This is the station of such-and-such a Buddha, such-and-such a Bodhisattva, a Vajra, or a Deva."
Having thus sequentially indicated each stage in order, one should then plaster the altar with mud so that the rising sun is not visible.
This concludes the brief explanation of the ritual procedures for the altar.
"Next, the methods for mudrās and dhāraṇīs are explained.
First, the Eleven-Faced Samādhi Mudrā. For the mantra, use the Great Mantra."

With the two thumbs and two little fingers held straight up with their tips joined, the remaining fingers slightly curved so that their tips do not touch, and the palms hollowed, move the two index fingers up and down while held upright.

This Dharma-seal mantra can eliminate all calamities caused by thieves, water, fire, and the like; if one recites and maintains it, even when passing through various perils, there shall be no fear whatsoever, due to the majestic spiritual power of Avalokiteśvara.
If one wishes to invite the various bodhisattvas, one must first perform this samādhi seal and mantra; thus one shall obtain the joy of all bodhisattvas.

2. The Body Seal (Kāyamudrā), Second: Join the wrists. The two thumbs of both hands stand side by side. Bend the middle joints of the two index fingers, each pressing its tip against the tip of a thumb. The tips of the two middle fingers touch one another. The two ring fingers stand straight, separated by one and a half inches. Open the two little fingers, leaving a distance of about one-tenth of an inch from the backs of the ring fingers. Keep the two elbows touching. Move the index fingers back and forth while reciting the Great Mantra above.
If one can maintain this Dharma-seal mantra, there will be no fear regarding any of the eight difficulties.
When performing the altar ritual and making formal offerings, one should use this seal-mantra while burning sesame seeds and other substances.
If there is an illness caused by spirits, by means of this seal and mantra, that illness will be cured immediately;

if it is not cured, one should recite the mantra and perform the seal one hundred and eight times while contemplating Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. For one who performs this rite, the illness will be cured immediately.

"If one washes their hands every day and chews on a willow branch, rinses the mouth until it is clean, puts on fresh and pure clothing, recites the mantra a full one hundred and eight times while also mindful of the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—one who performs this rite shall cause Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to rejoice."

Furthermore, take a ritual water jar (*śītalikā*) and fill it with pure water; seal it with this mudrā while reciting the mantra twenty-one times. After letting it sit overnight, use it to wash your hands and face; no evil persons, ghosts, spirits, or the like will be able to cause you harm.

3. The Great Heart-Seal Mantra, Third: "Following the previous body-seal, change only this: press the two index fingers upon the upper joints of the middle fingers; with the two thumbs, each press the side of the middle joint of the middle finger, moving the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is as follows:

“Oṃ ārya vairocanīya bodhisattva mahāsattva mahākāruṇika tadyathā hā hā hā hā īlī milī cilī vilī khilī helī svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. When performing any ritual involving a maṇḍala, one should use this seal-mantra to consecrate water, incense, flowers, robes, food, and other such items; it is also used when summoning the devas and others.

4. The Mantra of the Caṇḍālī Mudrā, Chapter Four: "Following the previous body mudrā, change only this: bend the tips of the two index fingers against the side of the middle joints of the middle fingers; the index fingers then move back and forth."
The mantra is as follows:

“Nama āryāya | Varakīrtiśabarāya | Bodhisattvāya | Mahāsattvāya | Mahākāruṇikāya | Tadyathā | Durdur dudur | Ha ha ha ha | Svāhā. If anyone recites and maintains this Dharma-seal mantra, [they shall attain... (Note: The Sanskrit transliteration provided in the source text contains several non-standard characters and phoneticizations;
the above rendering attempts to restore a plausible Sanskrit form based on the context of Mahayana dhāraṇīs.)
One should seek one hundred and eight stalks of lotus flowers,
bathe in river water,
and put on fresh, clean garments.
He returned to the river water,
where it reached his knees,
and stood facing directly east.
Having performed this mudrā and mantra, invite Avalokiteśvara;
as the thumb moves back and forth,
immediately form the sitting mudrā and place it before you.
With the left hand holding the prayer beads and the right hand grasping the flower,
recite the mantra seven times.
Thereafter, scatter them over Avalokiteśvara.
Recite the mantra seven times over each flower in this manner until all one hundred and eight stalks have been exhausted; immediately thereafter, one shall behold the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
If one cannot obtain one hundred and eight flowers in a single day, one should seek out five stalks of lotus flowers on that day to use for this rite.
In this manner, taking five stalks of flowers each day until the total reaches one hundred and eight, the performance of the rite is the same as before.
One should also use this mantra to consecrate the incense that is burned and the oil for the lamps, thereby making offerings.

5. The Jaṭāmukuṭa Seal Mantra, Fifth. In the Tang language: "Long Hair. Following the previous body seal, change only this: bend the middle joints of the two middle fingers so that their tips touch, placing them against the upper joint on the inner side of the ring fingers.
The mantra is as follows:

“Oṃ ārya vairocanīya bodhisattva mahāsattva mahākāruṇika tadyathā siri siri siri diri diri diri siri svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. Whether dwelling in a village or in the mountains, in a place free from clamor, where there are flowering trees, fruit trees, bamboo groves, and a pond, one should build a hut in the center of the water, bathe daily, and enter the maṇḍala.
Having first completed the mudrās for protecting the body and delimiting the boundary, invoke Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and perform the Flower Seat Mudrā to establish him upon his seat.

Then, having lit three lamps and finished making offerings of various incenses and flowers, as well as performing prostrations and praises, hold the prayer beads and single-mindedly recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
If a person performs this dhāraṇī rite daily for one hundred thousand recitations, they will immediately behold Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when entering a maṇḍala to offer flowers, incense, and garlands, one should first empower the flowers with this dhāraṇī seven times and scatter them over the image; then empower the incense seven times and apply it to the venerable image; and again empower the garlands seven times to adorn the venerable image.

6. The Mantra and Mudrā of the Flower Throne (Puṣpāsana-mudrā-mantra), Number Six. "Join the two forearms together; interlock the left and right thumbs and little fingers respectively and extend them upward. Leave the remaining three fingers all spread apart and fully extended. Thus it is formed."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ hūṃ kāmarā svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; whether one invites the Buddhas, Prajñāpāramitā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, or devas, for each one, this Great Flower Throne Seal-mantra is used to welcome them.

Seated upon it while turning the mudrā clockwise, once comfort and concentration have been established, one subsequently performs the Vajra-Caṇḍālī Samaya-mudrā to seal and close the gates and portals with strict secrecy; thereafter, one performs various ritual acts of offering.
The construction of altars, the healing of illnesses, and all other dharmas should be performed in this manner.

7. The Mudrā and Dhāraṇī for Avalokiteśvara’s Protection of the Body, Chapter Seven. "Following the previous body-mudrā, change only this: interlace the two ring fingers behind the backs of the middle fingers; place their tips above the first joints on the front side, ensuring the tips touch one another, and likewise let the tips of the two little fingers touch."
The mantra is as follows:

“Nama āryāya, vairocanīye, śabarāya, bodhisattvāya, mahāsattvāya, mahākāruṇikāya, tadyathā, sate saci, sate sate, sūdu sūdu, svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. When a practitioner of this dharma intends to perform various rites or recite mantras, they should use this seal to protect their body; only then should they perform the rite. Thus, Avalokiteśvara will come to protect the practitioner, ensuring that all performed rites are efficacious.
Furthermore, if one wishes to present offerings with this seal-mantra, one should first recite it.
One should consecrate the various flavors of food, drink, flowers, fruits, and so forth twenty-one times with the mantra, and only then present them as an offering.

8. The *Bharadvāja-mudrā-mantra*, the eighth. In the Tang language: "Following the Mind. "Stand up on the ground with the feet in the shape of a 'T'—the heel of the left foot at the head of the right foot's 'T', and the head of the right foot at the heel of the left foot's 'T'—with the right knee slightly bent."

Bend the left arm at the elbow so that the arm points toward the shoulder and the palm faces the body; grasp the flower stem with the thumb and index finger, bend the middle and ring fingers together without touching the stem, slightly curl the little finger, and flex the wrist.
Extend the right arm fully and point it downward, with the back of the palm resting against the side of the right thigh, but not touching the thigh itself.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ ārya vairocanīya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā asite site hulu hulu suru suru svāhā. This is the dharma-seal mantra; if one seeks the efficacy of the dharma, one should kindle a fire using *sumana* stalks.

Furthermore, separately take thirty-one segments of *sumana* stems, each about one inch long. Mix three substances—ghee, curd, and honey—and for each segment, individually coat the *sumana* stem with ghee, curd, and honey. Recite the mantra once and cast it into the fire. In this manner, burn all thirty-one segments in succession; by doing so, one will immediately obtain great efficacy.

"If a child falls ill, take thread of five colors and, for every recitation of the mantra, tie a knot; once thirty-seven knots have been made, fasten them around the child's neck. The mantra-practitioner shall then form this mudrā with his hand and seal the child’s nape; the illness will then be cured."
If the mantra-practitioner himself falls ill, he should first construct a water-maṇḍala, two cubits in length and breadth.
At the center of this maṇḍala, he should place a single water jar, filled to the brim with pure water, into which he places the five grains; he then seals the mouth of the jar with a willow branch.

When the boundary has been established, face due west and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times with single-minded concentration. Then, lift the jar and pour its contents over the crown of your head. Next, employ this left-hand mudrā as a protection seal, sealing seven places on the body; thus, the illness will be cured.
Furthermore, use this mantra to consecrate the fire for burning fuel. **The Ninth: The Mantra of Avalokiteśvara’s Staff Seal (Danda-mudrā)** [In Chinese:

*Cezhang*] "Cross the two middle fingers and ring fingers behind the palms, with the right hand pressing over the left. Bend the tip of the right index finger and press its nail against the tip of the left little finger. Bend the left thumb into the right palm. Bend the right thumb and press it against the middle joint of the left thumb, tucking its tip into the left palm. Extend the right little finger and the left index finger straight out, with the elbows of both arms touching."
The mantra says:

“Oṃ ārya vairocanaya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā iri miri ciri hiri svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. Having bathed with fragrant water and donned fresh, clean garments, enter the maṇḍala. Send forth a disciple to fetch incense, flowers, water, fire, grass, and white mustard seeds. The Ācārya silently protects his own body, recites the mantra over the water seven times, and scatters it in the ten directions to establish the boundary.
Next, recite the mantra over white mustard seeds seven times; having finished the recitation, scatter them to bind the boundary in the ten directions.
Next, hold the grass and recite the mantra seven times, then light a fire and circumambulate it three times to the right to bind the boundary in the four directions.
Next, form this mudrā and recite the mantra seven times to invite Avalokiteśvara, then perform the Flower Seat Mudrā.
Once the placement is complete, burn incense, scatter flowers, and finish making offerings of various superior flavors of food and drink, as well as prostrations; then dismiss the disciples.

The ācārya does not count the rosary but recites the mantra silently; sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), he forms with his hands the *ratnadaṇḍamudrā* before his chest, ensuring it does not touch his breast, while mentally keeping track of the mantra recitation.
"Practicing thus day after day for a full seven days, one immediately attains the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) and one's karmic obstructions are extinguished;
on the second seven-day period, by further performing this rite and making various offerings with sounds, one immediately attains śamatha;
on the third seven-day period, by further performing this rite and making various offerings..."

In this manner, for seven days, there is one specific occurrence each day: on the first day, one does not eat; the practitioner who performs this rite and recites the mantra shall smell various fragrances. On the second day, they see a great radiance. On the third day, they are able to see ghosts and spirits. On the fourth day, they see the Four Heavenly Kings. On the fifth day, they see the various devas. On the sixth day, they see the bodies of the various messengers of Avalokiteśvara. On the seventh day, they are able to see the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara himself.
If one performs this rite with a mind of equanimity, out of compassion for all sentient beings, such a verification shall be attained.
Furthermore, one may also use this mudrā to recite mantras and bind the boundary.

10. The Mantra of Avalokiteśvara’s Amṛta Seal, Chapter Ten "Join the left and right little fingers and ring fingers together and extend them straight upward. Extend the middle fingers straight upward, placing them against the side of the ring fingers with their tips separated by about two finger-widths. Separate each of the two index fingers and place them upon the backs of the middle fingers, with their tips aligned with the upper joints. Place both thumbs together, bent into the palms, with their tips resting against the middle joints of the two ring fingers. Bring the two wrists together and place the base of the two wrists at the level of the heart, with the palms hanging downward."
The mantra says: "Oṃ ārye..."

“Svāhā. Fifteenth. “This is the Dharma-seal mantra. When you have finished performing the rites for the practice of the Way and request my return to the palace, seal the water with this seal and recite the mantra over it seven times, then sprinkle it in the four directions; I shall then depart.”
“World-Honored One!

Although this divine mantra does not establish [anything in itself], it can accomplish various tasks; if one recites and contemplates it with a sincere heart, there is no wish that will not be fulfilled.”
"If one suffers from malaria—whether it manifests once every day, once every two days, once every three days, or once every four days;

or if one suffers from demonic illness, being struck by an evil spirit, struck by Hārītī, or afflicted by the actions of a Cāmuṇḍī, a Piśāca, a Kaṭapūtana, a mad spirit, a Rākṣasa, a seizure-demon, or any other various kinds of malevolent spirits—one should seal the patient with this mudrā and mantra. By reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, the ailment shall be immediately cured."

If one's karmic obstacles are heavy, take five-colored threads and for each mantra recited, tie a knot; having thus tied one hundred and eight knots, fasten them around the neck or upon the arm of the patient. The karmic obstacles will be extinguished and the illness will immediately be cured.

"If one suffers from carbuncles or epilepsy, or bodily ailments such as sores, boils, ulcers, scabs, and various other malignant lesions; or if one is wounded by knives, arrows, spears, or lances; or if one is stung by snakes, scorpions, centipedes, or venomous bees—one shall recite this mantra over them seven times, and they will immediately be healed."
If the obstacles are heavy, recite the mantra over yellow clay seven times and apply it to the afflicted area; one will then be cured.

If one suffers from wind-related illnesses—such as paralysis, hemiplegia, or tetanus—or from ailments such as facial palsy, convulsions, deafness, or nasal congestion, seal the affected area with the mudrā and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times with a sincere mind; the illness will then be cured.

If the obstacles are heavy, one should use sesame oil or cow’s ghee mixed with birch bark to prepare a decoction, or use *agaru* (sandalwood) mixed with sesame oil to prepare an ointment. By reciting this seal-mantra seven times over it each time, and then applying it to the body, dripping it into the ears or nose, or having it ingested, the illness will be immediately cured.
"If there are any other various illnesses, one should seal the site of the ailment with this mudrā and recite the mantra with a sincere heart; it will then be cured.

The spiritual power of this mantra is inexhaustible. If a practitioner of the Dharma, during the course of making offerings, must perform this mudrā and place it upon the heart while reciting this mantra, then out of compassion for all sentient beings, they bestow nectar upon all ghosts and spirits. All ghosts and spirits will then be greatly delighted, and they shall not cause any sentient beings to suffer from illness."

11. The Mudrā for Counting the Rosary (Akṣamālā-mudrā), Number Eleven: "Form a hole by pressing the tip of the left thumb against the tip of the ring finger; pass the rosary beads through this hole. Extend the middle finger straight and bend the tip of the index finger over the middle phalanx of the middle finger’s back. Extend the little finger straight. With the right hand, use the thumb and ring finger to grasp the beads, while the remaining fingers remain as on the left hand. There is no separate mantra for this; this mudrā is universally applicable to all mantras."

If one recites this mantra every day while forming this mudrā, mindfulness of the Buddha, and repentance, one will attain the four dhyānas and swiftly achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, with all vows fulfilled according to one's wishes.

12. The *Kuntī-mudrā* Mantra, the Twelfth. “Join the left and right wrists; from beneath the index fingers, let the tips of the four fingers touch one another. Place both thumbs side by side, bending them into the palms, and leave the center of the palms open.”
The mantra is as follows:

“Oṃ ārya vairocanatejorāja bodhisattva mahāsattva mahākāruṇika tadyathā siddhe vilokite aśuci śuci pāpame śvāhā. If one is unable to bathe every day, by washing the hands and rinsing the mouth each day and forming this mudrā while reciting the aforementioned mantra, although one has not bathed, it is as if one has bathed; the body will become exceedingly pure and clean.

"Upon entering the maṇḍala, one should protect the body and establish the boundary, then invoke Avalokiteśvara. Having formed this mudrā and recited the mantra twenty-one times, all Buddhas, Avalokiteśvara, Prajñā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and devas will all be greatly delighted."

The mantra says: "Oṃ ārye."

“Svāhā. (12) “If a woman who has no child desires to obtain one, she should construct a four-cubit altar using five-colored powders. In the center of the altar, she should place an image of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; in the east, Amitābha Buddha; in the north, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva; in the south, Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; and in the west, the Heavenly King Maheśvara.”

Take one pure jar and fill it with pure water; place five kinds of grain within it and seal its mouth with willow branches and the like. Further, bind those willow branches with fresh silk and adorn the jar with various beautiful flowers, then immediately place this jar within the mandala.

Hang banners of various colors; open four gates at the altar and light sixteen lamps. Furthermore, make offerings with all kinds of exquisite incense, flowers, and twelve platters of food. Outside each of the four gates, place a musical ensemble of fine and delicate sounds—if one cannot provide this, a single ensemble will suffice.

"Once the offerings have been meticulously prepared, the mantra-practitioner bathes, puts on fresh and clean robes, and sits outside the western gate of the altar facing east. He forms mudrās to invite Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Amitābha Buddha, and the others; having invited them in succession, each is established in their respective position."
He had the woman bathe in fragrant water, put on fresh and clean garments, and prepared a great lotus seat outside the western gate, upon which he spread fresh, pure grass.

Next, the ācārya holds a vajra in his right hand and takes the woman’s right hand with his left; he leads her to stand outside the northern gate of the maṇḍala. The ācārya recites the mantra twenty-one times with a sincere mind and instructs the woman to likewise recite the name of that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva twenty-one times with a sincere mind.

In this manner, next, having recited the names of Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Hayagrīva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, and King Maheśvara, have the woman perform three prostrations with a sincere heart, making vows and requesting for the child.
The ācārya, using thread of five colors, recites a mantra once for each knot until thirty-seven knots are formed, and ties them around the woman’s neck.
Next, he instructs the woman to sit upon a bed of flowers and grass and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva one hundred and eight times.
Next, the ācārya places his right hand upon the water jar, holds a rosary in his left hand, and recites the mantra over the water jar one thousand and eight times until it is completed.
Next, perform the protection of the woman's person and the establishment of the boundary.
Then, the Ācārya holds a water jar in his hand while standing beside the woman and makes this vow, saying aloud:

"I reverently invoke all Buddhas of the ten directions, the assembly of Bodhisattvas and holy multitudes, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, and all spirits and ghosts; may you bear witness with your knowledge of others' minds that today this upāsikā desires to conceive and give birth to a fine son or daughter. I pray that through your great compassion, you will swiftly fulfill her wish."

The woman joined her palms and called upon Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; the ācārya then poured water over her head, and she immediately gave birth to a son or daughter who was intelligent, handsome, and endowed with all the marks of excellence.
All methods for seeking and fulfilling wishes are likewise: according to one's vows, all shall bear fruit.

After performing the ritual, have the woman burn incense and pay homage while reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva without interruption; her wishes will surely be fulfilled, except in cases of a lack of sincere devotion.

“Svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. Every day, whether one has bathed or—if one has not bathed—has merely washed one’s hands and rinsed one’s mouth, one should enter the *maṇḍala*, form the mudrā, and recite the mantra. 17. The Mantra of the Avalokiteśvara Wheel Seal, Chapter Seventeen. "First, turn the left palm upward with the five fingers slightly curved and spread apart; do the same with the right hand. Next, place the right hand inverted over the left, pressing the tip of the right little finger against the tip of the left thumb, and the tip of the right thumb against the tip of the left little finger."
The mantra is as follows:

“Oṃ, Āryā, Vairocanīye, Bodhisattvāye, Mahāsattvāye, Mahākāruṇikāye, Tadyathā, Catre, Cakre, Mahācakre, Cakredhāri, Cakriṇi, Dhara dhara, Svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If a person daily performs this seal-method and mantra-offering, even if another should give rise to an evil mind and perform other rites intending to harm the mantra-practitioner, that evil will instead fall back upon the evil-doer.
If one constructs a *maṇḍala* for the establishment of the Buddha-dharma or a place for practicing the Way, one should form this seal and recite the mantra;

then no evil beings will be able to invade or harass them. 18. The Flower Garland Seal and Mantra of Avalokiteśvara, Number Eighteen. "First, join the two forearms together. Align the left and right thumbs and little fingers and extend them. Each of the two index fingers should touch the side of its respective thumb, opening about three finger-widths. The two ring fingers should also touch the side of their respective little fingers, their tips opening about four finger-widths. The middle fingers are held upright, their tips opening about two inches."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ āryā vairocanīye bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā dhara dhara pramācintye arugaye virugaye svāhā.
If a person desires to seek wealth by means of this Dharma-seal mantra, [they shall attain it].
Every day, having bathed and arisen,
one should enter the *maṇḍala*,
burn incense, scatter flowers, and perform various kinds of offerings.
Take one water jar, fill it to the brim with pure water,
adorn its neck with various flower garlands,
and stopper its mouth with branches of willow, cypress, or bamboo.
Place this water jar within the mandala,
fill it with the five grains,
and let the mantra-reciter rest his left hand upon the rim of the jar.
Holding the prayer beads with the right hand,
recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while focusing on the heart;
do this every day in this manner.
Upon seeing Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one immediately obtains wealth and resources. 19.

The Mantra of the Spear-Mudrā of Avalokiteśvara (Avalokiteśvara-śakti-mudrā-mantra), Chapter Nineteen. First, bend the left little finger; press the left thumb against the nail of the little finger to form a hollow. Next, hook the right little finger over the left little finger, and insert the right thumb from below upward into the hollow of the left palm, pressing against the nail of the little finger so that it resembles a hook-and-chain. The three fingers on each side should be held straight and upright with their tips touching; they must be kept close together and not opened.
When making offerings, keep the two elbows joined;
when treating illness, separate the joints of the two elbows.
The mantra is as follows:

"Oṃ ārya vairocanīye bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā mṛta mṛta bandha bandha bindha bindha huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra (*dhāraṇī*). If one can daily burn incense, form the mudrā, and recite this mantra, all rites will attain divine efficacy, and one will gain great power.

Twelve. “Regarding this Dharma-seal mantra: if a mantra-practitioner, while preparing medicine to take himself, has it suddenly snatched away by a ghost or spirit, he should construct a white water-mandala four cubits in size. At the center of the mandala, he should place a fire-pit and make offerings of incense, flowers, and food according to his means. While burning white mustard seeds and reciting the mantra repeatedly, the medicine taken by the spirit will immediately fall back onto the mandala.”
If one does not obtain the medicine within one day, but performs this rite for up to seven days, one will immediately obtain it.
Whether compounding the medicine for oneself or for another, one should prepare the altar as previously described, burn white mustard seeds, and recite the mantra repeatedly.

When these medicines are compounded, malevolent spirits and poisons cannot find an opportunity; all the medicines thus prepared will be fully effective, and those who take them shall have their illnesses completely cured.

21. The Pāśa-mudrā of Avalokiteśvara, the Twenty-first. First, bend the left ring finger and little finger, and with the thumb press upon the nails to form a hollow. Next, insert the right thumb from below into this hollow and grasp it with the remaining four fingers. Press the tip of the right thumb against the nails of the four fingers. Keep the left index and middle fingers straight and erect.
Using this great mantra to bind demons and cure diseases—if evil spirits wish to stop [the practitioner] from practicing, one who performs this rite will immediately cause them to cease and desist;
as for all ghosts and spirits who are difficult to subdue, by binding them with this seal, one cures all illnesses, which has proven to be of great efficacy;
if one engages in debate with others, one who performs this rite will cause the opponent to become tongue-tied and unable to respond.
All binding dharmas employ this seal; if one wishes to release them, by forming the mental perception of "releasing," one immediately attains liberation.

22. The Śaṅkha Seal Mantra of Avalokiteśvara, Number Twenty-Two. "Interlace the left and right index fingers and middle fingers within the palms. Place the left and right ring fingers and little fingers side-by-side, straight and upright, touching each other. Bend both thumbs together so that their tips press against the sides of the index fingers, and join the wrists."
The mantra is as follows:

“Oṃ ārya vairocanīya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā kuru kuru vidrāvaya samaye sthāpaya svāhā. If a mantra-practitioner recites this Dharma-seal mantra and, despite applying diligent effort, fails to obtain spiritual efficacy or is unable to behold the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, they should construct a water-maṇḍala four cubits in length and breadth, adorned with various ornaments.
Take one water jar and fill it with pure water; adorn the jar according to the ritual methods as previously described without variation.

Place this water jar within the mandala, bathe with fragrant water, and don new, clean garments. Enter the practice hall and perform various offerings: light sixteen lamps, burn incense of *kunduruka*, and with a sincere heart, confess all karmic obstructions while kneeling on the right knee and forming the mudrā.
When one recites this mantra one thousand and eight times, one will immediately behold Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and obtain great spiritual efficacy.
If no sign of efficacy is obtained after one day, then by the completion of seven days, one will certainly obtain spiritual efficacy.

"If a practitioner of meditation fails to attain *śamatha* and is thus harassed by all manner of spirits and ghosts, or if wind enters the body causing loss of mental resolve, one should construct an altar as previously described, begin from dawn, abstain from food for one day, and form this mudrā."

If, while walking on the path, one recollects the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, or while sitting performs mudrās and recites the mantra with a sincere mind without limit to the number of repetitions, one will obtain spiritual efficacy upon completing a full day.

23. The Śvāsa-mudrā Mantra (The Twenty-third). In Chinese, it is called "Emitting Light" (*fangguang*), also known as "Flame Light" (*huoyanguang*). "Bend the left arm upward, extend the palm vertically, and place it against the right side. With the right hand, form a fist with the fingers curled inward, placing it beneath the left wrist on the inner surface of the forearm, with the knuckles facing upward."
The mantra is as follows:

"Oṃ, ārya, vairocanīya, bodhisattva, mahāsattva, mahākāruṇika, tadyathā, agne, agne, mahāgne, vyalikari, svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. When establishing a *maṇḍala*, once this seal has been formed, one should circumambulate the four directions while reciting the mantra. When the count reaches twenty-one times, the fire-element realm is established and the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) is accomplished.
If one suffers from a demonic affliction that cannot be cured by other methods, performing this mudrā and reciting this mantra will cause the illness to be immediately healed.

24. The Great Heart Mudrā and Mantra of Avalokiteśvara. Second and Twenty-fourth: "Cross the four fingers of both hands behind the palms. Next, bend the tip of the left thumb and insert it into the palm; extend the right thumb straight, pressing against the side of the left index finger. Join the wrists, and move the right thumb back and forth."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ ārya vairocanīya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā oṃ aruḷ svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If a ghost or spirit transforms its appearance—whether taking the form of a large predator, a wild fox, or various other bodies—and enters a person’s body to cause illness, one should perform this mudrā and recite the mantra; the patient will then be cured.

"One should construct a circular water altar one cubit in diameter; take five bowls of the five pure substances and fill them with pure water—one placed in the center and one in each of the four directions—and furthermore, place a dish of food at the center of the altar."
Perform this rite at night, bringing the patient near the edge of the altar and having them sit facing east. Form the mudrā and recite the mantra twenty-one times.
Furthermore, take another jar and pour into it the water from the five bowls within the altar as well as the contents of the food plate, mixing them all together thoroughly.
The mantra-master holds [the vessel] in his hand and circumambulates the patient three times to the right.
Having gazed at the patient from a distance, he then places the jar upon the patient’s crown and pours out [the contents] toward the south.

When performing this rite, both the mantra-practitioner and the patient shall face east; the patient shall sit down. If the rite is performed for three days and the illness is cured, it was indeed caused by a spirit;
if it is not cured, then it is not a spirit-induced illness.
"If a person constantly performs this Dharma-offering for all Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will see them and rejoice greatly.

If one invokes the various Bodhisattvas with this seal and makes offerings to them, they will all be able to assist in accomplishing the power of Avalokiteśvara’s Dharma, and success will be swiftly attained."

25. The Mantra of the Flower-Sprinkling Seal of Avalokiteśvara, Number Twenty-Five. "Place the left and right palms facing upward and side by side, touching along their edges. Extend the left and right little fingers, ring fingers, and middle fingers in a row, keeping them close together without separating them."
Next, slightly bend the tips of the left and right index fingers and press them against the sides of the upper joints of the middle fingers.
Then, each thumb is individually bent at its tip and pressed against the sides of the lower joints of the index fingers, ensuring they do not touch the palms.
This seal is used universally for two dhāraṇīs. The first mantra is as follows:

“Oṃ ārya vairocanīye bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā oṃ pramudita-prabhāye svāhā. This dharma-seal mantra, when constructing any altar of Avalokiteśvara or other altars, one should place flowers within the seal and scatter them as an offering.

If one reaches the presence of the Buddha or various Dharma assemblies and forms mudrās, holding flowers and scattering them before the Buddhas and before Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara as an offering, one should maintain within the mind the thought of extinguishing all sins.
Furthermore, another mantra says:
"Namaḥ sarvabuddhadharmasaṃghebhyo nama āryebhyaḥ."

“This dharma-seal mantra is named the Mahāpuṣpābhikīrṇa-mudrā-dhāraṇī. If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or sons and daughters of good family who uphold this treasury of dharma-seal dhāraṇīs and various divine mantras, wherever they may be within the assemblies of all Buddhas, that place shall be a universal site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Forming this dharma-seal and holding various colored flowers and incense within the seal, they should praise and recite the aforementioned mantra.”

Having recited this three times, one scatters flowers and incense upon the assemblies of all Buddhas. Performing various rites, one extols and praises them with modulated melodies, circumambulates and prostrates, and produces sounds such as the Brahma-voice, the lute, and the chanting of hymns. These diverse sounds penetrate and blend with celestial music to enhance the resonance, naturally moving the hearts of all the Buddhas and their holy multitudes throughout the ten directions.
May all Buddhas who hear this give rise to joy, delighting in being together in one place and always acting as companions;
may all Prajñās and Bodhisattvas who hear this universally vow that sentient beings remain far removed from the evil realms, swiftly ascend to the other shore, and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and may all Bodhisattvas who hear this sound dance and leap for joy, attesting to and praising it, and augmenting its power.

"If one praises others at the time of their death, all Bodhisattvas will come to welcome them; the praiser shall not undergo the eight difficulties and will enter directly into the assembly of Buddhas.
All Vajras who hear this sound will give rise to joy, universally wishing that all Buddhas constantly practice compassion to rescue all sentient beings;
all devas who hear this sound will give rise to exultation, wishing that all sentient beings always experience peace and happiness."
All those on the paths of karma who hear this sound shall have all restrictive laws relaxed and great, vast grace bestowed upon them.

Sentient beings in the hells who hear this sound shall find their instruments of torture and shackles shattered all at once; the boiling cauldrons and burning furnaces shall cease their seething and flaming, becoming cool and blissful, the icy cold shall become warm, and the River of Ashes shall dry up.
"To state the essentials:
all those in the various hells will naturally be liberated from all their sufferings;

and all spirits and ghosts who hear this sound will all resolve to attain Bodhicitta, leave their bodies as spirits and ghosts, and be reborn among humans and devas to encounter the Buddhas and hear the Dharma."
All hungry ghosts who hear this sound shall receive the nectar of immortality; their food and drink will be fully provided, and they will no longer have thoughts of hunger or thirst.

All animals who hear this sound shall constantly attain peace and happiness, cease to experience the suffering of enmity, and immediately cast off their animal bodies; after their lives end, they shall follow the Buddha and receive his prediction of enlightenment.

Furthermore, when the practitioner performs this rite, all the Buddhas of the Dharma-realm—each Tathāgata, each Prajñā, each Bodhisattva, each Vajra, and each Deva, Nāga, and even the eight classes of spirits and deities—will individually bring forth various jewels, incense, flowers, necklaces, and ornaments; as well as banners, pennants, exquisite jeweled canopies, various decorative implements, diverse musical instruments, and manifold foods and drinks that fill the entirety of space, all joining together to assist the practitioner in making offerings.
Thus, when a practitioner forms mudrās and recites mantras, they praise and perfect the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattvas; such is their merit.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, every morning after washing their hands and face, stands before a sacred image with palms joined and single-mindedly recites the mantra three times, this surpasses the merit of making offerings of various incenses, flowers, and food to ten trillion Buddhas—how much more so for one who forms mudrās and makes offerings according to the Dharma?
The spiritual power of this mantra cannot be fully described; here it is explained only briefly. 26.

The Seal and Mantra for Prostration (Lī-bai-yin-zhou), Chapter Twenty-Six. "Sitting with both feet and knees touching the ground, first join the palms. Interlace all the fingers of both hands, keeping them level and even, with the right hand pressing over the left."

Having completed this mudrā, prostrate to Avalokiteśvara and pay homage to the Triple Gem; then, slowly lowering both knees to the ground, sit firmly and perform a full prostration with the head touching the earth.
The mantra says: "Oṃ ārye."
