“Svāhā, twelve. “This Dharma-seal mantra: if one constructs a *maṇḍala* or performs regular offerings, whenever one encounters a gathering of Buddhas and rejoices therein, one should form this seal, recite the mantra with a sincere mind, and praise the Triple Gem by performing a single prostration. All the Buddhas throughout the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and the *koṭis* of worlds, will all grant one a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). This shall extinguish and utterly eliminate the karmic obstacles of ten thousand lifetimes, leaving nothing behind.”

At the time of death, all the Buddhas whom one has venerated will come to welcome them; they shall cut across the path of karma, avoid all hardships, and enter directly into the assembly of Buddhas, where they will certainly realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and attain the stage of non-retrogression.

27. Viśvavāraka Seal (The Twenty-Seventh Viśvavāraka Seal; translated into Chinese as the "Gan-kuo-zi" [Sweet Fruit] Seal): "Join the two forearms together. Join the tips of the four fingers from the index finger downward on both left and right hands. Open the centers of the palms. Extend both thumbs straight upward, with their tips each resting upon the middle joint of the respective index finger. Then, bend them downward so that they emerge beneath the lower joints of the backs of the left and right palms."
This mudrā is the same as the aforementioned mudrā for the beggar mantra. 28. The Vajrāsana Mudrā (Vijurita-mudrā), the twenty-eighth;

in the Tang language, it is called the "Wrathful Mudrā. For the first face: Stand up with the big toes touching. Bend the little finger of the left hand and press the thumb against its nail. Spread the remaining three fingers straight out and place them horizontally across the forehead. With the right hand, cross the webbed space (the "tiger's mouth") at the side of the right waist, with the four fingers pointing forward. Form a wrathful expression on the face.

This is the Dharma-seal mantra; if one performs this seal, all evil Māras and non-Buddhists will be subdued and one shall have no fear. Wherever this seal is established, all ghosts and spirits shall forever cease to exist.

29. The Seal of Leaving Behind Pride (Līlā-mudrā), the Twenty-ninth. In Chinese, it is called the Seal of Arrogance. On the second face: "In accordance with the previous [instructions], change only this: bend the three fingers from the middle finger of the left hand into the palm; bend the index finger at its middle joint so that its tip is level with the tip of the thumb, leaving a space of about two inches. Place it above the space between the eyebrows with the fingertips pointing downward. Maintain a broad and gracious expression on the face; do not make a look of anger."
This is the Dharmakāya Seal. If one performs this rite, all sentient beings of the six realms shall be liberated from all suffering and hardship.

30. The Vajra-krodha Seal (The Great Wrath Seal). Third Face. As before, with the sole modification that the left thumb is bent toward the palm; the three fingers below the middle finger are bent to grasp the thumb; the index finger is extended straight, its tip pointing toward the mouth but not touching it; the mouth, tongue, and index finger move simultaneously; and the face is made wrathful as if to destroy the *sahasralokadhātu*. One assumes the form of great wrath.
This Dharma-body seal is also called Vīryakuñjiya. By performing this rite, all ghost-induced illnesses will be completely cured.

31. The Śāta Seal (The Thirty-first). In Chinese it is called the "Seal of the Softened Heart. Regarding the fourth face: "As before, stand upon the ground; place the left hand at the side of the left waist. With the right hand, bend the index, ring, and little fingers toward the palm, and press the thumb down upon the index and ring fingers. Extend the middle finger straight to touch the space between the eyebrows, with the tip of the middle finger pointing downward. Maintain a broad and gracious expression on the face; do not show a form of anger."

This is the Seal of the Dharma Body. If a person performs this seal-rite every day, offering incense and making offerings, they will receive the joy of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and whatever they desire shall all be fulfilled according to their wishes.

32. The Arudhara Seal (The Third-Twelfth). Translated into Chinese as the "Great Anger Seal. For the fifth face: Stand on the ground as before, but change only the right hand. Hold the middle finger straight and upright; place the tip of the index finger across the back of the middle finger, with its head aligned with the upper joint. Slightly bend the ring finger and little finger together, and the tips of the middle and ring fingers should be separated by about two inches. Hold the thumb straight up, with the tip of the thumb and the tip of the middle finger separated by about four inches. Place the tip of the thumb upon the crown of the head, while the tip of the middle finger points forward without touching the head.
This is the Dharma-body Seal (Dharmakāya-mudrā). If one forms this seal, all evil persons, malevolent spirits, and the like will have their minds transformed, turning toward a wholesome state.

33. The *Tatpūrṇaśani* Seal (The Thirty-third). In Chinese, it is called the "Seal for Breaking and Leveling Obstacles," also known as the "Seal for Rebuking and Expelling. Regarding the sixth face: "As before, stand upon the ground; however, change only the right hand by bending the elbow joint so that it extends outward at an angle, fully extending all five fingers with the palms held flat against each other. Position the side of the thumb against the chest, ensuring it does not actually touch the chest. This is the Dharma-body Seal."
If treating a disease caused by ghosts, one should immediately strike to the right with this seal-palm.

If one burns incense and forms this seal every day, one will receive the joy of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; all evil obstacles and difficulties will be extinguished without remainder, and all malevolent spirits and ghosts will be unable to approach or find any opportunity for harm.

34. Yamāntaka Seal (The Thirty-Fourth). In Chinese, this is called the "Seal of Attaining Victory. For the seventh face: "As before, stand upon the ground. With both left and right hands, bend each thumb into the palm; with the three fingers below the middle finger of each hand, grasp the thumbs. Bring the tips of the left and right index fingers together on their outer sides. Bring the middle phalanges of the backs of the three fingers below the middle finger of each hand together. Turn the seal upward above the eyebrows, with the tips of the index fingers hanging downward."
This is the Seal of the Foremost Dharma; if one forms this seal, all ghosts, spirits, devas, and so forth will be subdued and struck with fear, and it should be used for curing diseases.

35. The Vijaya Seal (Vijaya-mudrā), the thirty-fifth; translated into Chinese as "The Most Victorious Seal" (*Zuisheng yin*). Regarding the eighth face: "One should stand upright with the two feet separated by about two chi. The toes should be aligned side-by-side. Bend the middle joints of the middle fingers of both hands so that they rest within the palms. Next, place the two thumbs side-by-side pressing down upon them. The tips of the index, ring, and little fingers of both hands should all touch one another, while the sides of these three fingers are spread apart. Join the wrists and place the lower joints of the two thumbs against the forehead, with the tips of the fingers pointing upward."

This is the Seal of the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya-mudrā*). If, when constructing a great merit-field (*puṇyakṣetra*) or a ritual altar (*maṇḍala*), great clouds and rain arise or a great wind blows, one should form this seal and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Taking powdered salt mixed with white mustard seeds, one should cast a pinch of it into the fire with each recitation of the mantra; the clouds, wind, and rain will then cease immediately.
If a disciple who has entered the maṇḍala is possessed by a ghost such that they fall ill, if one performs the burning ritual as described above, the illness will be cured immediately.

If, while performing the rite, there is fear that wicked people may come to disturb or harass [the practitioner], if one performs the burning ritual as described above, the wicked people will depart and will certainly give rise to wholesome minds.
"When the ritual is completed and you wish to release [the seal], recite the mantra over clarified butter (*ghṛta*) once for each repetition and cast it into the fire;

after one hundred and eight repetitions, you will be released. 36. The *Amṛta-mudrā* (The Seal of the Incomparable), the Thirty-sixth. In the Chinese language: *Wúnéngyā yìn* (Seal of the Unconquerable). Regarding the Ninth Face: "One should stand upright with the left and right heels and toes facing one another. Greatly bend both knees as if sitting, though not actually sitting. The middle fingers of both hands and the three fingers below them are each bent into the palms. The middle joints of the three fingers on both sides face one another and touch. The two index fingers are held upright, their tips leaning against each other. The tips of the two thumbs also touch each other, pressing against the sides of the middle fingers. This is first placed upon the chest."

Next, raise the mudrā: place the upper joints of the three fingers below the middle fingers of both hands upon the forehead, with the tips of the index fingers pointing upward; thus, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva stands before the Buddha.

When this mudrā is formed, the celestial Māras of the desire realm all tremble with fear; all the spirits and ghosts fall prostrate upon the ground; and all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and devas are filled with great joy, simultaneously offering praise.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva spoke to the ghosts, saying:

"You malevolent spirits, do not fall down and do not be afraid. Arise and sit up! Today I shall perform this dharma-seal; let none among the fourfold assembly who study this dharma suffer premature death, illness, or other calamities."

If a person performs this seal-method and offers various kinds of worship day after day, they will immediately obtain great efficacy: at death, they shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha and draw near to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

37. Aparājita-mudrā (The Seal of the Invincible), the Thirty-Seventh. Translated into Chinese as *Wusheng Yin* (Seal of the Unconquerable). For the tenth face: Stand upright. First, bend the left knee deeply; keep the body straight and step firmly upon the ground with the toes pointing forward. Extend the right leg straight and slightly outward to the right, with the toes pointing forward. Cross the left and right index fingers and ring fingers behind the palms, placing the right over the left. Touch the tips of the left and right little fingers and middle fingers together. Hold both thumbs upright side-by-side, ensuring they do not touch the sides of the index fingers. Join the wrists and raise the seal, resting it upon the right armpit.

This is the Seal of the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya-mudrā*). Having completed seven recitations of the aforementioned Great Mantra, one should then raise it again toward the forehead and recite the mantra another seven times.

In whatever land this rite is performed, the five grains will ripen in abundance, the people will be free from disease, and it will be able to destroy all the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

38. The Seal of Mārasainya-pramardani (The Seal for Crushing the Army of Māra). The thirty-eighth [seal], translated into Chinese as "The Seal for Destroying the Army of Māra," is the eleventh face. "Join the wrists. Extend the left and right thumbs and little fingers together. Bend the left and right index, middle, and ring fingers so that their tips are each about one cun apart, and the sides of the finger tips are each opened by about half a cun. Raise them and place them beneath the wrists upon the crown of the head. Bend the right knee as in the previous seal, and extend the left knee; extend the left foot as in the previous seal, and bend the right foot."
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara stood before the Buddha and spoke these words:
"I now possess eleven faces, each of which produces a seal.

If anyone sees, hears of, or studies this dharma and practices it according to the law, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and sins as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will all be extinguished at once, just as a fierce fire consumes all grasses and trees."
"In whatever land this place of Dharma exists, it is no different from my own person currently residing here.
These eleven seals all employ the initial Great Dhāraṇī.

39. The *Ḍhṛtiśūla-mudrā-mantra*. The third and ninth [section], the *Ḍhṛtiśūla-mudrā-mantra*; in the language of Tang, the "Head-Spike Mudrā. [Procedure]: Bend the little finger of the right hand and press the thumb against its nail. Extend the remaining three fingers and cross them at the side of the right hip. Do the same with the left hand, except that the left arm is bent upward, placing the back of the wrist above the armpit. Sit with the body upright.
The mantra says: "Oṃ ārye."
1. Vajrapāṇaye, 2. Mahākrodhādhipataye, 3.
Bodhisattvāya, 4. Mahāsattvāya, 5. [Siddhi]mukhāya.
Mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā dhāraṇī.
9. Dhāraṇī; 10. Vidyā-dhāraṇī;
11. Krodha-nī (with the "upper tone" on the syllable *dha*).
“Piṇḍe (high tone) ni svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra.

If a person bathes daily with fragrant water—or if one cannot bathe every day, then bathes with fragrant water on the eighth, tenth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day—and enters the maṇḍala to construct a water altar two cubits in size;
Place a single incense burner at the center of the altar and burn aloeswood incense while reciting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*; in all matters, this shall yield efficacious results.

Regarding all the karmic obstacles of one's own being, if one forms the mudrā daily, repeatedly performs repentance, and recites the mantra with a sincere heart, all karmic obstacles will be entirely extinguished.

40. The Pāśa-mudrā of Avalokiteśvara, the Fortieth. "Flex the little finger of the left hand; with the thumb, press upon the nail to form a hollow. Insert the thumb of the right hand through this hollow, and grasp the three fingers of the left hand with the four fingers [of the right], holding them curled while the [left] three fingers are spread and held upright."
If one performs the above two mudrās, there will be no fear of any ghosts or calamities. 41. The Mudrā of Avalokiteśvarī, the Forty-first.

"Bend the little finger of the left hand and press the thumb against the nail to form a hollow. Insert the little finger of the right hand from below into this hollow and press its thumb against the nail, forming a shape like a hook-and-chain. The tips of the two ring fingers touch each other. Each of the two middle fingers is bent back so that their tips touch the backs of the nails of the two ring fingers. The tips of the two index fingers rest beside the base of the nails of the two ring fingers; their tips must not touch, but remain about one *aṅgula* apart. Move the index fingers back and forth."
The mantra is as follows:

“Nama āryāya | Varakīrtiśabarāya | Bodhisattvāya | Mahāsattvāya | Mahākāruṇikāya | Tadyathā | Kaṭa vikaṭa | Gaṃkaṭa | Kaṭa vikaṭa | Gaṃkaṭa | Bakabati | Viśaye | Svāhā. This mudrā and this mantra are applicable for all purposes.

42. The *Sāradā-mudrā* of the Mother Avalokiteśvarī. [The procedure is] as before; however, change only this: let the tips of the two index fingers touch each other. Use the previously mentioned mantra of the Mother.

43. The Mahāmāra Seal (The Forty-third). In the Tang language, it is called "the Flower Garland Binding Seal. Following the previous procedure, with the sole modification that the two ring fingers are opened; the two index fingers are bent at the middle joints with their tips touching each other, separated from the ring fingers.

"This Dharma-seal mantra: using the previously mentioned Mother-mantra, take a clean jar and fill it with scented water; one should form this seal and stir the scented water, reciting the mantra twenty-one times."

Next, raise this mudrā and seal one’s own crown three times; then, using the aforementioned mantra, bathe with fragrant water, put on fresh and clean garments, enter the maṇḍala, protect the body and bind the boundary, and invoke Avalokiteśvara, making various offerings, burning incense, and scattering flowers.

The mantra-practitioner, standing before Avalokiteśvara, should perform this mantra. Whatever one’s heart desires, all prayers made with both mind and mouth shall be verified. 44. The *Tāṇḍa-mudrā* of Avalokiteśvara. (The Forty-fourth. In Chinese:

*Ce qībǎozhàng yìn* (The Seal of Brandishing the Seven-Jeweled Staff). "According to the previous [instructions], change only this: join the tips of the two ring fingers; extend the right thumb; touch the tips of the two index fingers together; hook the right little finger around the base of the left little finger; and employ the *Mūla-mantra*."

"This is the Dharma-seal mantra; if a person performs this seal daily, they will attain the four dhyānas, and after the end of their life, they will be reborn in the Western Land of Immeasurable Life and achieve the state of non-retrogression (avaivartika)."
The above four seals are used in conjunction with the *Avalokiteśvarī-mātṛ-mantra*. **The Forty-fifth:

The Avalokiteśvara Kuñcika Seal Mantra** Standing on the ground with feet together: the left hand grasps the wrist and is bent upward; the forearm is positioned in front of the shoulder, not touching it, with the inner side of the wrist facing the shoulder. The right hand extends the arm downward; all five fingers are fully extended, and the back of the palm does not touch the hip.
The mantra is:

"Nama āryāya, vairocanāya, bodhisattvāya, mahāsattvāya, mahākāruṇikāya, tadyathā, oṃ, virāgani, svāhā. 46. The Aṅkuśa Seal (The Hook Seal). Fourth and Sixtieth. Translated into Chinese as "The Hook Seal":
Join the wrists, place the two thumbs side by side, and extend them straight.
Bend the middle joints of both index fingers so that their tips touch each other,
without allowing them to touch the tips of the thumbs.
The tips of the two middle fingers touch each other;
the two ring fingers are bent at the middle joints,
their tips touching each other.
The tips of the two little fingers, positioned at the sides of the upper joints of the middle fingers,
are held upright with their tips touching one another.
Do not place the tips against the side of the ring finger;
open them within the palm.

47. Padmamudrā (Lotus Seal). The forty-seventh: "Padmamudrā" (in Chinese, *liánhuáyìn*, Lotus Seal). "In accordance with the previous [seal], change only the middle fingers: open their tips by about two-fifths of an inch and place them toward the crown of the head."
This mantra is for universal application; it is used with white mustard seeds and ashes. 48. Vajramuṣṭi-mudrā (The Fourth-Eight).

Translated into Chinese as *Jīngāng juǎn yìn* (Vajra-Fist Seal). "According to the previous Aṅkuśa seal, change only the two index fingers: slightly bend them so that they each rest upon the upper joint of the middle finger without touching it, leaving a space of about one-fifth of an inch between them. Then, place both thumbs side-by-side, pressing against the sides of the middle joints of the middle fingers."

49. The *Akṣamālā-mudrā*, also known as the *Dānapāramitā-mudrā*. [The term] *Akṣamālā* is pronounced with the initial vowel *a* (ā). It is also called the *Dānapāramitā-mudrā*. (Forty-ninth. In the language of Tang, it is called the "Mudrā of the Ten Pāramitās," or also the "Rosary. Following the previous method, change only this: bend both little fingers into the palms; bring the sides of the two palms together; and bend the tips of both thumbs so that they rest against the side of the lower joint of the index fingers.
"The aforementioned five mudrās all generally employ the previously mentioned *junchi* mantra.

If a person bathes daily with fragrant water, enters the *maṇḍala*, performs this rite by protecting the body, establishing the boundary (*sīmābandha*), and making various offerings, that person will certainly attain *avaivartika* [non-retrogression]."

50. The Seal and Mantra of Amitābha Buddha, the Fiftieth. "Open the wrists slightly and join the two thumbs, bending the joints with the tips pointing downward. Bend each of the two little fingers and place their tips against the sides of the two thumbs. Bring the tips of the two middle fingers together. Bend the middle joints of the two ring fingers and the two index fingers so that their tips touch one another. Move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is as follows:

"Nama āryāya (1) Amitābhāya (2) Tathāgatāya (3) Arhate (4) Samyaksaṃbuddhāya (5). Tadyathā (6): Oṃ (7) Amitābha-pādavikse (8) Abhyāsāye (9) Svāhā (10). When performing the rite for constructing the maṇḍala, one should employ this seal and mantra.

51. The Mudrā and Dhāraṇī of the Eye of Śākyamuni Buddha, Number Fifty-one. "Interlace the two ring fingers and the two little fingers within the palms. Straighten the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another. Extend both thumbs straight forward. Bend the two index fingers at the middle joints so that their tips rest against each other, pressing down upon the tops of the two thumbs. Join the wrists together."

The mantra is: "Oṃ vīraśāni svāhā. The Fifty-second: The Seal-Mantra of the Earth Goddess (Pṛthivī). "Join the palms; interlace the two index fingers and the two little fingers within the palms, with the right pressing upon the left. Straighten the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers so that their tips touch one another. Hold the two thumbs upright side-by-side, pressing against the sides of the two index fingers, while moving the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ bhasundari anatarja prapratatni svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; when constructing a great maṇḍala or performing the rite for redeeming land, one should use this seal-mantra as the land-contract.
“The abbreviated explanation of the Mudrā-dhāraṇī is now complete.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If there are good men or good women who are able to rely upon the teachings of Avalokiteśvara to perform the rite of incantation, those good men or good women shall fashion an image of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara out of white sandalwood.

The wood must be of excellent quality, fine-grained, and solid; it must not be withered or hollow. The dimensions of the image’s body should be one *hasta* of the Buddha’s own measure—or, according to human measurement, two *hasta* or one *vitasti*. If these cannot be obtained, it may also be made at one chi and three cun.
"Construct eleven faces: the three faces in front should be made as bodhisattva faces;

the three faces on the left side should be made as wrathful faces; the three faces on the right side should resemble bodhisattva faces with canine fangs protruding upward; at the back there should be one face made as a laughing face; and the face on the crown of the head should be made as a Buddha face."
Each of its eleven faces is adorned with a flower crown, and within each flower crown resides an Amitābha Buddha.
The image’s left hand holds a water pitcher (*kundikā*), from the mouth of which a lotus flower emerges.
The right arm hangs down, with the right hand extended to hold a string of *ratnamālā* (jeweled necklaces), forming the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*).
On the body of the image, various ornaments are carved out to adorn its form.
If one uses gold, silver, brass, or painted images and so forth, one shall obtain them all.

At that time, once the person has fashioned this image and wishes to fulfill their heart's desire, they should enter the *maṇḍala* on the first day of the waxing moon and remain until the thirteenth day.

When entering the maṇḍala, one should bathe with fragrant water and put on new, clean garments—three sets of clean garments in total, changing them three times during the day, wearing one set each at dawn, midday, and dusk.
When ascending the screen, he would discard his clean robes and put on soiled garments.
"The practitioner of the Way observes a fast for a full meal at a single sitting, abstaining from all other flavors and consuming only barley and milk gruel."

"The place where the altar is established must be a clean room; the method for excavating and preparing the ground is as previously described in the section on the seven-day altar: it should be wiped clean with mud until fresh and bright, and the floor should be smeared with fragrant mud."

Furthermore, he sprinkled fragrant water everywhere upon that ground; within the chamber, he measured out a space of eight cubits, equal in length and breadth, erected pillars at the four corners, and hung banners all around.
"In the center of the main altar, set up a high seat and place an image of Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara, with the image facing west.
Scatter various kinds of flowers within the maṇḍala, and burn only aloeswood, storax, and other such incenses."
From the first day until the seventh day, recite the root great mantra one hundred and eight times during each of the three periods of the day; it is not necessary to offer food.

From the midday of the eighth day until the thirteenth day, offer various kinds of food and drink as well as other fruits once every day. The food offered should not be placed on a plate; rather, it should be contained in clean grass, new and pure earthenware vessels, or various leaves.

On the fourteenth and fifteenth days, he redoubled his offerings to the Buddha with various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers, various delicacies, and other assorted fruits, making them far superior to those previously offered.
"As for those who practice this rite, they shall spread only *śāla* grass as a sitting mat, kneel with the right knee on the ground in a posture of reverence, and face the image directly.

On the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the lunar month, they shall kindle a sandalwood fire before the image, take one *śroṇa* of *sumana* oil, place it in a clean copper vessel, and set it before the practitioner."
Furthermore, one must prepare agallochum incense, cut into pieces as thick or thin as a chopstick, with exactly one thousand and eight segments.

At that time, after midday on the fifteenth day following [the initial practice], the practitioner takes one piece of agallochum, coats it with *sumana* oil, recites the mantra over it once, and casts it into the previously kindled sandalwood fire. In this manner, he proceeds in succession until all one thousand and eight segments have been exhausted.
"At that time, the practitioner did not consume any food for two full days.
When the night of the fifteenth arrived and all was still, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva entered the practice hall, and the sandalwood image moved of its own accord."
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook all at once, and from the face atop the crown of the image, a voice issued forth, praising the practitioner, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
"O son of good family!
I have come to see you so that all your vows may be fully satisfied.
At that time, there were four vows.
What are the four?
First, may I, without leaving my seat, immediately fly up into the void and depart, moving with sovereign ease and without obstruction;
second, may I, amidst the assembly of all worthy and holy ones, be free from all hindrances and attain *sambodhi*.
Third, may I always become the king among the rishis who maintain mantras;
fourth, may I, in this very life, obtain the opportunity to follow and attend upon Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—these are called the four vows.
At that time, if the practitioner makes any request at will from among the four vows, Avalokiteśvara will immediately grant one vow.

If it is not obtained within those four vows, one should again establish a *maṇḍala* on the morning of the fifteenth day of the following month. Within that *maṇḍala*, place two images; if there is a relic (*śarīra*) within one of the images, place an image of Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara beside the image containing the relic. One must also have one thousand and eight stalks of fine flowers.

The practitioner of this rite shall, before the image, spread grass for a seat, kneel with the right knee on the ground in a respectful posture, take a single flower, recite the mantra over it once, and scatter it upon the image; in this manner, he shall continue until one thousand and eight flowers have been exhausted.
When the flowers have been exhausted, at that time, from the face of the Bodhisattva directly in front of the image of Avalokiteśvara, a great peal of thunder shall issue forth.
At that moment, the practitioner should settle the mind and fix the thoughts, and must not be terrified.
When the sound of thunder issues forth, everything trembles.
At that time, the practitioner should constantly recite the mantra; when the sound of thunder issues forth, one should immediately make a petition, raising one's voice and crying out:
"Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva!"
"Disciple, when will you be able to rescue all sentient beings from their various sufferings and afflictions?
When will you fulfill all the aspirations of all beings?
At that time, Avalokiteśvara granted these wishes immediately.
When making this vow, the eight classes of beings—gods, nāgas, and so forth—and all spirits will encounter no obstacles or hindrances.

One should place ox-gallstone on a blade of grass before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, perform the Avalokiteśvara Heart Seal and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times, then mix it with warm water to bathe the body; thus, all obstacles, all evil dreams, and all illnesses shall be completely cured.

"Take equal parts of the two substances, realgar and cinnabar, and place them upon grass leaves before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Recite the Avalokiteśvara Heart-Seal Mantra over them one thousand and eight times. Then, mix them with warm water and bathe the body; all obstacles, all evil dreams, and all pestilential diseases shall be completely cured."

"If, during a lunar eclipse, one takes three *liang* of cow's ghee and places it in a copper bowl, and sets it out in the open air before an image of Avalokiteśvara; having prepared a circular altar one chi and five cun in size by coating the ground with yellow earth, one places the bowl of ghee upon it."
"Recite the mantra from the moment of the first eclipse until this moon reappears; only then shall you cease.
Take the clarified butter for consumption, but you must eat it all and may not leave any remainder."
"Having consumed this ghee, all diseases within the body will be completely cured.

If there is an epidemic among the people of a land, or when all manner of livestock fall ill and die, one should establish a *maṇḍala*, take white mustard seeds and press them to extract an oil that fills one *śrōṇa*;
then take wood from the purple *kāśmarya* tree, as thick as a writing brush handle, and cut it into exactly one thousand and eight pieces, each an inch long."

First, burn purple acacia wood before the image; next, take small pieces of purple acacia wood cut into finger-width lengths and soak them in oil. Taking one piece at a time, recite the mantra once and cast it into the fire to burn, continuing in this manner until all one thousand and eight pieces are exhausted.
At that time, it will cause all epidemics among the people and all domestic animals to be completely cured.

Furthermore, if enemies or bandits from other regions intend to invade the borders, one should face this image of Avalokiteśvara directly toward the place where those enemies and bandits are coming, and make offerings of various incenses, flowers, food, and drink.

One should take red lac the size of a soybean; once one thousand and eight recitations of the mantra have been completed, smear it upon the wrathful face on the left side of the image, so that the enemy thieves shall be unable to advance.
"If a person suddenly contracts madness, one should take a white thread and recite a mantra over it once for each knot, making twenty-one knots in total.
Kneeling before the image, one should further recite the mantra over the thread one hundred and eight times and tie it around the back of the neck of the image directly in front."
After staying overnight, take the binding cord and tie it around the patient's neck.

If the illness is not cured after two days, take the mantra-cord again, recite the mantra over it one hundred and eight times, and fasten it around the neck of the image. After another night has passed, take it and tie it around the patient's neck; their illness will then be cured.

"If there are various ghosts who enter a person's house, one should light a fire before the image, take one hundred and eight grains of incense-resin (kunkuma), and recite the mantra once over each grain before casting it into the fire to burn."
When one hundred and eight seeds have been thus burned away, all malevolent spirits will disperse and flee, not daring to remain.

"If there are enemies who seek to find an opportunity against one, take white thread before the image; for every mantra recited, make a knot, until there are one hundred and eight knots. Tie them to the neck of the wrathful face on the left side of the image."

After staying there for one night, untie and take this cord; recite the name of the enemy once and cut one knot, continuing until all one hundred and eight knots are severed; thus, the evil schemes devised by the enemy shall not succeed.

"If a person harbors resentment toward another, they should take threads of five colors and twist them into a consecrated cord. Kneeling before the image, they should recite the mantra once for each knot, making one hundred and eight knots, and then tie it around the neck of the image's left side, facing the direction of their anger."
After staying there for one night, he untied what was bound upon his left arm and caused that angry person to reconcile and rejoice.

"If there are those who wish to seek auspicious matters, they should take five-colored thread and twist it into a cord; kneeling before the image in the *hu-ju* (half-kneeling) posture, they should recite the mantra once for each knot until seven knots are formed, and then tie them upon the neck of the image directly in front."
After staying there for one night, one should take [the image] and bind it to one's own body; then whatever one seeks will be fulfilled as desired.
"If a person knows that their own body has obstacles or difficulties, they should blend various exquisite fragrances and anoint the image, and further bathe the image with scented water."
Having finished bathing the image, collect the water again; recite mantras over it one hundred and eight times before the image and bathe your own body.
Once you have bathed yourself, all obstacles and difficulties will be completely extinguished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, standing before the Buddha, expounded the methods for the koṭi-seals and the dharanis, as well as the rituals for seven thousand maṇḍalas.
Having finished teaching these methods, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Those who wish to practice this dhāraṇī method must first enter the maṇḍala, and only thereafter proceed with the practice."
"If one does not enter [the path], one must not rashly teach this method of seals and mantras;
if one rashly teaches it, both the teacher and the disciple shall incur a grave and heavy offense.
When this chapter was spoken, the entire great assembly simultaneously praised, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

Great Being of Great Compassion, for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, you have taught the seal-mantras (*mudrā-mantra*) and the various altar rituals (*maṇḍala-vidhi*). We, this great assembly, shall likewise rejoice, receive them upon our heads, and uphold them.”
When this sutra had been spoken, the great assembly present at that time all rose simultaneously, circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, prostrated before him, and departed.
This concludes the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara Divine Mantra.
The Scripture on the Collection of Dhāraṇīs Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Four;
The Scripture on the Collection of Dhāraṇīs Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Five:
The Chapter on Avalokiteśvara (Middle Section), translated by the Tripitaka Master of Central India, Amoghavajra, during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The Heart-Seal Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva for One Thousand Recitations, Part One. This is identical to the Heart-Seal Mantra of all Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattvas.

*Form the mudrā:* Interlace the four fingers from the index finger downward, pressing them inward against one another. Bend the left thumb and insert it between the index fingers. Extend the right thumb straight inward, keeping it unbent. Join the two wrists together and move the right thumb back and forth.
The mantra is:
"Oṃ arulika svāhā. If one performs this seal-method, all Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattvas will behold it.

Having invited Avalokiteśvara to take his seat, performed the rite of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), and completed the offering of incense, next perform this mudrā; Avalokiteśvara will be delighted.
To perform it daily is most excellent and brings great benefit.
2. Furthermore, the second Thousand-Turn Seal Mantra: "The hand seal is identical to the Heart Seal of Avalokiteśvara mentioned previously; only the feet differ."

Interlace the four fingers from the index finger downward, pressing them inward against one another; bend the left thumb to enter between the index fingers, while the right thumb is extended straight and kept inward without bending; join the two wrists together.

The two legs form a cross-shape, with the right foot at the head of the cross and the left foot at its tail; thus, the right leg stands straight while the left knee is bent outward, the buttocks are thrust forward, and the body is inclined toward the left side.
Place the heart-mudrā before the right breast, ensuring it does not touch the breast; maintain a smiling countenance and turn the head toward the right.

On the fifteenth day of every month, bathe with fragrant water, enter a pure chamber, and perform this mudrā while reciting the Great Dharani that follows; thus, the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes will all be completely extinguished.
The Thousand-Turn Dharani says:
"Namaḥ muruṇḍānāṃ tathāgatānām | Nama ārya-valokiteśvarāya ||" (Namu molo da na tuo luo ye | Namu aliye bolu chi ti she bala ye) [Sanskrit:
*Namaḥ muruṇḍānāṃ tathāgatānām | Nama ārya-avalokiteśvarāya*].

Bhagavati saṃsārabhañji sarvabuddhaparokṣajñe cākṣuṣe. 15–17.

*Dharmaprabha-triṃśat-buddha-nīye svāhā.* (32) The *Sahasravartanī-sūtra* states:
Having recited this mantra, evil karma is extinguished;
upon reaching seven recitations, the five heinous crimes are extinguished;
if one completes a thousand recitations, there is no sin that is not extinguished.
Upon completing one hundred thousand recitations, one will behold Avalokiteśvara face-to-face, adorned with various ornaments.

During the seven days while first performing the rite, one may consume only milk gruel, butter, curd, white cakes, and non-glutinous rice; one must not eat salt, sauce, or vegetables, and on the final day, one must not eat at all.

On the fifteenth night, with an empty stomach, he recited the dhāraṇī continuously before the Buddha without a fixed limit of repetitions; he saw the image move and shake, and it uttered a voice, crying out:
"Excellent, excellent!"
He emits radiant light.
Furthermore, by placing genuine jewels and precious objects upon the head of the mantra-practitioner, one immediately knows that the efficacy has been achieved.
Having beheld Avalokiteśvara face-to-face, all virtuous aspirations will be fulfilled.

Furthermore, if one sees Avalokiteśvara adorned with various ornaments in a dream during sleep, all virtuous deeds will be accomplished and all evil karma will be extinguished; even those who merely recite this directly shall attain the destruction of their sins.
"When you wish to travel east or west, first recite the mantra over your hands seven times and rub them upon your face; wherever you go, no calamities or misfortunes shall occur.
If you can maintain purity according to the Dharma and constantly recite this without ceasing, you shall attain the First Ground."
"If there is a woman who can recite and uphold this, she shall later become a man and never again receive such a female form.
First, construct an altar, complete the arrangements for offerings, and only then recite the mantra."

Each of the four sides of the altar measures sixteen cubits; it is marked with four concentric circles. The appearance of the enclosures is white on the outside and four colors on the inside, each layer forming a wall-like structure, which constitutes eight layers in total.
Combine the colors of the five directions and open gates on the four sides—east, west, south, and north—aligned with one another; the single central layer need not have gates opened.

Take eight large earthen jars and four smaller pots, filling each completely with water, and insert branches of cypress and willow into the jars and pots. Prepare offerings of white cakes, non-glutinous rice, milk curd, clarified butter, honey, fragrant fruits, and the like, and light sixteen lamps.

Outside the four gates, insert sixteen unused arrows; hang five-colored threads upon the arrows. Take four pieces of khadira wood and purple ginger wood—two measuring five finger-widths in length and two measuring six finger-widths—and nail them into the four corners of the mandala. Scatter various seasonal and non-seasonal flowers upon the mandala.

Furthermore, take one thousand eight hundred small pieces of *pāka* wood or jujube wood, each one foot in length; using either a clay bowl or a copper bowl, coat these wooden branches with ghee and milk. Recite the mantra once over each branch and immediately cast it into the fire.
If khadira wood is unavailable, red jujube wood may be used as a substitute; one must paint an image of the Holy One Avalokiteśvara in white, making it according to one's means.
Furthermore, the *Fǎbiàn* (Transformation of the Dharma) states:

"The karmic obstructions accumulated over a thousand kalpas shall all be extinguished at once through recitation; one shall obtain the roots of goodness accumulated by a thousand Buddhas and reach the limit of backsliding from the cycle of birth, old age, sickness, and death for a thousand kalpas. After casting off this body, one will immediately see a thousand universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) who constantly uphold the ten wholesome paths."

If one wishes to be born in the pure lands of the Buddhas, one should recite [the mantra] twenty-one times during each of the three periods of the day and night. When thirty-seven days have been completed, according to one's aspiration, one will either see the golden form of a Buddha or the forms of Bodhisattvas within a dream; this is a preliminary sign by which one knows that one shall be born in a pure land.

Furthermore, regarding the practice of upholding the Dharma: take five *jin* of *tupoxiang* (translated in Tang as *maoxiang*) together with its sprouts, one thousand pieces of *zhumu* wood each one foot long, and ghee; recite the mantra over all of these one thousand times.
When one is about to burn [the offerings], smear clarified butter (*sarpis*) upon the wooden stem and the incense, reciting the mantra once over each before burning them.

"In advance, during the fifth or sixth month, take dried cow dung and mix it with *tūba* (turmeric) scented water to form a paste. Construct a circular altar two cubits (*hasta*) in diameter; upon this altar, arrange various flowers and incenses."
In the winter months, when there are no flowers, one should carve an image of a flower and place it upon [the object], then burn frankincense.
The incantation master sits facing east and recites the mantra one thousand times; thus the rite is accomplished.
Before the incantation, one should drink this consecrated water twenty-one or seven times.

One may use mantra-water to dissolve impurities, purify rooms, *dharma-śālās*, and Buddha halls, or sprinkle it upon the body; one may also use mantra-charged willow branches to strike away illness or mantra-charged water to cure disease—all of which are effective when recited twenty-one times each.

"If one can recite it twenty-one times each during the three periods of every day for the duration of one's life, the extinction of transgressions will be inconceivable, and it shall be effective for all purposes."
One who performs this rite will bring joy to Avalokiteśvara. 3. The Dharma Seal of the Body of Mother Avalokiteśvara, Part Three.

"Place the two thumbs firmly, each grasping the tips of the two little fingers. Hold both hands upright and pressed together. Interlace the two index fingers so they rest upon the two thumbs and little fingers; do the same with the two ring fingers. The two middle fingers are positioned above, their tips slightly apart without touching, while the palms below remain joined. Move the index fingers back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ kṣetradhṛti pāṇḍaravāsini stambhamukuṭa dhāraṇī svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there is anyone who can perform this daily, making continuous offerings by reciting the mantra once for each burning of a mixture of sesame seeds, ghee, honey, and *śāli* rice flowers into the fire—doing so up to one thousand and eight times, or even just one hundred and eight times of such recited burnings—it shall be accomplished.
If one performs this rite every day in this manner, all Avalokiteśvaras will be delighted.
Furthermore, regarding another method: if a child cries, one should recite this mantra over a knot or a cord and tie it around the child's neck; the crying will then immediately cease.

4. The Heart-Seal Mantra of the Mother Avalokiteśvarī. Fourth: "Join the palms. Bend the two index fingers, the two middle fingers, and the two ring fingers so that their tips touch one another and their first joints are level. Place the two thumbs side by side, pointing upward and touching, and press them against the sides of the tips of the index fingers. Extend the two little fingers upward with their tips touching. Move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ mahāśrīye svāhā. These two preceding dharma-seal mantras are called the Dharma of the Mother of Avalokiteśvara.
If there are those who recite and uphold it, they can eliminate the heavy sins of ten billion kalpas within their bodies.

All Bodhisattvas who hear this mantra shall attain śamatha; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they shall attain the stage of Buddhahood. Therefore, it is called the "Mantra Mother of Bodhisattvas."

Those who are able to receive and uphold it shall before long receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas; all Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattvas obtain the prediction of *śamatha* by means of this mantra-seal.

5. The Fifth: The Seal and Mantra for Holding the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Who Sustains All. "Join the two forearms; extend the two thumbs and the two little fingers straight upward with their tips joined, while the remaining fingers do not touch one another. Simply extend them straight up with the two thumbs separated and the tips of the little fingers not meeting—this is called the Eleven-Faced Seal, the Great Samādhi Seal. Move the index fingers back and forth; for the mantra, employ the Great Eleven-Faced Mantra."

"Those who practice this dharma can eliminate all calamities caused by kings, thieves, water, fire, blades, poison, and the like; they shall have no fear whatsoever, for it is due to the majestic spiritual power of Avalokiteśvara."
"If you wish to request the teachings from the various Bodhisattvas, you must first perform the Samādhi-mudrā; thus you shall obtain the joy of all Bodhisattvas. **Chapter Six:

The随心印咒 (Sui-xin-yin-zhou) of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva** "Interlace the middle, ring, and little fingers of both hands outwardly. Join the palms with the right hand pressing down on the left. Bring the tips of all the fingers together against the backs of the palms. Extend the two index fingers upright and touching each other; do the same for the thumbs, each thumb touching its respective index finger. Move the thumbs back and forth. The method for taking refuge is the same as that for the Eleven-faced [Avalokiteśvara] and others."
The mantra is:

"Tadyathā | Oṃ | Tāritāri | Dūtāri | Dūri | Svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If a person desires to attain intelligence, they should take a yellow ox and place it in a clean location, have a young boy observe the eight precepts, and then milk the cow.
The milk collected over the course of three days was returned daily to its cow for her to drink.
From the fourth day until the seventh day, the milk that was collected was immediately made into curd, and from the curd, butter was produced.
During a solar or lunar eclipse, one should bathe with fragrant water, don new and clean garments, and construct a five-colored water altar measuring four cubits.

This altar shall have no doors. On the eastern side of the altar, place a lotus seat; upon this seat, install the *kītamati* [image]. On the southern side, place a *tulasī* flower seat; on the northern side, place a *kurukulla* flower seat; and in the center, place a flower seat for the随心 (suixin) Avalokiteśvara.

Having made offerings with sixteen oil lamps, eight plates of food and drink, burning incense, and scattering flowers, the mantra-practitioner shall take the aforementioned ghee and place it in a new, clean vessel of red copper. On this day, the practitioner must not eat; they shall bathe three times, recite the Buddha’s name, and maintain no other thoughts.
Place the butter bowl at the center of the maṇḍala and have the butter-child look at the sun and moon from outside; do not let the child see what is within the maṇḍala.
The mantra-practitioner must not look at the sun or moon; if they do look at them, the rite will not achieve its efficacy.

If the sun or moon gradually rises, one should with a sincere mind form the *Tārā-hṛdaya-mudrā* and repeatedly recite the mantra over the vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Within that vessel of clarified butter, three signs will appear—namely, steam, smoke, and fire.
If it merely emits smoke, one who consumes the ghee will be able to recite seven hundred verses of scripture in a single day;
if it emits smoke, one who consumes the ghee will be able to recite seven hundred verses of scripture in a single day;
if it emits fire, both the one who consumes the ghee and others who consume it will become greatly intelligent, able to recite one thousand verses of scripture in a single day.
If one follows the usual practice, one will also be able to memorize [the teachings] with great facility.
As for the ghee, one may take one liang, two liang, three, four, or five liang, according to one's own preference.

7. Furthermore, there is the随心观世音印 (Avalokiteśvara-mānasānugata-mudrā). This seventh [mudrā] has no separate title and no separate mantra. "Both hands with all ten fingers extended upward, the tips joined, with a slight space within the palms, the two wrists touching, placed directly upon the heart—this mudrā is used for making offerings together with all other mudrā-rites."

8. The Seal for Requesting All Wishes by Contemplating Avalokiteśvara According to One’s Heart (Sui Xin Guan Shi Yin Qi Yi Qie Yuan Yin), Number Eight. "Bend the left thumb toward the palm; then bend the tip of the index finger so that its tip is about four or five *fen* away from the tip of the thumb. Extend the three fingers below the middle finger, keeping them pressed together. Place this seal horizontally and askew upon the heart, with the tips of the fingers pointing to the right. For the mantra, use the previously mentioned mantra."

"This is the Seal of the Single Dharma. When one wishes to make a vow, one should first prepare a water mandala four cubits in length and breadth, hanging various banners and canopies, and adorning it in various ways."

Within that mandala, place an image according to one's inclination. In front of the image, arrange four bowls; within these four bowls, place one type of substance each—namely, rock honey, granulated sugar, milk, and honey—offering them in their respective order. Scatter various flowers and burn aloeswood incense.

Having made offerings to the image, one should, before the image, with a sincere heart, confess and repent; having finished praying for one's aspirations as desired, one should form a mudrā before the image, covering it with a *kāṣāya* robe or using a clean cloth to cover the mudrā. Then, with a sincere heart, recite the mantra eight hundred times, without allowing any other distractions.
Having finished reciting this mantra, all that one desires according to the heart’s wish shall be fulfilled as intended.

Whether the matter is great or small, perform the rite for one day up to seven days, three times each day—at dawn, at midday, and at dusk—following the aforementioned ritual procedure, and the wish will certainly be realized, except in cases of lack of sincere devotion.

9. The Body-Seal Mantra of the Twelve-Armed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Chapter Nine. "Place the ring fingers of both hands one after the other on the backs of the middle fingers. Extend the two middle fingers vertically with their tips touching. Join and extend the two little fingers and the two thumbs, keeping them side by side. Bend the two index fingers so that their tips touch each other, pressing against the tips of the thumbs. Align the index fingers so that their second joints are level, and move the index fingers back and forth."

The mantra is: “Oṃ mahāśveti svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. Take one *liang* each of cow dung, cow urine, ghee, milk, and curd, and mix them all together. Bathe with fragrant water, put on new, clean clothes, face directly east, and squat with both feet together. Recite the aforementioned mantra over the medicine one hundred and eight times. Take it once every sixth month, or twice a year; thus one will remain free from illness oneself, and it is most auspicious for curing the diseases of others.

10. The Body-Seal Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Amoghapāśa, Part Ten. Following the previous Body-Seal of the Mother of Avalokiteśvara, one makes the following modifications: first, separate the two middle fingers by about one cun; second, slightly raise the two index fingers and the two ring fingers so that they do not touch the thumbs; third, leave a space between the index and ring fingers sufficient to accommodate the width of one middle finger; and finally, move the index fingers back and forth.
The mantra is as follows:

"Tadyathā | Oṃ | Śvetadhyā | Śvetabhujaṅga | Hūṃ hūṃ | Pramatha-sattva | Mahākāruṇika | Svāhā. This Dharma-seal mantra has manifold applications and possesses great power; it can subdue all malevolent spirits and ghosts, heal all diseases, and ensure that no calamities caused by thieves or bandits can cause harm.

If one is bound in shackles, one should take the *śulmala* herb, form it into an imprint with a mantra, and smear it upon the shackles; by further reciting the mantra with a sincere heart, one will immediately attain liberation.

11. The Dharani Seal of the Mouth for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Amoghapāśa, Number Eleven. "Insert the left and right little fingers inside [the palms] and stand them straight up. Hook the right ring finger over the back of the left ring finger and middle finger, entering into the space between the tips of the index and middle fingers. The left ring finger emerges from between the right middle and ring fingers, then enters into the space between the index and middle fingers. Stand both middle fingers straight up with their tips touching. Bend both index fingers so that each hooks the tip of its respective ring finger. Stand both thumbs straight up, with their tips touching and separated from the little fingers by about half an inch. Recite the aforementioned mantra together."

12. The Dharma Seal of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Amoghapāśa Fang (Tooth): The twelfth [section], "The Dharma Seal of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Amoghapāśa Fang," follows the previous oral seal, with the sole modification that the tips of the two middle fingers are slightly bent and each presses down upon the tip of its respective thumb; the two little fingers extend outward, the right pressing against the left, and all [fingers] grasp the back of the ring fingers. For the mantra, use the previously mentioned mantra.

"This single Dharma-seal can eliminate all calamities of water, fire, wind, bandits, and swords, as well as the perils of kings, yakṣas, rākṣasas, all ghosts and spirits, venomous dragons, poisonous snakes, and fetters."

If a person constantly makes offerings every day, they will cause Avalokiteśvara and all the bodhisattvas to feel great joy; at the end of their life, they will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, and furthermore, they may be reborn in any of the pure lands of the ten directions according to their wish.
"If you wish to stop the wind, first recite this mantra over ashes one hundred and eight times. Wrap a small piece of silk around them and carry them with you.

If the wind arises, take the ashes with your right hand and scatter them against the wind. Next, form a fist with the remaining fingers of your right hand and extend the index finger straight upward; facing the wind, recite the mantra repeatedly and shout fiercely, and the wind will immediately cease."
13. The Heart-to-Heart Core Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Amoghapāśa. The mantra is as follows:

“Oṃ, riṣṭi-lu-kā-viśaya, amogha-pāśa, mahā-kurudha, rājaya, ṛdhyaya, aparājitātta, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. This single dharma-mantra can extinguish karmic obstacles and afflictions. It is highly efficacious for repentance and healing diseases, as fully explained in the *Amoghapāśa Sūtra*.

The Method for Painting an Image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "All images of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva are entirely white in color, seated in the full lotus posture upon a lotus throne adorned with a hundred jewels. On his head he wears a flower crown adorned with the seven treasures, from which multiple rays of light emanate."
Within his floral crown stands a transformed Buddha; behind the floral crown emanates a light shaped like a winnowing basket, which is entirely red in color.
The back of the image rests against a couch embroidered with the seven treasures.
The image’s left hand has the arm bent at the elbow against the chest; furthermore, the middle finger is bent upward and held upright.
The right hand has the arm bent over the left hand, with the index finger and thumb bent and joined together, resting upon the top of the middle finger of the left hand.

The image has a jeweled necklace upon its neck, and each of its left and right arms and wrists is adorned with a jeweled bracelet. Furthermore, it is draped with a white silk garment decorated with jeweled flowers across the shoulders.
It wears a skirt made of white silk decorated with flowers; the waistband of this skirt is blue with a red inner lining, and it is fastened at the waist with a jeweled girdle.
"On both the left and right sides of the image, there is a bodhisattva serving as an attendant; these two bodhisattvas are entirely yellow in color, and both wear flower crowns upon their heads."
The Bodhisattva on the right side has his right arm bent, holding a white fly-whisk, and his left arm bent, holding a lotus flower.
The Bodhisattva on the left side has his right arm bent, holding a branch of various jeweled flowers, and his left arm bent and raised, with the hand grasping a white fly-whisk.
All were draped in morning mists above their jeweled necklaces; they wore white garments adorned with flowers bound around their thighs, and each stood upon a lotus pedestal.

Behind the attendants of these images, on the left and right sides respectively, there were three bodhisattvas each, arranged in ascending and descending order, leaning slightly to one side. Each faced the image, sitting in a posture of reverent gazing, assisting Avalokiteśvara in his sovereign spiritual powers to rescue and protect sentient beings.

"In the upper left chamber of that image is a bodhisattva whose entire body is yellow; there is a slight yellow tint upon his head, which is adorned with a topknot encircled by jewel-ornamented flowers. He has a circular halo of blue and wears white earrings."
He extends his right hand over his right knee, with all five fingers spread and the palm hanging downward; his left hand rests at his heart, grasping a lotus flower.
A white cloth is draped across his shoulders, and precious bracelets adorn both wrists; further, he wears a scarf of morning clouds, seated upon a blue lotus flower.
"Next, the Bodhisattva below has his entire body yellow in color; he wears a floral garland upon his head, has a red circular halo, and white earrings on his ears.
His breasts are large and high, and they are draped across with a light white flowered cloth."
The back of the right hand rests upon the thigh with the palm facing upward and the five fingers spread apart;
the left hand is placed face down between the left thigh and knee, with bracelets adorning the wrists.
Wearing a skirt of morning clouds, she sits upon a red lotus flower.
Next, the Bodhisattva below has a body that is entirely white, with a divine eye between her eyebrows on her face.
His hair is tied in a topknot that appears reddish; his head is devoid of flower garlands, and he has a circular halo of blue light. His ears are without earrings.

He possesses four arms: the first arm on the right side is bent at the elbow and turned backward, emerging from beneath his armpit and raised toward his head, with its fingers resting against his hairline.
One hand bends the arm, resting it upon the right knee, grasping a yellow rosary of twenty-one beads.
The left arm is bent at the elbow and turned backward; the hand emerges from beneath the armpit, extending upward to the shoulder with the fingers clenched into a fist.
With one arm resting between her thigh and knee, she holds a scripture box with her palm turned downward; a light green silk netting is draped over her shoulder.
A skirt of morning-glory red is crossed over her calves as she sits upon a purple lotus throne.

"Regarding the three bodhisattvas on the right side: the first bodhisattva from the top is entirely white in color, wears a floral garland on his head, has a circular halo of blue light, and has white earrings."
Her breasts were large and high, draped across with a white flower-patterned cloth.

Her left arm was bent over her left thigh as she grasped a lotus flower; her right hand rested upon her thigh, reaching upward to hold an object in the palm that resembled both a fruit and a flower, appearing variegated in color.
Her arms and wrists were adorned with bracelets, and she wore a skirt of morning clouds; she sat with her knees pressed together upon a purple lotus flower.
Next, there appeared a Bodhisattva whose entire body was yellow, wearing a crimson floral garland on her head, surrounded by a red circular halo, and having white rings in her ears.
The left arm is bent over the left thigh, grasping a lotus flower; the right hand rests upon the right thigh with the palm facing upward and the fingers spread like a mountain peak.
The wrists are adorned with bracelets, and a plain white cloth is draped across the upper arms. Wearing a skirt of morning clouds, he sits in the vajraparyaṅka posture upon a red lotus flower.

"Next, the Bodhisattva below has his entire body yellow in color; he wears a floral garland on his head and looks upward with his face raised toward the image. He has white earrings, a blue circular halo, and four arms."
Her breasts are large and high, draped across with a white jeweled cloth.

Her two hands are joined in *añjali*; furthermore, her left hand has its arm bent and rests upon her left thigh, grasping a lotus flower. The flower is purple; its stem is shaped like the shaft of an arrow, yellow in color, and its blossom faces upward.
The right arm is bent backward, with the hand emerging from the armpit and extending upward in front of the shoulder, holding a rosary of twenty-one beads.
He wears a skirt of red chrysanthemum-patterned fabric and sits with legs crossed upon a blue lotus flower.
"These bodhisattvas are all the retinue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; upon the image, near the light on both the left and right sides, there are two figures each of Srotāpanna devas."
The devas on the right side offered music as celestial gandharvas;
the devas on the left side made offerings to the Bodhisattva with scattered flowers and incense.

Furthermore, on both sides of the Flower Light [Hall], there were four birds each who assisted in the offerings: on the left side, two kalaviṅka birds stood side by side, followed by two śukas standing side by side; on the right side, two peacocks stood side by side, followed by two white cranes standing side by side.

Beneath the pedestal of that image, on the left side, there are two bodhisattvas. Their entire bodies are crimson; they have the appearance of youths, with handsome countenances and robust physiques. Their hair is short and appears as if dyed red, and between their eyebrows on their faces is a single *dhyāni* eye.
A white serpent emerged from behind him, turned toward the left with its head raised high, and gazed back at the face of this Bodhisattva.
His right hand was bent and extended, while his left hand, held near his breast, grasped a lotus flower.
He wore a light blue and white undergarment with vertical pleats and a short, narrow skirt tied at the waist over his loins; he stood upright and did not sit.
To the right, a bodhisattva was entirely yellow in color, wearing a morning-dawn skirt; with palms joined, he sat upright upon a purple lotus flower, looking up at the image while making offerings.

"It is spread upon a green ground; its image has Bodhi trees on both sides, with Indrānujā flowers upon those trees, and beneath the seat it is draped in blue, green, yellow, red, purple, and other colors."
"The Method for Drawing Images on the Jewel Ground of the Toilet is finished.
Chapter on the Dharma-Seals and Mantras of the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara and Vighnāntakṛt Bodhisattvas. There are twenty-one seals and forty-four mantras. Thus have I heard:

At one time, when the Buddha was in the city of Rājagṛha preaching various dharma-seals, dhāraṇīs, and mantras, he was surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable bodhisattvas and countless holy ones who uphold mantras; they came to where the Buddha was, attending him from before and behind.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, bowing his head to the Buddha’s feet.
Having paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, he circumambulated the Buddha three times and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have a heart-mantra named Vidyujjvālākarālī, which is profoundly deep and subtle, possessing secret spiritual powers, the seals of all dharmas, and the rites for the maṇḍala. It protects and sustains the world, universally causing all sentient beings—humans and non-humans alike—to escape all sufferings, so that every being may obtain its benefit.”
"I now wish to speak; I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to speak.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
For the sake of all sentient beings, you wish to expound the Dharma-seal dhāraṇī maṇḍala; I rejoice in your endeavor and shall support you as you explain it according to your intention."
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas present there were all filled with joy and simultaneously proclaimed it excellent.
Then, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, spoke this seal-mantra.

Slightly bend the index fingers so they appear as if not bent; moving the tips of the index fingers back and forth—if one bends both index fingers completely inward, this is the Flower Seat Seal.
The mantra says:
"Namaḥ sarvatathāgatapūjā arhadbhyaḥ. (1) "Arhat" is pronounced with the initial vowel *a* long, and "pūjā" is pronounced with the *u* sound as in "byuh" (the second syllable). (2)
