*Śvitiṣṭe che jñāne svāhā.* "When one wishes to recite this Dharma-seal mantra,
one should perform the bodily mudrā and recite it with a sincere mind."
All Buddhas who hear it will praise it;
all Bodhisattvas who hear the sound of the mantra will give rise to joy;
and all devas who hear it will prostrate themselves in worship.
All Vajras who hear the sound of this mantra shall be utterly terrified;
all spirits and ghosts who hear the sound of this mantra shall give rise to fear;
and all sentient beings of the six realms who hear it shall all resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
Those who hear of the sufferings endured in the hells shall all find relief from every agony;
such is the natural law. 2. The Great Heart Mantra of Vajrāṅkuśī.
Second: Application of the Body Seal. "The mantra says: Oṃ vīri-ku-ti ku-ti-ha. 3. The Middle Heart Mantra of Vajrāṅkuśī. Third: Application of the Body Seal. "The mantra says:"
“Oṃ vīri-cchindhi buddhāni svaḥ. The *Vijayā-hṛdaya-mantra* (The Small Heart Mantra of Vijayā), the fourth; using the body seal. The mantra says: “Oṃ vīri.
The *Vijayā-hṛdaya-madhyama-mantra* (The Middle Heart Mantra of Vijayā), the fifth; using the body seal. The mantra says: “Oṃ vīri-cchindhi svāhā.
The *Vijayā-āhvāna-mantra* (The Mantra for Invoking Vijayā), the sixth; using the body seal. The mantra says:
“Oṃ vīrikūci svāhā. (7) Vīkuci, the Mantra for All Uses; the seventh [use]. Regarding the Body Seal, also called the Great Heart Mantra, the mantra is:
“Oṃ pramabhaṣṭiri huṃ phaṭ. (8) Vīkuci, the Crown Mantra; the eighth [use]. Regarding the Body Seal, also called the Head Mantra, the mantra is: “Oṃ jñāni svāhā.

If anyone holds these eight mantras, including the aforementioned Great Mantra, and wishes to perform rites, they should all employ the aforementioned Body Seal; it will be efficacious in various ways.

9. The Dharma Seal and Mantra of the Bhṛkuṭī Incense Burner. This is the ninth [section]. The seal is the second; the mantra is the ninth. Following the previous body seal, the only modification is that the two thumbs are spread wide against the two index fingers, while the middle fingers are bent at their upper joints with their tips touching one another.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ, ci-kū-lu-kū-lu, vi-jaye, svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; when one wishes to perform the ritual and recite the mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajrakuṇḍalin, one should seal the incense burner with this seal.
Once the seal and incense have been applied, one then burns incense; holding the incense burner in hand, one makes a vow with both mind and mouth, saying:
"Now, for the sake of such-and-such a matter...
Having completed the offerings, one next seals the scented water.

10. The Dharani and Mudra for the Gandhodaka Incense Method. This is the tenth [chapter]. The mudra is the third, and the dharani is the tenth. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *Gandhatāradūpa*. "Extend the five fingers of the right hand, interlocking them, bend the elbow, and turn the palm sideways to seal the incense water; the left hand is not used."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ bodhi-tuḥ buddha-bhūte śodhani svāhā. When one wishes to perform a ritual and recite this Dharma-seal mantra, one should form the mudrā and seal the water, reciting the mantra seven times and sprinkling the water over one’s head and body.
Having likewise used this dharma-mantra to make offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, one next performs the ritual of the *Vijayā* Body-Protection Seal-Mantra.

**11. The *Vijayā* Body-Protection Dharma-Seal Mantra, Number Eleven.** This seal is the fourth; the mantra is the eleventh. "Cross the two hands so they are tilted and inverted, place the two thumbs side-by-side and upright, and let their tips resemble the shape of bird wings."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ bini hūḥ. When one wishes to perform the ritual and recite this mantra of the Dharma-seal, one should first protect oneself with this seal and then establish the boundary.
12. The *Vikṛti* Earth-Boundary-Sealing Mantra.

This twelfth seal for the earth-boundary-sealing mantra of the *Dharmamudrā* is the fifth [in this section]; the mantra is the twelfth. "With the middle fingers and those below them on both hands crossed in reverse within the palms, the right pressing down upon the left, the backs of the fingers resting against the palms, the two thumbs held together slantwise and upright, the two index fingers bent so that their nails touch and their backs are turned toward each other, and the two thumbs touching the ground."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ vettādi huṃ. When one wishes to perform the ritual and recite this mantra, one should seal the ground with this mudrā to expel all evil māras, gods, ghosts, and the like, both above and below the earth.
Next, perform the mudrā and mantra for binding the four directions. **The Thirteenth:

The Mudrā and Mantra for Binding the Four Directions with Vajrakuṇḍalī** This is the thirteenth [section], the sixth mudrā and the thirteenth mantra. In the Sanskrit language, it is *Parākara*. *Procedure:* First, tilt the left hand so that the five fingers are joined together. Press the right hand over the left forearm, with the backs of the hands touching. Hook the right thumb around the left thumb, and rotate to the right, following the path of the sun.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vīta-jñi hūṃ. This mantra is the same as the Earth-Boundary mantra. When one wishes to perform the ritual and recite the mantra, one should immediately rotate this mudrā three times clockwise, circumambulating toward the four directions to expel all demons, spirits, and the like belonging to the four quarters. Next, one performs the Upper-Boundary-Sealing Mudrā and Mantra.

14. The Dharma Seal and Mantra for Binding the Upper Realm by Vajrāṅkuśī. This is the fourteenth [section]. The seal is the seventh; the mantra is the fourteenth. “With both hands, interlace the three fingers from the middle finger downward, crossing them so that the right presses down upon the left. Place the backs of the fingers against the palms. With the tips of the two thumbs, lean them against each other at an angle. Bend the two index fingers so that their nails touch and support one another. Turn the tips of the thumbs downward to rest upon the crown of the head, but do not let them actually touch it.”
The mantra is:
"Oṃ tathā hūṃ. This dharma-seal mantra is able to eliminate all demons, evil spirits, and ghosts throughout the heavens and the void.

When one wishes to perform rites and recite mantras, by merely protecting oneself and establishing the boundary (*sīmābandha*), there is nothing further to fear; there shall be no obstacles whatsoever in performing various *Vaiśravaṇa* rites, all of which will possess divine efficacy.

The *Mudrā* of the *Vaiśravaṇa-Siṃhāsana*: This is the eighth seal. It employs the Great Heart Mantra; in the Sanskrit original it is called *Syeṅ-ga-san-na*. To form it: join the tips of the left and right index fingers, middle fingers, and ring fingers together; bring the wrists together; extend the two little fingers straight upward, leaving a space of about half an inch between them; bend the two thumbs into the palms as if drawing them inward; then extend the two thumbs straight outward—this is called "drawing in."

The *Vikṛti-harṣa-dharmamudrā* is the ninth seal. Using the Great Heart Mantra: "Bend the little fingers of both hands and press the two thumbs against the nails; extend the remaining fingers outward. Extend the right arm straight, place the left hand over the chest, stand up with the right knee bent, lean the body toward the right side, and keep the left leg slanted and upright at a distance of about four feet from the other. This is the Seal of the Messenger (*Dūta-mudrā*). To summon [the deity], use the right index finger: by bending it, they come; by extending it, they depart."
"This is the Seal of the Single Dharma (Ekadharmamudrā), which strikes all ghosts and asuras; wherever it is employed, it yields great efficacy.
If wicked people perform various evil rites intending to cause harm, by forming this seal and reciting this mantra, none of their efforts shall succeed."

The Seal for the *Vikūci* Offering Rite: This is the tenth seal. One employs the Great Heart Mantra (the Sanskrit text reads *āgamudrā*). Following the previous body seal, one makes this modification: separate the two thumbs by about two and a half inches. If one simultaneously bends the two thumbs and inserts them into the palms, this is the rite of "coming"; if one extends the two thumbs, this is the rite of "going."

"This is the Seal of the One Dharma. If one makes offerings of various flowers, incense, and food to the Triple Gem while forming this seal, one shall obtain immeasurable merit, and all Bodhisattvas will be greatly delighted."

The Eleventh Seal: The *Vikūci* Seal that Follows the Mind. To employ the Great Heart Mantra: bend the two ring fingers into the palms, with the right pressing upon the left; extend the two little fingers and the two middle fingers, keeping them touching; bend the two index fingers so they each rest against the first joint of the middle fingers; and bend the two thumbs so they lie along the side of the lower joints of the index fingers.

"This is the Seal of the Single Dharma. When one wishes to make offerings, one should form this seal and recite the Great Heart Mantra. Vajrakuṇḍalin will manifest before the practitioner, allowing them to see him; all their aspirations will be fulfilled according to their hearts' desires."

The twelfth seal, the *Vikṛti-dāna-sarvabhojana-dharmamudrā*: using the Great Heart Mantra, in Sanskrit *pāri*. With both hands turned upward, extend all eight fingers; join the little fingers to the sides of the wrists and press them together; then bend the tips of both thumbs and place them in the center of the palms.

"Once this Dharma-seal has been filled with various foods and drinks, it is offered as a gift to the Dharma-protecting deities and others; all sentient beings and all who receive it will give rise to joy."
"In the past, all five seals were recited together with the aforementioned Great Heart Mantra, and various efficacious results were obtained.

Regarding the Thirteenth Seal-Mantra for the Offering of *Vikucī* Flowers: [The Fifteenth Mantra]: 'Join the palms, leaving a hollow space between them; bend the two index fingers inward within the palms; extend the two thumbs side-by-side and upright, ensuring they do not touch the index fingers.'"
The mantra is:

"Oṃ śrī-jvala-mi suparadite pratyudhṛti-hṛtsna mayūpajidambushi svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If one performs the ritual services of Avalokiteśvara or the Bodhisattva Vidyujjvālākarālī, one must always perform this seal as an offering; thus one shall obtain the joy of all Bodhisattvas.
The Sixteenth Mantra for Offering *Vikucī* Incense: Use the Flower Offering Mudrā. The mantra says: “Oṃ pratyudhara hṛtsna durmāra-kule svāhā.

The Seventeenth Mantra for *Vikucī* to Extinguish Sins: Use the Flower Offering Mudrā. The mantra says: “Oṃ adhyadhi vihāre parati svāhā. Regarding these two mantra methods: if one performs the *Vikucī* rite, one should employ the aforementioned Flower Offering Mudrā for both and recite these two mantras.
All Buddhas who hear this mantra will give rise to joy, and all their sins from immeasurable kalpas shall be completely extinguished.
This is the Eighteenth Mantra for the Boundary-Formation and Offering of Vajrakilaya over Ten Thousand Li. Using the Dharmakāya Seal, the mantra says:

"Oṃ hrīḥ śūra-si uṃ phaṭ. If one wishes to establish various maṇḍalas, form a dharma altar, or perform extensive offerings, and fears the interference of māras, one should employ the aforementioned Dharmakāya Seal. When reciting this mantra, the rite will immediately be accomplished.

The Nineteenth Mantra for the Vajrāṅkuśī Altar Ground Offering. Regarding the mantra for the Vajrāṅkuśī altar ground offering: use the Fragrant Water Seal. The mantra is as follows: “Oṃ, teṣṭeṣṭa-jvati-tūre.

As for this mantra, if one wishes to establish an altar and extensively perform offerings, one should use the aforementioned Fragrant Water Seal to seal the fragrant water. Then, one should recite this mantra over the fragrant water one hundred and eight times and use it to smear the altar ground; thus, the rite will be accomplished.
Chapter on the Dharma of the Mudrā and Mantra of Vajracarcikā Bodhisattva for Subduing Māras, Chapter Twenty:
The Mantra is: “Oṃ bhañjaśani hūṃ phaṭ. Chapter Twenty-one: The Dharma of the Vajracarcikā Bow-Mantra.
The Mantra is: “Oṃ tārāsye hūṃ. Chapter Twenty-two: The Dharma of the Vajracarcikā Arrow-Shooting Mantra. The Mantra is: “Oṃ tārāsye hūṃ.”
“Oṃ trāsaya huṃ. This is the *Vijayā-dharmabāṇa-mantra*. (23) The mantra says: “Oṃ trāsani huṃ.
This is the *Vijayā-dharmabāṇa-mantra*. (24) The mantra says: “Oṃ vīrakrodha huṃ.
This is the *Vijayā-sarva-tīrthika-sarva-dharma-kārya-sīmā-bandhana-mantra*. (25) The mantra says:

“Oṃ śveti jaḍini svāhā. Regarding these and other such mantras: whether one constructs a Vajrapāṇi maṇḍala site, establishes various altars, performs boundary-binding for protection, or engages in offerings; or whether one treats illnesses, wards off spirits and ghosts, or breaks the difficult spells of non-Buddhist Brahmins—in each and every case, one must first form the body-seal and recite these six mantras as well as all other mantras, and they will all be efficacious.
The Fourteenth Dharma Seal of Vikuñcikācakra: Following the Buddha-wheel seal, the only modification is that the two index fingers are raised approximately half an inch above the middle fingers.

The Fifteenth Dharma Seal of Vajracarcikā, also known as the Seal of Wrath: Join the two hands; with both thumbs, pinch the lower joints of the ring fingers inside the palms. Bend both ring fingers together to press down upon the backs of the thumbs. Align the tips of the remaining three fingers of each hand, with the middle joints of these three fingers on both hands separated by approximately one cun.

The Sixteenth Seal: The *Vikṛti* Seal for Striking All Ghosts. As before, bend the left index, ring, and little fingers, and press them with the thumb so that the nails do not show. Hold the middle finger straight upright. Stand with both feet together and place the seal upon the forehead. Lower the middle finger until it reaches the space between the eyebrows. Make a wrathful facial expression; the right hand is not used. One should employ this seal to strike all ghosts.

The Seventeenth Dharma Seal of the Three Eyes of Vajrāṅkuśī: "Following the Seal of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, the only modification is that the three fingers below the middle fingers of both hands are crossed in reverse within the palms; the two index fingers are held upright with their tips touching. The two thumbs must not overlap the middle fingers, but each is held upright alongside the side of its respective index finger. Stand with feet together, turn the hands backward, and place them directly upon the forehead; the tips of the fingers should be aligned with the space between the eyebrows and hang downward. Form a wrathful expression on the face, identical to the Three-Eyed Dharma Seal of Cundī."

"This is the Seal of the Single Dharma. If one wishes to cure illnesses, or to subdue all evil Māras, great spirits, and the like, one should employ this seal while reciting the aforementioned Great Mantra; the rites will all be efficacious."

The Eighteenth: The Seal and Mantra for Counting the Rosary of Vikuñcī. The mantra (26) is identical to the method for counting the rosary in the section on Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara, with no further differences; one should employ the Great Heart Mantra.
Furthermore, the mantra for eliminating obstacles is as follows:
"Oṃ vīraśaraṅge ti so. This dharma-seal mantra is named "Elimination of Obstacles. The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi said:

"When forming the mudrā, counting the beads, and reciting this mantra, the karmic obstacles of the three types of action—past, future, and present—are removed; they are all completely extinguished, forever exhausted without remainder."
All who recited this mantra experienced its efficacy without exception.

Regarding the nineteenth *mudrā* and mantra for the *Vikṛti* (Pi-jū-chi) ash-gathering rite, the twenty-seventh mantra states: "With the right thumb and ring finger, pinch up some ash; recite the mantra seven times and place it upon the crown of the head."

The mantra is: “Oṃ uttara-tuṇḍi sīphalu svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If a person recites and maintains this *Vikurvaṇī* mantra method, whether they are traveling to or from a place and wish to protect themselves or protect the bodies of others, they should take ashes and recite this Dharma-seal mantra over them seven times. They should then apply the ashes to six locations—starting from the crown of the head down to the space between the eyebrows, the two armpits, below the throat, and the heart. Wherever one goes, there shall be no obstacles.

The Twenty-first Seal-Mantra for Dispatching All Departures by Vajrāṅkuśī. The mantra is twenty-eight [syllables]. To perform this: with the left hand, bend the tips of the middle and ring fingers so that they reach the second joint and are made flat; join the thumbs together so that the three fingers resemble a loom’s shuttle. Extend the little finger and the index finger straight, ensuring they do not touch the ring and middle fingers. Sit with knees bent and thighs joined, resting the right hand on the ground. Using the left hand, form the loom-shuttle seal with the three fingers and place it against the chest, leaning the torso forward.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vīre cici cu cu uṃ hūṃ ni ni krodha. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If one wishes to dispatch all [beings] or to command them, one should form this seal; having pressed the hands against the ground, lift the head and say aloud:
"Go! Go!"
"You must depart immediately.
This concludes the "Chapter on the Dharma-Seals of the Messengers of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi. Regarding the messengers of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, there are two:
the first is named Pramatha, and the second is named Prasanna.
These two messengers each spoke a mantra, requesting the use of the Bodhisattva’s former-life seal to subdue all beings.
Including the messenger *Pratama* mantra and the messenger *Pratama* mantra, there are twenty-nine mantras in total. The first messenger mantra is as follows:

"Oṃ vṛkūti varade karabhe svāhā. Including the messenger *Prasana* mantra and the messenger *Prasana* mantra, there are thirty mantras in total. The second messenger mantra is as follows: [The mantra is spoken].
"Oṃ bhagavati vīrakūṭe prajñe prabhāve svāhā. When Bodhisattvas hear these two mantras being recited, their hearts give rise to joy.

The two messengers followed the request to the Bodhisattva, who gave his seal of approval. This person who is able to recite this divine mantra can cause all beings to give rise to faith; furthermore, other mantras may also be requested for general use, along with various mudrās, to assist in accomplishing the Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual power.
At that time, the Buddha likewise simultaneously granted his seal of approval to all of them, and those messengers were all greatly rejoiced.
Those who practice the path of the bodhisattva should recite and uphold this.
This dhāraṇī method enables all the rites performed by the mantra-practitioner to receive the constant protection and mindfulness of the Bodhisattva.
He then spoke the mantra, the thirty-first: "Oṃ tathā huṃ jaḥ.
This is the third mantra for the binding of the boundary above the messenger, making thirty-two in total. The fourth mantra for the messenger is as follows:

“Oṃ vītadṛśi hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for binding the boundary; when combined with the previous ones, there are thirty-three. The fifth is the mantra of the Messenger, which says: “Oṃ śvetajñāni phaṭ.

When performing the rites of binding and protection with these two mantras, one employs the Bodhisattva’s Seal for Binding the Boundary and Protecting the Body; thus the method of reciting the mantras is accomplished.
The Dharma-mantra of the Messenger’s Head (Dūta-śīrṣa-dhāraṇī);
when combined with the preceding, it is the thirty-fourth. The sixth mantra of the Messenger: “Oṃ vāyanaśe svāhā. The Dharma-mantra of the Messenger’s Crown (Dūta-mauli-dhāraṇī);

when combined with the preceding, it is the thirty-fifth. The seventh mantra of the Messenger: “Oṃ trāsaya huṃ. The Dharma-mantra of the Messenger’s Eyes (Dūta-netra-dhāraṇī); when combined with the preceding, it is the thirty-sixth. The eighth mantra of the Messenger: “Oṃ...”
“Oṃ tala-saye phaṭ. This is the mantra for the mouth-rite of the messenger; combined with the preceding, it is the thirty-seventh.
The ninth mantra of the messenger is as follows: “Oṃ talasi hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for the heart-rite of the messenger; combined with the preceding, it is the thirty-eighth.

The tenth mantra of the messenger is as follows: “Oṃ vīrakucchi phaṭ. This is the mantra for the bow-rite of the messenger; combined with the preceding, it is the thirty-ninth. The eleventh mantra of the messenger is as follows:
“*Oṃ vīta jñi huṃ phaṭ.*” This is the mantra for the Messenger’s Arrow Method; when combined with the preceding [mantra], it is the fortieth. The twelfth Messenger mantra is as follows:
“*Oṃ ra jñi phaṭ.*” This is the mantra for the Messenger’s Staff Method; when combined with the preceding [mantra], it is the forty-first. The thirteenth Messenger mantra is as follows:

“*Oṃ vīta jñi phaṭ.*” All these mantras are universally applicable with the Dharma-seal of the Bodhisattva Vajravidāraṇa. They subjugate spirits and demons, cure all diseases, and protect sentient beings; they shall all be efficacious.
Cautionary Mantra, Cautionary Mantra. Combined with the preceding, this is the forty-second. The mantra says: "Oṃ kīṃ.

This is the Dharma Seal Mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajrānkuśī; it is the twenty-first seal, also known as the One-Syllable Seal Mantra. To perform it: With the four fingers of both hands, each grasp the thumb to form fists. First, place the right hand under the left armpit, then place the left hand under the right armpit. Bend the left knee, lean the body toward the left side, and stand the right leg straight and upright, following the bodily Dharma Seal of Kṣetrapāla.
The mantra is:
"Oṃ bhiḥ. Having formed this seal, recite the aforementioned great mantra seven times.

Once the seven recitations are complete, immediately draw back the hind leg so that the heel is positioned directly beneath the right knee, with the foot not touching the ground; rotate it once clockwise while uttering "Hūṃ."
Having uttered one sound, recite the one-syllable mantra and look around in all directions, giving rise to a great form of wrath.
This is the single Dharma-seal of Vajrāṅkuśī, known as Mahāmudrā; Vajrāṅkuśī should perform this rite when wishing to strike all beings.
At that time, the assemblies of the various Vajra-family retinues were struck with great fear; all the devas and māras were utterly shattered and simultaneously fell into a swoon.

"By the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Seal, reciting the one-syllable mantra even once is no different from reciting the mantras of the body of Avalokiteśvara; there is no distinction between the merit of the one syllable and that of the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa."

The Chapter on the Ritual Altar for Saving the Sick by Bhṛkuṭī. Regarding the ritual altar for saving the sick by Bhṛkuṭī: "If a mantra-practitioner wishes to save a patient, they shall go to the patient's home, bathe with fragrant water, don new and clean robes, and establish a ritual altar to alleviate their suffering."

The site for constructing the altar should be a favorable location, situated among water, trees, and flowering groves; or near the banks of the Ganges River, or at a place where there is a deep dragon pool. Having selected the most excellent spot according to one's residence, purify the ground in accordance with the ritual for the Eleven-Faced Seven-Day Altar.
When the purification of the ground is complete, smear the floor with fragrant mud and suspend various multicolored banners, canopies, and precious vessels.
Within that *maṇḍala*, one should construct a four-cubit ritual altar (*dharma-maṇḍala*) of five colors; at the center of the altar, place the seat of the Bodhisattva Vajrakuṭī.
In the east, construct a lotus seat, upon which place a large sword horizontally;
in the north, likewise construct a lotus seat, upon which set a clear mirror face upward;
in the south, again construct a lotus seat, upon which erect three arrows.
Outside the western gate of the altar, arrange the seat for the mantra-reciter.

Take five water jars, each with a capacity of one *śu* or less; fill them completely with pure water, place the five grains within, and seal their mouths with branches of green cypress, bamboo, pear, and crab-apple.
Having adorned the vases, they should be placed at the four corners and the center of the altar.

Ten plates of various superior-flavored fruits and foods, twelve lamps, and various incenses and flowers are offered with the recitation of mantras through various ritual procedures, continuing daily without interruption.

"When the seven days have passed, you should await the Seal of the Dharma that accords with your mind, taking its manifestation as the limit. By repenting with utmost sincerity, you shall eliminate your obstacles and swiftly achieve realization."

"In the future, if treating an illness, one should also rely on this method: have the patient sit facing north, to the east of the mantra-reciter; recite the mantra over white mustard seeds and circumambulate them around the patient's head, burning them for three days, and they will certainly recover."
"If one constructs this Dharma-maṇḍala, it will yield the greatest efficacy if one can wait for the time of a solar or lunar eclipse;
if one does not encounter such a time of eclipse, one should select an auspicious day within that month."
If there is no suitable location as previously described, one may instead construct a maṇḍala at a fine temple.
Furthermore, the mantra-practitioner must receive a white horse as an offering;
if there is no white horse, one should fashion a horse out of silver and give it to the mantra-practitioner.
If there is no silver for making the horse, one may use whatever object the mantra-practitioner requires as a substitute for the horse;

however, if there are no such objects, this rite should only be taught to those who are kind-hearted and filial, firm in their observance of the precepts, and capable of following the strict and decisive instructions of the ācārya without deviation.

The Efficacy of the Vidyārājñī Bhṛkuṭī Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī: “If there be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or sons and daughters of good family who uphold this great dhāraṇī-seal for the purpose of protecting the body and establishing boundaries, performing various rites, healing illnesses, repenting, and making offerings of incense and flowers without interruption, they shall receive the protective mindfulness of the Bodhisattva.”

"If one wishes to enter the palace of the asuras, one should recite the mantra three thousand times every day for eight years. Forming the Three-Eyed Seal (*tryakṣa-mudrā*), one uses the aforementioned great mantra to consecrate white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times; with each recitation, one scatters them upon the ground. The earth will then open to form a hole, through which the mantra-master may enter."
"If you wish to remain and behold Maitreya Buddha, you may stay as you please;
if you wish to come forth, do not enter the city.
If you see wealth or goods on the road, you may take them out with you without incurring any offense."
If there are fruits, one may take and eat them, and one's lifespan will be one thousand years.

"If you wish for the great ocean to dry up, you should go to its shore and, for three months, recite the aforementioned Great Mantra over white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times each day and scatter them into the seawater; by doing so daily, the seawater will then dry up."

"If one wishes to capture and seize a dragon, one should go to the side of a body of water where dragons dwell and perform the ritual and recite the mantra for one hundred days; the dragon will then emerge of its own accord and approach the mantra-reciter, who may then subdue it as desired."
"If one treats feverish illnesses with this, it is most efficacious and auspicious.

If a person wishes to obtain *āveśana* (possession), they should take equal parts of manaḥśilā (translated here as 'stone-orpiment') and mākṣika (antimony) and grind them together into a powder. Having refined it further for six months, they should bathe daily, wear fresh and clean garments, and at the three times of day—dawn, midday, and dusk—recite the mantra over the medicine one hundred and eight times with a sincere mind. Afterward, reciting it seven more times, they should apply it to their eyes; they will then achieve *āveśana* at will. It is visible only when sprinkled away [from the eyes], and the medicine must not be handled by anyone else."

"If you intend to enter the palace of the asuras, and there are obstacles such as malevolent objects, rākṣasas, snakes, and the like; or if there are hindrances such as doors not opening or darkness, you should beforehand prepare yourself by reciting the mantra over white mustard seeds one thousand and eight times. Carry them with you as you go, and wherever there is an obstacle, strike it with them; then, in every place, there will be no hindrance."

The Method for Painting the Image of Vajracarcikā: "If one uses white cotton cloth or paints the image upon silk, the artist must first observe the eightfold precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa). He should paint an image of Śākyamuni Buddha, with Vajrapāṇi on the left side and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva on the right side."

That Buddha’s body is golden and adamantine; his face is neither black nor white, and his form is like that of a sixteen-year-old youth; all his limbs are adorned in accordance with the dharmas of an adorned Bodhisattva body.

"The face and body of this Avalokiteśvara, as well as his crown, necklaces, celestial garments, and silk robes, are all adorned in accordance with the methods for painting Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva found elsewhere."

Below the left hand of Avalokiteśvara, another female deity should be painted separately; her body is entirely white, her garments are red and white, her countenance is exceedingly upright and beautiful, and she wears a flower crown upon her head.
Next, below [the central figure], draw the mantra-practitioner kneeling on his right knee, holding an incense burner in his hand and facing Avalokiteśvara.

Once this image has been completed, from the first day to the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, one should eat only barley and milk porridge while constantly reciting the following mantra; then, for three days and three nights until the eighth day of the waning moon, one must not eat at all.
"When making offerings to the image, the image of that goddess immediately emits light which enters into the toes of the Buddha's feet.
When this sign is seen, all heart-wishes are fulfilled."

Furthermore, if one wishes to see Pāṇḍaravāsini, on the thirteenth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day, one may enter the waters of the great ocean for three days and three nights to recite the mantra. One should display her painted image upon the water's edge and make offerings of a hundred thousand lotuses.

At that time, when the goddess Bandharāvasinī comes, those who cultivate the path with intelligence and wisdom, and those rishis who maintain mantras, shall all have their wishes fulfilled according to their desires.
Furthermore, there is the Vajuci mantra.
The mantra says:

“*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ bha-gavad-bhaye oṃ samaparyanāśani trāsani trāsani trāsayatrāsaya trase trasi bhijūti nijūti dhiti dhiti vedadhī vedadhī huluhuluvēdadhī śveti-jñāni svāhā.*” This mantra is also called the Vajra Mantra Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
"When reciting this mantra, all obstacles and difficulties will completely cease.
If one wishes to protect oneself, recite the mantra over ashes seven times and apply them to the forehead, the nape of the neck, and both shoulders; wherever one goes, there shall be no fear."

If one does this for another, by reciting the mantra over their hair and tying it into knots while constantly keeping the mantra in mind, they will encounter no difficulties in any place of fear—whether in government offices, walking alone at night, or among bandits. All wicked people will joyfully submit and take refuge, unable to create any obstacles.

"If you wish to subdue all beings, you should fast for one day and one night on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight. Using wood from a Bodhi tree as fuel, kindle a fire; recite the mantra once over a pinch of sesame seeds and cast them into the fire. When this is repeated eight thousand times, all will submit and come under your control—namely, the Śirīṣa tree and the Aśoka tree, which is the tree under which Kāśyapa Buddha attained enlightenment. Any tree under which a Buddha attained enlightenment may be used, and the *kukkuṭaka* tree may also be used."

"If one is afflicted by the malevolent incantations of all manner of enemies and consequently loses one's mental composure, one should take the bones of a man and fashion them into stakes. By reciting the mantra eight thousand times and driving these stakes into the ground at the base of the enemy's door, one will cause that person to likewise lose their mental composure."

"Furthermore, there is another method: take the ashes from a cremated corpse; on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, recite the mantra once over a pinch of ash and cast it into a fire. If this is done eight thousand times, the enemy will be extinguished."

"Furthermore, there is a method: on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, enter the water and stand until the water reaches the navel, and recite the mantra; all enemies and hosts of wicked thieves will be reconciled with one another, and both will give rise to wholesome minds."

"Furthermore, there is another method: if one wishes to establish a boundary (sīmābandha) in the four directions, take four pieces of khadira wood—each eight finger-widths in length and breadth—and after reciting the mantra over each eight hundred times, drive them into the ground at the four cardinal points. Then, no malevolent spirits or hostile enemies shall be able to enter within this boundary."

Furthermore, within the boundary, one constructs a maṇḍala; by reciting the mantra over water twenty-one times and sprinkling it upon the ground, the boundary is established, and within it, one is fit to perform the dhāraṇī rites.
"Furthermore, there is a method: recite the mantra *sattvamūrdhapāṭana hūṃ pūrīśa pi* seven times over mustard seeds.
Furthermore, regarding the method for prolonging life, it is said that if the necessary materials are lacking, it cannot be accomplished; this has not been translated."

"Furthermore, there is another method: take a small amount of Qin-ox ghee (āmalaka-sarpis), recite the mantra once for each incense offering and burn it. When these have been completed eight thousand times, all illnesses, pains, and obstacles will be entirely eliminated."
Furthermore, there is no need to observe the sun, moon, or specific seasons; perform the rite whenever it can be done, and use whatever firewood is available.
"Another method is to take firewood from the *khadira* tree (mushanzi) to kindle a fire for burning the medicine; as this tree does not exist in this land, it is omitted here."
"Furthermore, there is a method: when the thief of anger comes intending to trip me up, if one recites this mantra, the mind will immediately become joyful.

Furthermore, there is a method for legal matters: on the eighth day of the month, by the side of an image of Avalokiteśvara, one should consecrate white flowers with the mantra and cast them one stem at a time into a fire. When eight thousand repetitions are completed, the legal matter will be resolved."

"Furthermore, there is a method: if bandits come intending to invade and cause disorder, one should recite the mantra with a sincere mind before the image of Avalokiteśvara, and the bandits will immediately depart.

Furthermore, there is a method: whatever dharma one seeks, while reciting this mantra, one should burn smokeless charcoal and consecrate white mustard seeds with the mantra. For each repetition, one seed is cast into the fire. When eight thousand repetitions are completed, all that is sought shall be fulfilled."
"Furthermore, if one recites the mantra over white mustard seeds seven times, all *vetāla* spirits and the like will be completely bound.

Another method: if one recites the mantra over rock honey seven times and casts it into water, one may take this water to form a *maṇḍala* boundary; by reciting the mantra within it, none of the following can cause harm: lions, tigers, birds and beasts, water buffaloes, white elephants, *rākṣasas*, *cūras*, or water."
"The brief exposition of the *Vijayā* mudrā, mantra, and its ritual methods is hereby completed.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Scroll Five.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Scroll Six, Part Two: Avalokiteśvara and Other Bodhisattvas.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Ajita from India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Chapter on the Dharma-Seal Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Hayagrīva. In the Tang language, this is translated as the *Mātṛkā* (Horse-Head) Family Seal. There are eight seals and sixteen mantras. 1.

The Dharma-Seal and Mantra for Protecting the Body and Binding the Boundary of Hayagrīva. First: "Interlace the three fingers from the middle finger downward with the palms facing outward, each touching the back of the hand. Join the palms together; extend the two index fingers straight upward, spaced about five *fen* apart. Place the two thumbs side-by-side, each bent at one joint so that they do not touch the index fingers. Move the index fingers back and forth."

The mantra is: "Oṃ pravicāsta vajra śavara-ra-ji svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If one wishes to receive and uphold this Bodhisattva dharma, one must first protect oneself by reciting this Dharma-seal mantra. Furthermore, one should recite it seven times over wood or seven times over water; then, using the seal, one seals the water. Alternatively, one may recite it over white mustard seeds or ashes, sealing and reciting each seven times. Having done so, one should plant the wood at the four corners to establish the boundary, and scatter the mustard seeds, ashes, and water in the ten directions to complete the *kṣetraparigraha* (boundary-binding). Only then will all ritual activities performed yield their full efficacy.

2. The Great Dharmakāya Seal and Mantra of Hayagrīva, Part Two. "Interlace the three fingers from the index finger down with the palms facing outward; touch the tips of each finger to the back of the hand. Join the palms, align the two little fingers vertically so they meet, and join the two thumbs together. Bend the thumbs into fists, then move them back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ (1) duna duna (2) matha matha (3) khāda khāda (4) hāyagiri-va (5) hūṃ phaṭ svāhā (7). This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If a person is bitten by venomous insects or snakes, or encounters an evil person, once they have been sealed with this seal and the mantra is recited over them, they will immediately recover.

Furthermore, regarding the method for summoning a *mīgu* (yakṣa): take *sumana* flowers and recite the mantra twenty-one times before an image of Hayagrīva. Once you have finished scattering them at the feet of the image, take a flower with your right hand and follow behind the *mīgu* wherever it goes. Recite the mantra over the flower seven times and scatter it; he will immediately come.

"Furthermore, if both parties possess a mind [of desire], one should take a fruit or seed and recite a mantra over it twenty-one times. When sent by someone to deliver food, the recipient's mind will immediately become bewildered; they will feel such intense love and longing that no other thoughts will remain."

3. The Heart-Seal Mantra of the Hayagrīva Rite. Third: "Interlace the four fingers from the index fingers downward with the palms facing outward, so that the tips of the fingers each touch the back of the hand. Join the palms, place the two thumbs side by side touching each other, bend one joint of each thumb so they do not touch the index fingers, and move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:
“Oṃ amṛtodbhava huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This dharma-seal mantra is for when one wishes to engage in debate.
Take the three ingredients— cow bezoar, musk, and camphor— and grind them together;
recite the mantra one thousand and eight times over them,
then apply it to the crown of the head.
Then, over the two shoulders, the heart, the throat, the space between the eyebrows, the hairline, and the back of the head,
take white mustard seeds and recite the mantra twenty-one times;
holding them in the right hand, go to the gate of the place of debate and scatter them there.
Still, leaving a small portion of mustard seeds in the left hand,
when the formal debate is taking place, one should take the mustard seeds from the left hand with the right hand and secretly scatter them toward the opponent in the debate,
then immediately snap the fingers.
One shall thus attain the method for overcoming others.

4. The Dharma-Seal and Mantra of Hayagrīva (Horse-Head). The Fourth [Section]: The Dharma-Seal and Mantra of Hayagrīva. "Following the previous body-protection seal, change only this: join the tips of the two index fingers together; bend them so that the second phalanges protrude, with the small tips pointing outward."
The mantra is:

*Tadyathā* (1) *cakrābha* (2) *cakrākṣabha* (3) *cakrapadmodbhavakṣabha* (4) *amogha* (5) [insert the person’s name here] *śiracche* (6) *parasaṃghaccheda* (7) *svāhā* (8). [In other instances, the pronunciation of *kṣa* is the same. As for the ritual: if any person suffers from a headache, take their name and recite this mantra over water. After making the sound *huṃ*, strike the person’s head with this water and seal the site of the pain; the pain will immediately be cured. (This mantra is missing from the ancient manuscript.)

5. The Dharma Seal and Mantra of Hayagrīva’s Crown. Fifth. "Perform as before with the head seal, with this modification: raise the two index fingers so that their tips touch; align the two middle fingers in front of the index fingers so that their tips support one another."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ śrīla-ri-ti huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there is anyone suffering from pain in the head or crown of the head, one should seal the painful spot with this mudrā and recite the mantra; they will immediately be cured.

6. The Mudrā and Dhāraṇī of the Horse-Headed Face Ritual (Hayagrīvamukha-mudrā-dhāraṇī), Part Six. "Interlace the two little fingers behind within the palms; extend the two middle fingers straight upward with their tips touching; extend both thumbs side by side; press the tip of the right index finger against the tip of the right thumb; and extend the left index finger, slightly curved toward the side of the middle finger."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ hulu luḥ kuruḍāna huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This dharma-seal mantra cures all demonic illnesses immediately upon its application.

7. The Mudrā and Dhāraṇī of Hayagrīva, Part Seven. "The mudrā and dhāraṇī of Hayagrīva are performed according to the previous mudrā of Avalokiteśvara Amoghapāśa. The only difference is that the two middle fingers are raised straight with their tips touching, and the two thumbs are held side-by-side, pressed against the middle fingers. First, grasp the back of the right ring finger with the left little finger; then, grasp the back of the left little finger with the right little finger."
The mantra says:
"Namaḥ maṇidharāya | Nama āryāyai ||"
Parakite saṃparāye bodhisattvāya.
Mahāsattvāya (6) Mahākāruṇikāya (7) Tadyathā (8) Tārata (9) [Dhāraṇī]
Ṭaṭa ṭaṭa (10) maṭa maṭa (11) cchinda cchinda (12)
Phin da phin da (13) Hūṃ (14) Phaṭ phaṭ (15)

"Ṣā hā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If one wishes to shatter all dharmas and cause the mantra-rites performed by others to fail, one should construct a ritual altar using three-colored powders measuring four cubits.
On the northern and southern sides, draw lotus seats, upon which draw the shape of elephant tusks;
on the eastern side, draw the *vajra* mudrā upon the lotus seat.

Furthermore, twelve lamps were lit, and one hundred flavors of diverse foods were prepared in eight platters; these dishes were replaced with fresh ones every day, and this new offering was maintained for seven full days.

Each day, one must furthermore recite the mantra over one hundred and eight white mustard seeds; with each recitation, cast one seed into the fire to burn it. This shall destroy the ritual methods of all others, rendering them unable to achieve their aims—those "other people" being the heretics and evil persons.

8. The Dharani and Mudrā for the Begging Rite of Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Part Eight "Turn the left hand upward and extend all five fingers. Turn the right hand downward and touch the tips of the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb together."
The mantra is: "Oṃ na-śa-ri-ke. Recite this twenty-eight times. 9.

The Mantra and Seal for the Method of Releasing the Sword by Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva, Part Nine. "Extend both hands, with the left hand outside and the right hand inside; place the back of the left hand against the back of the right hand, and extend both thumbs upright."

The mantra is: "Oṃ āsamayiṇi svāhā. Chapter Ten: The Seal and Mantra for the Horse-Headed One’s Method of Healing Illness. [Method: Interlace both hands behind the back, extend the two middle fingers so they stand upright with their tips touching, and place the two thumbs side by side in front, slightly bent. Then, bend each of the two index fingers to grasp the base of the thumbs, ensuring the tips of the index nails touch the backs of the thumbs' nails.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ hulu lu jūrudhana uṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This dharma-seal mantra should be used to treat all manner of illnesses; it shall heal all those afflicted by spirits, ghosts, and the like, and their diseases will be immediately cured.

11. The Great Dharani of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva, the Eleventh. The Dharani says: *Namo ratnatrayāya | Namo 'ryavalokiteśvarāya* (Namo-mu-la-tuo-na-da-ra-ye | Namo-ari-ya-ba-lu-ji-ti-she-ba-ra-ye) (The first *na* is pronounced with an upward tone;

13. The Thirteenth Vidyārāja Mantra for Binding Vināyakas. "If one performs this rite, one must first bind and restrain the Vināyakas. Following the method of taking refuge at the beginning of the aforementioned Great Mantra, one should take refuge and prostrate, and then recite the binding mantra."

The mantra is: *Tadyathā: curu curu, vicuru vicuru, gata ye svāhā, mahāparā, sarvavidyāvināyakān, bhaṭṭapramukhān, pūjaye phaṭ.* As for the ritual method: one should perform this before an image of Hayagrīva. First, take wood of the *śrīvatsa* tree eight finger-widths long and cut it; when the fire has been kindled and flames have emerged, take *guggulu* incense and prepare eight hundred pills. Recite the mantra once and cast one pill into the fire, continuing until the incense is exhausted. Then the *vināyakas* will be bound of their own accord.
12. Another Dhāraṇī Method, the Twelfth. "Perform the preliminary acts of taking refuge and prostrating as before. The dhāraṇī is as follows:

*Tadyathā* (1) *buddhe buddhe* (2) *subuddhe* (3) *indrabuddhe* (4) *mamīśukālaṃ* (5) *paravācatur* (6) *svāhā* (7). Regarding its ritual application: if a person loses seminal purity at night, take a white thread and first recite this dhāraṇī over it eight hundred times. Then, fashion a consecrated cord, tying one knot for each recitation until there are twenty-one knots. Fasten it around the waist, and [the emission] will no longer leak."
13. Another Dhāraṇī Method, the Thirteenth. "Perform the preliminary acts of taking refuge and prostration as before.
The dhāraṇī is as follows:

*Tadyathā | hara hare | muhare | kuhare | sarvatuṣṭān | jambhaye me | nyavakrandite | navanśame | svāhā.* As for the ritual: having recited this dhāraṇī over a corner of the *kaṣāya* (monastic robe) seven times, tie it into a single knot; thus the accomplishment of the method for protecting the body is complete."
14. The Seal and Mantra for the Dispatching of Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara, Number Fourteen. "Perform the prostrations and take refuge as previously described."
The mantra for dispatching Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva is:

“Tadyathā | sarapara-sara | jaya-vijaya | vajra-kurapa-va | svāhā | kacchamudra-si | svāhā. As for the ritual: holding *sura-vibhuṣpa*—which in this context refers to cypress flowers—in one’s hand, recite the mantra once and strike the image once. Do this seven times, and Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva will immediately depart.
Regarding the method for painting the image: "Take a new earthenware jar that has never been used and dye it blue; upon this jar, paint an image of Avalokiteśvara with a horse's head."
The height of the image shall be one span (vitasti) of the Tathāgata, equivalent to one cubit (hasta) of a human; it should be painted with four joyful faces.
The face on the left side is painted black, with green eyes and canine fangs protruding upward;
the face on the right side is painted red and is named the "Face that Devours Mantras."
The front face in the center is that of a bodhisattva, made extremely upright and painted white;
above the crown of the central image, suspended in mid-air, is painted a blue face, from whose mouth a precious jewel is being spat forth.
On each of his four heads he wears a jeweled crown, and upon each crown sits a manifested Buddha.

The Bodhisattva’s left hand grasps a lotus flower, bent at the elbow and pointing upward, with the fist held before the shoulder; his right arm hangs down, all five fingers extended in the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), with jeweled bracelets adorning both wrists.

Around the neck of the image are worn precious necklaces; its body is adorned according to the methods for adorning the body of Avalokiteśvara as described elsewhere, and the image stands upon a precious lotus flower.

"Once this image was completed, he began in advance on the tenth day of the waxing moon to subsist on a gruel of barley and milk; thereafter, on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, for three days and three nights, he abstained from food entirely."

Take *pākabhiñca* incense and *gandhanakuli* flowers; consecrate these two substances with mantras, casting one into the fire with each recitation before one's face. Upon reaching eight thousand recitations, light will radiate from one's face and mouth.
Once that light has circled the body of the mantra-practitioner and returned into the mouth of the image, a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) shall emerge from within its mouth;

this one should immediately collect. Having taken this jewel, one shall obtain a lifespan of fourteen thousand years and will soon become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) possessed of the seven treasures.
After the end of his life, he shall be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, arising from beneath the feet of Avalokiteśvara.
"Furthermore, there is one dharma: when begging for food, one should eat barley and milk gruel while reciting [the mantra] seventy thousand times.
Upon reaching ten thousand recitations, the Vināyakas shall be bound;
at twenty thousand recitations, the dhāraṇī-vidyā is accomplished."

At the third ten thousand recitations, one immediately attains the accomplishment of the *āśana-mānava-cīra* medicinal rite. One should not eat for three days and three nights and perform the ritual while holding the medicine in hand. While reciting the mantra over the medicine, if three signs appear within it—namely, warmth, smoke, and flame—one knows that the medicine has been perfected. One then attains the accomplishment of *antarddhāna*, traveling through the air; one attains the accomplishment of a *vidyādhara* ṛṣi, entering the caves of the asuras at will.
At the fourth ten thousand recitations, one travels freely at a height of four finger-widths above the ground.
At the fifth ten thousand recitations, one attains the ability to ascend and travel through the air at will.

At the sixth ten-thousand recitations, one attains a lifespan of a thousand years; the mantra-practitioner becomes an accomplished mantra-seer (*vidyādhara*), and whatever he undertakes is spontaneously fulfilled, while all those he calls upon come to him.

At the seventh ten-thousand recitations, the mantra-practitioner’s hair transforms into a spiral topknot (*śikhā*), and whatever he requires arrives as soon as it is thought of. He draws near to and serves Avalokiteśvara, whereby he knows the death and rebirth of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, and thus achieves accomplishment.

"Furthermore, according to another method, if one wishes to produce the sound 'Rā-rā' (pronounced with the *yà* tone) toward the west, one should fast for three days and three nights before the image of Hayagrīva. One should smear the altar with incense and offer various kinds of fragrant flowers, as well as pure food, milk porridge, fruits, and other various offerings. One should grind *sajjārāsa* incense and mix it with white honey to form eight thousand pellets. After reciting the mantra once over each pellet of incense, one should cast it into the fire to burn. In this manner, one proceeds one by one until all the incense is exhausted."

When the western *ṛṣis* first see their heads transformed into those of crows, and after a short while their heads further change into those of *khañjarīṭa* birds, as the mantra-master gazes upward at that assembly with wonder, all the western *ṛṣis* completely disperse and vanish.
"Furthermore, according to another method: first, give barley to a cow to eat; then, take the barley from its dung, dry it, and pound and boil it to make milk-gruel (*pāyasa*).
Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, one should consume this milk-gruel until the thirteenth day, at which point one ceases eating entirely."

Before the image of Hayagrīva, having finished making offerings by anointing the ground with fragrant unguents, scattering various flowers, burning various famous incenses, and presenting various foods and drinks, one takes *kapittha* wood and grinds it into a fine powder; mixing this with water, one forms pills, numbering exactly eight thousand.

Take kāṣṭhara wood to serve as fuel and kindle a fire; take one incense pellet, recite the mantra once, and cast it into the fire. Continue in this manner until eight thousand pellets have been burned, at which point the charcoal will be transformed into suvarṇa gold weighing one hundred thousand *liang*.

"Furthermore, as for the method if one wishes to 'consume' the mantras of others: take a small amount of blood from one's own body and mix it with white mustard seeds to form eight thousand pills. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, abstain from food for the entire day. Take *khadira* wood and kindle a fire in a brazier; then, taking the aforementioned white mustard seed pills, cast one pill into the fire with each recitation of the mantra. Continue in this manner until all the mustard seed pills are exhausted. 'To consume' (chi) is a foreign term; its meaning is equivalent to the Chinese word for 'to destroy' (*po-mie*). 'Others' (*ta*) refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)."
"Furthermore, there is another method: by merely reciting the mantra while traveling through wildernesses and sandy deserts, the food and drink one requires will arrive spontaneously.

Furthermore, there is another method: during a solar or lunar eclipse, take one *liang* of pure cow’s ghee and place it in a new earthen bowl. Holding this bowl, look up at the sun or moon and recite the mantra over the ghee in the bowl until the ghee becomes warm, or until smoke and fire emerge. At that moment, one should drink this medicine."
Having consumed this ghee, wherever one wishes to go, one arrives as soon as the thought arises.
If one constantly recites this mantra, all fears will be dispelled so that one attains fearlessness, and all obstacles and difficulties will be entirely liberated.

"Furthermore, according to another method: if one suffers from *rūḍha* sores—those who suffer from these sores all die—or is bitten by various venomous snakes, such that the person dies upon seeing the snake; or if one suffers from *kambīṭa-kī* sores: for all such sores, one should recite the mantra over yellow clay and mud one thousand times and apply it to the sores; they will then be healed."
All fears are immediately dispelled by bringing them to mind.
Furthermore, according to another method, if a person should suddenly encounter any water-related peril, they will immediately attain the state of not being submerged by keeping this in mind.
“Such dharmas as these cannot be explained in detail; they are accomplished simply by following one’s intention.
If one constructs a great maṇḍala, one must not engage in sensual desire.
Regarding the ritual for creating an image of Kāyavajrapāṇi—furthermore, there is another method for painting an image: take a clean white cloth that has not been cut or torn.”

Engage a master painter of the highest skill, do not dispute his price, bathe him with fragrant water, dress him in fresh, clean garments, and have him observe the eight precepts every day in this manner.

In a pure location, construct a water mandala four cubits in length and breadth; the ritual for the water mandala is as described in other sections. Once the mantra-practitioner has completed the protection of his own body and the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), he should bestow that same protection upon the recipient.
Having finished making offerings within that maṇḍala by burning various incenses and scattering various flowers, one should paint a bodhisattva inside this maṇḍala.

The body of this bodhisattva is one span (vitasti) in length—measured from the tip of the thumb to the middle finger—which is equivalent to the forearm length (hasta) of an ordinary person; it possesses four faces in total.
The central face of the Bodhisattva is made extremely upright and handsome, with an expression of compassion; its complexion is reddish-white and the hair is purely blue.
The face on the left side manifests great wrath; it is black in color, with canine fangs protruding upward and hair standing erect like the color of a flame.
The face on the right side manifests a laughing countenance; it is reddish-white and as upright as the central Bodhisattva face, with hair that is purely blue.
Each of the three faces wears a celestial crown and ear-rings; upon each crown sits an emanation Buddha in the full lotus posture.
On the crown of the central face is formed a green horse’s head, which is kept with its mouth closed.
Around the neck of the Bodhisattva is a precious necklace; behind his neck and back is a circular halo composed of multiple layers of color.
His left arm is bent, with the hand placed before his breast, grasping a red lotus flower.
The lotus flower was level with the Bodhisattva’s head and positioned directly over his left shoulder.
Upon the flower’s pedestal appeared a manifested Buddha, wearing a crimson *kāṣāya* robe and sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), with light radiating from his neck and back.

The right hand has its palm facing upward with all five fingers extended; the arm and elbow are bent at equal angles. This palm supports a cintāmaṇi (in the Tang language, "wish-fulfilling jewel"), which is perfectly round and white in color, surrounded by a halo of red light. From this jewel, held directly in the right hand, various kinds of treasures rain down.

On her left shoulder she wears a *vyāghracarman* (Tang: "tiger skin"), which she wears like a *saṃkakṣikā*; she drapes the skin over her right armpit and fastens it with a sash. Furthermore, she covers her hips with tiger skin. Her outer armlets, celestial robes, and skirt are all to be depicted according to the rules for painting Bodhisattvas found elsewhere. Thus, the Bodhisattva is to be portrayed standing upright with body straight upon a red lotus flower, with a precious parasol suspended in the air above her head.
"In the space above, paint various musical instruments of the devas; in the space on both sides, depict the Śuddhāvāsa devas performing dances as offerings.
When painting this image, use fragrant liquid for the pigments; animal glue must not be used."

The Mañjuśrī Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara Dharma-Initiation Altar: "If there be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or any sons and daughters of good family who wish to receive and uphold the Bodhisattva Dharma, they should, according to the previous instructions, construct a four-cubit altar. They must seek out an excellent and pure location, sweep and sprinkle it until it is clean, and further smear the ground with scented water and cow dung. They should hang various multicolored banners, canopies, jeweled bells, pendants, mirrors, and various gold and silver ornaments, interspersing them in all manner of ways to adorn the site of practice."

“In the center of that maṇḍala, one should establish a five-colored altar measuring four cubits in length and breadth; first apply white, then yellow, then red, then blue, and finally black, and construct four gates.”
"At the center of the altar, construct a lotus seat and enshrine an image of Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara;
directly at the eastern gate, construct a lotus seat and enshrine the Eleven-faced Bodhisattva;
directly at the northern gate, construct a lotus seat and enshrine the Eight-armed Avalokiteśvara."
In the southern part of the altar, there is no further flower-seat;

instead, one should depict eight nāga kings. What are these eight? First is the Nanda Nāga King; second is the Vasuki Nāga King; third is the Takṣaka Nāga King; fourth is the Karkoṭaka Nāga King; fifth is the Padma Nāga King; sixth is the Mahāpadma Nāga King; seventh is the Śaṅkhapāla Nāga King; and eighth is the Kulika Nāga King.
These eight dragon kings may be offered only with milk-rice made from husked rice; however, they may also be offered various other kinds of food and drink.
Nevertheless, for the forty-five lamps, first summon the eight dragon kings and establish them there, using the body-seal of Hayagrīva Bodhisattva for their coming and going.

Once consecrated, they are cast into the fire and burned; this is done for each item in this manner until one thousand and eight recitations are completed.
"Next, invite Hayagrīva Bodhisattva at the center; next, invite the eight-armed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of the north, using the Bodhisattva-body mudrā for their coming and going."

"If the mantra-practitioner fasts for one day, and if unable to endure hunger, may eat only ghee; having bathed with fragrant water and donned new, clean garments, he shall enter the *maṇḍala* and perform offerings. Whether within the body, outside the body, above the stomach (āmāśaya), or below the large intestine (pakvāśaya); whether suffering from headaches, dizziness, bodily pain, heartache, or irregular chills and fevers—upon hearing this mantra of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja and the mantra of the Bodhisattva Varuṇa, the eighty thousand spirits and ghosts shall be unable to afflict the person’s body. This great divine mantra can cause all illnesses and sufferings to be completely healed and cured.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and the others, each expressing their original intent from within this assembly of Buddhas, expounded upon the inconceivable great majestic power and merit of the Dharma-seal Mantra Chapter. All the Buddhas praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

"Because you are able to provide such excellent protection and mindfulness, you have established these skillful means and sovereign spiritual powers to extensively rescue sentient beings, freeing them from all attachments, eliminating their karmic obstacles, and removing their afflictions. Having given rise to great compassion, you have diligently instructed and exhorted them, causing them to be moved to realization and awakening; I hereby grant my approval. At that time, the entire assembly was filled with joy, prostrated themselves, and departed.

Chapter One: The Dhāraṇī of the Dharma Seal of the Samādhi of Great Majestic Power of Vajragarbha, Spoken by the Buddha.
This chapter contains fifty-seven seals and thirty-two dhāraṇīs.
There are eighteen verses of praise and eleven seals; the mantra is the sovereign, while the others are its attendants. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Vipula together with an incalculable assembly of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as well as countless Arhats, and the eight classes of gods, nāgas, and others, surrounding him in front and behind. Together they were assembled there as he expounded the secret Dharma-treasury of dhāraṇīs and seals.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Vajragarbha in the great assembly; he rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and bowed his head at the feet of the Buddha.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! I have fourteen groups of followers, each of whom is accompanied by immeasurable retinues. They are currently present in this assembly at my command. Since ancient times, they have maintained the dhāraṇī methods, which are profound, clear, strictly secret, and pure; for this reason, they collectively praise and uphold my dharma, and they call me Mahāvajrapāṇirāja. Because of this name, I am known as the foremost.”

We also vow to firmly establish and protect the Buddha’s True Dharma; may these retinues stand in formation as majestic attendants at our left and right, expounding various skillful means for the great benefit of many.

In order to subdue all demons, evil spirits, and ghosts, we pray only that the World-Honored One will bear witness to our assembly and grant permission for us to recite the names of our retinues; only then shall we dare to recite them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vajragarbha:
"Excellent, excellent!
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you have now invoked their names; I likewise approve this, and you may now invoke their names as you wish."
At that time, Vajragarbha, having received the Buddha’s permission, was addressed by name:
“Vajrasūmahā, Vajrasubhāṣitīkara, Vajrasupāhu, Vajrakaniṣṭhuruḍa, Vajramitrakuṇḍali, Vajraucchuṣma, Vajratāhasa—these Bodhisattvas all dwell on my left.”
Vajramāmakī, Vajralocanā, Vajraśaṅkhala, Vajraṅkuśī, Vajrasūcī, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, and Vajranīlavaradā—these Bodhisattvas and others all reside on my right.

"In this assembly—whether gods, humans, or various demon kings, along with ghosts and spirits—whoever hears me invoke the name of Vajra shall each lose their color and remain entirely silent; they will harbor terror in their hearts, be filled with sorrow and unease, fearing a great calamity and dreading for their very lives."
At that time, Vajrapāṇi and the others perceived their thoughts from afar;

they feared that those present in the assembly might give rise to contempt, that spirits and deities might become violent and disorderly, fail to show reverence for the Dharma, and further, fearing slander and defamation, fall into the three miserable realms to undergo various sufferings.
And he addressed them, saying:

"I possess the profound intention (saṃdhi) endowed with all the characteristics of phenomena; the Buddha already knows this, and has granted his seal of approval for its fulfillment. This is not within the sphere of your knowledge."
"Therefore, it is called the Dharma Seal of the Great Dhāraṇī Divine Mantra, the Secret Treasury of the Dharma, which brings benefit to immeasurable beings, as realized by the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

At that time, the assembly of Vajra Bodhisattvas and others, having received the Buddha’s praise and confirmation, leaped for joy with exultation. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and addressed all those demons and spirits, saying:

"We have now accomplished the Dharma and have fortunately received the simultaneous seal of approval from all the Buddhas of the ten directions to benefit all beings. You should not be startled, nor terrified, nor give rise to evil thoughts."

In this assembly, whether gods or humans, śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, various kings of men, Śakra Devendra, as well as the eight classes of spirits and ghosts, multitudes of humans and non-humans, good sons and good daughters, and the hosts of heretical sages—listen all with focused attention!

I now offer to the Buddha this inconceivable, profound, and secret treasury of the Dharma, this most precious teaching; you all should believe and accept it, and together protect this sutra. This is identical to the rare and wondrous Dharma-treasury of the Mahāyāna of all Buddhas, and it is the dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī-seal and divine mantras that brings about accomplishment.

The Tathāgata, out of compassion, has established various skillful means to rescue and protect all classes of sentient beings. If you should intentionally give rise to opposition and fail to comply with my True Dharma, I shall split your heads into seven pieces, like the branches of an *ari* tree.
When the great assembly of people heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all filled with joy;

they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly. The Method for Painting the Image of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva: The entire body of the image of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva should be yellow in color. He stands with his left leg slightly extended and his right leg slung diagonally downward, appearing as if he is about to descend from his seat and then rise again. He sits upon a pedestal of a hundred-jeweled lotus flower, leaning his body slightly as he sits facing toward the right.
His head is adorned with a flower crown embellished with the seven precious gems, and his body is suffused with layered radiance; the image’s back rests against a pillow embroidered with jewels.

His left arm is bent, covering his left thigh, while his right arm is bent, resting upon his right knee; he joins his thumb and index finger together, bends his middle and ring fingers into the palm, and extends his little finger straight upward.

Beneath the neck of the image is a jeweled necklace; on each of the image’s two wrists is a jeweled bracelet; a single piece of plain white silk cloth is draped over its shoulders, with ribbons of two colors attached to the cloth.
Furthermore, she bound her navel and waist with jeweled cords; these cords ran across her abdomen, and upon their knots was fashioned a yellow circular ornament the size of a coin.

She draped a brocade of morning clouds over her hips and wore a skirt of pale yellow-white flowers; the skirt had a blue lining, and her ankles were visible through the folds, while jeweled cords served as a belt to fasten around her waist.

"On both the left and right sides, there stands a Great Attendant Bodhisattva upon a lotus flower; their entire bodies are yellow, with scarlet brocade sashes wrapped around their waists and hips, extending down to cover their knees, and all alike wear crowns of seven precious jewels upon their heads."
The attendant bodhisattva on his left side bends only his left arm, bringing it near his right breast to hold a white fly-whisk; the tip of the whisk is positioned directly above his left shoulder.
He extends his right arm, slightly bent at the thigh, with the fingers slightly curled; on his wrist he wears a bracelet.
The attendant bodhisattva on his right side is identical in flower crown and robes to the one on his left, except that he bends his left arm, bringing it near his left breast, grasping a *vajra*.
The right arm is bent upward, with the hand extended upward at the waist, grasping a white fly-whisk that hangs loosely with its head drooping downward.
To the left of the image, near the side of the Buddha’s thigh, there is a bodhisattva whose entire body is azure in color; from above his head emerges the form of a three-pronged *vajra*.
Beneath that vajra is a crimson band, which encircles the head.
Below that, there is further a yellow band, which wraps around the head, covers the navel, the temples, and the forehead, leaving only the face and eyes exposed.
The corners of his eyes are like those of a snake, slightly reddish, as if he were looking askance.
His physical form has an expression of wrathful anger; his two arms are crossed, with the right pressing down upon the left, tucked into the space between his armpits.
He sits with his legs crossed in a lateral position, with the left thigh raised.

From between his thighs emerges a red snake that coils around his belly and feet; its head protrudes from between the thighs as it gazes toward the elbow of his left arm at the reflected image of his body, which is seated upon a red lotus flower.
"On both the left and right sides of that image, there are four bodhisattvas each; they are all seated above and below, assuming majestic postures to assist Vajragarbha in subduing all beings."
"Next, the Bodhisattva in the upper-left position has a body that is entirely yellow; he wears a flower crown on his head and has white rings in his ears.
Behind the top of his image is a circular red light, and a white flower-cloth is wound around his right arm, emerging from behind toward the left armpit and looping across his shoulder."

The right arm is bent and placed upon the right thigh; the thumb and index finger are pressed together, while the middle and ring fingers are bent into the palm, and the little finger is held straight upright.
The left arm is bent and held horizontally across the thigh of the left leg.

With the palm facing downward, he grasps an object that is green in color; the object points upward, its tip tapering slightly and becoming gradually thicker toward the bottom, square yet circular like a Chinese boot-last, with a vertical blue line at its center pointing toward his body.
Wearing a skirt of morning clouds, she sits cross-legged upon a red lotus flower.
Next, there is a bodhisattva whose entire body is yellow; he wears a flower crown on his head and has a blue circular halo.
The image has jeweled earrings on both ears; the lips are red and the ear-piercings are white. A white, folded cloth is wrapped around the abdomen.
The right arm is bent, with the thumb and index finger pressed together while the remaining three fingers are extended; the hand is placed over the right breast.

With her left arm bent, she presses it firmly against the space between her left thigh and knee, holding upward the object resembling a boot-scraper that is grasped in the hand of the Bodhisattva before her.
Wearing a skirt of morning light, she sits in the *pralambapāda* posture upon a blue lotus flower.

"Below that, there are two bodhisattvas sitting side by side, one behind the other. The latter bodhisattva is yellow in color throughout his body; he has a small circular halo of blue light around his head, white earrings, and wears a garland of flowers upon his head."
Her breasts were large; she used a white flowered cloth to wrap crosswise around her breasts.
Her right arm was bent, with the tip of the thumb and the index finger pressed together while the remaining three fingers formed a fist.
With his left arm bent and his palm extended, he holds the object resembling a sandal-stand that was grasped by the Bodhisattva before him.
He wears a yellow flowered tunic and skirt, and sits with both knees kneeling upon a red lotus flower.
"The next preceding Bodhisattva is entirely yellow in color; his face is turned to the left, appearing as if he were conversing with the Bodhisattva behind him.

On his head is a single line of golden thread, which binds his topknot into a red circular halo. In one left ear, a jeweled earring is pierced, shaped like a clay water-jar; it has a red casing and white lips, forming a red circular halo."

Bend the right arm, bringing it close to the side of the breast; bend the middle and ring fingers so they rest within the palm, while the thumb, index finger, and little finger are extended upward, and turn the palm upward.
The left arm is bent, with the hand turned upward and resting upon the left knee, still grasping the object resembling a boot-scraper held in the hands of the Bodhisattva in front.
This scraper is directed toward the body; its head is slightly offset to the side, shaped somewhat like a hook, and curves outward slightly.
The arms and wrists are adorned with bracelets, and the body is clothed in a skirt of morning clouds; he sits in the *paryaṅka* posture upon a purple lotus flower.
To the left of the image, there is a bodhisattva whose entire body is yellow; his topknot is bound with a small amount of red silk, and behind it is formed a circular halo of red light.
In each ear she wore a pair of crimson jewels, small as chopsticks, inserted into her ears; each of these objects had a white dot at both ends.
She draped a green gauze cloth over her shoulders and wore a skirt of white flowered gauze, which revealed a slight flush of dawn-red at her waist.
Bend the left arm over the left knee with the palm facing upward toward the body; using the thumb and index finger, hold a *vajra* upright between them, with the palm turned upward.

Next, the Bodhisattva below has a body entirely red in color, wears a floral crown on his head, has a blue circular halo, white earrings, and a full, fleshy form.
