“Svāhā. [Twenty-fifth] “This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If one wishes to eliminate illness, one may form this seal and place it upon the afflicted area, reciting the mantra repeatedly with continuous sound for a full thousand times; the illness will then be immediately halted and cured.”

Furthermore, if one recites the mantra over the ashes of a cremated corpse one hundred and eight times and scatters them at the threshold of an enemy's gate, anyone who steps upon them will immediately contract a fever.
"If one wishes to cure an ailment, take black sugar, recite this mantra twenty-one times over it, write down the name of the patient, and burn it; the illness will be cured.
Furthermore, if one wishes to enter the palace of the asuras, one should recite this mantra two hundred thousand times, and one will then be able to enter."

"Furthermore, there is a method: incant the cow’s milk, ghee, and fire, and while doing so, write the name of the patient and cast it into the fire; the illness will be cured immediately. Furthermore, there is a method:
mix poison with human blood, and for each incantation, burn [a portion of it] one hundred and eight times; all ghosts will die."
Furthermore, take leaves of the *nimba* tree; recite the mantra once for each leaf and burn them one hundred and eight times, and all demonic illnesses will be cured.

8. The Mantra and Seal for Throwing [Offerings] to Ucchuṣma, Chapter Eight. Following the previous body-seal, change only this: bend the middle joints of both index fingers toward each other and let their tips hang down.
The mantra says:

"Oṃ vajra-kuruta mahāphala paramadhāruna makāramukha taṭa taṭa vimā vimātiye āgata āgata ha ha rāha rāha rāla rāla tāpa tāpa tāpaya tāpaya svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra (*dhāraṇī*). If one wishes to cure illness, the master of mantras should perform this seal and recite the mantra within the patient’s house; he should consecrate white mustard seeds twenty-one times and scatter them all around to establish a boundary (*sīmābandha*).

Thereafter, construct a water-maṇḍala. At the center of the maṇḍala, place a jar filled with the five grains—namely, first, millet; second, wheat; third, barley; fourth, small beans; and fifth, rice—all intended for later use. Place several platters of food and sixteen oil lamps. Next, summon the patient to sit outside the maṇḍala.

At the center of the altar, place a fire pit. The mantra-practitioner forms the mudrā, takes white mustard seeds, and circles them once above the patient’s head; for each recitation, one seed is burned, repeating this twenty-one times.

Afterwards, bring a water bowl and place it upon the altar. Take the burnt remains of the white mustard seeds along with their ashes and a small amount of food and drink, mix them together in the water bowl, and pour the mixture into a vessel of the five grains placed upon the altar. Then, carry this vessel outside and offer it as food to the ghosts and spirits, saying aloud:
"May this person’s illness be cured."
After this is concluded, he shall then dismiss [the deity], and the illness will immediately be cured.

9. The Dharani of the Uṣṇīṣa-mālā-pāśa Dharmamudrā, Ninth. "Following the previous body-seal, one only changes the position of the index fingers so that they are behind the middle fingers, with their tips touching."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ ānī maṇi kṣaṇi khurṇaduvaṃ svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If one wishes to eliminate a disease caused by a ghost or spirit that refuses to submit, one may perform this rite and recite the mantra to bind it; it shall then be sent far away.
After it has departed, perform the rite of establishing a boundary (sīmābandha), so that the afflicted ghost or spirit can never enter again.

10. The Dharma Seal and Mantra of the Ucchuṣma Cakra. Tenth: "Cross the left and right index fingers and ring fingers inward; extend the middle fingers of both hands vertically with their tips touching; extend the thumbs and little fingers with their tips touching; and open the wrists."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vajrakrodha mahāparavara śvabhrapiṅgale prasara prasara svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If a person suffers from a cold disease, the mantra-practitioner shall hold a grass torch in hand and perform the ritual with grains, flour, and other implements over the fire, according to the method of Cundī.
Furthermore, if one encircles the perimeter of the patient’s house with this fire and repeatedly recites the mantra to establish a boundary (*sīmābandha*), the illness will be cured immediately.

11. The Mantra of the Great Body Axe Mudrā of Ucchuṣma (Ucchuṣma-mahākāya-paraśu-dharmamudrā-mantra), Number Eleven. "Rise up; bend the left knee; grasp the big toe of the right foot with the left hand, placing the elbow directly upon the knee; keep the body standing upright."

With the right hand, form the axe mudrā (paraśu-mudrā), holding the axe within it; the thumb should rest upon the handle of the axe, with the elbow bent, and the mudrā should be placed at the breast, about five inches away from it.
If an actual axe is not available, it is also permissible to simply form the axe mudrā.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vajra-kuruta mahāvara rīpayu mahāmanrye varavara karame varavarā prasaraṇaye svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If a person suddenly suffers from ailments such as qi-stasis, spirit-possession, back-gas, or heaviness in the back and shoulders, one may form this seal and recite the mantra while striking the painful area; the condition will be cured immediately.

"Gopāye svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra.

If one wishes to eliminate illness, one should construct a water mandala four cubits in size beside the patient. At the center of the mandala, place one plate of food and drink; likewise, place one plate of food each in the east, north, and south directions.
The mantra-master sits in the western direction, and the patient is seated on the mantra-master’s left side.

In front of the mantra-master, a fire pit is established to burn white mustard seeds; for every recitation of the mantra, one seed is burned, repeating this one hundred and eight times, and the illness will be cured immediately.
If the illness does not subside within one day, perform the ritual on the third day and it will certainly be cured;
if it still does not subside, know that it is not a disease caused by spirits.
It should be performed during the day; do not perform the ritual at night.
"Place one image of Ucchuṣma; to the south, install a fire pit, and take white mustard seeds, red flowers, and a small amount of one's own blood, mixing them together."

If one wishes to cause the sufferer of *śatru-ruja* (hostile fever) to fall into distress, one should take the aforementioned medicine and burn it once for each incantation, repeating this one hundred and eight times; the *śatru-ruja* will then become distressed.

If one wishes to cause them to recover, take sugar, water, and white flowers, and burn them once for each incantation, repeating this one hundred and eight times while reciting "Namaḥ" at every repetition; the afflicted person will then recover, and thereafter their poisonous mind will naturally be extinguished.

13. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of Ucchuṣma. Regarding the Dharma-Seal Mantra of Ucchuṣma, number thirteen: "Following the previous body-seal, change only this: press the tip of the right index finger against the upper joint of the middle finger; extend the left index finger forward toward the middle finger and bend it."
The mantra is:
“Oṃ ānāli kunāli kṛṣṇapiṅgali subhoke kṛtāvasāne svāhā. This dharma-seal mantra is fully capable of curing all diseases caused by spirits; its efficacy is great and rapid.

14. The Dharma Seal and Mantra of the Crown of Ucchuṣma. Regarding the Dharma Seal and Mantra of the Crown of Ucchuṣma, Number Fourteen: its efficacy has not yet been witnessed. "It follows the previous head seal, with the sole modification that the left index finger presses upon the second joint on the outer side of the middle finger."

The mantra is: “Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vajrakrodha oṃ khaṅgali ke tumāśi khe svāhā. 15. The Mouth-Dharma Seal of Ucchuṣma. Regarding the Mouth-Dharma Seal of Ucchuṣma, the fifteenth: it follows the previous body-seal, with the only difference being that the left head-finger is bent slightly behind the left middle finger, and the right head-finger is bent slightly in front of the right middle finger; the mantra used is the aforementioned offering mantra.

"This Dharma Seal Mantra: if a woman is in labor and the child dies in the womb and cannot emerge, take a small amount of water in the palm of the hand and mix it with a little asafoetida medicine. Recite the aforementioned Offering Mantra one hundred and eight times and give it to her to drink; the dead child will then come forth."

16. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of Ucchuṣma-vajramuṣṭi. Regarding the Dharma-Seal Mantra of Ucchuṣma-vajramuṣṭi, the sixteenth: "With the left hand, press the thumb against the lower joint of the ring finger, and clench the remaining four fingers into a fist."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vajra-kuruta mahāphala bharu bharu siri siri sama sama prabhā ha ha svāhā oṃ dhṛti hūṃ phaṭ. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; if one forms this seal and recites the mantra, one will immediately attain universal joy and be free from all obstacles.

17. The Seal for Purifying Defilements through Ucchuṣma (Ucchuṣma-kalmaṣa-viśodhana-mudrā), Number Seventeen. "Interlock the two little fingers within the palms. Straighten and press the two ring fingers, middle fingers, and index fingers against one another. Place the two thumbs upon the two little fingers inside the palms, and join the wrists."
The mantra is:

"Śūrimaule (1) mamamale male (2) śuśūri (3) svāhā (4). This is the Dharma-seal mantra. Place water within the seal, recite it seven times, and sprinkle it upon the face; thereafter, one may recite and maintain the various other mantra methods.

"If a practitioner of mantra sees a corpse, a woman giving birth, livestock being born, or a place where blood flows—and upon seeing such various impurities—one must immediately form this mudrā and recite the Mantra for Dispelling Impurity. Thus one attains purity, and all the mantras one practices will be efficacious.
If one does not do so, it will cause one to lose the efficacy of the mantras and suffer calamity, with sores breaking out on one's face."

"One must never forget the Mantra for Dispelling Impurities. The practitioner should daily fumigate their body with incense and, within the *maṇḍala*, hang an image of Vajrapāṇi on the eastern wall. They should then spread out a pure Vajra seat and sit upon it—using *śara* grass; if this grass is unavailable, white *mūla* grass may be used as a substitute."
The mantra-practitioner shall wear red garments and use a red sitting mat, then sit upon a mat of sweet flag (khañjana).

Furthermore, taking yellow radish seeds and white mustard seeds, he shall recite the mantra over them seven times and scatter them in the four directions; thus, no malevolent spirits or celestial Māra deities shall be able to cause disturbance.
The mantra-practitioner scatters two kinds of flowers—red and purple—with both hands before the Vajra.

"Āḥ Vajrajñāna Svāhā. This one dharma-mantra is named the Great Dharma-Spell of Ucchuṣma-vajra.

20. The Ritual for Painting the Image of Ucchuṣma and its Mantra, Number Twenty. "Have a young girl weave white cloth or silk, and first recite the mantra over cow urine one hundred and eight times."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vajra dṛḍha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having consecrated the cow urine with this mantra, one should sprinkle it upon the undergarments and other items. On the eighth, ninth, or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should prepare a maṇḍala on a clean and excellent patch of earth.
Take an image of the Buddha, sprinkle it with scented water, and place it within the altar; offer various kinds of incense, flowers, food, and drink, and light eight lamps.

Summon a master painter who is most skilled at painting; give him whatever amount he requests without allowing him to offer a price in return. Day after day, have him observe the eight precepts of the fast, bathe him with fragrant water, dress him in fresh, clean garments, and have a ritual master perform protective mudrās for him. Only then shall he paint the Fire-Head Vajra.

"The image is approximately one cubit of the Buddha’s height, or two chi and three and a half cun; excluding its halo and pedestal, it is further made tall and grand, exquisitely refined and beautiful, with harmonious colors and the use of liquid incense from *kunduruka* resin, rather than animal glue."
Place one water jar at the center of the altar; every day, you should provide a vegetarian meal for seven persons—if this cannot be arranged, even for one person will suffice.

The image is blue in color and has four arms: the right hand reaches toward the shoulder holding a *vajra*, and the left hand reaches toward the shoulder holding a red cord, which is coiled and curved like a snake in a circle.
The right hand is extended downward; the thumb is turned upward to touch the tip of the index finger, which is stretched straight down, while the remaining three fingers are slightly bent upward.
The left arm is bent upward, holding a rosary, with the tip of the middle finger used to count the beads.
The facial features are upright and exceedingly beautiful.

"Paint two dragon kings draped over their left shoulders; the two dragon heads are hooked together, looking upward toward the chest, while their tails rest upon the back, all being a pure crimson color."
Furthermore, four dragon kings, all blue in color, each entwined one arm.
Moreover, two other dragon kings, likewise all blue in color, each entwined a shank.
Above the head of the image is a white nāga king, his body coiled and his head held upright.
Below the waist of the image, tiger-skin trousers are wrapped around the hips, and the hair on the head blazes with flames, all of which are made to stand erect.
"Not only upon the head, but also on the nape and back, there is the light of flaming fire.

Above the halo of the head, to the left and right, paint a lotus seat each; upon the left lotus, depict one image of Akṣobhya Buddha—some say Śākyamuni Buddha—sitting in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), with the left hand palm-upward held horizontally below the navel, and the right hand palm-upward resting upon the right knee, with all fingers hanging down."

Upon the lotus to the right, one should visualize an image of Amitābha Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). His hands form the *Amitābha-cakra-mudrā*: that is, the left hand is turned with the palm facing upward; the thumb and ring finger touch at their tips, while the index, middle, and little fingers are all extended. The right hand is formed in the same manner as the left, except that it covers the left hand, with the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands aligned and touching.
"On the image of the Buddha, paint figures of various devas scattering flowers, with clouds above them colored like flashes of lightning.

On the base of the Vajra-image, paint the ocean; within it, there is a lotus flower, upon which a vajra stands. In the ocean, paint eight asura kings—four on the left and four on the right—all of whom are depicted in the form of bowing their heads in prostration."
"On the right side of that vajra base, one should further paint the image of the mantra-practitioner (dhāraṇī-sādhaka), holding an incense burner and kneeling on his right knee in worship.

Having created this image, the mantra-practitioner should daily burn agallochum incense to make offerings to the Vajra, confessing and repenting. Once he has first recited the mantra one hundred thousand times within the water mandala, all his aspirations will be fulfilled."

"If one wishes to enter the palaces of the asuras, one should recite this mantra two hundred thousand times; then one will be able to enter, after which one should perform offerings at a colored mandala."

21. The Mantra for Binding the Four Directions at the Vajra-Āśvāsana Offering Maṇḍala. The Mantra for Binding the Four Directions at the Vajra-Āśvāsana Offering Maṇḍala, Chapter Twenty-one. "The Mantra for Binding the Four Directions."
The mantra is:
"Oṃ vajrakrodha mahāparakrama adhuradhipate tiṣṭha svāhā. One should recite this mantra twenty-one times and perform the ritual boundary-binding (sīmābandha) by encircling the four directions.
22. The Fire Boundary-binding Mantra, the Twenty-second. The mantra says:

“Oṃ vajra-kuruta mahāvala vajrāṅkura vajra-rūra vajrapraharaṇa vajrinna tiṣṭha tiṣṭha ākrama svāhā. This is a single dharma-mantra. Take a torch and recite this mantra twenty-one times; it binds the boundary all around and protects the body. It cures all diseases and possesses great spiritual efficacy.
23. The Twenty-third Mantra for Consecrating Water and Powdered Clay. The mantra is as follows: "Oṃ vajra-vajriṇi vajra-sudatini vajra-sudantike svāhā.

This is a single dharma-mantra. One should take water and powdered clay to make fragrant mud, recite this mantra twenty-one times over it, and then smear it upon the ground to construct a four-cubit altar. Various colored powders may all be used interchangeably.
24. The Twenty-fourth Chapter on the Mantra for Consecrating Water.
The mantra says: “Oṃ vajradharāya svāhā. This single dharma-mantra is used with water that has not been purified; it may be employed in all circumstances.

26. The Twenty-sixth Mantra for the Garland of Flowers. The mantra says:

27. The Mantra for Vajra (Vajravidāraṇa-mantra), the Twenty-seventh.

The mantra is as follows: “Oṃ hrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ śivāya huṃ phaṭ. This is a single dharma-mantra. Recite this mantra over the *vajra* one hundred and eight times, then drive it into the center of the sandalwood [image].
28. The Mantra for Binding the Boundary with Fire, the Twenty-eighth.

The mantra says: “Oṃ dhipiṇḍu savideva sarvakāra siddhāśvaje svāhā. This is a single dhāraṇī-mantra. When constructing the maṇḍala, one should recite this over a torch seven times, three times over (twenty-one times in total), and then circumambulate the four sides of the maṇḍala to bind the boundary all around.
29. The Great Boundary-binding Dhāraṇī, Chapter Twenty-nine. The dhāraṇī is as follows:
“Oṃ prasarā akṣanye svāhā. This dharma-dhāraṇī is used to bind the great boundary at the place where the dāna is performed.

"If one wishes to construct a maṇḍala, first seek out a secluded, quiet, and pure location within a fine hall or chamber. Construct a maṇḍala measuring four cubits; within a space of six cubits, excavate and remove all manner of bones, wood, tiles, and stones. Thereafter, bring in separate pure soil to fill it, making it firm and solid, and ensuring it is perfectly level."
Upon that ground, construct a mandala measuring four cubits; the method for marking it with colored powder lines is as explained in the *Buddhottama* and other sections.
Those who wish to receive the dharma should bathe in scented water and put on new, clean garments.

Above, below, and in the four cardinal directions, hang various banners, canopies, bells, ribbons, precious flowers, and mirrors—all adorned in accordance with the descriptions found in the ritual manuals of other schools.

For the lower section, use powders of five colors; each of these colored powders must be consecrated with one hundred and eight recitations of the mantra before being used—this applies to all altar rituals involving powder; if the powder is not consecrated, the ritual performance will not be accomplished.
As for the five-colored powders: first, white, which is rice flour;
second, yellow, such as saffron powder or yellow earth powder;
third, red, such as vermilion powder or red earth powder, and so forth.
Fourth, blue: such as powdered indigo or dried lac dye;
fifth, black: such as powdered ink or powdered charcoal. All these powders are to be mixed with powdered agarwood.
30. The Mantra for White Powder. The thirty-first mantra for white powder:
“The mantra says: ‘Oṃ ajaneye śvetadhāye svāhā. 31. The Mantra for Red Powder. The thirty-second mantra for red powder:
“The mantra says: ‘Oṃ ajaneye aruṇadhāye svāhā. 32. The Mantra for Yellow Powder. The thirty-third mantra for yellow powder: “The mantra says:”
“Oṃ ajaneyi pidhaye svāhā. (33) This is the third and final mantra for blue powder.
The mantra says: “Oṃ ajaneyi kṛdhaye svāhā. (34) This is the mantra for black powder. The mantra says:

“Oṃ ajane kuruṣvaya svāhā. These are the mantras of the five dharmas. If one wishes to construct a maṇḍala, one should take a vajra and seal each portion of the powder with its respective mudrā, reciting the fundamental mantra one hundred and eight times for each. Once the mantras have been thus recited, one should install them according to the ritual rules.

"Construct a mandala four cubits in size; first, use white powder to mark out the boundary lines. The mandala shall have four gates, and at its center, construct a lotus seat upon which to place the image of Ucchuṣma.
At the eastern gate, further construct a lotus seat and place Vajraśekhara there.
At the southern gate, likewise construct a lotus seat and place Mīlūśrīka there."
At the north gate, construct another lotus seat and install Han-tuo Shi Jizhi;
at the west gate, install Va-jra-du-di, and outside the west gate, place the seat for the mantra-reciter.

"In the northeast corner, place the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; in the southeast corner, place Virūḍhaka; in the southwest corner, place Virūpākṣa; and in the northwest corner, place the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. These Four Heavenly Kings should also be offered universal worship, equal to that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
"When performing the ritual, one should use sixteen lamps, prepare twelve platters of food and drink of a hundred flavors, burn agalloch incense, and make various offerings."

Outside the western gate of the maṇḍala, at a distance of approximately eight finger-widths toward the southwest corner, construct a fire pit intended for burning ghee, honey, sesame seeds, incense, and so forth; on that day, the mantra-reciter shall recite the Great Mantra one thousand and eight times.
If one performs this rite, Vajrāgnimukha will be pleased; all rites performed will yield great efficacy.

Furthermore, invite [the deity] to sit within the vajra fire-pit and burn ghee, honey, sesame, and rice-awns while reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times. Each of the fire-head disciples should likewise recite their respective mantras one hundred and eight times, and each of the Four Heavenly Kings’ mantras seven times.

35. The Dharma-Seal Mantra for Summoning the Messengers of Ucchuṣma. Third and Fifty: "Place both thumbs upon the nails of the little fingers. Extend both index fingers and ring fingers straight upward. Touch the tips of the two middle fingers together. Join the wrists. Move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:

“Irimī (1) Irimī (2) Limi Rimi Limi (3) Svāhā (4). This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If one wishes to perform the seal for the purpose of curing illness, one must first burn incense by the side of the patient and perform this seal-mantra to summon and settle all spirits and ghosts. Thereafter, performing the seal and reciting the mantra to treat the disease will yield great efficacy in all cases.
36. The Mantra for Sprinkling Water on the Face: *Ucchuṣma-mantra* The third and thirty-sixth [chapter], "The Mantra for Sprinkling Water on the Face with the *Ucchuṣma-mantra*:

"The mantra is recited as follows: 'Namaḥ vajrakrodhāya | oṃ | jñānini | svāhā. This is a single dharma-mantra; one should recite it seven times over water and sprinkle it upon the face, and all will be filled with joy."

37. The Ucchuṣma Mantra for Stopping Crying, the Thirty-Seventh. “Namaḥ mātṛgaṇāya | Vajrakrūradhyāya | Tadyathā | Curuṭe | Curuṭe | Curūcuruṭe | Svāhā. This is a dharma-mantra. One should transcribe this mantra-text upon plain silk, enchant a cord with it at its center, and tie this mantra-text [to the child].

Furthermore, by reciting this mantra once for each knot, one makes one hundred and eight knots; when a young child or girl cries out at night, if these are tied around the neck, they will not fear any ghosts or spirits, will cease crying, and the child shall attain a long life.
38. The Ucchuṣma-Ḍauṣṭhika Dhāraṇī, the Thirty-eighth. The mantra says:

“Namo bhagavate vajrakrodhāya | tadyathā | īkhe īkhe | mahābala | amukam | śaphariṇa | kṣūṇa | hulu hulu | ṭhaṭha ṭhaṭha | svāhā. This is a dhāraṇī-mantra. If one wishes to subdue a person and summon them, yet they do not come when called, one should perform the *ḍauṣṭhika* rite: take black sheep’s wool and fashion it into a consecrated cord.
Carve stakes from purple *śiṃśapā* wood, each eight finger-widths long. Take the aforementioned mantra-cord and wrap it around the grain tree;

recite the mantra over the stake and the cord one hundred and eight times, then drive the stake into the tree. Immediately, the *pala* (Sanskrit; in the Chinese commentary, "disease of leprosy") will be bound.
If you wish to effect a cure, extract the stake, recite the mantra over cow’s milk one hundred and eight times, and place it back into the hole;
then the person will immediately recover. 39. The Ucchuṣma-ratudeti Dhāraṇī, the Thirty-ninth. The mantra says:
“Oṃ vajra-kurudhaye kañci kañci amuka śānti-pāyami svāhā. This is a single dharma-mantra. If another person is angry, recite it repeatedly, and that person will become joyful.
40. The Ucchuṣma Subjugation Mantra, the Fortieth. The mantra says: “Oṃ vajra-kurudhaya kubbi-kuru-mukhi svāhā. This is a single dharma-mantra.

If one recites this mantra over a fired clay bowl one hundred and eight times and covers it, the four syllables of the Brahma-language *tśyang-gyu-li* (the name of the demon) will be unable to escape. *Tśyang-gyu-li* is the transliteration of the Sanskrit *ucchuṣmali*.
If one wishes to go out, one may leave immediately after setting aside the alms bowl.
41. The *Uṣṇīṣasitātapatrā-yoga-mantra*, the Forty-first. The mantra is as follows:

“Oṃ (1) Vajra-kurudaya (2) Ugu-ri (3) Migu-ri (4) Cikhari (5) Śimili (6) Amuku (7) Amogha-sa (8) Tippiṭṭhu (9) Bhabhodu (10) Vicchitsiṭṭhu (11) Svāhā (12). This is a single dharma-mantra; one should recite it over rice husks one hundred and eight times.
Near the southern wall, install an image of Vajrapāṇi, facing north.
The mantra-practitioner faces south and sits before the image.

He should then construct a small water-maṇḍala and place a fire-pit within it. Taking paddy chaff before him, he recites the mantra once for each burning, performing this one hundred and eight times while chanting the *Namo* in its original Sanskrit sound.

Having performed these rites, if the two persons desire to compare their wisdom, their Brahma-voices, or their physical marks of excellence, they should take incense of *kunkuma* mixed with white flowers and, reciting the mantra, burn them in the fire; they will then immediately attain *yoga*.
42. The Ucchuṣmamukha-vaśīkaraṇa-dhāraṇī, the Forty-second. The mantra says: “Oṃ svahana svahanapana kalandakuliśa śrīraye svāhā.

This is a dharma-mantra. If one recites it twenty-one times over ashes or soil and applies it toward an evil rival, that rival will be brought under control, and one shall achieve *mukha-vaśīkaraṇa* (subjugation by means of the mouth).
If one wishes to restore [an injury] to a good state, one should recite the mantra over water twenty-one times and sprinkle it toward the *mukha* (face);

it will then be restored. The Efficacy of the Ucchuṣma Dhāraṇī Method: "If there are bhikṣus, upāsakas, or others who wish to receive and uphold the Ucchuṣma Vajra Dhāraṇī, they should construct a water-maṇḍala. Every morning at dawn, they should offer various incenses and flowers with a resolute mind to the Buddhas of the ten directions, Prajñā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, Devas, and so forth. Having made vows with both mind and speech, they should then sit in a single session and recite the dhāraṇī eight hundred times;
at midday, in the evening, and at midnight, they should likewise recite it eight hundred times each, making offerings according to the previous procedure."
When reciting the mantra, one must not joke or laugh with bystanders, nor engage in idle chatter or whispering.

The mantra-reciter should maintain an expression of extreme wrath; when first receiving this dharma, one must be firm and resolute. If one can recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, maintaining continuous mindfulness in every thought without interruption and without pursuing other distractions, then nothing that is undertaken will fail to be accomplished.

"For the incense used in this offering, one should burn exclusively agallochum; red flowers or purple flowers may also be used. As for counting beads, it is appropriate to use either red beads or lapis lazuli beads."
Furthermore, he dons red robes and sits upon a mat of calamus, spreading a layer of fine cotton cloth beneath the mat.

Once he has settled in, he recites the mantra over water seven times seven times and scatters it in the four directions, above, and below to establish the boundary. Afterward, having recited the mantra over white mustard seeds seven times seven times, he scatters them everywhere throughout the four directions, above, and below to complete the boundary.
"Next, having invited Vajrapāṇi and his retinue and established them upon their seats, take a fire pit and place it outside the western gate to the south, in front of the mantra-reciter.

Taking rice-grain blossoms mixed with high-quality cow’s ghee, kindle firewood in the pit; then, striking [the offering] with a willow branch while reciting the mantra once, burn it within the fire for eight thousand times. At that time, the mantra-deity will descend and manifest its form, or you shall see the deity's form in a dream."
When you behold the deity, do not be afraid; let the hairs on your body remain unmoved, maintain a calm and settled visualization, and make various vows according to your heart's desire.
Once you have obtained this sign of efficacy, you may proceed to the summit of a high and precipitous mountain that is inaccessible from all four sides.
He again established a ritual altar and made offerings according to the Dharma; having completed one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra, he cried out in a loud voice:
"O Gate of the Sages!"
"The gates of the asuras shall all open of their own accord.

Furthermore, take half a *śeṣa* (half-measure) of radish seeds and mix them with one's own blood; for every pinch of seed, recite the mantra once and burn it in the fire. When eight thousand repetitions are completed, the asura women and the daughters of the ṛṣis will come out to welcome the practitioner, lead him inside, and provide offerings, constantly giving him the drink of *amṛta* (ambrosia)."
The practitioner’s teeth, hair, and skin will all naturally fall away and be replaced by new growth.
The person’s body will become like the color of gold; the mantra-holder shall live for a thousand years, with strength like that of a vajra.
After a thousand years, when his life ends, he will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he himself shall become the King of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

Furthermore, there is another practice: on the day of a solar or lunar eclipse, one should prepare a water altar four cubits in length and breadth, smear the ground with cow dung, burn agalloch incense, scatter flowers of various colors, and place an image of Vajrapāṇi in the center.
Furthermore, take high-quality ghee and place it in a vessel of red copper before the image.

The mantra-practitioner sits facing east, reciting the mantra before the image until the completion of the lunar cycle, at which point he should cease according to the original instructions. Thereafter, he may take the ghee himself and consume it; he will attain great intelligence, and all undertakings he performs will yield great efficacy.
"The weapon for the Fire-Head Vajra for subduing māras should be made from clean, high-quality, well-smelted bīṇa iron as a vajra, one foot in length.
Both ends of the vajra should have six-sided prongs, each two inches in height and width, with a four-sided narrow waist, shaped like the vajra-wielding strength of a Vajrapāṇi grasping a mace."
As for the method of constructing the wheel: it is complete with hub and rim, shaped like a chariot wheel.

The wheel is one foot wide, and its length and breadth are likewise; it has six ridges within, with six peaks as well, and twelve ridges on the outside, with twelve peaks as well, all encircled by sharp blades.
Next, one should fashion an axe with blades on both ends; it should be six inches in length and have a handle two feet long. One should also make a single knife.
Furthermore, one must make a spear approximately four feet in length, with a wooden shaft and an iron point.
All the iron used must first be consecrated one hundred and eight times, purified, and bound by a protective boundary.
Once the weapons have been fashioned, each object must be consecrated one hundred and eight times.

Once each mantra has been completed, one should place them within the ritual altar for receiving the dharma; day and night, one should recite the mantras according to the previously established number of times, continuing until the weapons manifest great supernatural powers and majestic might as the limit of the practice.

If a vessel manifests signs of heat such that it cannot be approached by hand, one should know that this rite has already been accomplished; the practitioner who recites the mantra shall live for a thousand years.
If smoke issues forth, the practitioner who recites the mantra shall live for ten thousand years.
If flames issue forth, the practitioner who recites the mantra shall fly up into the heavens.
"If one performs this rite, one must go to a secluded place or to the summit of a high mountain peak. If one seeks only minor results, it may also be performed within a clean room;

however, if one desires to become an immortal or to obtain great efficacy, one must perform it atop a high mountain peak in the wilderness, for one will certainly attain the most supreme and great efficacy."

Furthermore, there is another method: by consecrating water, white mustard seeds, and so forth with mantras and scattering them throughout the ten directions to establish a boundary, all evil Māras and malevolent spirits thereafter shall be unable to cause disturbance.

"For one who recites mantras, among all phenomena, none are permitted to be defiled; however, the Vajra-dharma of Ucchuṣma is an exception, for whether defiled or pure, it is subject to no prohibition.
If a person can eliminate all greedy and defiled attachments, that dharma becomes even more excellent, and its full efficacy cannot be fully described."

“Svāhā. (54) “If one upholds this mantra, for twenty-one days one should observe the fast and precepts with purity, bathe with fragrant water, wear new and clean garments, and keep a single room pure.”
Take pure cow dung, steam it to remove its odor, and after steaming it once more, mix it with yellow earth to form a paste for smearing the altar.

The altar should be one zhang and two chi in length and breadth, or perhaps one zhang and six chi; prepare five-colored seats for the banners and lamps according to the diagrams, and likewise, following the prescribed method, spread five-colored powders upon the surface of the altar ground.

"Once this altar has been constructed, sit in the southwest corner of the altar, facing northeast. With a sincere mind, recite the mantra six times each day, one hundred and twenty times for each session."

Recite for a full three weeks, circumambulating the altar while practicing the Way; once the limit for reciting the mantra is reached and the required number of repetitions is complete, one may then treat the illness, succeeding without fail in ten thousand cases.
When reciting up to one thousand times, if the rain falls excessively, it will stop the thunder, wind, and rain; at the appointed moment, all will settle.

When reciting up to one thousand times, fresh blood will flow from a great sword. If one recites the mantra over the sword one thousand times and points the blade at the clouds, blood will fall from within the clouds.
"If one recites this mantra over a tree a thousand times, the tree will bear flowers and fruit.

If, while traveling alone in the mountains or wilds, you are disturbed or harassed by mountain spirits, aged demons, tigers, leopards, lions, bears, elephants, or similar beasts, you should recite this mantra and point with your finger; they will all be subdued and dare not cause harm."
"If one recites this mantra two hundred times, when treating an illness—regardless of whether it is light or grave—it shall be cured instantly upon hearing the sound.
If one recites the mantra one hundred times for someone who has just begun to run a fever, the fever will be immediately halted."
"If a person has a white haze or clouding in their eyes, by reciting this mantra one hundred times, it shall be immediately cured.
If one suffers from the illness of the 'cat-demon' (mārjāra-graha) or the 'wild-path' disease, by reciting the mantra one thousand times, the cat-demon will manifest, and all people shall see it."
"If one suffers from possession by ghosts or demons, recite the mantra six or seven hundred times; the possessing spirit will manifest its body so that all may see it.
If one suffers from seasonal epidemics or contagious diseases, strike them with a peach staff, and the illness will be immediately cured."
"If one is afflicted by a suppressed *gū* (demon), reciting this mantra two hundred times will result in immediate recovery.

If one suffers from bone-consuming fever (*asthisāda*), lingering fevers, or the transmissible pestilence of the *pishī* demons, reciting the mantra one thousand times will cause the illness to be cured."
"Furthermore, if a woman’s menstrual flow is obstructed, she should recite this mantra six or seven hundred times; her ailment will then be cured and her flow will be restored.
If she suffers from leukorrhea, by reciting the mantra according to the aforementioned method, her illness will likewise be cured."
"If one suffers from diseases such as insanity or epilepsy, reciting the mantra up to a thousand times will cause the illness to be immediately cured.

If one suffers from a spirit-induced illness—whether characterized by compassion, anger, joyful singing, fondness for laughter, or shouting and crying out—one should likewise rely on the aforementioned mantra, and the illness will be immediately cured."
"If one suffers from swelling of the entire body or edema caused by soil vapors and the like, it shall also be cured immediately by reciting the mantra according to the aforementioned method.
If one suffers from any great swelling or chronic swelling, by reciting the mantra over *soma* [swelling], that swelling shall be cured."

"If husband and wife hate each other as much as water and fire, one should recite mantras over five-colored threads, making one knot with each recitation until seven knots are formed. By tying them behind the elbow, all relatives will rejoice."

"If there is litigation, verbal dispute, or legal contention with government officials, one should recite the mantra over five-colored threads, making one knot for each recitation until seven sets of seven knots (forty-nine knots) are formed; by following the aforementioned method, one will immediately attain liberation."
"If wicked people cause disturbance, one should likewise rely on the aforementioned method, and they will naturally be subdued.

This is but a brief explanation and does not exhaust its full efficacy; it should be shared only with those who possess a sincere heart and act with straightforwardness. Aside from such individuals, do not transmit it recklessly."
"If one merely clenches the fists while reciting mantras with others, the efficacy will certainly be achieved.
Once the recitation reaches twenty-one rounds, one must raise one's voice; regardless of the number of repetitions, the efficacy will then be attained."

"Whenever one wishes to treat an illness, first recite the names of the yakṣas of the five directions along with their retinues to cause them to enter the room. The household being treated must absolutely not consume alcohol, meat, or the five pungent vegetables; if they do so, it will greatly harm the patient."
"When inviting the deity, do not attempt to call them by name individually; instead, chant internally 'Come quickly' seven times, and the deity will arrive immediately.
When sending the deity away, chant internally 'Naragaṇa' fourteen times. Do not recite this mantra aloud, but maintain it as a protection for your person."

The Heart Mantra of the Yakṣas, Chapter Two. “*Vateṭa svāhā | Mahāmahālu svāhā | Uhu uhu svāhā | Rājñāte svāhā | Svāhā.*” When first intending to treat a patient in a household, one must first reverently invoke the yakṣas of the five directions. First invoking the yakṣa of the eastern direction as the leader, one reverently invokes the Blue Yakṣa of the East, whose body is thirty-two feet tall and who exhales blue breath from his mouth;
together with his retinue, he enters this room—“this altar” meaning within the altar, and “this house” meaning within the house.
The others are to be understood accordingly. One should establish the form of a yakṣa at the northeast corner of this maṇḍala.

The Yakṣa Standing-Body Seal and Mantra** Third: "With the right leg straight and the left foot planted on the ground, separated by about one cubit; with the three fingers of the left hand held upright and the thumb pressing upon the nail of the little finger, cross the arms over the waist with the four fingers pointing forward; with the five fingers of the right hand resting against the face, make the face express an angry expression. Perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) around the maṇḍala, circling to the right once for each mantra."

Then he spoke the mantra: “Oṃ, devayakṣa, bandha bandha, ha ha ha ha ha, svāhā. 4. The Fourth Seal for Summoning the Body of a Rākṣasa: Join the two palms together; hook the two little fingers; place the two thumbs side by side and touching; join the wrists; and move the index fingers back and forth.
5. The Yakṣa Hook Seal, Fifth: "Following the previous body seal, place the tip of the right hand’s index finger upon the third joint of the middle finger; this is called the Yakṣa Hook."

Having bound this upon the heart, one should proceed by circling to the right; all yakṣas and their retinues will be filled with joy, constantly providing protection and serving the mantra-practitioner.

6. The Yakṣa Fire-Wheel Mudrā, the Sixth: "Place the left middle finger against the right index finger, and the right middle finger against the left index finger. Bend both ring fingers into the palms so that their two joints face one another. Keep the two thumbs and the two little fingers straight and upright, with their tips touching each other. Recite the Great Heart Mantra."

7. The Body Seal of the Yakṣa (Yakṣakāyamuḍrā), the Seventh. Regarding the three yakṣas who cure all diseases of ghosts, one should rely upon the body seal—this body seal is identical to the *Kuntali* standing body seal. With the two thumbs bent into the palms, the two ring fingers press down upon the nails of the two thumbs; the index, middle, and little fingers are held straight and upright with their tips touching one another. One should extend the elbows to the sides at a distance of five inches from the breasts and recite the Great Body Mantra (*Mahākāyavidyā*).

8. The Seal for Summoning Yakṣas and Deva-Demons, Part Eight. The seal for summoning yakṣas and deva-demons is identical to the seal for assembling the host of devas of Mahāmāyūrī (translated into Chinese as *Kongque Wang*, or "Peacock King"). Interlace the eight fingers with their backs facing each other within the palms; likewise, bend the two thumbs so that their tips enter the palms. Only the middle finger of the right hand remains upright, moving back and forth while reciting the Great Body Mantra of the Peacock King.

9. The Seal for Subduing Māra, Ninth. "As before, with this modification: only change the two middle fingers so that they are held upright with their tips touching, and place the seal upon the crown of the head while extending the two arms. This is also the Māyūrī Seal for Subduing Māra; recite the Great Body Mantra."

For the Fire Wheel Mudrā: place the left middle finger against the tip of the right index finger, and the right middle finger against the tip of the left index finger. Bend the two ring fingers within the palms so that their two joints face one another. Extend the two thumbs and the two little fingers straight upward, with their tips touching each other, while reciting the Great Heart Mantra.

The Tenth: The Dhāraṇī of Joyful Delight “*Namo kili (1) kumari (2) hūlū cālū (3) svāhā (4)* If one is in a place where government officials are angry, or where other people are enraged, if one quickly grasps [the mantra] in the left hand and recites this *bǎozhòu* (beating-spell) seven times for oneself, they will immediately become greatly delighted and their anger will be extinguished; it is highly efficacious.”

11. The Bow Seal (Cāpamudrā), the Eleventh: Press the right thumb against the left thumb. Bend the right index and middle fingers so they rest upon the left thumb. Extend the left index and middle fingers straight upward. Place both ring fingers and both little fingers together, bent within the palms.

12. The Arrow Seal (Śara-mudrā), the Twelfth. Regarding this arrow seal: the two thumbs are held upright. The left index finger is bent to rest upon the left thumb; the right index finger is pointed upward and slightly bent. The right middle finger is bent so that its tip is close to the tip of the left index finger. The three fingers below the left middle finger—the ring finger and the little finger—and the ring finger and little finger of the right hand are all bent together within the palms.

13. The Great Bow Seal (Mahācāpa-mudrā), the Thirteenth. "Extend both thumbs straight upward; extend both middle fingers straight up with their tips touching one another; slightly curve both index fingers so that their tips rest against the side of the upper joints of the middle fingers; interlace both ring fingers and both little fingers together, with their tips protruding outward."

14. The Sword Mudrā (Khaḍgamudrā), the fourteenth: "The two thumbs are held straight upright; the right index finger is bent, remaining about half an inch away from the right thumb; the left index finger is slightly curved upward; the middle fingers of both hands and the three fingers below them are all bent together within the palms."

15. The Mudrā for Binding the Great Powerful Ghost (*Mahābalaka*). Fifteenth. "The two thumbs are held straight upright. The left index finger is bent, its tip resting within the base of the left thumb; the right index finger is slightly curved. The middle fingers and the two fingers below them (the ring and little fingers) of both hands are all bent together into the palms."

16. The Mudrā of Eating, the Sixteenth: "The two thumbs are bent with their tips pointing downward; the two index fingers are held straight and upright; the two middle fingers are also upright and slightly curved; and the two ring fingers and little fingers are both bent together within the palms."

17. The Fang-tooth Seal (Dantamudrā), the Seventeenth: The two thumbs point upward and stand straight. The two middle fingers stand straight. The left index finger stands slightly curved. The right index finger is bent to rest upon the right thumb. The two middle fingers stand straight, their tips separated by about half an inch. The two ring fingers and the two little fingers are both bent together within the palm.
"If you wish to obtain verification, you must first construct an altar. The altar shall measure one *zhang* and nine *chi* in both length and breadth.
Outside the altar, only the eastern gate shall be opened; the northern, southern, and western sides shall have no gates.
At a distance of about one and a half *zhou* from this outer enclosure, another layer shall be constructed with four gates opened."
In the center, construct another small square altar that does not require doors; within it, fashion a large lotus seat.
This altar has two tiers, both adorned with steps made from powders of five colors.
In the outer courtyard, ten arrows shall be placed facing each direction; each arrow is to be wrapped with five-colored threads according to its respective quarter. There shall be eighteen swords.
In the inner courtyard, it is unnecessary to place additional arrows; instead, thirty swords shall be erected at the four corners of the altar.

Within the outer courtyard, twenty-two trays of food were arranged, with a new, clean water jar placed at each of the four sides; in each jar, branches from various trees were inserted, all including their leaves.
Within the inner courtyard, two trays of food and one water vessel were placed in each of the four directions.
In front of each square seat, one tray of food was set out, along with one water vessel and six incense burners.
"The mantra master stands in the western direction, holding an incense burner, and first with a sincere heart [should pray]:

'I respectfully invite the Yakṣas of the five directions and their five sovereign emperors, each leading eighty-four thousand retinues, to enter this maṇḍala, so that my mantra phrases may be accomplished as desired.'"
Three times each day and three times each night, recite the aforementioned mantra thirty-one times during each session; by practicing in this manner for seven days, the rite will be accomplished.
To know whether success has been achieved: if the sword moves or the water moves, one knows that the proof of accomplishment has been attained.
If the practitioner of the mantra obtains these signs, from that time forward, all that they do will succeed.
"If one wishes to cure diseases caused by ghosts and spirits, the illness will be healed immediately after reciting the mantra no more than three or five times.
Whether one commands them to be bound or commands them to be released, whatever one does according to one's will shall be accomplished."
The Method for Painting the Images of the Five Yakṣas: "Each has one body and four hands; on the left side, the upper hand holds a trident and the lower hand holds a staff;
on the right side, the upper hand presses against a wheel and the lower hand holds a lasso."

His body is blue in color and his mouth is wide open; his canine fangs protrude upward, and his three eyes are red as blood. He wears a skull upon his head, and his hair stands erect like the color of flames. A great snake winds around his neck, and from each of his two shoulders hangs a dragon, their heads facing one another.

"The image has two large red snakes coiled around its waist, and large red snakes are also coiled around both of its ankles. From each shoulder hangs a dragon, with their heads facing one another; a large red snake is coiled around its waist, and a large snake is likewise coiled upon the staff it holds."
The hips are covered with tiger skin, and there is an ornament of skulls.
Beneath each of the two feet of the image, a ghost should be placed.
On both the left and right sides of the image, a youth dressed in blue robes should be fashioned; their hair is tied in two topknots at the corners, and they hold incense burners in their hands.
To the right of the image, two yakṣas are depicted—one red and one yellow—holding a sword and a lasso;
to the left of the image, two yakṣas are depicted—one white and one black—holding a spear and a trident; their forms are all extremely terrifying.
Both his hands and feet are those of a yakṣa, and his claws are long and sharp.

Once the image has been painted, during a solar or lunar eclipse, quickly construct a mandala and prepare as much food and fruit as your means allow to offer; recite the mantra until the sun or moon returns to its normal state, at which point you may cease.
Those who receive the Dharma must abstain from the five pungent roots, alcohol, and meat; if they consume these, there will be no divine efficacy.
The nature of the spirits is impetuous and fierce, and they may fearlessly harm people; one must therefore exercise great caution.

"When wishing to recite the mantra, place the image within the altar, starting from the southwest. Holding an incense burner in hand, stand at the entrance and with a sincere heart make this invocation:

'All Buddhas, all Great Bodhisattvas, all worthy sages, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, celestial youths, and powerful yakṣas—may you all bear witness through your great compassion, divine eye, divine ear, and knowledge of others' minds, so that as I, your disciple, today recite the Great Majestic Mantra of the Five Yakṣas, it may be brought to fulfillment without any hindrance.'"
Having spoken these words, he should recite the mantra seven times with a loud voice and immediately close his eyes to perform this visualization:
"May the sound of this mantra reach all the Vajras, Yakṣas, and so forth throughout the infinite Dharma-realm of the ten directions, serving as a summons to them."
Focus your thoughts and maintain this visualization, intending that the yakṣas of the five directions and their retinues will all come.
Then, sit in a composed posture and recite the mantra twenty-one times; if you can recite it as many as forty-nine times, that is most excellent.

"When the deity of the mantra arrives, the mantra-practitioner himself feels uneasy while seated; his body hair stands on end, and he feels as though he might topple over. It is as if someone were suddenly approaching from all four sides to press against him."
If such signs appear, one should know that the mantra deity, his generals, and all their retinues have arrived.

The mantra master must fashion a golden vajra about two feet in length; holding the vajra in his right hand, he strikes the ground with it while reciting the mantra continuously, keeping his left hand across his waist.
Regarding such incantations, the deity will appear no later than three or five recitations.
Unless there is a matter of great urgency, one should not summon them hastily;
if one summons them with haste when it is not urgent, the deity may become resentful, which will surely lead to harm.

"If there is an enemy who repeatedly causes you distress, you should establish an altar. Upon the altar, fashion the form of that Śatru using charcoal and ash from a cremated corpse. While reciting the mantra, strike it with a pestle."

In this manner, after reciting it no more than twenty-one times, all illnesses and afflictions—other than those caused by one's mother or father—will be cured at will; there is no need for further elaboration.
"As for the method of making the pestle: combine gold, silver, and copper—these three substances—and cast them together to form the pestle.
The pestle has eight facets; its shape is like that of a Vajrapāṇi holding a mace, and the pestle is one chi and two cun in length."
"If the three aforementioned substances are unavailable, one should take the root of an eastward-growing peach tree to perform it.

Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty great arhats,
as well as an immeasurable multitude of great bodhisattvas, headed by Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and others.
...and the son of Māri, surrounded before and behind by the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In future ages, during the final period, what dharma must sentient beings practice to escape all calamities?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now explain this matter for you."
At that time, the assembly rejoiced and leaped for joy, and they urged the Buddha once more to speak.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, there was a deity named Mārīcī who possessed the great power of sovereign supernormal faculties. She always travels before the sun; the sun does not see her, yet she can see the sun. No one can see her, no one can know her, no one can seize her, no one can harm her, no one can deceive her, no one can bind her, no one can demand her wealth, no one can punish her, and no enemy can find an opportunity to take advantage of her."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If there is anyone who knows the name of that goddess Mārīcī, that person cannot be seen, cannot be known, cannot be seized, cannot be harmed, will not be deceived by others, will not be bound by others, will not have their wealth confiscated by others, will not be subject to punishment by others, and no enemy will be able to find an opportunity against them."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family knows the name of that goddess Mārīcī, they should speak thus:

‘I, the disciple so-and-so, because I know the name of that goddess Mārīcī, no one will be able to see me; no one will be able to know me; no one will be able to seize me; no one will be able to harm me; no one will be able to deceive me; no one will be able to bind me; no one will be able to demand my wealth; no one will be able to punish me; nor will any enemy be able to find an opportunity against me.’”
This mantra possesses great supernatural power; its applications are accomplished, and it destroys all evils.
If used to establish a boundary, no evil whatsoever within a hundred yojanas will dare to enter.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this mantra:

*Namo buddhāya* (1) *Namo dharmāya* (2) *Namaḥ saṃghāya* (3) *Tadyathā* (4) *Aragamase* (5) *Māragamase* (6) *Sudumase* (7) *Cipramase* (8) *Mahācipramase* (9) *Mārīcīyamase* (10) *Antardhānīyamase* (11) *Namuci-tute* (12) *Svāhā* (13) Furthermore, another version states:

*Namo buddhāya* (1) *namo dharmāya* (2) *namaḥ saṃghāya* (3) *tadyathā* (4) *arukamas* (5) *margamas* (6) *adumamas* (7) *jīvalamas* (8) *aṇḍadhānayamas* (9) *maricivaramas* (10) *namo śrutadhe* (11) *svāhā* (12). The note states: The Sanskrit manuscripts mostly agree with the preceding version. Among the virtuous masters of the Western Regions, most recite the former;

both the ancient and modern traditions of upholding it have yielded verified results. There is no lack of efficacy in either the former or the latter mantra. Thus, while the wording of the former is more complete and comprehensive, determining which is correct is beyond the scope of ordinary perception. Whether to use the former or the latter is left to one’s own convenience.

Then the Buddha spoke these words: “May I be protected amidst the perils of kings; may I be protected amidst the perils of thieves; may I be protected while traveling on the road; may I be protected in the wilderness when lost from the way; may I be protected by day; may I be protected by night; may I be protected amidst the perils of water; may I be protected amidst the perils of fire; may I be protected amidst the perils of *rākṣasas*; may I be protected amidst the perils of *caṇḍāla* ghosts; may I be protected amidst the perils of poisonous drugs. May I be protected by the true word of the Buddha; may I be protected by the true word of the Dharma; may I be protected by the true word of the Saṅgha; may I be protected by the true word of the devas; may I be protected by the true word of the ṛṣis.”

The Invocatory Spell of Mārīcī, also known as the Body-Spell of Mārīcī.
The spell is as follows:
*Namo ratnatrayāya | Mārīcī-dharāye | Māpadevi-samaye | Tadyathā | Varale | Vardhare | Varāhamukhi | Sarvatuccheṣṭe | Vandha vandha | Svāhā.* The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there be anyone who knows that Bodhisattva Mārīcī, all obstacles and difficulties—including those caused by kings, thieves, fierce beasts, poisonous insects, water, fire, and so forth—shall be eliminated."
"If there are those who wish to practice this dharma, among all dharmas this one is the most supreme.
For one who upholds this mantra, even facing a hundred *yojanas*, no ghosts, spirits, or evil persons shall be able to find an opportunity to harm them."

"If, while traveling through difficult terrain, one rises at dawn and recites the aforementioned mantra, sprinkling a handful of water in the four directions and upon oneself; and if one ties knots—whether on the lapel, the sleeve, or a corner of the *kāṣāya*—reciting the mantra once for each knot and making three knots in total, and then proceeds into the difficult terrain while continuously reciting the two great mantras mentioned before, then all obstacles and hostile military commanders will become utterly stupefied and intoxicated, such that none shall have any awareness or perception of them."

"If anyone wishes to make offerings to Mārīcī, they should fashion an image of Mārīcī using gold, silver, red copper, white sandalwood, red sandalwood, or other materials, according to what their means allow."

"As for the method of making the image, it resembles the form of a celestial maiden (*devī*). The image’s left arm is bent upward; at the level of the front of the left breast, the wrist forms a fist grasping a celestial fan, similar to the fan held by the celestial maiden before Vimalakīrti."

In the center of the *śaṅkha*, draw a western-style *svastika* (卍), similar to the *svastika* on the chest of a Buddha. Within each of the four inward-curving arms of the *svastika*, draw four sun-discs and place them one by one. Upon the celestial *śaṅkha*, draw the form of blazing light.

Extend the right arm and stretch out all five fingers with the fingertips pointing downward; as for its length, it may be one or two inches, up to even a cubit—among these, the best is one or two inches.
"The person commissioning the image shall dispatch a master artisan of the highest skill, who observes the eight precepts and fasts, bathes daily, and wears clean white robes while working.
Regarding the price, it shall follow the master's word; the price must not be exceeded."
"On each side of that image, fashion one attendant; these attendants should also be in the form of celestial maidens (devakanyā), adorned with various ornaments.
Once this image has been fashioned, if a bhikṣu wishes to travel a long distance, he should wrap the image within his kāṣāya robe;
if it is an upāsaka, he should conceal the image within his topknot."
When performing the functions of nature, one must leave the body and not discharge them upon it; furthermore, one must not perform these functions in a secluded place while on the body.
Next, the methods for the mudrās and the maṇḍala are explained. 1. The Body Mudrā (Kāyamudrā), First:

Interlace the two little fingers and the two ring fingers, placing them within the palms with the right pressing down on the left. Straighten the two index fingers so that their tips touch each other. Place each of the two middle fingers across the backs of the respective index fingers so that their tips touch. Hold the two thumbs upright side by side, each touching the side of its corresponding index finger, and move the thumbs back and forth.

2. The Head Mudrā, second: Following the previous body mudrā, bend the upper joints of both middle fingers so that their tips point toward the thumbs with the fingernails facing each other; this is the head mudrā.

3. The Crown Seal (Uṣṇīṣa-mudrā), the third: Following the previous body seal, simply change it by bending the two thumbs at their upper joints and placing their tips within the palms; this is the crown seal.
"If a bhikṣu wishes to travel a long distance, he should wrap the image within his *kāṣāya*;

if it is a layperson, they should place the image within their topknot. Then, forming this 'Crown-of-the-Head' mudrā (*mūrdhna-mudrā*) and placing it upon the head of the image, one should recite the mantra twenty-one times while walking on the road; wherever one goes, there shall be no fear."

4. The Seal for Protecting the Body (Kāyarakṣā-mudrā), the Fourth: "Following the previous seal for the body, simply change it by opening the two index fingers by about two finger-widths; this is the seal for protecting the body, used for self-protection."
5. The Mudrā of Joy (Ratimudrā), Fifth: "Press the tip of the left thumb against the first joint of the ring finger, and clench the remaining four fingers into a fist; this is the mudrā of joy."
If one forms this mudrā and recites the mantra, the rākṣasas and the *tadukpādas* will immediately become joyful toward that person. 6.

The Manu Mudrā, the sixth: "Bend the left arm with the palm facing the chest; clench the fist by grasping with the four fingers starting from the index finger, pressing the thumb over the nail of the index finger, and leave a small opening as a hole in the center of the palm."
Using the fingernails and palm of the right hand, rub from the knuckles of the left hand toward the palm; once reaching the opening, cover the opening with the right hand.
One should contemplate thus:

"The palm of the left hand is the heart of Mārīcī; the palm of the right hand is the body of Mārīcī. Within the center of the palm of the left hand, my own body is concealed. This text is hidden within the heart of the Mārīcī-mantra, and it places Mārīcī upon the crown of my head to protect my body—this is the Seal of Good Knowledge."

7. The Seventh: The Seal of the Messenger. "Bend the four fingers of the left hand and press the tips of the two middle fingers with the thumb to form a hollow. Place the right hand under the armpit of the left arm without covering it, with all five fingers extended. Recite the mantra seven times, then place this hand over the hollow of the left hand."
The mantra is: "Namo Māricyai, sarvasattvānām adṛśyāyai, svāhā. The Buddha said:

"O practitioners who uphold this mantra, if you wish to seek exclusively the dharma of Mārīcī and obtain various benefits that manifest as spiritual efficacy, then after reciting the mantra according to the previous method until the full number of repetitions is reached, you should establish a ritual altar for receiving the dharma on the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month."

"If one wishes to construct a mandala, on the morning of the eleventh day of that month, one should seek out a favorable site and prepare the ground. One must remove all harmful substances exactly according to the aforementioned method, then firmly level and smooth the earth, and immediately perform the ritual for protecting the body and binding the boundaries."

"If one wishes to perform the protection of the body, one should begin on the eleventh day of this month; recite the mantra three times each day, using the aforementioned mudrā method to protect oneself, and perform the boundary-binding (sīmābandha) three times."

As for the method of binding the boundary (*sīmābandha*), one again employs the previously mentioned method of the body-protection mudrā; having formed the mudrā and recited the mantra five times, one turns the mudrā clockwise, whereby the boundary is established.

On the morning of the fourteenth day, one should again perform a great boundary-binding (*mahā-sīmābandha*). Reciting the mantra over ashes seven times, one should cast them in the four directions to establish the inner boundary.

Furthermore, one should prepare ten lumps of clay; having recited the mantra over each one seven times, one should throw them into the eight directions as well as the zenith and nadir. This is called the great boundary-binding.
Having thus performed the boundary-binding protection, one should take scented water mixed with earth to form mud and smear it everywhere over the ground of the altar.
Once the site of practice has been established, hang various banners, canopies, and diverse precious objects.

Having encircled the four sides of the altar with five-colored threads, next take a small portion of incense and flowers into the *maṇḍala* hall; burn incense, perform the mudrās, invoke Mārīcī, make offerings, and practice the path, and then dismiss her.

"On the morning of the fifteenth day, take clean cow dung mixed with fragrant clay to plaster the ground of the altar site. Having performed the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) once more, use various kinds of famous incense mixed with water and a small amount of pure earth to coat the altar ground a second time. Once it has dried, take powders of five colors and spread them over the altar ground, making it as magnificent and beautiful as possible."
Construct a mandala four cubits in size; in the center of the mandala, fashion a lotus seat, and upon that seat place an image of the goddess Mārīcī.
To the east, arrange the seat of the messenger named Bhadrāśrīyā;
to the south, arrange the seat of the messenger named Mārīṇī.
To the north, one should further establish the seat for the messenger, named Keśinī;
at the western gate, one should arrange the seat for the mantra-practitioner.

At night, light twenty-five lamps. Take five water jars—one in the center and one in each of the four corners—and having arranged them, make offerings of various incenses, flowers, cakes, fruits, and food and drink. Adorn the water jars as described in other sections.

"Once various kinds of ritual implements have been arranged, the mantra-practitioner sits upon green grass; thereafter, he forms mudrās to summon Mārīcī and others, making various offerings while maintaining those mudrās."
Upon exiting the ritual enclosure, one should distribute various foods and drinks as alms to all the spirits and deities (*bhūta*).

Once the distribution is complete, the mantra-practitioner holds a blade of green grass while reciting the mantra; he then rubs it from the head down to the feet one hundred and eight times, forming the *rakṣā-mudrā* (protection seal).

Within that mudrā, he again placed green grass upon the crown of his head, and dispatched a disciple to pour water from the jar at the center of the maṇḍala over the crown of the head of the recipient of the empowerment.

Having completed the consecration, one puts on new, clean garments and enters the maṇḍala; there, one receives the protection of the body and, with single-minded devotion, recollects the Buddha and pays homage to the image of Mārīcī.
"When constructing this dharma-maṇḍala, the mantra-practitioner himself and the disciple receiving the dharma shall subsist only on non-glutinous rice and milk porridge as their food.

When the rites are completed and the deities have been dismissed, one should subsequently sweep the site of the maṇḍala; once the plastering and all preparations are finished, the remaining offerings of food and drink must not be consumed by either the mantra-practitioner himself or the disciple receiving the dharma."
"Once these rites have been performed, they may then be put into practice; all [methods] will yield great efficacy.
If one wishes to receive the teachings and realize their miraculous effects, one must first construct a mandala and perform the hand-seals (*mudrā*);
if one does not do so, one's efforts will be in vain."

"Furthermore, construct a water mandala by purifying a single room, smearing the ground with cow dung to a square of one cubit, two cubits, or four cubits, and place an image of Mārīcī at its center."
"The practitioner should bathe every day; if one does not bathe, one should at least wash the hands and rinse the mouth before entering the maṇḍala.

The mantra-master sits here on the western side of the altar, facing directly east, invokes Mārīcī to be established within the altar, and makes various offerings by burning agallochum incense and other fine fragrances."
Recite the mantra every day while seated, one hundred and eight times, or one thousand and eight times, or ten thousand and eight thousand times.

The mantra-reciter takes handfuls of sesame seeds and non-glutinous rice mixed together and burns them in the fire-pit before the altar; for each handful, he recites the mantra once as it burns. In this manner, he completes one hundred and eight or one thousand and eight repetitions, maintaining continuous mental focus without allowing the mind to dwell on other matters.

From the first day of the month to the fifteenth, one should make offerings according to one's ability of food and drink, ghee, honey, milk, curd, fruits, flowers, incense, and lamps; however, one must exclude alcohol, meat, and the five pungent vegetables. Desiring to complete one hundred thousand recitations, one should increase the offerings twofold, continuing in this manner until the full one hundred thousand recitations are finished.

Thereafter, in a suitable location, one should clear the ground, uprooting all undesirable things such as tiles, gravel, bones, and hair; then, having firmly packed the earth, one should make it level.

Regarding the day on which this altar is constructed: the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month is most excellent; furthermore, according to another method, the gengzi day or the first day of the first month may be used, while for other months, one should take the jian day as the starting point.
Construct a mandala using five colors; at the center of the mandala, place a *mārīcī-āsanapīṭha*, upon which one scatters five-colored powders to create a flower seat, along with its form or seal.
The messenger stationed on the eastern side is named Bhadralakṣmī;
the messenger stationed on the northern side is named Keśinī;
the messenger stationed on the southern side is named Mālinī.
"Then the mantra-practitioner shall call them in succession from Mārīcī to Mālinī, seating each according to their respective position.

Once they have been seated, one should present various offerings—eight plates of incense, flowers, and food, and sixteen lamps—twice as many as those previously mentioned. The practitioner shall then sit outside the western gate facing east, reciting the mantra one thousand and eight times while making these various offerings."
In this manner, after seven full days have passed, one should then dispatch [the deity].
There is another method: if one performs this rite of the maṇḍala on the day of a solar or lunar eclipse, one will obtain great efficacy.
The above has completed the explanation of the method for constructing the maṇḍala, making offerings, and receiving and upholding [the mantra].

Furthermore, there is another practice: on the day the mandala is constructed, as well as at other times, having risen at dawn and finished washing one's hands and face, one should recite the mantra for removing obstacles and difficulties, and sprinkle water consecrated by that mantra in the four directions, above, below, and upon one’s own body.

Upon reaching the place where the mantra is recited, one should use this single mantra to consecrate cow dung with which the altar is smeared; likewise, the food and drink offered, as well as the lamps, flowers, incense, the bathing water for the mantra-reciter, and the protective garments—all these items should be consecrated with this single *buddhagaṇapati* mantra.
The mantra says:
"Namo cūdāmaṇe kaṭa kaṭa."
