"‘Svāhā’ means ‘dispersed. Since this mantra is for the purpose of seeking wealth and material goods, it lacks ‘svāhā’; therefore, the word ‘svāhā’ is not appended. This is called the first root seal.

2. The Flower-Body Seal of Śrīdevī (The Second). "Following the previous [instructions], change only this: extend the two index fingers straight upward, separated by about two inches. Interlace the two middle fingers with their tips entering the palms, the right pressing down upon the left, with the tips slightly bent. Bring the tips of the two little fingers together and the tips of the two thumbs together. Open the wrists so they are separated by about four inches."

The mantra is: “*Paci-hulu-da* (1), *Buli-dina-hulu-da* (2), *Uṭa-ku-hulu-da* (3), *Na-mu-hulu-da* (4), *Buli-ti-na-hulu-da* (5), *U-she-fu-hulu-da* (6), *Svāhā* (7). 3. The Mudrā for Delimiting the Boundary of Śrīdevī. Third: The mudrā for delimiting the boundary of Śrīdevī is as follows: Interlace the two little fingers behind the palms; interlace the two index fingers outwardly, with the right pressing against the left; extend the two middle fingers straight upward with their tips touching; join the backs of the joints of the two ring fingers by pinching them with the respective middle fingers; bring the tips of the two thumbs toward the body so they touch; space the wrists about three inches apart, and then recite the mantra.

4. The Seal of Śrīdevī Bestowing Precious Jewels, Chapter Four. "Interlace the middle and ring fingers of both hands, inserting them into the palms. Interlace the two little fingers outwardly, with the right pressing down upon the left. Curve the right index finger upward and keep the left index finger straight and upright. Bend the two thumbs into the palms. Joining the wrists, recite the Great Mantra."

5. The Mudrā for the Goddess of Merit Bestowing Various Kinds of Food and Drink upon All Ghosts and Spirits. Fifth. Interlace the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers so they enter the palms; interlace the two little fingers with the right pressing over the left; extend the two index fingers straight upward, separated by two inches; bend the two thumbs into the palms; join the wrists and employ the Great Mantra.

6. The Seal of the Flower-Throne of Merit (*Puṇyapuṣpāsana-mudrā*). Sixth. "Extend the three fingers from the index finger downward of the right hand upward, appearing slightly bent but not fully so; extend the right little finger upward straight, its tip about one and a half inches away from the ring finger; bend the right thumb onto the palm. Grasp the five fingers of the right hand with the left hand, pressing the left thumb over the right thumb. Join the wrists and palms. There is no mantra."

7. The Seal of the Merit of Universal Food, Number Seven. "Place the three fingers below the right middle finger upright and pointing upward. With the right thumb, press against the side of the upper joint of the index finger. Clench the left hand into a fist with the three fingers below the middle finger; the left index finger is slightly curved upward, and the left thumb presses against the side of the middle joint of the middle finger. With both hands, open them wide with palms facing upward and join the wrists, then recite the Great Mantra."

8. The Seal for Causing a Household Afflicted by Illness to Become Bustling, Blessed Goddess Śrī. Eighth: Bend the right thumb onto the palm; clench the remaining four fingers into a fist with the back of the fist facing upward. Grasp the right wrist with the left hand, placing the left thumb upon the back of the right wrist.
If a person forms this seal every day and makes offerings by scattering flowers, precious jewels will come to them spontaneously.

9. The Ninth: The Seal of the Heart-Mind of the Merit-Heaven Deity (*Guṇadevatā-hṛdaya-mudrā*). "Interlace the left and right ring fingers and little fingers behind the palms. Raise the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another. With the tips of the two index fingers, pinch the back of the upper joints of the middle fingers respectively. Keep the two thumbs upright and side-by-side."

10. The Mudrā for Making Offerings to Śrīdevī, the Tenth. "Interlace the little fingers of the left and right hands within the palms, with the right hand pressing down upon the left. Bend the two ring fingers and grasp the two little fingers; point the tips of these fingers toward the body. Straighten the two middle fingers slightly curved, their tips separated by one *fen* (inch). Also straighten the two index fingers, their tips separated by four *cun*. Straighten the two thumbs side-by-side, each pressing against the back of the middle joint of its corresponding ring finger."

11. The Mudrā of Śrīdevī’s Joyful Delight, Number Eleven. "Follow the previous Flower-Body Mudrā; however, change only the two index fingers so that they press slightly upon the nails of the two middle fingers from behind, positioned at the chest."
The mantra is: “1. Jibuditi liṇa, 2. Ajibuditi liṇa, 3. Mikiḍiti liṇa, 4. Usuditi liṇa, 5. Jyaptaditi liṇa, 6. Śisuditi liṇa, 7. Svāhā. If one has legal affairs, one should form this seal.

“Śrīdevī’s *dhāraṇī* seal causes the members of the mantra-practitioner’s household to be joyful. If one forms this seal every day and makes offerings of scattered flowers, precious jewels will arrive of their own accord.

12. Furthermore, Śrīdevī’s Heart Seal, the twelfth. As before, using the *pramuditā-mudrā*, place the two index fingers upon the nails of the two thumbs; the two middle fingers are held upright and slightly bent, with their tips touching one another.”
The mantra is as follows:

"Nāgīphulu (1), Udrāphulu (2), Nāgarukṣaphulu (3), Upacaphulu (4), Arāgīphulu (5), Vīratināphulu (6), Sujñāphulu (7), Svāhā (8). These words of consecration are certainly auspicious, true, and not false.

“Sentient beings of equal practice who possess middling roots of goodness should uphold, recite, and master this [teaching]. For seven days and seven nights, they should observe the eight precepts, purify their minds morning and evening, and make offerings of incense and flowers to the Buddhas of the ten directions.”
One should dedicate [the merit] for oneself and all sentient beings toward the fulfillment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, making this vow:
"May all that I seek attain auspiciousness."

He himself shall thoroughly clean and sweep the dwelling or house where he resides—whether it be his own quarters or a forest hermitage—smearing the ground with fragrant clay, burning exquisite incense, arranging pure and fine seats, and scattering various flowers and perfumes upon the ground to await me.

At that time, in the space of a single thought-moment, I entered his house and sat upon his seat; from that day and night forth, I ensured that this household—whether it be a village, a monastery, or an open space—lacked for nothing, so that whatever was required, whether money, gold, precious jewels, cattle, sheep, or grain, was all obtained in full abundance, and everyone experienced complete happiness.

"If you can dedicate the most excellent portion of the roots of goodness you have cultivated to me, I shall never again oppose that person throughout my life; I will protect and keep them in mind with a sincere heart wherever they dwell, and I will cause whatever they seek to be accomplished according to their wishes."

"You should all, with a sincere heart, pay homage to these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—namely: Ratnottama Tathāgata, Vimala-jvalana-ratna-prabhāsa-rāja-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata, Suvarṇajvālā-prabha Tathāgata, Suvarṇa-śata-prabhā-saṃbhāra-garbha Tathāgata, Suvarṇaparvata-ratna-cchattra Tathāgata, Suvarṇajvālā-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata, Maholkā Tathāgata, Ratna-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata...
You should also reverently pay homage to the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇaprabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Nityapralāpa, and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata;

you should also pay homage to Akṣobhya Tathāgata of the eastern direction, Ratna-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata of the southern direction, Amitāyus Buddha of the western direction, and Sūkṣma-svara Buddha of the northern direction."

The Ritual for the Image of Śrīdevī: "Take an unmarried girl of fifteen years of age and have her weave one *zhang* and four *chi* of silk. Recite the Great Body Mantra of Śrīdevī over yellow cow urine one thousand and eight times, and sprinkle the urine upon the surface of the silk."

From the eighth day to the fourteenth day of the month, one should cleanse and prepare a plot of earth with fine mud, constructing a water altar measuring four cubits on each side. One should take a single image of Śākyamuni and place it within the altar, making offerings of various incenses, flowers, food, and drink, and lighting five lamps.
“Summon a master painter—one of the most skilled—and have him observe the eight precepts every day, bathe in purity, and provide the painter with protection seals.”
First, one must agree upon the artisan’s fee; whatever is required, the mantra-practitioner must not violate the price.

The body of the image should be one cubit—specifically one chi, three cun, and five fen—in length, excluding the halo and pedestal; furthermore, it should be made even taller and more exquisitely crafted.
Use frankincense, aloeswood, and white sandalwood mixed with milk-juice as pigments; do not use any animal hides or glues, and consecrate the pigments with the body-mantra of Śrīdevī.

Take five jars of water and place them at the center and the four corners of the altar; before the entrance of the altar, perform a vegetarian feast for twenty-one persons—if such are unavailable, seven persons, or even as few as three, will suffice.

"The image of that Goddess Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhā has a well-proportioned body, is reddish-white in color, and her two arms are depicted with various necklaces, bracelets, armlets, earrings, celestial garments, and a jeweled crown."
The celestial maiden holds a cintāmaṇi jewel in her left hand and bestows the mudrā of fearlessness through incantation with her right; she sits upon a preaching dais.
To her left, paint the Brahmā-Indra holding a precious mirror;
to her right, paint Śakra-devendra scattering flowers as an offering to the celestial maiden.

Behind each [deity] is painted a mountain of the seven treasures; above the celestial image, five-colored clouds are formed, upon which rests a six-tusked white elephant. The elephant’s trunk holds a crystal jar from which various precious objects pour forth into a vessel placed atop the crown of Śrīdevī.

"Behind the celestial deity, paint a grove of flowers made of a hundred jewels; above his head, paint a thousand-petaled jeweled canopy; atop the canopy, depict the various musical performances of the devas scattering flowers as an offering."

"Below the image, on the right side, further depict the form of a mantra-practitioner (dhāraṇī-vidhāyin) wearing fresh white robes, holding an incense burner in his hand, kneeling in the *hu-kuei* posture to make offerings, and seated upon a white silk cloth."
"The above concludes the ritual method for the image of Guṇakārandavatī.
Furthermore, there is another ritual method: fashion an image of a celestial maiden from *kapiñjala* wood, one inch in height."

"From the first day of the first month, the mantra-practitioner shall bathe and arrange various kinds of offerings before the image, increasing the quality of the ritual implements each day. Continuing in this manner until the fifteenth day is reached, whatever one seeks shall be attained according to one's wishes."
"When one wishes to disperse the altar, one should burn *apāmārga* grass—here translated as *niuxi cao* (ox-tongue grass)—at the center of the altar.

If one wishes to perform the ritual, one should enter the altar during the first, third, or seventh month; the celestial maidens will rejoice in these months, while in other months it is not permitted."
"If one wishes to subdue powerful spirits (*bhūta*), first burn *ariṣṭaka* wood—this is called the *mu-huan-zi* tree.
Furthermore, there is another method: recite the mantra over *kunduru* incense—which is *guggulu*—*nyagrodha* tree leaves, and various kinds of fragrant flowers."

Furthermore, light a lamp using ghee from a yellow cow, maintaining this practice constantly; take the aforementioned flowers and fruits and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, casting each item into the fire once for every recitation.

Three times each day for fifteen days, once the ritual at the *cīvara-maṇḍala* is completed, all wealth and treasures, various garments, and the five grains will become abundant, with nothing lacking.

"Furthermore, there is another method: take all the painful spots on the body of the patient, and using a cord made of black sheep's wool, tie twenty-one knots and fasten them upon the painful spots; thus, they shall be healed."

"Furthermore, there is another method: beneath the patient's bed each night, burn manaśśila (translated as 'realgar'), white mustard seeds, salt, and so forth. When the spirits smell the scent of these medicines, their bodies will split apart, and they will retreat, scatter, and flee."

"Furthermore, there is another method: take *gorocanā* (translated as 'cow bezoar') and *sumana* flowers (translated as 'silk-cotton'), grind them into a powder, and recite the mantra over it one hundred and eight times. By applying this to the forehead, all obstacles and difficulties will naturally disperse and vanish."

"Furthermore, there is another method: take clove leaves and camphor and grind them into a powder. Recite the mantra over it one thousand and eight times, then apply it to the heart center. Take another portion and place it inside a vermilion pouch, which is then worn upon the crown of the head. All sentient beings who see this will feel love, respect, and mindfulness."
"If one wishes to cause an enemy to fall ill, one should establish a water-maṇḍala measuring one cubit before an image of Śrīdevī.

At the entrance of the maṇḍala, burn *dhāra* wood—this refers to *candana* (red sandalwood)—and take the arm bone of a person who died in the marketplace, wild mustard seeds, and *harītakī*, burning them together to make ash. Mix this with milk and fashion the likeness of that enemy."
The mantra-practitioner recites the mantra while holding a sword with his right hand and grasping it with his left; with a mind of wrath, he recites the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Furthermore, he treads upon the heart of the drawn human figure with his left foot twenty-one times, adding the syllables *hūṃ phaṭ* during the recitation.

"Furthermore, according to another method, if the mantra-practitioner wishes to cause all sentient beings to come of their own accord to make offerings, he should establish a water mandala two cubits in size before an image of Śrī-devī. At the western gate of the mandala, he should dig a fire pit one cubit deep."

The mantra-practitioner sits to the south of the altar gate, holding one hundred and eight grains of square-shaped salt in his right hand. He recites the mantra once for each grain and casts them into the fire pit.

In this manner, for fifteen days, three times each day—at one thousand and eight recitations per session—he also burns ghee, honey, white resin, aloeswood, storax, and other fragrances. A hundred flavors of food and drink will spontaneously appear as offerings; the mantra-practitioner shall lack for nothing.

"Furthermore, according to another method, if one wishes to behold the goddess Puṇyavatī, one should go to a large lotus pond. Holding an incense burner in the left hand, one should enter the lotus pond, pluck a single flower from within the pond, recite the mantra over it once, and then cast it back into the water."
When these have been completed ten thousand times, at that time, Puṇyavatī (Gongde Tian) shall appear from within the water of her own marks and signs upon a throne of the seven treasures.
At that moment, the practitioner, having filled a silver bowl with camphor-scented water, shall sprinkle it upon the place where she has emerged.
Thereupon, Puṇyavatī said these words:
"What kind of object do you wish for me to create?
At that time, the practitioner replied:
"May the deity Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhā grant me a portion of her merit.
Having spoken these words, Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhā immediately returned to her own abode.

Thereafter, wherever the practitioner went, he encountered wealth and treasures; those who sought things had their desires fulfilled, and all manner of things were provided according to their hearts' content, never lacking in any way.

"Furthermore, there is another method: take śamī wood—this is called *gouqi* [dog-rose] in Chinese—and cut it into one hundred and eight pieces, each an inch long; recite the mantra once over each piece and cast them into the fire."

Three times each day, recite one hundred and eight times; when this is completed over the course of one hundred and eight days, the practitioner will immediately attain self-realization of the threefold supernormal knowledge (*trividya*).

"Furthermore, there is another method: whether in a temple, or within a chamber, or at a site containing śarīra, one should adorn the *maṇḍala* and place an image of Puṇyadevī facing west. Take pieces of *candana* (red sandalwood) and *niṃba* wood (the bark of this tree is called *kudrū*); these two types of material should both be smeared with curd, clarified butter, and honey. Smear one segment of wood and recite the mantra over it once, then cast it into the fire. Continue in this manner until one hundred and eight segments have been offered, then cease."
If one performs this practice three times a day for twenty-one days, the practitioner will obtain five hundred silver coins daily.

Furthermore, there is another method: take *utpala* flowers—if these are unavailable, take freshly blooming blue lotuses—and combine them with *śarīpani*, *viśatapani*, *madana* incense, *maruka* incense, and *manasija*. These six ingredients should be taken in equal parts, ground into a powder, and mixed with snow-water to form pills the size of small jujubes. Place these medicinal pills within a double-layered casket of gold or silver, and recite the mantra day and night without ceasing according to the previous method, until the medicine moves spontaneously.

Upon moving, he immediately casts the medicine into his mouth; once the practitioner has swallowed it, all who see him are filled with great joy, and he can travel three thousand li daily without any fear.

"Furthermore, regarding the method for ensuring that the Goddess Puṇyavatī is always joyful: take *nāgakesara* (translated here as 'dragon-flower'), which grows on Mount Kunlun, along with *sukandana* and *mākarani*, in equal parts. Grind them into a powder and mix the medicine with snow water to form pills the size of small jujubes. Store the medicine in a golden casket and burn one pill daily before the image of the Goddess Puṇyavatī; all obstacles and difficulties will naturally be dispelled."

"Furthermore, there is another method: take a one-cubit length of *śālmalī* wood—here called the *saheuan* tree—which is as thick as a finger, and smear the branches of the *saheuan* with the sap of the *sāla* tree."

The mantra-practitioner holds a branch in his hand and recites the mantra repeatedly before the image of the deity; when one hundred and eight days have been completed, the goddess will be pleased, and whatever ailment there may be will be cured by leaning upon this mantra-staff.

"Furthermore, there is another method: one must take grains, wheat, and small beans, recite the mantra over them once and cast them into the fire. Do this until it is completed one thousand and eight times.
Three times each day, continue in this manner for forty-five days; then all the grains, wheat, and beans within the house will naturally sort themselves by color and gather together."

"Furthermore, there is another method: if one wishes to eliminate all calamities within the household, one should take branches of the *kara* tree—or if this wood is unavailable, take branches of the pomegranate—and cut them into inch-long pieces. Anointing them with ghee, curd, and honey, one should recite the mantra over them once and cast them into the fire, burning them for one thousand and eight repetitions; then all calamities will naturally be extinguished."

"Furthermore, there is a method for removing all calamities and obstacles within the home: on the eighth and fifteenth days of each month, take charcoal and ash, mix them with curd, recite the mantra over them one hundred and eight times, and scatter them in the four directions of the house."
When standing within the house, if one recites the mantra one thousand and eight times, no evil spirits will dare to advance.

If the mantra-master wishes to cause the celestial maidens to rejoice, he should construct a water altar measuring four cubits before the image. In the center of the altar, he should dig a fire pit one cubit wide and seven inches deep, drawing the shape of a twelve-petaled lotus flower within it. Inside this, he should burn pieces of red sandalwood and mulberry wood as fuel, each piece one cubit long and arranged in separate bundles.

In this manner, one should burn [the offerings] before the image three times each day, making various kinds of offerings, including burning ghee, curd, rice flowers, and buckwheat flowers, while reciting the Great Body Mantra until it reaches one hundred thousand recitations.
By relying on this dharma, the celestial maidens will rejoice and constantly possess great spiritual efficacy.
"One who recites this mantra must not engage in sexual desire.
One who recites this mantra shall attain fearlessness; neither asuras, ghosts and spirits, nor nāgas shall be able to harm them."
Having spoken this mantra, Ānanda and all the bhikṣus came forward, prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and withdrew.
This concludes the ritual of the goddess Puṇyavatī.
*The Sūtra of the Collection of Dhāraṇīs Spoken by the Buddha*, Scroll Ten.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Volume Eleven, Section on the Various Devas, Part Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Ajita from India during the Great Tang Dynasty.

Chapter on the Devas and Others Offering to the Buddha to Assist in Accomplishing the Dharma-Seal Dhāraṇīs of Samādhi. Chapter on the Devas and Others Offering to the Buddha to Assist in Accomplishing the Dharma-Seal Dhāraṇīs of Samādhi.

At one time, the Buddha was at Mount Vipula, amidst a great assembly, expounding the secret treasury of dhāraṇīs, mudrās, and divine mantras, as well as the methods for maṇḍalas, concerning all the vajras.

At that time, the Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, Maheśvara, Sūryadeva, Candradeva, the stellar deities, Pṛthivīdeva, the Four Great Kings, Agnideva, and others were all present in the assembly. Each of these celestial kings was accompanied by immeasurable retinues, and they all gathered together to hear the Dharma being preached.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, various great spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and their retinues; upon hearing the efficacy of this Vajra-Abhijñā-Svatantra-Dhāraṇī, they were all greatly terrified and knew not where to flee.
The Buddha said:
"Stop, stop! Do not be greedy. This treasury of the Vajra Dharma brings great benefit; listen attentively as I explain for you the matters of skillful means that bring such benefits."

At that time, when the assembly of the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, had heard what the Buddha said, their hearts were filled with joy; each felt shame and remorse for their transgressions. Rising from their seats, they prostrated themselves on the ground, touching it with their five limbs, and bowing their heads in reverence, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Each of us in this retinue has one hundred and twelve great generals; each of these generals leads a retinue of forty thousand yakṣas, and each yakṣa leads four hundred million *koṭis* of spirits. Together they roam throughout the Sahā world, filling all lands, constantly watching for opportunities to harm others, greedily devouring flesh and blood, causing various calamities, acting with violence across the land, destroying the True Dharma, deceiving the Triple Gem, and perpetually performing unwholesome deeds.
"We were ignorant and did not know that the Buddhas, out of their great compassion, pity all sentient beings and provide them with manifold benefits.

We and our retinues, each failing to perceive this and losing mindfulness of our minds and speech, have now made a great vow to take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Together with the devas, we offer this divine mantra to assist and protect the Triple Gem; we dare not disobey these instructions and shall follow as authorized by the Buddha."
Before the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and others, they bind these essential vows:

"We, along with all the retinues we lead, wherever there may be monasteries, shrines, or sites for practice where the Dharma wheel of the Mahāyāna is expounded, or where there are those who recite, uphold, and employ the dharanis, treasuries of divine mantras, and mudrās—if anyone at such places causes disturbance, inflicts injury, or fails to provide protection, we, the members of our retinues, shall be as if we have deceived and violated the Triple Gem; we all vow that in future ages we shall not attain the fruit of the Buddha-way."
“May the Buddha bear witness to and certify this Dharma-mantra; we, too, shall likewise benefit all beings, just as the Buddhas do. 1. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of the Great Brahmā Deva King.

First: “Turn the palm upward; extend the little finger and the index finger straight; bend the middle joints of the ring finger and the middle finger so that their tips point upward and stand erect; place the thumb alongside the side of the index finger; then move the thumb back and forth.”

The mantra is: "Oṃ śrūci simrici dhāraṇī maṃ hūṃ haḥ. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there are those who uphold this dharma, practice this mantra, and wish to obtain a sign of efficacy by making offerings to Brahmā, they should wash their hands and face every day; having done so, they first kneel on the ground, holding the water-pitcher between their left armpit and chest with the mouth of the pitcher facing forward. Having then formed this seal with the left hand, they pour water from the pitcher into the palm of that hand, bring their mouth close to the palm, and recite the mantra over the water three times before drinking it themselves.
Furthermore, fill the mudrā with water and wipe one’s own mouth, reciting the mantra three times.
Again, fill the mudrā with water and recite the mantra over it three times; then, using this water, sprinkle it upon one’s right foot, followed by the left foot.

Again, using the thumb and ring finger of the right hand, press upon both eyes, both nostrils, the mouth, the right ear, and the left ear in succession; then, passing the hands over the top of one's head, release them.
"If it is a good matter, insert the tip of the index finger between the tips of the middle and thumb fingers, then extend the tip of the index finger outward and snap the fingers with a sound;
if it is a bad matter, pinch the thumb and middle finger together and snap the fingers with a sound."
"Whoever performs this rite shall obtain various efficacious results; the ritual will be accomplished immediately, and they shall prevail in doctrinal debate.
Furthermore, when establishing a great mandala, one should likewise employ mudrās and mantras to summon the Brahmā and devas to provide assistance, protection, and offerings."
If one can recite this mantra every day and make offerings to all the Buddhas and others, all [practices] will be efficacious.

2. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of Śakra Devendra, Part Two First, turn both hands upward. Then, hook the two ring fingers together. Bend the two middle fingers and the two little fingers toward the palms. Extend the two index fingers slightly upward so that their tips touch each other. Likewise, extend the two thumbs slightly upward, placing them alongside the sides of the index fingers, and move the thumbs back and forth.
The mantra is:

“Oṃ kṣābhamrikha kṣābhagmrikha nārāmaṇi amavaha akhaśumukha sagati śinavara svāhā. This is the Dharmamudrā-mantra. If there are those who receive and uphold this mantra-seal and make offerings to the Lord of Devas, various efficacious results will manifest.
If one remains before the Buddha and daily maintains the intention to constantly make offerings, that person will always receive the protection of all devas, and all beings will rejoice.

3. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of the Deva Maheśvara. Third. "Join the palms. Interlace the two thumbs, the two index fingers, and the two little fingers, holding them all upright and touching one another. Then, interlace the right middle finger with the left middle and ring fingers, extending the [left] ring finger outward. Next, interlace the left ring finger with the right ring and middle fingers, extending the [right] middle finger outward. Then, interlace the left middle finger with the right index and middle fingers, extending the [right] index finger outward. With the fingers thus interlaced and turned outward, place each finger against the knuckles of the back of its respective hand, while the thumbs move back and forth."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ vītarasani pramathani cchindani bhindani svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there are those who daily receive and uphold this seal, recite this mantra, and make offerings to the deity Maheśvara, they will obtain various efficacious results.
Whenever one forms this mudrā and recites the mantra to make offerings to all Buddhas, all the Buddhas likewise give rise to joy; furthermore, it is efficacious for curing all manner of illnesses.

4. The Spell for Seeking Horses from the Deva Maheśvara Using the Ancient Seal. The Fourth: "Bend the lowest joint of the middle finger of the right hand toward the palm; extend the remaining two joints straight. Then place the ring finger across the base of the back of the middle finger. Next, bend the tip of the little finger toward the center of the palm. Then bend the index finger, pressing the pattern of its middle joint against the nail of the ring finger. Next, bend the thumb, pressing the pattern of the thumb against the nail of the index finger, and finally press the tip of the thumb against the nail of the little finger."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ, Gambhīra-vikrīḍita, svāhā. If a person wishes to seek out a horse, they must abstain from all food for seven days. Day by day, they should form this mudrā with the middle finger of the hand, smear it with ghee and honey, and recite the mantra repeatedly while saying aloud the name of the sought-after horse followed by the words, "Come quickly! On the seventh day, the horse will arrive and knock at the door.
When performing the rite at night, do not allow others to know;
if you perform it during the day, keep the doors firmly closed so that others do not know.
Furthermore, there is another method: fashion four images out of clay, resembling celestial beings, each three or four finger-widths in length.
What are the four?
First is named Śaya, second is named Viśaya, third is named Asita, and fourth is named Aparasita.

Furthermore, fashion an image of the deity Maheśvara out of clay. Place Maheśvara in the center; on the right side, place Aja and Vijaya; on the left side, place Āsīta and Aparāsīta. Set up a fire-pit in front. Take cat excrement—this is the name of the "ghost-eating cake" (piṇḍa) in the Western Regions—along with human fingernails and human hair. Mix these three together and burn them as an offering. Repeatedly perform mudrās and recite mantras, saying aloud: "O horse named [insert name], come quickly to look!"
In this manner, perform the rite day by day for seven days. On the seventh day, [the deity] will come and knock at the door; grant whatever is wished for from the heart.
Regarding the consumption of food during this rite, there is no hardship; however, when performing the rite at night, do not let others know.
If you wish to perform the rite during the daytime, close the door firmly and ensure that no one sees you.
When the ritual matter is completed, collect the image and store it away for future use.

5. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of the Eastern Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Part Five. "Place the left palm facing upward; curl the three fingers below the middle finger; bend the middle joint of the index finger so that its tip is slightly curved; extend the thumb straight and askew, ensuring its tip does not touch the top of the index finger."
The right hand is performed in the same manner, with the exception that one raises the wrist and places it upon the upper part of the left forearm, while the thumbs move back and forth.

The mantra is: "Oṃ dṛḍhīkuru ra ra ra parāntana svāhā. Sixth: The Dharma Seal and Mantra of the Southern Heavenly King Virūḍhaka. Tilt the left wrist and place the side of the right wrist against the base of the left wrist. Turn the two palms away from each other and hook the two middle fingers together, extending them like a rope. Curve the two little fingers, the two index fingers, and the two thumbs individually, and move the index fingers back and forth.

The mantra is: “Oṃ vīrutaka yakṣadhipataye svāhā. Seventh: The Dharma-Seal Mantra of the Western Heavenly King Virūpākṣa. Method: Place the right wrist upon the base of the left wrist. Bend the three fingers below the middle finger of both hands into the palms to form fists. Hook the two thumbs, each pressing down upon the nail of its respective middle finger. Interlace the two index fingers like a rope and extend them, while moving the thumbs back and forth.

The mantra is: "Oṃ vīrabhojanāgā dīpate svāhā. Eighth: The Dharma Seal and Mantra of Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Northern Quarter. [Method: With the left hand, bend the index finger and place the remaining four fingers in the palm to form a fist; then bend the thumb to press down upon the index finger.
The right wrist is also tilted and formed into a coil, as with the left hand; however, the thumb is extended straight upward and placed upon the coil of the left hand, moving back and forth.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ veśramaṇa dānadattā svāhā. These are the Dharma-seal mantras of the Four Heavenly Kings. If any persons, when receiving and upholding the various dhāraṇīs of the Buddhas, Prajñāpāramitā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and Devas, establish a site for a sacrificial assembly, a Way-place, or a Dharma-altar, and perform this mudrā while reciting the mantra to summon the gods and arrange offerings, they will immediately cause all people to rejoice.

"In the past, these Heavenly Kings and others also made offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as to the Bodhisattvas and Vajras; their mantra-seal methods were identical, approved by all Buddhas, and manifested the Image Dharma complete with all its characteristics, serving the Buddhas with majesty to benefit all beings."

9. Furthermore, the Heart-Penetrating Seal Mantra of the Four Heavenly Kings. Ninth: "With both hands, interlace the thumb, middle, and ring fingers and join the palms; extend the two index fingers so that their tips touch, bending them at the first joint; then turn the two thumbs inward toward the center, moving them back and forth."

"Once these images have been fashioned, arrange them in a row facing south within the northern part of the *maṇḍala*. When the arrangement is complete, the mantra-practitioner shall sit to the south, facing north. He shall then form the aforementioned ritual mudrā with his hands; each deity shall perform their respective mudrā and recite their respective mantra, calling upon each one individually."
Having seated [the deity], burn agalloch incense and present various offerings.
Next, perform the Universal Mind Seal and recite the Universal Mind Mantra.
The mantra is as follows:

10. Furthermore, the Heart-Seal Mantra of the Four Heavenly Kings. Regarding the tenth mantra: use the final [mudrā] with the right hand’s thumb, middle finger, and little finger all extended upward; bend the index finger and ring finger and tuck them onto the palm; the palm faces forward; the elbow is bent upward—this is not a method for coming or going elsewhere.
The mantra is as follows:

"Namaḥ vīrutakāya | namo vīrupakṣāya | namo veśarāvaṇāye | namas tīriti-ra-sthālāya | tadyathā | taṇḍa taṇḍa | taṇṭāṭā taṇṭāṭā | damari | svāhā. If one can purely uphold this Dharma-seal mantra according to the ritual, the Four Great Heavenly Kings will lead the twenty-eight divisions of benevolent spirits to the site of practice to assist and protect the practitioner. They shall cure all illnesses; if one recites the mantra for seven days, all ailments will be completely eliminated.

The Ritual for the Images of the Four Heavenly Kings: Regarding the ritual for the image of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra: the image should be made with a body one cubit (*hasta*) in length. The body is adorned with various celestial garments and decorations, which must be rendered extremely exquisite and in perfect proportion to the body.
The left arm is extended downward, grasping a sword; the right arm is bent forward with the palm facing upward, holding a jewel from which light radiates.

Regarding the iconographic method for the celestial king Vīrutaka: the size and attire of the image are according to the previous [standard], and the left hand is likewise as in the method for the preceding celestial king—extending the arm to grasp a sword—while the right hand holds a spear, the base of which rests upon the ground.

Regarding the ritual method for the image of the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa: the size of the image and its clothing shall correspond to the previous description; the left hand is the same as before, differing only in that it holds a spear, while the right hand grasps a red cord.

Regarding the ritual method for the image of King Vaiśravaṇa: the dimensions of the image and its clothing shall correspond to those previously described; the left hand is as before, holding a spear planted upon the ground, while the right hand is bent at the elbow, supporting a Buddhist stūpa.

"Once these images have been fashioned, one should arrange them in a row facing south on the northern side of the *maṇḍala*. When the arrangement is complete, the mantra-practitioner sits facing north and, forming the aforementioned mudrā with his hands, recites the mantra while calling each deity by name one by one."
Having seated them, burn agalloch incense, present various offerings, and recite the heart mantra.
The mantra is:
"Oṃ jvala śvetarāja svāhā. This dharma-seal mantra is called the Heart-Penetrating Seal Mantra of the Four Heavenly Kings.

If one creates an image of the body and performs mudrās day after day within the maṇḍala, reciting the aforementioned mantras and the heart-mantra before the image, the Four Heavenly Kings will be delighted and bestow their grace.
If one can recite this mantra ten thousand times, it will be highly effective for curing illnesses and one will obtain much wealth.

11. The Mantra of the Dharma-Seal of the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva-dharmamudrā-mantra), Number Eleven. First, turn the backs of both hands toward each other. The middle, ring, and little fingers are held upright and aligned. The two index fingers are extended diagonally with their tips touching. The two thumbs are bent sideways to press against the side of the base joints of the index fingers, moving back and forth.
The mantra is:
"Oṃ sahasraraśme svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there are those who uphold this seal and recite this mantra, making daily offerings to the Sun Deity, they shall all be free from illness.
If one makes offerings before the Buddhas, all Buddhas will rejoice.

Chapter Twelve: The Seal for Offering to the Sun Deity (Āditya). No separate mantra is seen here. [The mudrā is formed as follows: Bend the ring finger and little finger of the right hand into the palm. Press the thumb down upon the upper joints of the ring and little fingers. Hold the middle finger straight upright. Slightly bend the tip of the index finger and place its side against the upper joint of the middle finger. Then, grasp the wrist with the four fingers of the left hand; let the thumb grasp the back of the right wrist. Extend the little finger slightly and bend it. Keep the right arm and elbow straight and pointing upward.

13. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of Candrādevī, the Thirteenth. "Cross the two little fingers; place the ring fingers within the palms, with the right pressing upon the left. Stand the middle fingers upright, their tips touching one another. Press the two index fingers respectively upon the third joints of the middle fingers. With the two thumbs, pinch the two ends of the ring fingers within the palms, moving the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ, tiṣṭha tiṣṭha patti, svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; when constructing a great maṇḍala or a universal altar, one should perform this mudrā, recite this mantra, and make offerings, whereby all shall rejoice.

14. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of the Constellation Deities (Nakṣatra-devatā-dharmamudrā-mantra), Chapter Fourteen. "First, extend the right hand upward and cross the left hand over it in reverse. With the tip of the ring finger of the right hand, align it to press upon the inner root joint of the middle finger of the left hand; with the middle finger of the right hand, press upon the inner root joint of the ring finger of the left hand."

Again, with the left ring finger, press back against the inner root joint of the right middle finger; then, with the tip of the left middle finger, pinch the inner root joint of the right ring finger, twisting them together firmly like a cord.
Straighten and erect the two little fingers so that their tips touch.
Extend the two index fingers obliquely upward so that their tips touch.
Point the two thumbs toward the body so that their tips touch, and move the thumbs back and forth.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ nakṣatrarā devatāye svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there is a mantra-practitioner who, day after day in succession, performs this mudrā before the Buddha and recites this mantra as an offering, their body will always be free from illness.
When constructing the central altar, this [rite] is also included in the count; one recites the invocation and makes offerings, and all rejoice. 15.

The Dharani of the Seal of the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī-devatā-dharmamudrā-mantra), Number Fifteen "Join the palms. Cross the two index fingers and the two little fingers behind in the center of the palms, with the left pressing against the right. Straighten the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers so that their tips touch one another. Stand the two thumbs side by side, pressing them against the sides of the index fingers, and move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vāsundhari dhanadhānya prabhārati svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. If there are those who continuously receive and uphold this seal day after day, recite the mantra with a sincere mind, and make offerings to the Earth Goddess, they shall obtain all manner of rare treasures.
When constructing the universal altar (*sāmānyamaṇḍala*), it also applies to a single station; one summons [the deity] and makes offerings, whereby all rejoice. 16.

The Dharma-Seal Mantra of the Fire God (*Agnideva-dharmamudrā-mantra*) No. 16: "Extend the three fingers of the right hand straight upward, slightly bend the index finger, and place the thumb folded within the palm; move the index finger back and forth."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ āgneye hā bhe bhe vaḥnaye dīpe dīpe dīvaye svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. When a mantra-practitioner performs any ritual of the maṇḍala or makes offerings, they should first summon the Fire God (Agnideva) to sit upon the flower seat within the fire-pit. After burning various offerings such as clarified butter and honey, they shall then move the Fire God and install him seated by the side of the fire-pit.

Thereafter, in due order, one should invite all the Buddhas, as well as the Prajñāpāramitā, each of the Bodhisattvas, each of the Vajras, and also the devas; having thus established them within the flower-seated fire-pit, one completes the offerings by burning ghee, honey, and so forth, along with the five grains, various flowers and incenses, various cakes and fruits, and scented water.
One by one, they revert to their original mudrās, recite their respective root mantras, and send them back to their original positions.
Once the offerings are complete, one forms the dismissal mudrā and causes them to disperse.

17. The Seal of the Heavenly Manifestation of the Fire Deva Assisting the Mantra-Practitioner (Agni-devaputra-mantradhārin-sahāya-divyadarśana-mudrā), Number Seventeen. "Bend the right arm at the elbow and extend it straight upward. Curl the tips of the index, middle, and ring fingers toward the palm, but do not let the tips touch the palm. Extend the thumb straight up and press its tip against the side of the index finger."

18. The Dharma-Body Seal and Mantra of King Yama. The Eighteenth: The Dharma-Body Seal and Mantra of King Yama. "Bend the three fingers of the right hand, leaving the index finger protruding by about three parts of its length. Place the thumb flat against the lower joint of the index finger, and move the index finger back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ yamarāja ugrapiśāca ajara svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. When performing a great maṇḍala offering to all the Buddhas and others, if one forms this seal and recites the mantra seven times, King Yama will immediately come to receive the offering, and his heart will be greatly gladdened.

19. The Dharma-Body Seal Mantra of All Dragon Kings, Chapter Nineteen. It is also called the Seal of the Dragon King Upananda. "Place the right elbow inside the left elbow. Then, with the right hand, slightly curve the last four fingers; with the thumb, press against the index finger and slightly curve it. Reverse-curve the left hand toward the right hand; the right hand is likewise."
With both hands facing each other in the shape of a snake’s mouth, open and close the four fingers of both hands while moving them back and forth;

for the mantra, use the following mantra. 20. Furthermore, there is the Dharma-body Seal of the Dragon King (Nāgarāja). For the twentieth [seal]: "The left and right arms and wrists remain as before without change; however, simply cross the left and right little fingers and ring fingers within the palms, with the right pressing upon the left. Straighten the two middle fingers so their tips touch one another. Rest the two index fingers against the joints on the backs of the middle fingers. Slightly curve the two thumbs so that each rests against the inner middle joint of its respective index finger. Move the index fingers back and forth while reciting the following mantra together."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ puṣpe puṣpe puṣpavati hūṃ svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra. When performing a great assembly for making offerings at the altar, if one forms this seal and recites this mantra while summoning those who enter the general assembly to join in the offerings, everyone will become entirely joyful.
"If you wish to pray for rain, you should prepare an altar and perform the ritual of offering; by following this prayer, it will suffice that rain shall fall immediately. 21.

The Flower-Throne Seal of the Five-Directional Nāga Kings (The Twenty-first [Chapter], No Separate Mantra Found). "The two hands: the eight fingers [excluding the thumbs] are neither curved nor straight, all pointing upward and held vertically. The tips of the two little fingers are separated by two *aṅgula*. The tips of the two ring fingers and the two middle fingers are each separated by approximately two *cun*. The tips of the two index fingers are four *cun* apart. Both thumbs are held upright, with the two [thumbs] touching each other."

22. The Tooth-Seal of the Five Directional Dragon Kings (Dvāviṃśatitamaḥ pañcadig-nāgarāja-daṃtamudrā). No separate mantra is seen [for this]. "Fold the right arm at the elbow and extend it straight upward. Bend the ring finger and little finger into the palm. Extend the middle finger straight upward. Then bend the tip of the index finger so that its side touches the middle joint of the middle finger, and press the tip of the index finger with the thumb."

The Ritual Altar for Praying for Rain: "If one wishes to pray for rain, one should go to a superior location within the kingdom that commands the four quarters, or to a place with fine ponds and springs where dragons reside. Having cleared and leveled a site near the edge of such a pond, measuring exactly fifty paces on each side, and having donned clean garments and completed the establishment of the ritual arena (dharma-śālā), one should construct a mandala twelve cubits square at its center—eight cubits is also acceptable."

The four sides of the altar shall all be surrounded by curtains and canopies of black cloth, with the upper part likewise covered; within these curtains, many black banners should be suspended, and the four boundaries should be encircled with powder of five colors.
The boundaries of the altar shall consist of a single enclosure with four gates opened.
At the eastern gate of the altar, one shall fashion the body of a nāga king out of clay; it shall be three cubits in length, with one body and three heads.
The dragon stands upon the ground; one cubit of its body is within the altar, while two cubits remain outside.
Next, at the southern gate, one should again fashion the body of a nāga king out of clay, five cubits in length, with a single body and five heads.
The dragon stands upon the ground; one cubit of its body is within the altar, while four cubits remain outside.
Next, at the western gate, one should again fashion the body of a nāga king out of clay, seven cubits in height, with seven heads on a single body.
The body of the dragon stands upon the ground; the dragon’s body is one cubit long within the altar and six cubits long outside it.
Next, at the northern gate, one should again fashion the body of a nāga king out of clay, nine cubits in length, with nine heads on a single body.
The body of the dragon stands upon the ground, with one cubit [of its length] inside and eight cubits outside.

Furthermore, at the center of the next altar, one should fashion the body of a nāga king out of clay; it shall be eight cubits in height, with a single body and a single head, the dragon’s head facing east.
"In front of each of the five Dragon Kings, place a large earthenware jar; on each jar, apply white powder.

Upon the body of each jar, use genuine cow bezoar to paint four images of Subhūti, seated in the full lotus posture. Fill the mouth of each jar to the brim with various flowers—if there are no fresh flowers, use colored paper flowers—and wind flower garlands around the necks of the jars."

"At each of the four corners of the altar, place a separate water jar made of red copper; each jar should have a capacity of about one *dō*, filled to the brim with pure water, and need not be decorated with paintings."
Insert willow or cypress branches—bamboo branches may also be used—into their mouths, taking each with its leaves.
Furthermore, tie five-colored silks, each five feet long and of a distinct color, around the branches; these shall be bound together into a single bundle.
"On the inside and outside of the altar, many small dragonlets were fashioned from clay to serve as retinues.
Before each of the five Dragon Kings, various kinds of cakes, fruits, and food were offered, served upon a large lacquered tray; these offerings were replaced daily with fresh and excellent ones."
"When performing this rite for the altar to pray for rain, every day one should cook one *shí* of the five grains and distribute it as food upon the ground for the spirits and deities.
When performing the ritual, eight disciples—each of whom has previously entered the Great Dharma Hall (*dōjō*)—should be employed as attendants; no others are permitted to enter at will."
Those who perform the ritual are permitted to eat only dry non-glutinous rice, non-glutinous rice milk porridge, cakes, fruits, and the like; they must not consume vegetables.
Bathe with fragrant water, put on fresh and clean robes, and enter the maṇḍala to perform the ritual.
Whenever one goes to the toilet, one must bathe once and put on fresh, clean robes before entering the maṇḍala again.

"Dispatch a mantra-reciter to sit within the altar; burn various incenses profusely and recite the mantras with a sincere mind. Perform only the protection of the body; do not perform the rite of boundary-binding."

In this manner, these eight persons shall enter the mandala in turn to recite the mantra, ensuring that the interior of the mandala is never left empty. They must recite the mantra day and night so that the sound of the chanting does not cease, and every night they shall light one hundred and twenty lamps.
"When entering or exiting, coming or going, one must always enter and exit through the western gate; the other three gates must not be entered at will.

Outside the curtains, a separate gate shall be opened on each of the four sides. At each gate, various multicolored banners shall be suspended, and a curtain shall be set up at each gate. Many woolen rugs and cushions shall be spread out, and fragrant oils, food and drink, and bedding shall be provided."

Furthermore, he invited a community of virtuous and disciplined monks who were diligent in their practice; having himself observed the fast and bathed in fragrant water, he donned new, clean robes and entered the inner curtains to recite the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*, the *Mayūra-rāja Sūtra*, and the *Mahāmegha-cakra Sūtra*. Throughout the six periods of the day, he circumambulated the altar, performed prostrations, and assisted those praying for rain.
"If one performs the ritual for requesting rain in this manner, rain shall fall within three days;
if it does not, a great rain will surely fall within seven days.

23. The Body Seal and Mantra of Nārāyaṇa Deva, the Twenty-third. It is also called the 'Summoning Seal'; the procedure for the upper and lower parts is the same. 'Interlace the four fingers of both hands with the backs facing each other, turn the palms upward, and extend the fingertips straight up. Place each of the two thumbs against the side of its respective index finger, and move the thumbs back and forth. "

The mantra is: “Tadyathā | Oṃ | Nārāyaṇadevana | Klyū klyū | Svāhā. 24. The Seal of the Boundless Power of Deva Nārāyaṇa, Number Twenty-Four. [Perform] the seal as before, but rotate the palms upward toward the body with the wrists joined. Insert the left thumb bent into the space between the fingers of the right thumb; press the right thumb down upon the left thumb, and recite the aforementioned mantra.

By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, one can move mountains and cover the seas; however, one must not harbor enmity toward others. If one seeks revenge and causes harm to another, [the consequences will surely follow]. Be careful, be careful!

25. The Gandharva Body Seal Mantra, the twenty-fifth. "Interlace the two little fingers of the left and right hands with one another. Hook the two ring fingers to grasp the two little fingers within the palms. Straighten the two middle fingers so that their tips touch. Slightly bend the two index fingers so they rest against the sides of the two middle fingers. Place the two thumbs side by side and extend them upward; then move the thumbs back and forth."

The mantra is: "Oṃ sarva-gandharva-nā karuṇāya paṇḍa paṇḍa svāhā. The Twenty-sixth Mantra of the Kiṃnara Body Seal: "Join the middle, ring, and little fingers of both hands together, interlacing them with the right hand over the left. Extend the two index fingers upright so that their tips touch, leaving a space of about one inch between the palms. Spread the two thumbs upright and move them back and forth."

The mantra is: “Oṃ vajrakinnarāya panta panta svāhā. The Twenty-seventh: The Body Seal and Mantra of the Mahoraga. “Grasp the two hands in a fist with the palms facing upward and the sides touching. First, extend the two index fingers. Then, with the two thumbs, each press upon the side of the second phalanges of the two middle fingers. Move the index fingers back and forth.”
The mantra is:
"Oṃ sarvamahoraga gharāṭaye svāhā. (28) The Mahāmāyūrī Body-Seal Mantra, the twenty-eighth. [In Chinese it is called] the Peacock King Seal;
use this to bind the boundaries and fetter the māras. First, insert the middle finger of the left hand between the back of the fingers of the right hand.
With the index, ring, and little fingers of the left hand, grasp the back of the middle finger of the right hand;
with the index, ring, and little fingers of the right hand, grasp the thumb of the left hand,
such that the tip of the left thumb protrudes between the two thumbs of the right hand.
Press the right thumb against the nail of the right index and middle fingers while they are held together;
the left index finger is held upright, moving back and forth.
The mantra is:

“Tadyathā | Oṃ | Mahāmāyūrī | Sarvagaṇapade | Phaṇṭa phaṇṭa | Hūṃ phaṭ | Svāhā. 29. The Seal for Assembling the Hosts of Devas by Mahāmāyūrī (Second Ninth). This is identical to the Seal for Repelling Devas and Ghosts by Cāmuṇḍā. 30. The Mantra Method for Summoning the Lion King.
First, stand up and bend the second joint of the index finger of the left hand.
Furthermore, with the left hand, press the thumb upon the index finger,
and press the middle finger upon the tip of the thumb;
keep the ring finger and little finger straight and upright.
Raising the hand so that it is level with the left shoulder,
then bend the thumb of the right hand into the palm while the other three fingers grasp and curl;
[raise this hand] so that it is also level with the right shoulder.
Turn the palms toward the shoulders and extend the index fingers straight up while moving back and forth.
The mantra is as follows:
“*Tadyathā | Oṃ | Huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ | Ho ho ho ho | Svāhā.*” When this seal is formed, all spirits and deities will arrive immediately upon being called.

31. The Mantra of the Lion King’s Boundary-Protecting Seal (Siṃharāja-sīmābandhana-mudrā-mantra), Number Thirty-One. This is identical to the previous One-Syllable Subduer of Māras Seal of Cundāvajra; the only difference is that the tips of the two middle fingers are placed against the space between the eyebrows.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ hūṃ (1) dhu dhura dhu dhura (2) hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ (3). Having circumambulated the maṇḍala three times and let out a great lion’s roar, once this mantra has been recited, all the vināyakas who hear the sound of this mantra shall be utterly dispersed and extinguished.

32. The Mudrā and Mantra for Summoning Garuḍa. The thirty-second [chapter]: "The mudrā and mantra for summoning Garuḍa: Turn the palms upward with both hands, placing the right over the left. Hook the thumb of the right hand around the thumb of the left hand; do the same with the left hand."

Bend the middle, ring, and little fingers of the left hand into the palm of the right hand; press the middle, ring, and little fingers of the right hand against the three nails of the right hand, while the index finger is held straight up, moving back and forth.

The mantra is: "Oṃ vajragaruḍa cchinda cchinda matha matha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. 33. The Mantra of the Seal for Summoning the Great Eloquence Heavenly King (Mahāpratisarā-devaputra). First, bend the right thumb into the palm; curl the middle, ring, and little fingers inward. Then, with the left hand, grasp the right wrist from the front, while moving the right index finger back and forth.

The mantra is: "Tadyathā | Oṃ | Mahādevaputra | Kṣapaṅga | Hastyadaye | Svāhā. 34. The Ritual for the Mudrā and Mantra of Summoning Yama-dhanda. Method: Interlace the middle, ring, and little fingers of both hands. Extend the two index fingers upright with their tips touching. Place each of the two thumbs against the side of its respective index finger. Open the palms as if holding water, and move the thumbs back and forth.

The mantra is: “Tadyathā | Oṃ | Yamatandana | Śiṅkarī | Vajrīdudde | Ḍhe Ḍhe | Svāhā. 35. The Mantra and Seal for Summoning Varuṇa. To perform this seal: join the tips of the little fingers of both hands together. Place the two ring fingers behind the little fingers, with their pads pressed together; do the same for the two middle fingers. Place the tips of the two index fingers upon the first joints of the backs of the two middle fingers. Turn the palms upward in the manner of cupping water. Then, place each thumb against the side of its respective index finger and move the thumbs back and forth.
The mantra is: "Tadyathā:

Udgatidevana, khe khe, svāhā. If one wishes to perform this ritual of the Water Deity’s mudrā and mantra, one should construct a water mandala four cubits in length and breadth, with four gates opened in the mandala.
On the northern side of the altar, place the seat of Varuṇa and arrange sixteen plates of food and drink as offerings, while burning frankincense.
The mantra-practitioner shall bathe, don new and clean garments, sit facing north, and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times; thus, he will first obtain the rain.
"If one enters the water and performs this mudrā-rite, one may tread upon the water as if it were solid ground.

Regarding the ritual for creating an image of the Water Deity (Varuṇa): carve an image from white sandalwood, five inches in height, resembling the form of a celestial maiden. Her face shall have three eyes, her head shall wear a celestial crown, and her body shall be clothed in celestial garments and adorned with necklaces and ornaments, holding a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) in both hands.
It is also permissible to make an image two and a half inches in height."
Having fashioned this image, place it within a wooden casket and enclose it in a brocade pouch, binding it to the left arm; all one's aspirations will then be fulfilled.
Next, perform the bodily mudrā.

36. The Mudrā of Varuṇa’s Body, the Thirty-sixth: "Stand upright with feet together, join the palms at the level of the space between the eyebrows, and press the tips of the two index fingers against the tips of the two thumbs."
For one who forms this seal, the body of Varuṇa (Water Deity) manifests. **37. The Dharma Seal and Mantra of Vāyu (Wind Deity), No.

37.** “Rising to one’s feet, with the two legs separated by about two chi, the toes aligned side-by-side. Bend the middle joints of the left and right middle fingers so they rest within the palms. Next, place the two thumbs side-by-side, each pressing down upon the upper side of the respective middle finger. Hook the index, ring, and little fingers of both hands so that their tips touch one another; the sides of these three fingers are all spread apart. Join the wrists and place the lower joints of the two thumbs against the forehead, with the tips of the fingers pointing upward.”

The mantra is: "Oṃ vāce ākhye svāhā. The Dharma-seal of the Eleven-faced One emerges from the seal of no coming or going; this mantra belongs to this particular division. **The Dharma-seal Mantra of the Asura King, Number Thirty-Eight:** "Form the fist with the middle fingers of the left hand, leaving them about three finger-widths away from the palm. Curve the index fingers, and likewise slightly curve the thumbs so that they correspond with the index fingers. Move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ vimalacitra asura dīpate svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; when performing the Great City Ritual Mandala, one should invoke [the deities] with this seal-mantra for their entry and offering, and they will all rejoice.

39. The Dhāraṇī of the Seclusion Mudrā (Cāmuṇḍā-dhāraṇī-mudrā), the Thirty-ninth. "Interlace the middle fingers and ring fingers of both hands by twisting them together in reverse; interlace the two little fingers; interlace the two thumbs with their tips pointing upward; likewise interlace the two index fingers; and move the thumbs back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ hulu hulu cāmundi svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; when constructing a great Dharma-maṇḍala, one should invoke [the deities] with this seal-mantra for their offering, and they will all rejoice.

40. The Cāmuṇḍā Devī Trisampuṭa Body-Protection Seal, Number Forty. "Bend the two thumbs into the palms; press the two ring fingers against the upper surfaces of the two thumbs; extend the two index fingers, middle fingers, and little fingers straight upward with their tips touching one another; brace the two elbows. Holding the seal five inches below the breasts, recite the Great Body Mantra."

41. The Fire-Wheel Seal of the Deva Cāmuṇḍā, the Forty-First. "Place the tip of the right middle finger against the tip of the left index finger; place the tip of the left middle finger against the tip of the right index finger. Bend both ring fingers into the palms so that their middle joints face away from each other. Keep both thumbs and both little fingers straight and erect, with their tips touching one another, while reciting the heart mantra."

42. The Seal of the Deva Cāmuṇḍā for Subduing Demons and Ghosts, Number Forty-Two. "Interlace all eight fingers from left and right within the palms; raise only the two middle fingers straight up with their tips touching one another. Join the wrists and place them upon the crown of the head, extend the elbows like wings, and recite the heart-mantra."

The ritual application for receiving and maintaining this mantra, as well as its efficacy, are as described below: "If one wishes to receive and maintain the Mārīcī (Moṇḍagā) mantra, first construct an altar seven feet in length and breadth, using cow dung to smear the ground over a square area of seven feet and seven inches."
One should take a staff, measuring it according to its length; a length of seven chi is also acceptable. One may take willow branches six chi long or bamboo.
Holding pure water in the mouth, one should spray half of it and swallow the remainder.
First, hold water in the mouth and strike the teeth seven times; then, spray half of it away and swallow the remaining half while reciting the mantra.
The same applies to consecrating the alms bowl.

When consecrating a sick person, take ash—if there is no ash, take earth and water—and having recited the mantra over whatever is obtained, apply the ash and water to the patient’s body, and then consecrate the burning of white resin incense (śrīkhaṇḍa).
Draw the figure of a ghost upon the ground. The mantra-practitioner shall hold a branch of pomegranate or, alternatively, a willow branch, and recite the mantra over it.
When striking the patient, if a ghost has possessed them, it will immediately ask for its name and the reason for its inflicting the illness;
if it does not speak, recite the mantra once and sprinkle water [upon it], and it will then speak of its own accord—using mustard seeds instead of water is also permissible.

Regarding the method for establishing a boundary: take water and mustard seeds, recite the mantra over them either three times or seven times, and scatter them in the four directions while forming this thought in your mind:
"May they provide protection for me within a distance of so many paces."

"Whenever one intends to cast a spell upon a boy or girl to send them out to observe auspicious or inauspicious signs, one should bathe and purify oneself, burn agalloch incense, hold a pomegranate staff in hand, and strike the ground with the staff while reciting the mantra."
If one strikes the ground with four fingers or strikes the body, it is a case of spirit possession.

For those suffering from malarial fevers that recur every day, every two days, every three days, every four days, or every seven days, one should recite a mantra over a white thread, making one knot for each recitation; after tying twenty-one knots, fastening them around the head will cause the illness to be cured.

"If a person wishes to sever the affliction of yakṣas and pūtanas, they should take a blade of tempered iron—of whatever size they prefer—and brandish it above the head of the patient; the illness will then be immediately cured."

"If a person wishes to obtain money, wealth, grain, silk, or the necessities of life, they should take seven kinds of grain and use purple ginger wood to construct a well-railing. Then, lighting a fire with firewood, they shall recite the mantra over the seven kinds of grain and cast them one by one into the fire of the purple ginger; doing this one hundred and eight times, their heart's desire will be fulfilled."
"If a person wishes to gain mastery over women, they should take sesame seeds, recite the mantra over them, and burn them.
If a person wishes to expel all malevolent spirits and ghosts, they may recite the mantra over raw meat and burn it upon fire."
"If a person wishes to eliminate a fever, they should burn *śrīkhaṇḍa* (sandalwood) and recite the mantra; the illness will be cured immediately.
If a person wishes to eliminate the venom of a snake, they should burn its skin and recite the mantra."
"If a person desires to obtain wealth and clothing, they shall burn *sumana* flowers and recite the mantra; they will obtain them immediately.

If a person wishes to perform the *āveśana* rite, they should take *dhūpa* resin, fine ink, and sesame oil, grind them together, and smear the mixture upon the fingernails of a child. Facing the sun, they shall recite the mantra over it, and they will immediately see various auspicious and inauspicious visions."

"If there is someone who suddenly contracts the demonic illness of the Kṛtya ghost, its symptoms resembling those of wind-epilepsy, or appearing like a madman, sometimes weeping and sometimes laughing—such being the symptoms of this disease, if it is not treated for forty-nine days, that person will certainly die."
The mantra-practitioner shall construct a water-maṇḍala four cubits in size at a secluded spot outside the city gate by the side of an eastward-flowing stream, making various offerings.
He shall call the patient near the entrance of the maṇḍala, form the fire-wheel mudrā, and recite the previously mentioned heart-mantra.
With his right hand, he grasps white mustard seeds and scatters them over the face of the afflicted person; once the spirits obtain the mustard seeds, their bodies shatter as if scorched by fire.
With his left hand, he holds a willow branch and strikes the patient.
"If one repeatedly performs this rite and burns ghee, curd, and sesame seeds in this manner for three days, the deity of the mantra will be pleased.

Furthermore, as for the method [for healing]: rub ghee and oil upon the patient's body at all painful locations, and further recite the mantra while applying it below the heart; thus, one shall obtain immediate recovery."

Furthermore, regarding the method for obtaining great efficacy: when one desires to achieve this, one should perform offerings of various incenses and flowers and light lamps before an image of Cāmuṇḍā. One should dig a fire pit, one cubit square in measurement, and within the pit, draw the shape of a lotus flower. One should burn one hundred and eight pieces of mulberry wood, reciting the mantra once for each piece as it is cast into the fire.

Furthermore, by burning ghee, curd, non-glutinous rice, rock honey, buckwheat flowers, mustard seeds, and agallochum incense, and so forth, one thousand and eight times, the mantra-practitioner will be able to obtain great treasures.
"If one can perform this rite daily, the celestial deities will be delighted and it will constantly possess great efficacy, such that one shall not be troubled or disturbed by ghosts or spirits.
Any practitioner reciting the Cāmuṇḍā mantra must not eat coriander, black pepper, ginger, lentils, or cumin; these five items must all be avoided.
If a person eats them, it will cause them to lose their spiritual efficacy."

48. Furthermore, the Method for Transferring Swellings by Means of the Vemacitra Seal and Mantra, Number Forty-Eight. "Form a fist with the three fingers below the middle finger of both the left and right hands, each bent inward. Join the tips of the two index fingers together. With the two thumbs, pinch the sides of the middle fingers to form fists, ensuring that the backs of these three fingers are pressed against one another."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ cāmuṇḍe ilimili svāhā. Having received this Dharma-seal and observed the fast for seven days in advance, on the day of the great fast, one should burn aloeswood incense before an image of the Buddha; once the offering is complete, one should silently recite this mantra twenty-one times.

Next, one should tap the teeth twenty-one times and then silently chant "Kill. After receiving and upholding [this rite], it may be used as one wishes. For men, use the left hand; for women, the right.

When performing the rite of subduing a man, use the index finger of the left hand to press upon the swelling. Then, take a bone and write the character for "swelling" (*zhòng*) on its surface. Place it on the ground and recite the aforementioned mantra twenty-one times.

Next, one should tap the teeth twenty-one times while silently chanting "sha" (śa). Then, lead the afflicted person to stand beside a tree and use the index finger of the left hand to write [the name] upon the tree; immediately, it will transfer onto the tree. This possesses great spiritual efficacy.
The brief exposition on the efficacy of the Cundā-dhāraṇī is concluded.

49. The Dharma-Seal and Dhāraṇī of All Vināyakas, Part Forty-Nine. To form this seal: Hook the two little fingers and the two ring fingers together toward the palm. Then, interlace the two middle fingers vertically. Next, extend the two index fingers vertically and place them against the middle fingers. Finally, extend the two thumbs vertically, positioning them close to the sides of the index fingers, moving the thumbs back and forth.
The mantra is:

“Oṃ bhagavate āryāvatī svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; when performing a great *maṇḍala* ritual, one should invoke [the deity] for the offering by forming this seal and reciting this mantra, whereby all shall rejoice.
