(Verse 11) "If one wishes to perform this rite, one must first fashion an image, using white tin, copper, wood, or similar materials; it may be cast or carved into the form of a couple standing in an embrace. Each figure should be five inches tall—seven inches is also acceptable—and both bodies should have the heads of elephants with human bodies. The price paid for the creation of these images must not be reclaimed."
"Once the image has been fashioned, on the first day of the waxing moon, within a clean room, one should prepare a circular mandala using pure cow dung, of whatever size is desired.
One should take one *śīrṣa* of clear sesame oil and, using the aforementioned mantra, consecrate that pure oil one hundred and eight times, then warm the oil."
Place warm oil in a clean copper vessel, then set the image within the oil and install it inside the mandala.

Using a clean copper spoon or ladle, pour the oil over the crowns of the heads of the two images one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, every day recite the mantra over the old oil one hundred and eight times and pour it over them seven times in a single day—four times at dawn and three times at midday, totaling seven times. If one performs this ritual in this manner for up to seven days, whatever one’s heart desires will be fulfilled according to one’s wishes.
"While performing the ritual oil-bath, one should repeatedly make vows.

Furthermore, one should prepare balls of parched grain mixed with ghee and honey, along with radish roots and a cup of wine; by making fresh offerings of these every day, all virtuous undertakings will be accomplished as desired and all calamities will be entirely extinguished. The food thus offered must be consumed by oneself in order to gain strength."

51. The Dharani and Mudra for Harmonizing the Vināyakas, Number Fifty-One. To perform the *Tiśula-mudrā*: Interlace the two little fingers and the two ring fingers within the palms; extend the two middle fingers so that their tips touch one another; place each of the two index fingers upon the lower half of the first joint of the back of the middle fingers; this is the invocation of all the devas. Move the thumbs back and forth.
The mantra is:

"Oṃ śodhulu paramadhānye svāhā. Regarding the ritual for subduing Vināyakas: if the practitioner of the mantra experiences terrors in dreams or perceives various evil omens such as wild animals, one should know that this is because the king of spirits, Vināyaka, is angry.
Having awakened from the dream, he immediately felt ashamed and begged [the deity], saying:
"Do not be angry; tomorrow I shall provide food and drink as an offering of gratitude.
As for the method of offering: one should moisten the ground with water and create a water-altar two cubits in size—it may also be circular, as large as a shallow basin.
Take five steamed cakes and three radish roots, roast them over a fire until cooked; place flowers upon them, and together with burnt white resin and frankincense, install these within the altar.
The mantra-master sits facing east on the western side of the altar; having recited the mantra of Maheśvara one hundred and eight times, he says aloud:
"I am ashamed; go in peace."
Having spoken thus, one places various items from within the maṇḍala upon a tray, exits through the gate, and discards them toward the west—or toward the northwest is also acceptable—while reciting:
"Sarvayakṣarāja āveśaya svāhā sabhājagaccha. Having spoken these words, one discards the items and immediately returns.
The mantra of Maheśvara is as follows:

“Oṃ vitarasani parāmaridhani cindani bindani svāhā. If one recites this one hundred and eight times, the mind will immediately become joyful; not only in dreams, but even while awake, if demonic activities occur, one should simply perform the aforementioned rite and it will be auspicious.

52. The Dharma-Seals and Mantras of All Yakṣas, Part Fifty-Two. "With the four fingers of the right hand pointing downward, hook them with the four fingers of the left hand; the two thumbs are extended straight, moving back and forth."
The mantra is:

"Oṃ kumbhira svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; when performing a great *maṇḍala* ritual, by forming this seal and reciting this mantra to summon [the deities] for the offering of food, they all rejoice.

53. The Dharma-Seal Mantra of All Rākṣasas, Part Five and Thirty-Three. “With the right hand, press the thumb against the tips of the ring finger and the little finger; keep the remaining three fingers upright, and move the thumb back and forth.”
The mantra is:

"Oṃ khaḍgādhīpataye svāhā. This is the Dharma-seal mantra; when performing a great *maṇḍala* ritual, one should invoke [the deities] with this seal-mantra for their offering, and they will all rejoice.

At that time, the Buddhas, seeing that these devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, the kings of the various ghost spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, and others had each offered divine mantras—which bring great benefit and accomplish rare and great merit—addressed the assembly, saying:

"I authorize them all; do not contradict their original vows, but allow them to employ skillful means to protect and uphold the True Dharma. You must not treat our orthodox teachings with contempt, for they show compassion for all classes of sentient beings."

At that time, the various heavenly kings and others, having received the Buddha’s approval, were all greatly rejoiced; they simultaneously paid homage with minds free from regression, thereby accomplishing the foremost and most supreme merit.

The Buddha’s Teaching on the Chapter of the Seals of the Samādhi-Maṇḍala for the Great Assembly of All Buddhas’ Great Dhāraṇīs.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of Arhats, as well as various Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, along with the Vajrapāṇis and their retinues, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, the six masters of external paths, humans, non-humans, and others, all gathered there. He expounded the secret treasury of the Dharma, including various dhāraṇīs, samādhis, divine mantras, dharma seals, and maṇḍalas, to benefit all beings.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Avalokiteśvara of the Eleven Faces, who, together with his retinue, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the earth, and bowed his head at the feet of the Buddha.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit on one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Buddhas, out of their great compassion, have skillfully employed expedient means to preach before this assembly of noble ones this secret treasury of Dharma—the dhāraṇī, samādhi, divine mantra, dharma-seal, and maṇḍala. From the past until the present, all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have attained the fruit of sainthood by means of this Dharma.”

This assembly, with deep-seated devotion and joy, attained what they had never experienced before; they then each proclaimed dharma-mantras within the gathering to provide protection and mindfulness, and upon hearing this, our hearts were filled with great delight.
Furthermore, there is the method for the accomplishment of merit at the Great Assembly Dharma Altar, which delivers all sentient beings and enables them to swiftly attain Buddhahood.

Should there be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, upāsakas, upāsikās, or any sons and daughters of good family who, though they cherish it in their hearts, desire to study and uphold the dhāraṇīs, divine mantras, and dharma seals (mudrās) spoken by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, yet have never entered my Great Assembly Altar, nor have they been able to realize the names of the secret definitive teachings and achieve realization—fearing that those who would rashly employ such dharma seals and the like might be terrified by the afflictions (kleśas) that invade and disturb their bodies and minds.

People such as these do not understand my intent; they act with negligence and recklessness, causing the various māras to stir their thoughts and scatter the power of the mantras so that they become ineffective.

Therefore, I now wish to protect the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as devas and humans, desiring to enable them to penetrate all the dharmas of perfect completion taught by all Buddhas without obstruction. Once the great assembly has heard this, it shall truly be called no falsehood.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Quickly explain it to me."
And he spoke in verse:
“In each and every Buddha-field, the mind delights in and clings to many dharmas;
he extensively draws forth the secret treasury and skillfully explains expedient means.”
Exhorting all sentient beings, protect yourself with compassion;
upon hearing this dhāraṇī, all shall submit and take refuge.
Or, within the universal Dharma altar, may all minds gather together in harmony.
"Through the seal of approval of the Buddha-dharma, one realizes the truth and severs all doubt.

At that time, when all the Buddhas, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the retinue of Vajras, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, yakṣas, ghosts, and others had heard these subtle and wondrous verses spoken by the Buddha, they were all filled with great joy; their minds were free from doubt, and they attained definitive faith.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, addressed the great assembly, saying:

"If there be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or sons and daughters of good family who wish to request the essential decision of the Secret Dharma-treasury and desire its accomplishment; or if kings, having resolved in their hearts, wish to seek repentance for the extinction of all sins and aspire to see and hear the ritual procedures of the Great Way Maṇḍala, they must all prepare in advance during the three months of spring, the three months of autumn, or the three months of winter—these being the superior months. Within these, one should begin on the first day of the third month of spring, the first day of the ninth month of autumn, or the first day of the twelfth month of winter; such are the most excellent and foremost superior days. One should take the first ten days (the *śukla-pakṣa*) as the start, and the ritual proceedings shall be completed in total over seven days and seven nights."

"If you wish to perform the ritual procedures for the accomplishment through mental application (*manasikāra*), you must first seek out a pure location—a spacious and large courtyard, a place with a magnificent great hall, or even a temple or a Buddha shrine; it may also be performed in the open air."

Having ascertained the location, on the morning of the first day of the waxing moon, the Ācārya and his disciples bathe with fragrant water, put on fresh and clean garments, and take various incenses and flowers to that site.
The Ācārya, holding the vajra, should ask those disciples:
"Are you all able to resolutely receive this secret treasury of the Dharma taught by me and the Buddhas, without giving rise to doubt or hesitation?"
The assembly replied:
"We possess firm and sincere faith within the Buddha-dharma and do not give rise to doubt.

After the preceptor had thus asked three times and the assembly had answered three times, he then took the hand-seal (*mudrā*), the incense burner, the pure water, and so forth; he applied the Hayagrīva seal to the pure water, recited the mantra twenty-one times, and holding the incense burner while kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he offered incense and addressed all the Buddhas, Prajñā, Bodhisattvas, Vajra-devas, and all the hidden sages of the path of karma:

"This ground is my own land; I now wish to establish for seven days and seven nights an assembly of the Great Dharma Altar of the Universal Path. I shall make offerings to all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the worlds of the ten directions, to all the Prajñāpāramitās, to all the great Bodhisattvas of the earth, and to the Vajras and Devas. I reverently entreat the Buddhas and their retinues to preside over this assembly, so that we may definitively realize the inconceivable Great Dharma Gate of the Secret Dharma Treasury and thereby attain full certification."

I now wish to perform the ritual for protecting the body, establishing the boundary, and making offerings. All evil spirits, ghosts, and the like, whether they dwell within this courtyard or in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below—depart all from this place of my established boundary to a distance of seven *li*.
As for benevolent spirits and ghosts who are beneficial to our Buddha-dharma, you may remain as you please.
Having spoken these words, he next uses the aforementioned water to circumambulate to the right, sprinkling it everywhere upon the ground of the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).

He then performs the previously mentioned *muñjakeśinī* rite once to bind the boundary; the mudrā and mantra for this boundary-binding are as explained in the *Muñjakeśinī* section, with no other method required.
When establishing the boundary (*sīmā*), the Ācārya may determine its extent—whether distant or near, broad or narrow—according to his own intention.
As for the dimensions of the ritual mandala: if it is for a sovereign, it shall be one hundred and twenty cubits;
if it is for receiving the Dharma, it shall be sixteen or twelve cubits square, and so forth.

Whether it be for a repentance altar or a healing altar, both should be constructed as water altars; those measuring from one *zhou* above to four *zhou* below may all be used interchangeably—the length of a *zhou* being determined by the length of the mantra-practitioner’s own arm—as the ground must be perfectly square and level on all sides.

"If one constructs a water-maṇḍala, there is no need to select specific days, months, seasons, or times; wherever a suitable site is found, one may construct it in that pure place. On a level and even ground, one must smear the surface with fragrant mud, and this constitutes the maṇḍala ritual. Furthermore, one must erect markers at the four corners as signs."
"If one constructs a great maṇḍala, as previously described for the boundary-binding, one should erect markers at the four corners.
Once the marking is complete, summon people to dig the ground and remove the inferior soil."
"If one attains the superior stage, dig out a span;
if one attains the intermediate stage, dig out a cubit;
if one attains the inferior stage, dig out three cubits."

One must completely remove all impurities within it—bones, hair, charcoal ash, tiles and rubble, gravel, tree roots, grass, wood, husks, and other such foul things—and having cleared away all these impurities, reach the good, solid ground. Then, bring good soil to fill the base; sprinkle it once with scented water, add a layer of earth, and immediately strike it with a mallet to compact it until it is level and full, ensuring it is firm and resilient.
If one obtains a high foundation, it is the most excellent.

On the following day, at the time of dawn, the ācārya and his disciples bathe in fragrant water, put on new and clean garments, and four or five disciples follow the ācārya into the maṇḍala, diligently exerting themselves to adorn the maṇḍala.
Regarding the external deportment: the four gates and four corners must all be majestic and imposing, with one pair of *śrīmaṇḍala* deities stationed at each gate.

Furthermore, banners of *śrīmaṇḍala* deities shall be suspended from the left and right aisles, and thirty-six banners of various colored silks shall be hung at each of the four openings of every gate; this applies to each gate individually.
The banners are new and fine, each eight feet in length.

At each of the four corners, one divine king banner is suspended, along with various multicolored banners; there are four such openings at each gate, and the banner poles are likewise arranged accordingly.
"If the dwelling has only two gates, one at the front and one at the rear, place a pair of divine king images on each side of the front gate facing each other;
likewise, place a pair of divine kings on each side of the rear gate facing each other, all of them being new and well-crafted."

"At the entrance to his place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), four stakes are driven into the ground on each of the left and right sides, and a cord is wound around them. Within the area enclosed by the cord, he smears fragrant mud to establish a boundary of protection (rakṣā-sīmā), wherein all manner of offerings are to be placed."

"Next, the Ācārya shall further perform the *kuntaḷī* ritual for establishing the boundary once more; having completed this, he shall immediately prepare a jar of various fragrant muds, stir them with a willow branch, and recite the Great Heart Mantra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*."
The mantra is: "Tadyathā:
gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. As for the number of recitations of this mantra: if one recites it for the sake of a king, one must complete one hundred and eight recitations;
if one recites it for those of the third rank or above, fifty-six recitations are required.
If it is for those of the fourth or fifth grade, recite seven times seven;
if for those of the sixth or seventh grade, recite five times seven;
if for those of the eighth grade and below, as well as the common people, recite three times seven.

All maṇḍala rituals are to be performed with this mantra. Once the recitation over the clay is completed, use the clay to smear the ground; as for the method of smearing the ground, rub it with the palm of the hand following the direction of the sun.
When the smearing of the ground is finished, once again perform the *kuntali* ritual for boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) as previously described.

Next, on the morning of the third day, one should bathe and prepare pure cow dung—taking the dung without letting it touch the ground and receiving it in a clean vessel—and mix it with fragrant water. Having performed the incantation as before, one should smear it over the entire ground.

Next, take a cord and measure its length in cubits (*hasta*) as required; determine the dimensions according to the width and narrowness of the courtyard at that time, marking the measurements by tying knots. Then, pull the cord taut toward the four directions of the site for the ritual arena and mark the points below with white powder.
"The Ācārya first stretches a cord from the northeast corner to the southwest corner to fix it, marking a point four finger-widths away from the pillar;
next, he stretches a cord from the southeast corner to the northwest corner to fix it, marking a point four finger-widths away from the pillar."

At the exact point where the central strings intersect, mark another dot; at each such dot, pierce a small hole about one *zhè* (a span) in depth. Within these, one intends to bury the seven treasures and the five grains. As for the seven treasures: first, gold; second, silver; third, pearls; fourth, coral; fifth, amber; sixth, crystal; seventh, lapis lazuli—these are called the seven treasures.
As for the five grains: first, barley; second, wheat; third, rice; fourth, small beans; and fifth, sesame seeds—these are called the five grains.

Crush those jewels into pieces, mix them with the five grains, wrap them in a piece of silk, and tie the ends with thread of five colors. Bury this within the five openings, leaving the ends of the threads protruding from the ground to a length of about five finger-widths.
Once these treasures have been lowered, they shall never emerge again; from this point upward, the ground is demarcated by golden cords and composed of the seven precious jewels.
This is the place where all Buddhas dwell to preach the Mahāyāna and turn the wheel of Dharma; it is to be made into a Buddha-hall and is therefore the most supreme.
If ordinary people dwell above it, there will be no benefit whatsoever.

Next, perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*). Regarding the method for binding the boundary: take a *vajra* (translated into Chinese as *jin'gangchu*, or "Vajra-pestle") and, according to the *Cundī* ritual, bind the boundary by circling three times to the right outside the mandala; furthermore, perform the mudrā and recite the mantra for the expulsion of *vināyakas*.
Having thus completed the demarcation of the boundary for the four directions, the zenith, and the nadir in succession, one lights lamps at night.

On the morning of the fourth day, the demarcation of the boundary is performed as previously described; one then mixes cow dung with fragrant water and mud, recites the mantra over it as before, and dispatches the disciples to rub the ground with their hands.

Beginning from the northeast corner, rub the ground clockwise day by day; do not rub counter-clockwise toward the left. Rubbing in this successive order, cover the entire ground until you reach the northeast corner again.

Within the site of enlightenment (maṇḍala), when a disciple moves any object or more for the purpose of ritual arrangement, they must always follow the sun by moving to the right; they must not move against the sun to the left.
“The site for the ritual ground shall be square in its length and breadth, with four gates opened; rafters are erected at the four corners, and these rafters are buried deep.

At the upper ends of the four corner rafters, one rafter is laid horizontally on each of the four sides; all these rafters must be of a uniform thickness and large size, while their four faces are to be finely smoothed and planed until they are perfectly square.”

The vertical pieces are notched at their tops, and the horizontal pieces are bored with holes; these are interlaced like bracelets, forming a square and straight structure. The length and breadth are determined according to the occasion, depending on the width and size of the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), and cannot be fixed in advance. For the time being, one may roughly approximate it using coarse bamboo to serve as rafters and the like. Upon this wooden framework, one wraps colorful silks, with various hues interspersed.

Next, take large banners and cover them over with eight longitudinal and transverse lines, intersecting in the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions; this is called the method for adorning the upper direction.

Upon the great banner, a pair of green banners are suspended in the east, a pair of vermilion banners in the south, a pair of white banners in the west, a pair of deep blue banners in the north, and four yellow banners are suspended in the center; all are attached to the great banner and hung to signify the vital energies presiding over the five directions.

Next, large banners were affixed to each of the four sides to form a decorative border; then, above these borders on all four sides, golden and copper *ghaṭa*-flowers, as well as gold and silver vessels, precious mirrors, and other such items were attached, arranged in regular intervals throughout. Furthermore, the four pillars were likewise adorned in this same sequence of ornamentation.

Next, cords were extended to encircle the four sides and fastened to the pillars; upon these cords hung various multicolored banners, clusters of precious bells and ribbons, and assorted jeweled pendants, interspersed and arrayed in magnificent adornment.
Next, it was encircled on all four sides with pearls, and further adorned with various precious lattices.

Once the adornments were complete, next to the western gate of the site of enlightenment—at a distance of about two chi from the southern side—a square pit was excavated, equal in dimension on all four sides, each measuring two chi in length and two chi in depth.

In the center of that pit, leave a mound of earth; upon this mound of earth, fashion a lotus seat with pure cow dung mixed with fragrant water, taking great care to prepare it with meticulous refinement.

Furthermore, one canopy was made of purple silk and another of vermilion silk; the frames for both canopies were fashioned from bent bamboo, each nine feet in length. These were intended to be carried as attendants followed, used to cover the ācārya and the initiates entering the maṇḍala, serving as a mark of solemn deportment during their coming and going.
"In the northeastern area of the ritual site (maṇḍala), at a distance of two or three feet, construct another four-cubit white-water altar.

Next, outside the ritual site toward the southwest—this may also be done in the central courtyard—erect yet another separate four-cubit white altar. At the four corners of that altar, plant four banner-poles; hang banners upon the poles, fill the holes where they were inserted, and sweep and wipe it clean. Perform once more the Great Boundary-binding Rite (mahā-sīmā-bandha) to seclude and purify the ritual site, then light lamps and candles and burn various kinds of incense."

On the fifth day, at dawn, the ācārya bathes the two disciples, and they don new, clean robes. He instructs one disciple to hold a silver bowl containing scented clay water, and another disciple to hold a gold bowl containing scented powder water along with a small, thin cord. Following the ācārya, they enter the maṇḍala.

Upon arriving at the site of the altar, the Ācārya performs one circuit of the ritual path, offering praise and prostrations. He then dispatches a disciple holding fragrant mud to enter the mandala; starting from the northeast corner, he rubs the ground with his hand using the same method as before, until the area where the mud is applied becomes damp and then gradually dries.
Next, the Ācārya and the disciple, who holds the powder-water and the perfumed water, together enter the maṇḍala. Taking a cord measured by cubits (*hasta*), they determine its length.

Having pulled it taut from the northeast corner of the sacrificial altar toward the southeast corner and fixed it, they mark each end with a dot. Next, they move it toward the southwest and mark it with a dot; then they move it toward the northwest and mark it with a dot as well.

Using a cord and colored powder, he sent a disciple to hold the end of the cord while kneeling on the ground at the northeast corner of the altar; he then placed the end of the cord at the point where the first mark had been made at the exact corner of the altar and pulled it taut against the ground.

The ācārya takes one end of the cord and places it at the southeast corner, at the very point where the altar was first marked; then, the two of them pull it together with equal force at the same time.

He sent one disciple to hold the center of the cord and stretch it across the ground; then, the disciple at the northeast corner rose and sat facing the southwest corner, stretching the cord according to the previous method.
Next, at the southeast corner, the Ācārya rises and sits facing the northwest corner, marking the line as before.
Next, at the southwest corner, the disciple rises and sits facing the northeast corner, marking the line as before.
Next, within the distance of one cubit from the plumb line, mark points again according to the previous method.
Once all four corners have been thus marked, dye the cord with colored powder and stretch it out according to the same procedure as before.

Next, take an eight-cubit cord and bend it at its midpoint; place it starting from the first mark previously made outside the square of the altar. Again, bend the cord at one cubit from its center, and further measure from the central point of one side of the altar using a two-cubit length of cord, marking two additional points to the left and right of the central point.

Next, on one side of the wall of the gate, at a distance of five finger-widths from the altar, the wall should be further bent toward the left and right edges for a width of five finger-widths; next, both sides of the gate of the altar should be made five finger-widths wide.
Next, along the edge outside the gate, stretch the lines straight.
As it is for one side, so it is for the other three sides.

Next, construct the central courtyard; the outer line of the [outer] enclosure shall be four cubits [from the wall], and between the inner line of that outer enclosure and the outer line of the central courtyard, leave a path one cubit wide.

Regarding the gateways of the inner courtyard, the walls on all four sides and the left and right edges of the openings shall each be three finger-widths wide; the outer edges of these gates are joined with straight cords, according to the method previously described.
Within that middle court, at a distance of one cubit from the inner boundary ropes on each of the four sides, further mark lines with chalk.
In the center of that altar, construct a courtyard measuring two cubits; do not form a door.

"On the sixth day, the Ācārya shall take five-colored threads and, according to the number of persons receiving the Dharma, tie them into knots to form a consecrated cord (*mantra-sūtra*), which he shall then empower with the Great Heart Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva."
He then spoke the mantra:
"Oṃ amṛtodbhava hūṃ phaṭ. One should recite this mantra once for each knot; thus, one should complete fifty-four knots.

Having fashioned the mantra-ropes, next take pieces of silk, the seven precious gems, and the five grains, wrapping them together in one place; bind their ends securely with thread of five colors, according to the number of persons.

"When the sun is setting, the ācārya and all the disciples who are to enter the maṇḍala have completed their ritual ablutions; they put on fresh, clean garments and cause the disciples to sit in a row outside the maṇḍala, near the western side."
Next, the ācārya performs the ritual for establishing the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) and protecting the bodies of the disciples.
After sunset, the ācārya enters the maṇḍala hall and invites the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattvas, the Vajras, and the various devas to enter the altar and take their seats.

The Buddha sat at the center, Avalokiteśvara and others on the northern seats, and Vajragarbha and others on the southern seats; having completed the ritual of making offerings with various sublime incenses and flowers, five-dish foods, and the lighting of sixteen lamps.
Next, the ācārya exits the maṇḍala and leads the disciples and others to the maṇḍala; they stand in a row near the western gate and perform a brief offering of incense, worship, and prostrations.

"Once the ritual procedures have been completed, the ācārya shall next perform the protection-seal (rakṣā-mudrā) for each disciple one by one, reciting the mantra and forming the seal upon each disciple's body as before. Thereafter, he shall instruct them to take their seats and kneel, each facing east."

The Ācārya shall chant the mantra over white mustard seeds and strike each disciple’s head, face, and heart three times; thereafter, he shall perform the ritual for protecting the body using the seal and mantra of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva as previously described.
"Next, the ācārya kneels on his right knee and asks the seniormost disciple:
'Do you wish to receive this dharma?
The disciples reply:"
"May we obtain such dharmas as these.

Having completed the exchange of questions and answers, the ācārya next takes a vessel of perfumed water and sprinkles it over the head of each disciple one by one. He then places his right hand upon the chest of each disciple one by one, reciting the heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva Bodhisattva to bestow protection. Once this is finished, he ties a mantra-cord around the left arm of each disciple one by one.
"Next, the ācārya leads the disciples back to their positions and descends from the eastern staircase to sit on the ground at the foot of the western staircase.
Then the ācārya sprinkles fragrant water made from *śāla* tree sap in succession before each disciple, circumambulating them three times to the right;
next, he uses a flaming torch to circumambulate them three times to the right, following the same procedure as before."
Next, provide willow branches and then various flowers; following the same procedure as before, circumambulate to the right and bestow them upon the disciples.

Once the disciples have received the willow branches, they shall kneel with their bodies slightly drawn back and chew the tips of the *yāñzhī* (willow twigs), after which they shall cast the willow branches forward.
The ācārya shall observe the place where each willow branch falls one by one. If the chewed end of the branch points toward the body, it is a great omen of good fortune;
if it points toward the south, it is an ill omen;
if the chewed end points toward any other direction, one should know it to be neutral.
Having thus completed the trial in this sequence for all, he then successively pours scented water into their palms and gives it to them to drink, with each person drinking three times.
Once the palm-pouring has been completed for each disciple, the ācārya next drinks from the water using the *vajra* mudrā.

"Once the ritual procedures have been completed, lead the disciples up to the site of practice (*maṇḍala*). Ascend by the western stairs and sit in a row along the side of the site of practice; perform one round of the incense-offering ritual for them."
Next, the ācārya says to the disciples:
"Go to sleep; if you have any signs in your dreams, report them to me individually tomorrow morning. Each of you must apply your minds with care; do not speak rashly, nor disclose this to others."
Having spoken these words, the Ācārya next leads the disciples down from the eastern stairs, and they each disperse to return to their quarters.
Next, the Ācārya enters the maṇḍala and addresses the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and others, saying:

"These disciples wish to enter the maṇḍala and each seek certification. I have completed the ritual procedures for my disciple [Name] and finished all the inquiries. These disciples wish to come and enter the maṇḍala tomorrow to make offerings."

"I pray that the Buddhas, Prajñā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and all the devas and their retinues, who dwell tonight within the sphere of great compassion, will deign to accept my invitation tomorrow. I, the disciple [Name], shall universally invite the Triple Gem and all their attendants to perform extensive offerings. I pray that, out of great kindness and compassion, you will all attend tomorrow and receive these offerings, witnessing this dharma-rite. (Recite this three times.)
Thereafter, dismiss the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajras within the maṇḍala, dispersing them according to their conditions.

Next, the Ācārya, having placed a fire-pit at the northern edge of the maṇḍala, recites the Great Heart Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva. He consecrates white mustard seeds with the mantra, burning one seed into the fire-pit for each recitation, one hundred and eight times in total, to cause all disciples to extinguish their sins and eliminate their obstacles.
Next, the ācārya, together with two or three disciples who have previously entered the maṇḍala, shall, during one night, spread five-colored powders within the maṇḍala to adorn the ground.
As for the application of this method, one first lays it out from the interior, using white powder first, followed by yellow powder, then red powder, then blue powder, and finally black powder.

Once the [powder] has been distributed on all four sides, proceed immediately to the outer enclosure. Starting from the northeast corner, perform the rite by circling clockwise; distribute the five-colored powders according to the same method as before.

When the distribution on the four sides is complete, appoint Dīpaṃkara as the presiding master (ācārya). In the center, spread a great lotus throne; this presiding master is the transformation Buddha upon the crown of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, named Buddhoṣṇīṣa Buddha. If one does not take Buddhoṣṇīṣa as the presiding master, it is also permissible to substitute him with whichever Buddha or Bodhisattva one intends in one’s mind.

Except for the presiding master of the seat, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas remain in their respective positions while receiving offerings; unless it be the Buddhas, Prajñāpāramitā, or Bodhisattvas such as Ekādaśamukha who take turns, none others may serve as the presiding master of the great assembly Dharma altar.

Regarding other water mandalas for healing illnesses and those involving repentance rituals lasting one night, one should appoint a Buddha or Bodhisattva from the specific family (kula) appropriate to the rite as the presiding master; all such various offerings will be excellent.

"Once the seat for the presiding master has been established at the center, next place one flower-seat for the Prajñāpāramitā in the middle of the eastern side of the inner enclosure; second, to its right, place a seat for Śākyamuni Buddha; third, to its left, place a seat for the Buddha who is the Heart of All Buddhas."

"Next, in the north, directly opposite the center of the door, place the seat of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva (4); next, on the right side, place the seat of Avalokiteśvarāmātṛ (5); next, on the left side, place the seat of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (6)."

"Next, directly facing the door on the southern side, place seven seats for the Vajrarājas; next, on the right side, place the seat for Māmakī, known as the Vajramātṛ; next, on the left side, place the seat for Mātaṅgī, known as the Vajradūtī."
"Next, to the south of the western courtyard gate, place the seat of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (10); next, to the north of the courtyard gate, place the seat of Maitreya Bodhisattva (11).

Next, in the northeast corner of the courtyard, place the seat of Aśani (12); next, in the southeast corner, place the seat of Vajrasūksma (13); in the southwest corner, place the seat of Vajrakānta; and in the northwest corner, place the seat of Agni."

"Next, on the northern end of the eastern side of the outer enclosure, first install fourteen seats for Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; next, to the south, install fifteen seats for all the Buddhas of the ten directions; next, install the seat of Candanaprabhāsa Buddha; and next, install the seat of Akṣobhya Buddha."

"Within the courtyard gate, first place the seat of Amitābha Buddha (18); next, place the seat of Lakṣaṇaguṇa Buddha (19); next, place the seat of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva (20); next, place the seat of Uṣṇīṣa (21); and next, place the seats of all the Uṣṇīṣas of the Buddhas of the ten directions (22)."

"On the north side of our temple, proceeding from east to west: first, we install the seat for the Dhāraṇī-piṭaka, number twenty-three; next, the seat for Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, number twenty-four; next, the seat for Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara, number twenty-five; next, the seat for Amoghapāśa, number twenty-six; and next, the seat for Ekajaṭī, number twenty-seven."

"Twenty-eighth, place the seat of the随心 (Sui-xin) Avalokiteśvara at the center of the courtyard gate; twenty-ninth, place the seat of Mahāśrīya; thirtieth, place the seat of the Six-Armed Avalokiteśvara; thirty-first, place the seat of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi (Vikurvaṇa) Avalokiteśvara."

"On the south side of the temple, starting from the east, first place the seat of Aukṣasama (translated into Chinese as *Bùjìng Jīngāng*, Impure Vajra), number thirty-two; next, place the seat of Vajratāḍaka, number thirty-three; next, place the seat of Vajramuṣṭi, named *Jīngāng'ér* (Vajra Son), number thirty-four; and next, place the seat of Vajrāṅkuśī, named *Jīngāng Xiǎonǚ* (Vajra Little Girl), number thirty-five."

"Next, one should place thirty-six *sumahā* seats at the temple gate; next, place thirty-seven *vajraśaṅkarā* seats, known as the Vajra Goddesses; next, place thirty-eight *kaṇikuruta* seats; next, place thirty-nine *yathācitta-vajra* seats; and next, place forty *vajramantramuṇḍarī* seats."

"To the south of the western gate of this temple, first place seat number forty-one for Umādevī; next, place seat number forty-two for Nīlabhadrā; and next, place seat number forty-three for all the devas."
"Next, to the north of that gate, place the seat of Maheśvara (44); next, place the seat of Mūrdhataḥkha; this is the primary position (45); next, place the seat of Vīraṇīrici (46)."

"In the northeast corner of this temple, place forty-seven seats for the *Vajrapāṇi* (Vajrapiṅga); in the southeast corner, place forty-eight seats for the *Mucilinda*; in the southwest corner, place forty-nine seats for the *Kanakakūṭa*; and in the northwest corner, place fifty seats for the *Vajraśrīṇī*."

Proceeding to the northern end of the eastern side of the outer enclosure: first, place the seat of Vināyaka (51); next, place the seat of Vidhyadhara (52); next, place the seat of the Śuddhāvāsa devas (53); next, place the seat of Dhṛtarāṣṭra (54).

"55. To the north of the entrance to the *Cīvara-kṣetra* (Robe Hall), place the seat of Śakra’s disciple. 56. To the south of the entrance to the *Cīvara-kṣetra*, place the seat of the deva Śakra. 57. Next to the south, place the seat of the deva Candra (Moon). 58. Next, place the seat of the deva Varuṇa. 59. Next, place the seat of the deva Nakṣatra (Star). 60. Next, place the seat of the Buddha’s messenger."

"In the first position at the eastern end of the northern side of this temple, place the seat of the King of Ghosts, Īśāna (61); next, place the seat of the ghost Bālāhi (62); next, place the seat of Cāmuṇḍā (63); and next, place the seat of Lambikā (64)."

"Place the seat of Vajrakanda (Vajra-Health) sixty-fifth at the eastern gate of the medicinal hall; place the seat of King Vaiśravaṇa sixty-sixth at the western gate of the medicinal hall; next, place the seat of the yakṣa Kubera sixty-seventh; next, place the seat of the bodhisattva Cāndraprabha sixty-eighth; next, place the seat of Maṇibhadra sixty-ninth; and next, place the seat of Sthavira seventy."

"On the eastern end of the southern side of this temple, first place the seat of Agni (the Fire God), number seventy-one; next, place the seat of Vīrabhadra, number seventy-two; next, place the seat of Nārāyaṇa, number seventy-three; and next, place the seat of Mīḍhuṣīkara, number seventy-four."

"Seventy-fifth: to the east of the gate of the *Cīvara-kāraṇa* (Robe Hall), place the seat of Vairocana. Seventy-sixth: to the west of the gate of the *Cīvara-kāraṇa*, place the seat of the maṇḍala of Yama. Next, to the west, place the seat of Yama’s disciple (seventy-seventh). Next, place the seat of the Kinnara King (seventy-eighth). Next, place the seat of the Piśāca King (seventy-ninth). Next, place the seat of the Rākṣasa King (eightieth)."

"To the south of the western gate of this temple: first, place the seat of the Dragon King Nanda, number eighty-one; next, place the seat of the Sun Deity, number eighty-two; next, place the seat of Mārīcī, number eighty-three; next, place the seat of the Asura King, number eighty-four; and next, place the seat of King Yama, number eighty-five."

"To the north of the gate of the Medicine Hall, place the seat of the Dragon King Anupānananda as number eighty-six; next, place the seat of the Earth Deity as eighty-seven; next, place the seat of Virūpākṣa as eighty-eight; next, place the seat of the Gandharva as eighty-nine; and next, place the seat of the Wind Deity as ninety."

"In the northeast corner of this court, place the seat of Akṣi-akṣi-kuruta (91); in the southeast corner, place the seat of Vajra-sīdana (92); in the southwest corner, place the seat of Bāhubhiga (93); and in the northwest corner, place the seat of Vajra-śikhara (94)."
"As previously described, within each of the three enclosures, excluding the positions occupied by the four corners, construct lotus seats one after another.
This concludes the brief explanation of the ritual for the twelve-cubit mandala."

"The sixteen cubits are as described in the diagram; the number of seats, their quantity, and the width of the intervals between positions should be increased or decreased according to the amount of offerings provided by the patron. This is called the method for adorning the lower section."
"Next, within the fire-hearth, one should decorate a lotus flower using red and white powder.

Then, on a four-foot square area to the northeast of the mandala, one should construct a four-cubit altar; on this altar, one should use exclusively red and white powders to delineate the boundary lines and fashion a lotus seat."

Next, within the central courtyard, upon the consecration altar, one should fashion a lotus seat using only white powder for the boundary lines; having thus completed the arrangement of all the various positions on the ground.
“The Ācārya stands before the western gate and observes the arrangement of the seats within the maṇḍala: which are excellent?
Which are not excellent?
Which are well-proportioned?”
Why is it not complete?
Examine it thoroughly; report any areas that are incomplete so they may be further repaired.
Perform once more the ritual for the Great Boundary-delineation (*mahā-sīmā-bandha*), wielding the *vajra* and establishing various protections.
Having briefly completed the offerings, leave the disciples who have previously entered the mandala to guard it, and do not allow others to enter the ritual arena at will.
This concludes the explanation of the rites for the adornment of the sixth day.

"Next, on the morning of the seventh day, the ācārya shall bathe with fragrant water and don fresh, clean robes. He shall wrap three feet of yellow cloth around his head from the crown, and then bind four feet of vermilion cloth around his forehead; this is called the method for wearing the celestial crown."

Next, having tied the previously consecrated five-colored mantra-cord below the wrist of one’s right arm, one should immediately perform the horse-headed (Hayagrīva) body-protection mudrā, seal one’s own body with it, and enter the maṇḍala.

Next, taking hold of the vajra, one should immediately perform the great-body mudrās and mantras of Vajrasenācārya and others, circling three times to the right, performing various rites on the outer edge of the maṇḍala.
Next, perform the mudrā of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva and recite the Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara mantra to seal the boundaries of the ten directions.

Then, take golden and silver vases for ablution; fill each one with pure water. Into each vase, place a small amount of the five grains, along with *kakkola* (camphor) incense and the seven precious substances wrapped in the aforementioned silk. Immediately, plug the mouths of the various vases with willow branches, bamboo branches, pear branches, and cypress branches, each together with their leaves, while leaving the ends of the threads wrapping the seven precious substances exposed.

"When about to confer the empowerment, each disciple shall hold this jewel; then, having placed a fine pomegranate inside each of the stoppers of the water jars, one should tie three feet of raw silk to the branches and leaves atop each jar-stopper."

Next, take four precious basins: fill two golden basins with scented water and two silver basins with various flowers; then, insert individual jeweled trees bearing flowers and fruits into the pedestals one by one, and set them upright upon the altar.
Next, take ten five-colored precious candles and place them upon bronze candlesticks, arranging them in rows within the corded enclosure at the hall entrance.

Next, prepare food trays upon bronze platters; in each tray, place various kinds of fruits and foods, including exquisite pastries, rock honey, grapes, granulated sugar, ghee and honey, and milk porridge.
Next, prepare oil lamps, placing oil in each one and lighting them all.

Then, prepare vessels made of gold, silver, and *sāla* wood, as well as copper bowls, filled with ghee, honey, fragrant oils, and various flowers; together with the mantra-cord, white mustard seeds, sesame seeds, rice blossoms, and water of eight virtues—all these should be fully and appropriately prepared. Furthermore, provide copper incense burners equipped with precious censers, one for each of the four gates at the center.

Next, prepare six food trays, fully equipped with various types of cakes such as thin pancakes, *ḍālika*, and *pūpa*, twenty pieces of each; mince them all finely and mix them with milk porridge, assorted sweetmeats, and so forth, placing the combined mixture into a single tray in preparation for the burnt offering (*homa*).
Next, place clarified butter, honey, milk-curd, and pure oil, each in its own vessel.
Then, prepare one *śuṅgī* of honey-water in a copper bowl, providing it with a silver ladle.
Next, prepare a full measure of the five grains—small beans, barley, wheat, and large beans—and place them together in a basket along with a single ladle, setting it before the hall.
Next, add two copper water-jars: one intended for pure use and one intended for impure use.
Next, prepare firewood, pine torches, charcoal, and so forth.
All items intended for use within the ritual arena must be thoroughly prepared and arranged in pairs on both sides inside the corded enclosure outside the hall door.

"Next, the Ācārya shall inspect each item one by one to ensure they are complete on all sides; he shall pass his hand through them to verify they are within the cord. Flowers, incense, and water of eight virtues shall be placed outside to the west of the door, while wax candles, food trays, lamps, firewood, and charcoal shall be placed to the east of the door."

Next, the two divisions of *qingle* (pure music), including the long flute, transverse flute, sheng mouth organ, bi-li reed instrument, pipa lute, zhizhu percussion, konghou harp, fangxiang gong, zhenye zither, and copper cymbals—each with two instruments—are arranged in pairs, facing each other on the eastern and western sides of the entrance to the ritual hall.
Furthermore, he dispatched two disciples into the maṇḍala hall to spread felt mats near the base of the western wall;

having thus completed these preparations, the ācārya next performed ritual acts at the eastern and western entrances to maintain the sanctity of the site, ensuring that not a single person should sit in disorder within its precincts.
Next, the ācārya dispatches the assembly of disciples to bathe in scented water; they don fresh, clean robes and each takes their seat in a row within the courtyard of the maṇḍala.
When the sun has set, the ācārya emerges from outside the hall, holding an incense burner in his hand, and enters the maṇḍala, circumambulating it once to the right.

Having completed the circumambulation, perform three prostrations, then set down the incense burner. Stepping forward with your own hands, take a golden water pitcher and, proceeding to the western gate of the altar, kneel in the *hu-gui* posture and recite the mantra of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva one hundred and eight times with a sincere heart. If you have invited various Buddhas to serve as presiding masters, recite their respective root mantras one hundred and eight times according to their particular division.
Having entered the mandala, place them upon the seat of the presiding master. Subsequently, the disciples shall hold up each jar one by one and present them to the ācārya.

Next, place one jar at each of the four corners of the inner court and one jar at its center; furthermore, place one jar at each of the four corners of the outer court; again, place one jar at each of the east, north, and south gates of the outer court; and finally, place one jar on each side—left and right—of the west gate of the mandala.

At the western gate, one winds five-colored threads around the jar upon a bundle of miscellaneous branches; having measured them by circling the maṇḍala once, one then draws those threads to encircle the maṇḍala for one full circuit.
Next, bring the precious trees into the inner courtyard; place one tree at each of the four corners of the seat master’s position, and place one tree in the center of each of the four gates.
Next, place multicolored silks, flowers, fruits, trees, and so forth; let there be a separate tree for each seat.

Next, take five-colored precious candles and place them within the inner courtyard. Place three precious *ratna*-candles before the seat of the presiding master. Directly opposite the seats of the Venerable Ones at the center of each of the four sides of the outer courtyard, place one candle each. Finally, place one candle at each of the four corners of the outer courtyard.

Next, light the lamps: first, place four lamps at the four corners of the inner courtyard, positioned between the seats of the presiding masters; for each of the other seats, separately place four lamps.
Next, arrange various incense burners, flower trays, and the like; next, arrange the food trays.
First, place four plates of food before the seat of the Abbot in the inner courtyard; place one plate before each of the other seats. Next, arrange the offerings:

for the positions of the Buddhas and Prajñāpāramitā, place gold and high-quality silk brocades such as *kīra*; before each of the Bodhisattvas, place silver and various colored silks and fine fabrics; before each of the Vajras, place copper coins and plain or patterned silks; and before each of the Devaputras and others, place coins and items of a single color. As for precious objects and the like, let them be offered according to the donor’s intention and their means.

"On the day of dispersing the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), the items before the Buddha shall be used for the service of the Buddha; the items before the Prajñāpāramitā shall be used for copying the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and other sūtras; the items belonging to the Bodhisattvas shall be used for the service of the Bodhisattvas; the items belonging to Vajrapāṇi and the devas shall be incorporated by the *ācārya*, who shall use them according to the Dharma; and the silk for the crown, the two parasols, and the silk for tying the water jar shall also be incorporated for the use of the *ācārya*."

"Next, prepare the large incense burners: first, place one incense burner before the seat of the presiding master in the inner courtyard; next, place one incense burner at each of the four gates of the outer courtyard; furthermore, place one incense burner at each of the four gates of the outer courtyard; finally, place a large incense burner near the water jar by the western gate, intended for the *ācārya* to carry back and forth while performing ritual acts. In each burner, separately burn various kinds of exquisite incense, ensuring that smoke is produced from all of them."
Next, place one water jar beside the hearth, and likewise set out one food tray and one lamp.
Then the Ācārya stands at each of the four gates in turn, examining them most carefully to ensure that everything is perfectly arranged on all sides.

Having completed the inspection, the ācārya takes the incense burner in his hand, circumambulates the outer edge of the maṇḍala once clockwise; having finished walking the path, he places the incense burner back in its original position.

Next, take one end of the five-colored thread from atop the water jar outside the western gate; having grasped one end, lead it around to the right, circling the outer edge of the altar and the poles of the ritual site, returning to the western gate where you fasten it after completing one circuit.

Next, outside the western gate of the disciple’s altar, a mat and rug shall be spread for the ācārya; the seat shall be about three feet from the gate of the altar, with all ritual implements, incense, flowers, and other offerings arranged in rows before it.

"Next, the Ācārya holds up the incense burner and performs a *brahman* hymn of praise (*vandana*). He goes out to welcome the incense, flowers, and articles of offering. Four disciples follow the Ācārya, carrying the offerings and vessels containing perfumed water."
The ācārya, holding an incense burner in his hand, leads [the practitioner] into the maṇḍala and circumambulates it once to the right.

He places [the practitioner] outside the western gate of the altar before the seat, where they stand in successive rows. One by one, the incense burners, flower trays, ritual implements, ghee and honey, milk and curd, sesame seeds, various other foods, firewood, charcoal, and pine torches—all such items as these—are arranged and set out near the side of the hearth.
Furthermore, two canopies were set up leaning against the side of the *bodhimaṇḍa*: a purple canopy to the north and a vermilion canopy to the south.
Additionally, on a white altar outside the northeastern side of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, five trays of food and five bowls of lamps were placed; having thus completed all these arrangements.
"Next, the ācārya exits the maṇḍala. Before the two śrīdevīs on the left and right of the gate, he places incense burners, lamps, and food trays, assigning one item to each."
Next, descend the hall steps and proceed to the center courtyard upon the white altar, where place four oil lamps and four trays of food and drink.
Then set out one *xuántái* (proclamation platform) and one bed for each; these constitute the positions for the assembly’s consecration (*abhiṣeka*) altar.
Next, the musicians shall form a procession in order and sit in two rows outside the entrance of the maṇḍala.
Then, the ācārya shall once again conduct a thorough inspection of the entire perimeter.

Once the inspection was completed, he immediately entered the *maṇḍala* hall and sat in the *hu-kuei* (half-lotus) posture at the western gate of the altar. Holding an incense burner in his hand, he again made a formal declaration; after offering worship and praise once, the sound ceased. Simultaneously, the various musical instruments outside the gate began to play as flowers were scattered, and they stopped as soon as the Buddha’s song ended.

"Next, the ācārya takes the flowers from within the tray and places them in scented water so that they remain slightly moist; he then places these flowers in his own palms and performs the mudrā for inviting the Buddhas."
First, invite the presiding master of the inner court to recite the mantra seven times; the method for coming and going is as previously described.
Once invited, perform the mudrā of the flower seat and recite the mantra seven times, also as previously described.
Having established the seats, he immediately released the flowers held in his palms.

Next, proceeding eastward within the inner courtyard, he performed the mudrās and made the invocations one by one in sequence, reciting each respective mantra seven times; the methods for the coming, going, and seating are all as described above in the ritual for the flower-seats.
Next, he invited [the deities] to proceed northward, following the same method as above.
Next, request [the deities] to proceed southward, following the same method as above;
next, request them to proceed westward, also following the same method as above.

Next, arriving at the inner and outer courtyards, first proceed from the east, forming each mudrā and reciting its respective root mantra seven times for both the coming and going, exactly as prescribed in the original rite; the formation of the flower-seat mudrā is also according to the method above.
Next, invite [the deities] to proceed north, following the same method as above;
next, invite them to proceed south, following the same method as above;
next, invite them to proceed west, following the same method as above.

"Next, proceed to the outermost enclosure; first walk from the east, performing the mudrās one by one and reciting each respective mantra seven times as you go back and forth, arranging flower seats for all as before;
next, invite [the deities] to walk north, following the same method as above;
next, invite them to walk south, also following the same method as above."
Next, invite [the deities] to proceed to the west, following the same ritual method as above, and arrange flower seats for all of them as previously described.
If there are no specific mudrās or mantras for a particular division, then if inviting the Buddhas, use the mudrā and dharma methods of all Buddhas;
if inviting the Bodhisattvas, use the mudrā and dharma methods common to all Bodhisattvas.
If one invites the Vajras, one likewise employs the ritual methods of all Vajra seals;
if one invites the various devas, one likewise employs the ritual methods of all deva seals;
if one invites all the spirits and ghosts, one likewise employs the ritual methods of all spirits and ghosts, completing the general invitation in this sequential order for each one.
"Next, perform the Great Samaya Boundary-binding Rite. The mudrā method is as follows:

Interlace the left and right ring fingers and little fingers within the palms and hold them upright; extend the two middle fingers obliquely with their tips touching; bend the two index fingers to press against the back of the upper joints of the middle fingers; and place the two thumbs alongside to press against the base of the index fingers."
The mantra is:

“Oṃ vajra-saṃkāli samara samayaṃ bhaṇḍa bhaṇḍa svāhā. Recite this mantra seven times while performing this dharma-mudrā, turning it clockwise three times; this is called the Great Boundary-Seal (Mahā-sīmā-bandha), which provides comfort and stabilizes the seated posture.

Next, take powdered incense and scatter it over the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and others within the altar. Next, perform the ritual of scattering flowers once. Then, prostrate three times and circumambulate the path three times. Thereafter, have the various instruments outside the gate played in succession to perform the *Amitābha Buddha* melody; when the melody ends, they shall cease immediately.

"Next, the Ācārya takes up the incense burner and leads six disciples, each disciple holding a specific item—one holds flower-water, two together carry a vessel of cooked five-grains, one lifts a food tray, one holds a cup of honey-water, and one grasps a torch. They follow behind the Ācārya, universally bestowing [offerings] upon all the accompanying attendants as well as the various protective spirits and deities, extending even to all classes of hungry ghosts (preta), causing them all to be fully satisfied."

"Having completed the general distribution of offerings in the four directions, above, and below, the Ācārya next washes his hands and rinses his mouth. Having entered the maṇḍala and performed three prostrations, he further performs hymns of praise and completes the ritual procedures. Outside the gate, music is played to perform the *Avalokiteśvara* melody; when the melody ends, it stops."
"Next, the ācārya takes up the vajra and calls the ten disciples to stand before the hall.

One person holds a wax candle, one person grasps an incense burner, one person holds a flower tray, one person holds an incense tray, and one person holds a handkerchief; these five persons lead the way with the ācārya walking at the front, while the ācārya follows behind them as they proceed."

Furthermore, he had five men follow behind the Ācārya: one holding a water pitcher, one carrying the three robes, one carrying a tray of white mustard seeds, one carrying a tray of powdered incense, and one carrying a tray of guggulu incense; subsequently, musicians followed in successive order, both before and after them.
"The Ācārya, holding a vajra and repeatedly rotating it, performs a Brahma-hymn chant while proceeding to welcome the assembly of disciples who have come to receive the Dharma."
At that time, when the assembly of disciples saw the ācārya approaching, they rose and formed a procession.

Once the ācārya had arrived, the incense burner was led around him as he stood before it; the candles, incense, flowers, and musical instruments were all positioned on both sides of the gate, standing in rows.

"Next, the Ācārya proceeds to the side of the gate; the person holding the water pitcher, the person with white mustard seeds, and the person carrying the three robes—these three shall follow the Ācārya, ensuring they do not part from him."
Next, the Ācārya orally transmitted the Buddhist teachings, proclaiming them to his disciples and addressing the assembly, saying:
"Do you all wish to study such secret dharmas as these?"
The assembly replied,
"We wish to joyfully see and study it.
Next, the ācārya takes water from the ritual pitcher, places it in his right hand, and recites the heart-mantra of Kuṇḍalī.
Having consecrated the water with mantras, he struck each member of the assembly on the crown of their heads.
Next, he used white mustard seeds, consecrated with mantras, to strike the assembly in the same manner as described above.

When he had thus struck them one by one in succession, the Ācārya then performed a Brahma-praise and led the assembly forward, having the musicians follow behind so that the sound of their instruments did not cease.

The members of the assembly each contemplated virtuous matters with their minds and mouths; they proceeded toward the site of the *bodhimaṇḍa* and stood near the southwest corner of the hall’s steps. With focused minds, they knelt and sat, causing the moving music to cease as soon as the final note was struck.
Next, the ācārya takes white mustard seeds and recites the mantra of Hayagrīva Bodhisattva seven times; having done so, he strikes each head three times.

Next, perform the protection-seal (rakṣā-mudrā) and place it upon the body of each disciple one by one to provide protection for their bodies; the method for sealing the body is as described in the Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta ritual.

Next, he provided each of his disciples with water from the ritual pitcher; once they had washed their hands and rinsed their mouths, he spread out mats upon the steps of the maṇḍala directly in front of the entrance, intending for the musicians to sit there.

"Next, the Acharya leads the assembly of disciples up the western stairs and stands upon the seats; they immediately perform three prostrations, confessing all transgressions of the three karmas of the past, present, and future, without concealing even the slightest bit, but rather fully revealing them all. Then, the musicians below the stairs perform their music, which ceases as soon as the final note is struck."

"Next, the Ācārya enters the maṇḍala hall and instructs his disciple to take a clean woolen mat and spread it within the hall. He should place there vessels for incense, flowers, and wax candles; however, the water-pitchers and such items need not yet be placed there. Subsequently, carrying them forward as offerings and performing prostrations, he shall reverently address and praise the Dharma-activities of the myriad practices and meritorious virtues of the Buddhas."
And he praised him, saying:
"Homage to the Buddha’s wisdom and diligence, whose body is a lattice of bones with the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
This Prajñāpāramitā is the treasury of eighty-four thousand Dharma gates."
"The root of the merit of the myriad practices, the Great Compassionate Father constantly and universally acts for the sake of all classes of sentient beings within the six realms.

Having performed this praise and circumambulated the path once, he prostrated three times, withdrew, and exited the door of the *cāitya* hall; outside the door, the music all began simultaneously and ceased as soon as the melody ended.
"Next, the Ācārya further bestows upon the assembly the Great Method for Protecting the Body; he strikes each person once with white mustard seeds.
Furthermore, they form the body-mudrā to subdue the demons of the mind."
Next, using water from a ritual vessel, chant the mantra over each disciple’s heart one by one, once for each person.
Next, perform hand gestures (*mudrā*) and seal each of them individually.

Next, sprinkle scented water over their bodies one by one. Next, fumigate them with incense from an incense burner to ensure their protection and purity. Next, apply the *vajra* seal to the crown of each disciple’s head one by one. Finally, provide scented water for them to wash their hands and rinse their mouths; having finished these rites, cease the music.
"Next, the ācārya calls his assembly of disciples and instructs each one, beginning with the eldest, to proceed to their mats by the door, prostrate, and sit in a kneeling posture.

Then, the ācārya takes yellow silk and, in order, places it over the eyes of the senior disciples; he takes the hands of the disciples and teaches them the *samādhi-mudrā* of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva."

Once the seal has been impressed with flowers, the ācārya leads the disciple by the head into the maṇḍala. Standing before the western gate of the altar, the disciple faces the altar; the ācārya stands to the north of the gate, and the disciple stands to the south of the gate.
Next, the ācārya recites the Avalokiteśvara-samādhi-mantra.
The mantra says:
“Oṃ bhamu bhavaye svāhā. Reciting it seven times, he instructs the disciple to scatter the flowers from his hands, allowing them to fall freely onto the maṇḍala.
Once the flowers have been placed upon the lotus seats of the Buddha and the others, the preceptor removes the silk veil to reveal the positions on the ground.
After the disciple has performed three prostrations, the ācārya says:

"You have scattered flowers upon the positions of such-and-such a Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā, such-and-such a Bodhisattva, such-and-such a Vajra-being, and such-and-such a Deva; you must remember well each of these according to where they fell and not forget them."

When those who have finished scattering flowers have completed their task, they kneel and sit to the south of the gate within the *maṇḍala* hall. They wait for the subsequent disciples to arrive, at which point they are instructed to withdraw and exit, taking their seats on the western side.
All other disciples shall follow this procedure one by one until the entire assembly has completed the rite.

Next, the Ācārya also follows this same method to scatter flowers himself; he then calls the musicians to ascend the steps toward the altar, where they sit in a horizontal row and perform several pieces of music.

Next, the Ācārya, assuming a solemn and majestic demeanor, leads the disciples to perform prostrations and offer their greetings; they then proceed together in meditation, circumambulate the altar three times, and take their seats according to their assigned positions.

Next, the ācārya himself takes the water jar from the position of the presiding master within the maṇḍala and steps out through the western gate. He dispatches a disciple to hold a vermilion canopy behind him as they circumambulate the site of practice (maṇḍalagṛha) to the right. They proceed to the consecration altar in the central courtyard, enter through the western gate, and stand upright beside the platform.
The Ācārya performs the mudrā for the empowerment rite: standing on his left foot with the heel firmly planted, he places the right foot about three inches away; the left knee remains straight.

His right hand hangs down, extending the little finger, slightly bending the tip of the index finger, and folding the middle and ring fingers so that they form a hook-like shape; the thumb is also slightly bent, positioned about two *fen* from the middle and index fingers.
The left hand is likewise positioned.
Next, take the water jar and hold it aloft with both hands; from above the crown of the head, recite the heart-mantra seven times while pouring the water, letting it flow directly downward.
While performing the consecration, make vows with both mind and speech as follows. Having finished, put on clean robes and enter the maṇḍala.

Beside the entrance to the *maṇḍala* was a disciple who held a purple canopy over the head of the *ācārya*; they proceeded to the western gate of the altar and circumambulated the *maṇḍala* once, walking clockwise.
"Next, the Ācārya shall again call each disciple into the maṇḍala in turn; having fetched a water jar as before, he shall exit and enter the Abhiṣeka-maṇḍala through the western gate."
The one holding the crimson parasol follows behind the Ācārya according to the ritual procedure, covering the disciple as they proceed to the outer mandala.
Next, the Ācārya bestows the *dharmamudrā* and holds up a water jar; the Ācārya then asks:
"To which Buddha’s position did you previously cast your flowers—among the Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattvas, the Vajras, the various devas, or the spirits and ghosts?"
"According to his response, bestow upon him the primary mudrā.

Having placed the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown) mudrā, with the seal facing upward and a flower held in the palms, receive the water with the seal and pour it over his head while reciting the primary mantra. The disciple shall then make vows with mind and mouth as previously described, and so forth."
Then, take the wrapping containing the treasures from within the jar and fasten these treasures to the aforementioned mantra-cord, never to be separated from the body.
When the time of death approaches, one must use these treasures as a token of verification.

"Once the consecration is completed, he shall immediately don pure garments and enter the maṇḍala. Adorned with a purple canopy, he shall perform the rites of welcoming and prostration, following the master’s (ācārya) deportment and movements exactly. Upon reaching the western gate of the altar, he shall be instructed to perform three prostrations and take his seat according to his assigned position."

"Next, the Ācārya enters the maṇḍala once more to fetch the water jar; each step follows the sequence of the previous procedure for the rites of welcoming, escorting, and conferring empowerment, without the slightest variation."

Having completed the general circumambulation, the *ācārya* next performs prostrations and offerings, leads the assembly of disciples in performing three circumambulations of the path, and returns to sit in his original place.

Next, the *ācārya* sits at the western gate of the maṇḍala, near the western end of the fire-pit, with his body upright. Once firewood made of grain has been ignited within the fire-pit, he should first form the mudrā of the Fire God (*Agnideva*), recite the root mantra to summon him to sit within the fire-pit, and offer him incense, flowers, ghee and honey, food and drink, sesame seeds, and other such items.
Having recited the root mantra seven times for each and performed the fire offering, the Ācārya records in his mind:
"The Fire Deity, please emerge and sit outside the hearth; now I wish to make offerings to the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā, and all the Bodhisattvas."
Next, perform the seal of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva and recite the root mantra, requesting him to form the lotus seal and sit within the fire pit.

Next, the ācārya takes hold of the *vajra* and successively calls the disciples who have entered the maṇḍala; one by one, they come to the right side of the ācārya, prostrate, kneel with palms joined, and are instructed to hold the head of the *vajra* in their hands.

The ācārya shall hold a *vajra* in his right hand upon the disciple’s hand; with his left hand, he shall grasp sesame seeds and recite the fundamental heart-mantra seven times while burning them, followed by taking ghee and reciting the mantra twenty-one times while burning it.

When the cremation was thus completed, he had his disciples prostrate and withdraw to sit in their original positions; as for the remaining disciples, each performed the ritual duties exactly as before, without any difference.
Having completed the general circumambulation, one returns to form the primary mudrā and recites the heart mantra, escorting the Bodhisattva Hayagrīva back to his original seat.

Next, one requests the presiding master to form his primary mudrā and, while reciting the primary heart mantra, to form the lotus mudrā and sit within the fire pit. There, he recites his own root mantra and burns various incense, flowers, sesame seeds, human figures, ghee, honey, milk, curd, food and drink, assorted fruits, oil, and other such substances.
When the offerings have been completed, revert to the original mudrā and recite its root mantra to escort [the deities] back to their respective positions.

Next, one by one in sequence from the inner court, invite each of the Buddhas, Prajñā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and Devas; for each, perform their respective original mudrā and recite their respective root mantras. Form the lotus mudrā and sit within the fire altar, reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times, or seven times seven; either method may be employed.

Having finished making offerings by burning various incenses and flowers, along with sesame seeds, ghee, honey, milk, curd, food and drink, assorted fruits, oil, and other such items, one should again perform the primary mudrā and send [the deity] back to its original position.
In this manner, each of these positions shall be invited in turn; the offerings and the ritual of sending forth the Dharma are no different from those described previously.
"In all instances of inviting and sending, one must first proceed from the northern end of the eastern side to the first seat at the southern end, completing the sequence for the eastern side;
next, proceed from the eastern end of the northern side to the first seat at the western end, completing the sequence for the northern side."
Next, starting from the first seat at the eastern end of the southern side, proceed until the first seat at the western end; thus the southern side is completed.
Next, starting from the first seat at the southern end of the western side, proceed until the first seat at the northern end.
As it was in one courtyard, so it was in all the others; in this manner, they proceeded sequentially until every place had been completely circumambulated.
Next, for the sake of the sovereign, the Emperor, and the Empress, they burned incense, offered flowers and other articles, and recited the mantra forty-nine times.
Following that, for the sake of the Crown Prince, the various princesses, and the royal consorts, they likewise made offerings and recited the mantra forty-nine times.
Next, perform such offerings for the great ministers and the civil and military officials, reciting the mantra forty-nine times;
next, perform offerings for all teachers of the past, present, and future kalpas, as well as for all parents, reciting the mantra forty-nine times;
next, perform offerings for all the officials of the paths of karma, reciting the mantra forty-nine times.
Next, for the sake of making offerings to all donors throughout the ten directions, recite the mantra forty-nine times;

next, for the sake of making offerings to all sentient beings throughout the entire void of the Dharma-realm across the six paths and four modes of birth, including those in the eight difficulties and suffering from the eight miseries, recite the mantra forty-nine times;
next, for the sake of making offerings to oneself as the ācārya, recite the mantra twenty-one times to completion.
Next, for the sake of the host of the site of the *maṇḍala* and their entire household, one should perform offerings while reciting the mantra the same number of times as before.
