From the sovereign of the state down to the host, all together shall recite the Great Heart Mantra of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; this applies universally to all ritual applications of offering.

"Next, the ācārya shall perform the mudrās of the respective classes for all Buddhas, Prajñā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, Devas, and so forth; it is not necessary to recite mantras, but he should display them one by one in sequence to the assembly as an offering."

When all various ritual matters have been completed in their entirety, next perform the Prajñā Sin-Eradication Seal, placing it upon the heart. Verbally recite the transgressions of the three karmas of the past and present, detailing each one in full, and repent with a sincere mind, forever severing their continuity. Sit without wavering while the disciples repeatedly prostrate to the Buddha.
"Next, the Ācārya performs the Vajragarbha-Kuṇḍalī Praise and the Seal for Accomplishing the Fulfillment of Wishes within the Maṇḍala, reciting its divine mantra.
The mantra is as follows:
‘Oṃ sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite prahemini gagana-kānta samanta svāhā. Having thus recited it seven times sevenfold, he utters words of praise from his mouth and speaks this verse:"
"Homage to the Buddha’s wisdom and diligence, To the body of bone-joints with the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
This is the Prajñāpāramitā, The treasury of eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates,
The root of the merit of the myriad practices, And the universal gateway treasury of dhāraṇīs."
Having spoken these verses, they each made this vow:

"May our disciples and followers in this single assembly, all classes of sentient beings who move, and those on various paths of karma—from this day forward, whether dwelling among humans—constantly hear the Mahāyāna sūtras of profound dharma, the treasury of dhāraṇīs, and the names of the Great Compassionate Ones, the Buddhas of the ten directions; may they not see evil things, not hear evil teachings, not encounter non-Buddhists, and not suffer the nine untimely deaths, the eight difficulties, or the eight sufferings."
At the time of death, one will be reborn at will in the pure lands of the ten directions and constantly behold all Buddhas.
All sentient beings shall likewise be so.
At that time, the assembly of disciples all exclaimed, "Excellent!
Next, the ācārya called the disciples one by one in order and performed the protection of their bodies (*kāyarakṣā*) for each.

When the protection was completed and it was about to become dawn, the ācārya took a censer in hand, led the assembly of disciples to circumambulate the path three times, and withdrew after performing prostrations.
Next, the Ācārya looks upward and offers this expression of thanks:

"The various incenses, flowers, food, and drink offered as sustenance have been largely improper; I feel profound shame and remorse. I pray that the assembly of noble ones will bestow their great compassion and grant me joy."

Thereafter, perform the mudrā of dismissal with the hands; rotate the mudrā to the left and recite the mantra seven times. Then, from the presiding master downward, each person individually performs the mudrā of dispatching and recites their respective root mantra to dismiss them, no differently than when they were invited.
Rotate the mudrā to the left to disperse it; this is called the rite of dismissal.
Once the dismissal is complete, next dispatch a disciple to collect the offerings, money, silk, and other items, to be used according to the previously established rules for distribution.

He sent a disciple to collect the food within the altar area; subsequently, the ācārya divided it into three portions: one portion was sent to the monastery to be offered to the assembly, one portion was bestowed upon the poor and beggars, and one portion was distributed as alms to all sentient beings of the water, land, and space.
None of the disciples who have entered the maṇḍala, nor the ācārya, nor the host, etc., should eat; if they do so, the ritual will have no efficacy.
Once the arrangements are complete, the ācārya next takes a torch and leads the disciples one by one in sequence to circumambulate and enter the maṇḍala, pointing out to the assembly:

"This is the place where such-and-such Buddha sits; this is such-and-such Prajñā; this is such-and-such Bodhisattva; this is such-and-such Vajra; this is such-and-such Holy Saṃgha; this is such-and-such Deva; this is such-and-such Spirit; this is such-and-such Ghost; this is such-and-such Nāga."

"In this manner, each item shall be presented in successive order, fully displayed so that they may be memorized. Afterwards, using pure clay, one must completely sweep away all the colored seats upon the altar before sunrise. All remaining ritual implements shall likewise be treated in this way; everything else shall be cleared away and discarded thereafter."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the vajradharas, arhats, and the rest of the great multitude, saying:

"Now, at this gathering, while I am expounding the treasury of the subtle, profound, and secret dhāraṇī-seal methods, there are present immeasurable devas and humans, along with the eight classes of beings, great spirits and ghosts, and the retinues of various non-Buddhist paths. Whether they be bhikṣus, brahmins, upāsakas, virtuous sons, humans, or non-humans—all who hear me speak of these rare matters concerning the divine mantras and dharma-seals—will not fail to rejoice."

At that time, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas of the ten directions—immeasurable, innumerable, and as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—together with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, Vajrapāṇis, great arhats, assemblies of śrāvakas, and the eight classes of beings including devas, nāgas, and spirits, each brought incense, flowers, food and drink, clothing, and various kinds of music to scatter as offerings. Simultaneously, they offered praise, filling the entirety of space.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all greatly rejoiced; each expressed their own intention and proclaimed dhāraṇī methods for the common benefit [of all].

At that time, there were also immeasurable devas in the assembly who offered various dhāraṇī methods, declaring that they possessed divine power to protect the treasury of the Buddha-dharma and to awe all beings, saying, "We also approve of this."

Therefore, they shall all enter my secret treasury, extensively establish the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), complete the rites of the universal altar, and be arrayed by name within their positions of dharma-sovereignty.

If there are those who encounter or hear this Dharma, they will immediately be able to extinguish and eliminate all their various transgressions; how much more so for those who further behold the extensive opening of the gateways of the *dhāraṇī* treasury?
This is called the first rare attainment.

This secret Dharma-treasury of the dhāraṇī is truly sincere and subtle; it is difficult to see, difficult to hear, difficult to transcribe, difficult to read, difficult to receive and uphold, and difficult to understand the principles of its meaning and skillful means.

If there are bhikṣus, brahmins, upāsakas, sons of good family, or others who love and delight in this sutra, constantly practicing and reciting it, forming the seals of all dharmas, and extensively establishing places of practice; if they offer incense, flowers, and ghee lamps daily without ceasing as an offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions; if their deportment is flawless and they constantly perform ascetic practices, reciting the sutra and mindfulness of the Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm; if they repent of the offenses of the three karmas of the past and present, diligently cultivating such gates of merit and dharma without weariness of body or mind, persevering with diligence day and night, always practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and protecting and cherishing all sentient beings with compassion—then they will be able to eliminate the obstacles and difficulties of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; within a single thought-moment, all shall be utterly extinguished.

"Furthermore, if there are those who resolve their minds on Bodhi and rescue all from illness, I deeply exhort you all that you too must employ skillful means to show loving-kindness to all suffering beings. You should know that such persons who resolve their minds in this way will constantly obtain various rewards in their present lives; I and all the Bodhisattvas shall protect these practitioners, remembering them day and night without ever abandoning them, so that no sudden evils may afflict their bodies."
After the end of their lives, they will be reborn at will in the pure lands of the ten directions and constantly behold all Buddhas.

"If one practices this Dharma yet gives rise to unwholesome thoughts, habitually deceives and oppresses sentient beings, speaks with falsehood and flattery, greedily seeks fame and profit, or recklessly scolds and reviles gods and ghosts while assuming an air of great authority to constantly perform evil deeds—such persons as these will be constantly watched for by gods and ghosts seeking an opportunity to harm them; they will frequently encounter untimely calamities, and various forms of suffering and affliction will press upon their bodies."
If, at the time of death, you further inflict harm upon one another, you shall fall into hell with no prospect of escape.
"All of you sentient beings must listen attentively and receive my words with faith, free from any doubt."

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking these words, the entire assembly gathered there heard the Buddha’s instruction; they all simultaneously exclaimed, "Excellent! and, having paid their respects, withdrew.
The Buddha’s Teaching on the Methods for Adorning the Site of Enlightenment and Preparing the Materials for Offerings.
The following text in bold characters is the original scripture; the fine characters represent the interpretations of later scholars.
"Golden and copper bell-bands, forty-eight in number, each seven feet long; large pendants, twenty-eight..."
There are twenty-eight cords for the paths, each six feet long; twenty-eight small pendants, each four feet long;
twenty-eight large mirrors, each one foot wide; forty small mirrors; four hundred glass bubble-flowers, each one foot in diameter;
and twenty-four large multicolored banners, each one hundred feet long.
A length of forty-nine chi is also acceptable; there shall be two hundred and twenty new and fine multi-colored banners, each one zhang long;
two hundred strands of new and fine pearls, each five chi long;
a vermilion net four chi wide and eighteen sections long, each section one zhang; and forty-six gold and silver jars, each with a capacity of one sheng.
Four hundred large bronze bowls, each one chi and five cun in diameter; two hundred small bronze bowls, each seven cun in diameter;
four silver trays, each two chi and five cun in diameter; eighty miscellaneous gold and silver vessels;
four gold trays, each two chi and five cun in width; and forty gold and silver *sarā* (strainers).
Eight pieces each one foot or more in width; one golden ladle, one silver ladle;
six sets of copper incense burners and censers; one set of gold incense burners and censers;
two golden and silver *sāra* vessels with a capacity of one *sheng*, one of gold and one of silver; and five trees of seven-jeweled gold and silver lotuses.
Each was four feet high, newly made and magnificently adorned; there were one hundred artificial flowering trees of various colors, each newly made and fine;
twelve copper candle stands; forty-eight gold and silver cups and goblets;
ten five-colored wax candles; and twenty-six copper wash-basins, each with a capacity of more than five sheng.
Three clean cotton towels, one *sheng* of cleansing powder (*kaṣāya*), forty pieces of soapberry (*karañja*),
one *sheng* of charcoal ash, and a bundle of *śīrīṣa* twigs— if one adorns the *maṇḍala* with such various precious implements as these,
it will cause the donor to obtain various kinds of immeasurable merit.

"Take sixteen long rafters, each with a diameter of three inches at the head and a length of twenty-five feet; plane, pare, and bore holes so that they may be strung together according to the prescribed method. Take sixty small bamboo poles, each twenty feet long and about three finger-widths in thickness. Prepare eighteen banners painted with Vajrapāṇi, twenty-four banners painted with *rājapuruṣa* (kings/spiritual guardians), and four banners painted with the Four Heavenly Kings (*caturmahārāja*). Prepare one hundred miscellaneous banners of various colors, each ten feet long, using fresh and fine pigments. Take twelve cords of eighty feet each, as thick as a writing brush handle. Use twenty *liang* of five-colored thread—purple, blue, crimson, white, and yellow—ensuring the quantities are equal for each color, and wind them separately by color."
Wind them onto a single reel, ensuring that each color and type is distinct and not intermingled.
Take four hundred feet of thread as one section, and the remaining fifty feet as another section; furthermore, approximately four such sections are required for use.
There must also be five-colored small banners, including the body and the feet, with a total length of three feet.
Five inches wide, there are two pieces each of the following colors: two deep blue, two light blue, two crimson, two white, and four yellow.
There are eight figures of the Armor-Vajra, each five feet high, magnificently adorned with new and fine colors;
and there are eight figures of the Armor-Devaputra, each five feet high, likewise magnificently adorned.
For those who prefer new items: sixty segments of five chi each of raw silk; two *zhang* of pure white cloth;
one *zhang* of white gauze; one *zhang* of crimson brocade; one *zhang* of purple brocade; three chi of yellow brocade; four chi of crimson brocade;
and two pairs of clean thread shoes—one pair intended for pure use and one pair for impure use.
Regarding the socks, two sets are prepared: one set for pure use and one set for impure use; the same applies to the sock-strings.
From the laces of the shoes up to the sock-strings, each person must possess their own.
With various such colorful articles, the ritual site (maṇḍala) is adorned; when the patron sees this, they shall obtain immeasurable and boundless varieties of merit.
The passage beginning with "Satisfying the first [requirement]" and above is from the Sūtra.
It states: "Take five *liǎng* of pure cow dung—[dung] from a calf that has not eaten dregs or beans—and receive it in a clean basket or vessel;
this is called 'pure. Also take fifteen *liǎng* of *kunkuma* (dragon-brain incense) and fifteen *liǎng* of *suheta* (suhe incense)."
Fifteen *liang* of saffron, one *jin* of high-quality blended incense, two *jin* of aloeswood (*agaru*), two *jin* of frankincense (*guggulu*),
two *jin* of benzoin (*gandha-māṃsī*), one *jin* of resinous incense (*śrīparṇī*),
two *jin* of powdered sandalwood, two *jin* of sandalwood chips, five *jin* of miscellaneous herb-incense, and five *jin* of miscellaneous herb-flowers.
...various tree blossoms, five *sheng* in measure; if no cut silks are available, let silk cloth suffice, all of which must be fresh and fine.
There are three *sheng* of rice-grain blossoms and three *sheng* of buckwheat blossoms. By making offerings of such various flowers and incenses, the patron shall attain purity of the three karmas;
their body will be perpetually fragrant and clean, and all who see them will give rise to [faith].
Rejoicing, in every birth and in every place, their bodies shall always be upright and handsome, and they shall attain great renown.
As for the musicians of the two divisions of pure music, have them bathe in fragrant water, dress in new and clean garments, and do not let them consume pungent or mixed foods.
[Give] two *liang* of gold, two *liang* of silver, and two *liang* of coral. Water...
Two *liang* of camphor, two *liang* of amber, two *liang* of pearl, and two *liang* of Persian glass;
these should be purchased in sufficient quantity according to the number of persons entering the Dharma.
As for the five grains—rice, small beans, wheat, barley, and millet—one may beg for one *sheng* of each at the market, but this is not permitted [if obtained by improper means].
It was purchased with the intention of wrapping it together with the seven treasures in a piece of silk; then, by offering various garments,
the seven treasures, the five grains, and musical instruments as gifts, all the karmic calamities of the donor's three actions from past lives were entirely eliminated,
and they constantly attained peace and happiness— this is the aforementioned sutra.
One *shi* of finely ground red earth, one *shi* of finely ground yellow earth, one *shi* of finely ground dried indigo dye,
one *shi* of finely ground charcoal, two *shi* of fine-sieved rice flour, one *sheng* of sesame seeds,
one *sheng* of high-quality honey with impurities filtered out, and seven *jin* of high-quality cow’s ghee with impurities filtered out.
One *dō* and five *shō* of pure sesame oil for burning as an offering;
one *dō* and five *shō* of white mustard seeds, sufficient for seven days of use; twenty *kin* of pine torches;
five bundles of wood from grain trees—drying those that are wet; one hundred and fifty *kin* of charcoal; five hundred lamps; and five [measures] of oil.
For the location where the lamps are lit, one must prepare five hundred plates of fruit offerings, complete with various colors and varieties:
three hundred high-quality pomegranates, five hundred large chestnuts, five hundred large dried jujubes,
five hundred dried persimmons, five hundred pears, and five hundred walnuts.
Twenty-five *liang* of granulated sugar, one and a half *jin* of dried grapes, and other such fruits—all must be of superior quality, free from insects, defects, or damage.
There shall be five hundred thin flatcakes, five hundred *mò* (stuffed cakes), and five hundred *dòutóu* (sweet dumplings).
As for other types of cakes, they shall be provided according to the local customs of the country.
"Whatever is esteemed by people may be used, with the exception of impure food; seasonal fruits must all be provided in full.

Three *śoṇa* (three *liǎng*) of dried non-glutinous rice, two *shēng* (two *liǎng*) of non-glutinous rice milk porridge, and five kinds of colored powders such as red earth, in quantities calculated according to the standard of one hundred and twenty *zhǔ*."
If the altar is sixteen cubits or less, the various ritual platforms should be prepared accordingly.
Have those who prepare the food wash with fragrant water and observe the fast with purity; do not allow them to taste the offerings prematurely or to discard any portion.

"Two *śu* each of these five grains—barley, mung beans, millet, wheat, and soybeans—are cooked together and placed in a clean basket; a small ladle is also set therein. Two *śu* of honey-water are poured into a silver bowl, which is also provided with a silver ladle; this is placed near the basket of cooked grain. This is intended for distribution as an offering to the various benevolent deities who protect the boundary. This is the ritual manual."

"When such ritual implements are prepared with purity and on a vast scale to establish the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and further adorned and provided as offerings with various garments, they can eliminate all evil offenses—the four grave pārājika transgressions, the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), and those of an icchantika—accumulated over ten billion Ganges-sands of kalpas. Within a single thought-moment, these are entirely extinguished, so that the karmic retribution of evil deeds can no longer be realized."

"As for that donor, in this present life they shall fully attain the six pāramitās, and their three karmas shall be purified. In every place of rebirth, they shall be endowed with supernatural powers, their physical form shall be upright and majestic, and they shall possess mastery according to their will. All their aspirations shall bear fruit, and they shall always receive the protective mindfulness of the Triple Gem as donors. At all times and in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—their body and mind shall be peaceful and secure; by the power of such merit, they obtain this great retribution."

The Diagram of the Sixteen-Cubit Adornment Beneath the Universal Assembly Mandala In the center, there is one courtyard measuring two cubits in length and breadth. In the very center of this courtyard, construct a lotus seat; upon the seat, fashion a wheel complete with all its parts—the hub, spokes, and rim. This is the position for the presiding master of the *maṇḍala*. According to the preferences of the patron, deities such as the Buddhas may serve as the presiding masters of the *maṇḍala*, and even Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattvas may be installed therein as desired.
"Next, the outer enclosure is four cubits in length and breadth, containing twelve positions.

At each of its four corners, one should fashion an earth-seal *vajra* in the shape of a *vajrapāṇi* holding a mace; the two maces are crossed like a cross, with their heads resting against the four corners, all being dark blue-black in color."

"The seal at the northeast corner is named Sumahā; the seal at the southeast corner is named Svaḥsiddhikara; the seal at the southwest corner is named Vajrakānta; and the seal at the northwest corner is named Agni. These are called the Vajra-Earth Seals."

"Facing east, at the northern end, the first flower seat is named the station of the Mother of the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā. Upon the lotus seat, one forms a square seal (*mudrā*) with two pairs of intersecting lines reaching to the corners of the seal; one places this seal upon each corner pillar of the flower seat, surrounded by blazing light."
"The second flower seat is the position of the Buddha’s heart; upon the lotus seat, one forms the head and face of the Buddha, surrounded by flames of light.
On the eastern side of the southern face, the first flower seat is the position of Vajramātā Māmaki; upon the lotus seat, one places a *vajra*, surrounded by flames of light."
"The second is the position of the Vajra King; upon a lotus seat, one forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light.
At the southern end of the western row, the first presiding master is named Śuddhāvāsakāyika Deva; upon a lotus seat, he forms the light of flaming fire."
"The second presiding master is named Varāma; upon his lotus seat he manifests flames of light.
At the western end of the northern side, the first presiding master is named Avalokiteśvararāja; upon his lotus seat he manifests a lotus bud, surrounded by a halo of radiant flames."
"The second presiding seat is named Avalokiteśvarī; she holds a lotus bud upon a lotus pedestal, surrounded by a halo of light-flames.

All her *vajras* are golden in color, and all the forms of the light-flames are yellowish-red; the same applies to what follows. This concludes the first enclosure. Generally, the seals at the four corners are called 'Seizing the Positions' (*saṃgraha-sthāna*), while those on the flower pedestals are called 'Principal Positions' (*mukhya-sthāna*); the subsequent cases follow this pattern."
"Next, the second courtyard is eight cubits in length and breadth, containing twenty-six positions; the ground seals, shapes, and arrangements of its four corners are as previously described."

"The seal at the northeast corner is named Vāyavyaka; the seal at the southeast corner is named Agnikūṭa; the seal at the southwest corner is named Khargalāśira; and the seal at the northwest corner is named Pātālacayeṣa."
"On the first seat at the northern end facing east is the presiding master named Subhāṣitaruta-uṣṇīṣa; an alms-bowl shaped object is placed upon a lotus throne, surrounded by radiant flames."
"The second presiding seat is named Amitābha-uṣṇīṣa; upon a lotus throne, it takes the form of the Buddha’s crown, surrounded by blazing light.
The third presiding seat is named Sarvabuddha-uṣṇīṣa; upon a lotus throne, it takes the form of a Buddha’s uṣṇīṣa, surrounded by blazing light."
"The fourth presiding seat is named Śākyamuni Buddha; upon a lotus throne he takes the form of a Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, surrounded by blazing light.
The fifth presiding seat is named Akṣobhya-uṣṇīṣa; upon a lotus throne he takes the form of a Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, surrounded by blazing light."

"The sixth seat-lord is named Southern Jewel-Phase Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa; his lotus seat is shaped as a long rectangle of jewels, with the jewel being narrow from east to west and long from south to north, surrounded by encircling flames of light."
"The first seat master on the eastern side facing south is named Ucchuṣma; he forms a vajra upon a lotus throne.
That vajra has a slender waist and three prongs, with upper and lower triple-forked tips that are sharp and keen; its color is as previously described, and it is surrounded by blazing flames."
"The second presiding master is named Vajraśikhara; upon a lotus seat he forms the vajra, surrounded by blazing light.
The third presiding master is named Amṛtakuṇḍalī; upon a lotus seat he forms the vajra, surrounded by blazing light."
"The fourth presiding master is named Kaniṅkula; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light.
The fifth presiding master is named Pratālavajra; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light."
"The sixth presiding master is named Vajrayakṣi; he forms the *vajra* upon his lotus seat, surrounded by blazing light-flames.
At the southern end of the western side, the first presiding master is named Śaṅkhala; he forms the *vajra* upon his lotus seat, surrounded by blazing light-flames."
"The second seat-holder is named Umādevī; upon a lotus throne he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light.
Next, two cubits of ground constitute the entrance to the maṇḍala."
"Next, the first presiding master at the northern gate is named Maheśvara; he sits upon a lotus throne forming a *vajra*, surrounded by blazing flames."
"The second presiding master is named Pārvatī; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light.
On the western end of the northern side, the first presiding master is named Six-Armed Avalokiteśvara; upon a lotus seat he holds a lotus bud, surrounded by blazing light."
"The second presiding seat-holder was named Bandhulāmā; upon the lotus throne, he fashioned a *kundikā* vessel with a side-opening, which is called a *kundikā*, surrounded by a halo of light."

"The third presiding seat-holder is named Nine-Armed Avalokiteśvara. Upon a lotus throne, he forms a precious flower-stalk with five nodes; each node has a bud shaped like a lotus rhizome, which lies upon the seat with its head resting toward the west, surrounded by a halo of light and flames."
“The fourth presiding deity is named Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara; upon a lotus seat he holds a lotus bud, surrounded by a halo of light and flames.
“The fifth presiding deity is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta Avalokiteśvara (translated into Chinese as Dàbái Guānshìyīn); upon a lotus seat he holds a lotus bud, surrounded by a halo of light and flames.”
"The sixth presiding seat is named Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara; upon a lotus pedestal he assumes the form of a precious vase, surrounded by radiant flames.
The second enclosure is completed."
"Next, the third courtyard is exactly twelve cubits in length and breadth, with forty-two positions; the ground seals, shapes, and arrangements of its four corners are also as described above."

"The seal at the northeast corner is named Vajrasvāhā; the seal at the southeast corner is named Mudrāṭaka, which constitutes the stationing of the positions. The seal at the southwest corner is named Kani-kuruta; the seal at the northwest corner is named Vajraśrī, which also constitutes the stationing of the positions."

"On the eastern side, at the head of the north, the first seat-holder is named Saṃkusumitarājendra Buddha; he appears in the form of a Buddha upon a lotus throne, surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
The second seat-holder is named Amitābha Buddha; he appears in the form of a Buddha upon a lotus throne, surrounded by a halo of blazing light."
“The third presiding master is named Śākyakāñcanacakravarti-uṣṇīṣa.
The fourth presiding master is named Śākyadharmacakrapravartana.
The fifth presiding master is named Candanaguṇa.”
"The sixth presiding master is named Śvetābhā-buddhoṣṇīṣa.
The seventh presiding master is named Aśokaśrī-buddha.
The eighth presiding master is named Sarvabuddha-daśadig."
“The ninth presiding seat is named Vipaśyin Buddha.
The tenth presiding seat is named Emitting Light Buddha-Crown.
All such seats are fashioned as lotus flowers; upon these lotus seats are fashioned images of Buddhas, surrounded by blazing flames.”

"In the first seat at the eastern end of the southern row is the presiding master named Vajratāṭaka; he forms the *vajra* upon a lotus throne, which is purely yellow in color and surrounded by blazing flames."

"The second presiding master is named Aśani; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, its color and form as described before, surrounded by radiant flames; all subsequent *vajras* are identical in color."
"The third presiding master is named Nīlabhadra, which in this language means 'Blue Vajra. Upon a lotus seat, he forms the *vajra* [mudrā], surrounded by blazing light."
"The fourth presiding master is named Mucilinda; this is the position of the true seat. Upon the lotus throne, one forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light."
"The fifth presiding master is named Suvāhu; upon the lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light.
The sixth presiding master is named Suvajraśrīṇī—this is the position of the true rank; upon the lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light."
"The seventh presiding master is named Vajramudrārāja; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light.
The eighth presiding master is named Kṣitigarbha-vajra; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light."
"The ninth presiding master is named Vajramuṣṭi; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra* [mudrā], with fists formed at its sides, surrounded by blazing light."
"The tenth presiding master is named Muśala; upon a lotus seat, he forms the shape of a slender waist-mallet, resembling a Vajrapāṇi holding a mallet, surrounded by a halo of blazing light."
"On the western side, at the southern end, the first seat-holder is named King Vaśavartin; upon a lotus throne he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light."
"The second presiding master is named King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati); upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light-flames.
The third presiding master is named King of the Tuṣita Heaven; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light-flames."
"The fourth presiding seat is named King Yama; upon a lotus throne he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light.
Next, two cubits of ground constitute the gateway to the maṇḍala."
"Next, the first presiding master in the northern gate is named Gandharva; upon his lotus seat he forms the shape of a small drum, surrounded by blazing flames.
The second presiding master is named Peacock King; upon his lotus seat he forms the shape of blazing flames."
"The third presiding seat is named Garuḍa; it takes the form of a lotus throne.
The fourth presiding seat is named Nārāyaṇadeva; upon the lotus throne is the form of a golden wheel, surrounded by blazing flames."
"In the north, at the first seat on the western end, the presiding master is named Vikuñci; upon his lotus seat he takes the form of blazing flames.
At the second seat, the presiding master is named Arida (in the Tang language, 'Following the Mind'); upon his lotus seat he takes the form of a rosary, surrounded by blazing flames."
"The third presiding master is named Hayagrīva-hṛdaya; upon a lotus seat, he forms the shape of a lotus bud, surrounded by blazing light.
The fourth presiding master is named Ekajaṭā-karālī; upon a lotus seat, he forms the shape of blazing light."
"The fifth presiding master is named Amoghapāśa.
Upon a lotus seat, he forms a noose with his hands, surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
The sixth presiding master is named Four-Armed Avalokiteśvara. Upon a lotus seat, he holds a white lotus, surrounded by a halo of blazing light."
"The seventh presiding master is named Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara of the Small Mind; upon a lotus throne he holds a lotus bud, surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
The eighth presiding master is named Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara of the Great Mind; upon a lotus throne he holds a lotus bud, surrounded by a halo of blazing light."
"The ninth presiding master is named Sarvalokiteśvarahṛdaya; upon a lotus throne he forms the mudrā of holding a lotus, surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
The tenth presiding master is named Mahāśrīye; upon a lotus throne he forms the mudrā of holding a lotus, the flower being red in color, surrounded by a halo of blazing light."
“The third court is completed.

Following this sequence, the fourth court is sixteen cubits in length and breadth, consisting of fifty-eight positions; the ground-seals at the four corners, their shapes, and their arrangement are also as described above.”

"The seal of the northeast corner is named Kīlikīlukuruta; the seal of the southeast corner is named Vajrasena; the seal of the southwest corner is named Bāhudantaka; and the seal of the northwest corner is named Vajraśṛṅkhala."

"The first seat-master facing east at the northern end is named Vināyaka; upon a lotus throne he assumes the form of a mallet, with the head of the mallet pointing upward and standing on the flowered seat. The mallet head has eight petals, and the handle is of varying length, extending downward from the head for several inches."
Fashion it into the shape of a crescent moon blade; the base of the blade is attached to the handle, and the body of the blade is raised with sharp ridges.
Between the head and the blade, fashion two or three joints like the edge of a small knife, surrounded by blazing flames.
"The second seat-holder is named Vidyottama; he sits upon a lotus throne with a head like that of Trailokyasundara, surrounded by a halo of blazing flames."

"The third presiding seat is named Bodhisattva Śuddhānanda; upon a lotus throne he forms a vajra pedestal, and upon the vajra pedestal he arranges spread lotus flowers. Two-thirds of their petals hang downward and one-third points upward, and upon these flower petals he forms the shape of blazing flames."

"The fourth presiding seat is named Maitreya Bodhisattva; upon a lotus throne, he appears like the point of a spear. The blade of the spear-point is somewhat broad, with a slender neck and a large belly, entirely of golden hue, rising with a ridge from its center and surrounded by radiant flames."
"The fifth presiding seat is named Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; upon a lotus throne, he appears in the form of radiant flames.
The sixth presiding seat is named Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva; upon a lotus throne, he performs the mudrā for extinguishing transgressions, surrounded by radiant flames."
"The seventh presiding master is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra; upon his lotus seat he forms a vajra, surrounded by blazing light.

The eighth presiding master is named Indrasena (translated into Chinese as *Dìshì shìzhě*, Attendant of Śakra); upon his lotus seat he forms the head of Trailokyavijaya, which is pure yellow in color, surrounded by blazing light."
"The ninth presiding master is named Indra, another name for Śakra; he forms a *vajra* upon a lotus seat, surrounded by radiant flames.
The tenth presiding master is named Candradeva; he forms the shape of a lunar disc upon a lotus seat, its color being pure white."
"The eleventh seat-holder is named Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; upon his lotus throne, he takes the form of blazing light.

The twelfth seat-holder is named Sarvarkastadeva (All Star Deities); upon his lotus throne, he appears like a precious jar, with a large belly and a thick neck, encircled by a string of pearls around his abdomen."
The mouth of the jar is painted the color of empty space, shaped like a parasol, and its interior is filled with numerous white dots surrounded by a halo of light and flames.
"The thirteenth seat-holder is named Buddhajita; he is depicted in the form of a Buddhist stūpa with a four-tiered base, surrounded by a halo of light and flames."
"The fourteenth seat-holder is named Dhāraṇīgarbha; upon a lotus seat he takes the form of a precious treasury, surrounded by blazing flames.
At the eastern end of the southern side, the first seat-holder is named Agnideva; upon a lotus seat he takes the form of a precious vase, from the mouth of which flames emerge."
"The second presiding master is named Bodhisattva Makhādeva; upon his lotus seat, he takes the form of blazing light.
The third presiding master is named Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha; upon his lotus seat, he appears like a precious vase, yet without a base."
The mouth of that vase is shaped like two crescent moons joined together and lying face upward.
The vase is blue in color, while the crescent moons are pure white, surrounded by a halo of light and flames.

"The fourth presiding deity is named Viśvānara (the first syllable pronounced with an *ū* vowel); upon a lotus seat he assumes the head of Trailokyavijaya (in Chinese, the head of the double-pronged halberd), surrounded by a halo of light and flames."
"The fifth presiding lord is named Yamāraja; upon a lotus throne he assumes the form of Maheśvara, surrounded by a halo of blazing flames.

The sixth presiding lord is named Yamadanda; upon a lotus throne he takes human form, with a head and face resembling that of a Buddha but with slightly larger eyes, wearing fish-scale armor and emerging from the body halfway, surrounded by a halo of blazing flames."
"The seventh presiding master is named Sūcittavajra; upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light.
The eighth presiding master is named Bāyupiga, who is of the true station (*samyaktva*); upon a lotus seat he forms the *vajra*, surrounded by blazing light."
“The ninth presiding master is named Vairambha-jūṭa; upon a lotus throne he forms the head of Trailokyavijaya, surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
The tenth presiding master is named Puṇyadattā; upon a lotus throne he forms a wish-fulfilling jewel, surrounded by a halo of blazing light.”
"The eleventh seat-lord is named Mahāpratibhāna-deva; upon his lotus throne he takes the form of blazing flames.
The twelfth seat-lord is named Mīḍhuśikha-ra; upon his lotus throne he takes the form of the head of Trailokyasura, surrounded by blazing flames."
"The thirteenth seat-lord is named Sarvabhūta; upon a lotus seat he forms the shape of a *vṛttaka* sword, surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
The fourteenth seat-lord is named Sarvarākṣasa; upon a lotus seat he forms the shape of an upright sword, surrounded by a halo of blazing light."
"On the western side, the first seat-holder at the southern end is named King Asura; upon his lotus throne he forms a vertical horn-bow, surrounded by blazing light.

The second seat-holder is named Deva Mārici; upon his lotus throne he forms the shape of a celestial fan, with the *svastika* (万字) of the Western lands depicted in the center of the fan, surrounded by blazing light."
"The third presiding master is named Devaputra; upon his lotus seat is the form of a sun disk, purely yellow, surrounded by red-colored flames.
The fourth presiding master is named General Vajrapāṇi; upon his lotus seat is the form of an upright sword, surrounded by flames."
“The fifth presiding master is named Sarvadeva; he takes the form of blazing light upon a lotus throne.
The sixth presiding master is named Nandana-gara-ja; his form is like a python, with its head raised as it gazes.”
"Next, two cubits of ground shall be made the entrance to the *maṇḍala*.

Next, to the north of that entrance, the first seat-master is named Upānandana-karāja; his physical appearance is like that of the previously mentioned Nanda, and he likewise raises his head and gazes."
"The second presiding master is named Bhūmideva; upon his lotus throne he assumes the form of a precious *stūpa*, filled with the seven treasures and surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
The third presiding master is named Vairocana; upon his lotus throne he assumes the form of blazing light."
"The fourth presiding master is named Kiṃnara-svara; he forms a lotus seat.
The fifth presiding master is named Mahoraga; he forms a lotus seat."
"The sixth seat-master is named Virūpākṣa; upon his lotus seat he forms a noose held in a cleft hand, surrounded by blazing light.
At the western end of the northern side is the first seat-master, named Vāyu-deva; upon his lotus seat he holds an upright banner-pole with a banner suspended from it, surrounded by blazing light."

"The second presiding master is named Varuṇadeva (translated into Chinese as Tiānshui). Upon the lotus seat there is the form of radiant flames, and beneath the lotus seat are patterns of rippling water."
"The third presiding master is named Sthita; he forms a shape of blazing light upon a lotus throne.
The fourth presiding master is named Maṇidhara; he forms a shape of blazing light upon a lotus throne."
"The fifth presiding master is named Candraprabha Bodhisattva; upon his lotus seat he forms a blue lotus, held within its sheath but not yet blossomed, surrounded by encircling flames of light."
"The sixth presiding seat is named the Yakṣa Kubera; upon a lotus throne he assumes the head of Trailokyavijaya, the color of pure blue iron, surrounded by a halo of blazing flames."

"The seventh presiding master is named King Vaiśravaṇa, stationed at the entrance. Upon a lotus seat, he holds a five-jointed mallet, perfectly formed with eight facets, resembling a jeweled pillar, of pure golden hue, and surrounded by a halo of blazing light."
"The eighth seat-holder is named Vajragandha; this is the position of the true state. Upon the lotus throne, one should form the vajra, surrounded by blazing light."

"The ninth presiding master is named Śaṅkhinī. Upon the lotus seat, she takes the form of a vessel with a small, slender belly; it has vertical ridges within, and the openings at the top of these ridges are like the mouths of bells. Her color is purely yellow, surrounded by a halo of blue light and flames."
"The tenth presiding master is named Lambika; he forms a lotus seat.
The eleventh presiding master is named Carvaka; upon the lotus seat he forms what resembles a silver bowl, with a circular jewel supporting its base."
On the left side of the bowl’s belly, there is a single eye opened slightly, like the eye of a spirit-king (*śrī-deva*), surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
On the twelfth seat, the presiding master is named the *Bharahe* ghost; upon his lotus throne, he forms the shape of an upright sword.
"The thirteenth seat-holder is named Īśvara; upon the lotus seat, he has the head of Dṛḍha-Śūra and is made entirely yellow.
The fourteenth seat-holder is named the Ghost-King Īśāna; upon the lotus seat, he has the head of Dṛḍha-Śūra and is made entirely yellow."
"This sixteen-cubit *samāja-maṇḍala* has both extensive and abbreviated versions.
Regarding the extensive version, within the sixteen cubits, there are two hundred and nine lotus seats;
regarding the abbreviated version, within the sixteen cubits, there are one hundred and thirty-nine lotus seats."

"As previously stated, if one is a king, a minister, or a householder who possesses various kinds of exquisite offerings and vessels of the seven precious gems, and the ācārya has many disciples who are intelligent and sharp-witted, one should construct an extensive maṇḍala.

If the patron lacks various kinds of exquisite offerings and vessels of the seven precious gems, and the ācārya does not have many intelligent and sharp-witted disciples, one should construct an abbreviated maṇḍala."
"The ritual for the sixteen-cubit maṇḍala has been fully explained.
This concludes the Universal Assembly Maṇḍala from the *Buddhabhāṣita-dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Volume Twelve.
